lessons.title: JavaScript: the big picture
lessons.summaryHtml:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web. Every modern browser runs it, and with Node.js it also runs on servers, in command-line tools and inside desktop and mobile apps.

The language is standardised as ECMAScript by a committee called TC39, which publishes a new edition every year. An engine such as V8, SpiderMonkey or JavaScriptCore reads your code, compiles it to machine code on the fly and runs it.

JavaScript runs your code on one thread. Slow work such as timers and network requests is handed to the host (the browser or Node), and an event loop runs your callbacks when that work is done. In this course every example is live: edit it, press Run and watch the console.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

JavaScript is the language that makes web pages do things. HTML describes what is on a page, CSS describes how it looks, and JavaScript describes how it behaves: what happens when you click Add to cart, type in a search box or submit a form.

Today JavaScript runs far beyond the browser. The same language powers web servers, command-line tools, desktop apps and, through frameworks, mobile apps. If you learn it well once, you can use it almost everywhere a program runs.

Think of JavaScript as a language like English, and of the engine as a person who reads and acts on it. The host is the room that person works in. In a browser tab the room contains a page, a network connection and timers. In Node.js the room contains files, processes and the terminal. The language is the same; the tools on the table change.

Why it matters

Almost every website uses JavaScript on the client side, and it has been one of the most widely used programming languages for many years. For a junior developer this means three practical things:

  • One language, many jobs. Front-end work (React, Vue, Svelte, plain DOM code), back-end work (Node.js, Deno, Bun) and tooling (build scripts, tests) all use JavaScript or TypeScript, which is JavaScript with types.
  • Your code runs on the user’s machine. A slow loop freezes the page the user is looking at. Understanding the single thread and the event loop is what separates a smooth app from a janky one.
  • The language keeps improving. New features arrive every year, so knowing where they come from (TC39) and how to check support (MDN, caniuse.com) is part of the job.

How it works

A short history: from Netscape to ES2025

Brendan Eich created JavaScript at Netscape in 1995, in a famously short time, to make web pages interactive. Despite the name it is not related to Java; the name was a marketing choice of the time. To stop each browser inventing its own version, the language was handed to Ecma International and standardised as ECMAScript (the document is called ECMA-262).

EditionYearWhy it matters
ES31999The version the early web was built on.
ES52009Strict mode, JSON, array methods such as map and filter.
ES2015 (ES6)2015The big one: let/const, arrow functions, classes, modules, promises, template literals.
ES2016 onwardsevery yearSmaller yearly releases: async/await (2017), optional chaining and ?? (2020), array copy methods (2023), Object.groupBy (2024), Set methods and iterator helpers (2025).

The committee that designs the language is TC39. A proposal moves through stages 0 to 4; at stage 4 it has shipped in at least two engines and joins the next yearly edition. That is why you will often use a feature in Chrome before the edition that contains it is published. When a lesson uses something very new, it tells you to check the MDN compatibility table or caniuse.com.

Engines: how your code becomes machine instructions

An engine is the program that runs JavaScript. The three big ones are V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node.js, Deno), SpiderMonkey (Firefox) and JavaScriptCore (Safari, and the Bun runtime). They all follow the same specification, so correct code behaves the same in each.

Underneath, a modern engine does roughly this:

  1. Parse the source text into a tree that represents its structure. Syntax errors are found here, before any line runs.
  2. Interpret it quickly as bytecode so the program starts fast.
  3. Watch which functions run often (“hot” code) and what types they see.
  4. Optimise hot code into fast machine code, and throw that code away again if its assumptions break, for example when a function that always got numbers suddenly gets a string.

This is called just-in-time (JIT) compilation. You do not control it directly, but it explains a useful habit: functions that always receive the same kinds of values tend to stay fast.

Try it: Your first program

JavaScript

// A first program: variables, a calculation and some output
const learner = 'Asha';
const course = 'JavaScript: Zero to Job-Ready';
const lessons = 31;
const minutesPerLesson = 45;

console.log('Hello,', learner + '!');
console.log(`You are starting "${course}".`);

const totalHours = (lessons * minutesPerLesson) / 60;
console.log(`That is about ${Math.round(totalHours)} hours of study.`);

// Values can be numbers, text, true/false, lists and objects
const plan = { daysPerWeek: 5, topics: ['basics', 'functions', 'async'] };
console.log(plan);
console.log('Weeks at one lesson a day:', Math.ceil(lessons / plan.daysPerWeek));

Change the name or the prices and press Run. Every console.log prints one line below the editor.

Hosts: the browser, Node.js and friends

The engine only knows the language itself: numbers, strings, objects, functions, arrays, Math, JSON, promises. Everything that touches the outside world comes from the host.

HostAdds, for exampleTypical use
Browserdocument (the DOM), fetch, localStorage, events, timersWeb pages and web apps
Node.jsfs (files), process, http, timers, fetchAPIs, servers, scripts, build tools
Deno and BunNode-like APIs, built-in TypeScript and toolingServers and scripts
FrameworksReact Native, Ionic/Capacitor, ElectronMobile and desktop apps

This is why document.querySelector works in a browser but not in Node.js, and why process.version works in Node.js but not in a browser. The next example checks which names exist in the current host.

Try it: Language vs host: what exists here?

JavaScript

// Built into the language (works in every engine)
console.log('Math.max:', Math.max(3, 9, 4));
console.log('Array:', [3, 1, 2].toSorted());
console.log('JSON:', JSON.stringify({ ok: true }));

// Provided by the host. Here the host is a browser tab.
const check = (name, value) => console.log(name.padEnd(12), typeof value);
check('document', globalThis.document);
check('fetch', globalThis.fetch);
check('setTimeout', globalThis.setTimeout);
check('localStorage', globalThis.localStorage);
check('process', globalThis.process); // Node.js only, so 'undefined'

Arrays and Math come from the language. document, fetch and setTimeout come from the browser, and process only exists in Node.js.

One thread and an event loop

JavaScript runs your code on a single thread: one line at a time, one function at a time, using a call stack to remember which function is running. It never runs two of your functions at the same moment on that thread.

So how can a page wait for a network response and still react to clicks? The host does the waiting. When you call setTimeout or fetch, the browser starts a timer or a request in the background and your code carries on. When the work finishes, the host puts your callback into a queue. The event loop takes callbacks from the queues and runs them, one at a time, whenever the call stack is empty.

  • Tasks (also called macrotasks): timers, clicks, network events. One runs per loop turn.
  • Microtasks: promise callbacks. After each task, all pending microtasks run before anything else.
  • In browsers, the page can repaint between tasks. A long task blocks painting, so the page freezes.
console.log('order placed');
setTimeout(() => console.log('email sent'), 0);
console.log('thank-you page shown');
// order placed
// thank-you page shown
// email sent

The example below goes further: it blocks the thread on purpose with a busy loop, so you can see that a “0 ms” timer really waits for the stack to clear. Lesson 5.1 draws the whole loop step by step.

Try it: One thread and an event loop

JavaScript

console.log('1. Script starts');

setTimeout(() => console.log('4. Timer callback (a task)'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3. Promise callback (a microtask)'));

console.log('2. Script ends... after some heavy work');

// Block the only thread for about 300 ms
const start = performance.now();
setTimeout(() => {
  const waited = Math.round(performance.now() - start);
  console.log(`5. A 0 ms timer actually waited ${waited} ms`);
}, 0);
while (performance.now() - start < 300) {
  // busy: nothing else can run on this thread
}

The timer asks for 0 ms, but it must wait until the busy loop ends. The promise callback (a microtask) runs before the timer (a task).

JavaScript in a web page

In a browser, JavaScript usually arrives through a <script> tag. The browser parses the HTML into the DOM, then runs your script, and your code can read and change that DOM. The live page below is a tiny but complete example: the HTML draws a card, and the script greets you by time of day and counts clicks.

<button id="hello">Say hello</button>
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

Try it: JavaScript on a web page

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <section class="card">
    <div class="top">
      <span class="logo">JS</span>
      <span class="tag">Lesson 0.1</span>
    </div>
    <h1 id="greeting">Welcome to Ralfiz Academy</h1>
    <p class="sub">This card is HTML and CSS. The button, the greeting and the counter are JavaScript.</p>
    <div class="row">
      <button id="hello" class="btn" type="button">Say hello</button>
      <span id="count" class="pill">0 clicks</span>
    </div>
    <p id="msg" class="msg" aria-live="polite">Press the button to run some code.</p>
  </section>
</main>

CSS

* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body {
  margin: 0;
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #eef2ff, #f8fafc);
  color: #0f172a;
}
.wrap { min-height: 100vh; display: grid; place-items: center; padding: 16px; }
.card {
  width: 100%; max-width: 420px; background: #fff;
  border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 16px; padding: 24px;
  box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.08);
}
.top { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; }
.logo {
  width: 40px; height: 40px; border-radius: 10px; display: grid;
  place-items: center; font-weight: 800; background: #facc15; color: #1e293b;
}
.tag {
  font-size: 12px; color: #4f46e5; background: #eef2ff;
  padding: 4px 10px; border-radius: 999px; font-weight: 600;
}
h1 { font-size: 22px; margin: 16px 0 8px; }
.sub { margin: 0 0 16px; color: #475569; font-size: 14px; line-height: 1.5; }
.row { display: flex; gap: 12px; align-items: center; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.btn {
  font: inherit; font-weight: 600; border: 0; border-radius: 10px;
  padding: 10px 16px; background: #4f46e5; color: #fff; cursor: pointer;
  transition: transform 0.1s, background 0.2s;
}
.btn:hover { background: #4338ca; }
.btn:active { transform: scale(0.97); }
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #c7d2fe; outline-offset: 2px; }
.pill {
  font-size: 13px; color: #334155; background: #f1f5f9;
  border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; padding: 6px 10px; border-radius: 999px;
}
.msg {
  margin: 16px 0 0; padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 14px;
  background: #f8fafc; border: 1px dashed #cbd5e1; color: #334155;
}

JavaScript

const greeting = document.querySelector('#greeting');
const button = document.querySelector('#hello');
const countEl = document.querySelector('#count');
const msg = document.querySelector('#msg');

// Greet by time of day
const hour = new Date().getHours();
const part = hour < 12 ? 'morning' : hour < 17 ? 'afternoon' : 'evening';
greeting.textContent = `Good ${part}, welcome to Ralfiz Academy`;

let clicks = 0;
button.addEventListener('click', () => {
  clicks += 1;
  const time = new Date().toLocaleTimeString('en-IN');
  countEl.textContent = `${clicks} ${clicks === 1 ? 'click' : 'clicks'}`;
  msg.textContent = `Hello! This code ran at ${time}.`;
  console.log('Button clicked', clicks, 'time(s)');
});

console.log('Script ran after the HTML was parsed. Greeting:', part);

The HTML and CSS draw the card. The JavaScript tab greets you by time of day and reacts to clicks. Try changing the greeting text.

How this course works

Every lesson follows the same rhythm, so you always know what to do next:

  1. Read and run. Each concept has a live example. Change the code and press Run (or Ctrl+Enter). Breaking things is encouraged; the Reset button brings the original back.
  2. Predict the output. Before running a snippet, choose what you think it prints. Being wrong here is cheap and teaches a lot.
  3. Lab. Download the exercise files and solve the TODOs in VS Code, running them with Node.js. Compare with the solution folder only after trying.
  4. Quiz. Four questions check the ideas, not the syntax.

Example: your first program

The lab’s first program introduces itself, calculates your weekly study time and shows the event loop in action. Here is the finished version, which you run with node index.js:

const learnerName = 'Asha';
const city = 'Perinthalmanna';
const daysPerWeek = 5;
const minutesPerDay = 45;

console.log(`Hello, I am ${learnerName} from ${city}.`);
const weekly = daysPerWeek * minutesPerDay;
console.log(`I will study ${weekly} minutes a week.`);

console.log('Node.js', process.version, 'on', process.platform);

console.log('A: start');
setTimeout(() => console.log('D: timer'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C: promise'));
console.log('B: end');

Walk through it line by line. The first four lines create constants: names bound to values. The template literals (text in backticks) insert values with ${…}. process is a Node.js host object, so this line would fail in a browser. The last four lines print A and B first, because the script itself runs to completion; then the promise callback (a microtask) prints C; and finally the timer (a task) prints D.

Common mistakes

1. Thinking Java and JavaScript are related. They share some syntax from C, and nothing else. Saying so in an interview is a red flag.

2. Expecting host APIs everywhere. Browser code in Node.js, or Node.js code in a browser, crashes:

// Wrong in Node.js: document does not exist there
document.querySelector('h1');
// ReferenceError: document is not defined

// Fix: check the host first, or keep DOM code in browser files
if (typeof document !== 'undefined') {
  document.querySelector('h1');
}

3. Believing setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately. It schedules a task. The callback runs after the current code finishes and after all microtasks:

// Wrong assumption: total is ready on the next line
let total = 0;
setTimeout(() => { total = 500; }, 0);
console.log(total); // 0

// Fix: use the value inside the callback (or await a promise)
setTimeout(() => {
  const total = 500;
  console.log(total); // 500
}, 0);

4. Blocking the main thread. A long loop in a click handler freezes the whole page, including scrolling and animations. Keep handlers short and move heavy work out (lesson 7.4 shows chunking and Web Workers).

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What is JavaScript?” A high-level, dynamically typed, garbage-collected language with first-class functions, standardised as ECMAScript and run by engines such as V8 inside hosts such as browsers and Node.js.
  • “Is it compiled or interpreted?” Both: modern engines interpret bytecode first and JIT-compile hot code to machine code.
  • “How does it do async with one thread?” The host does the waiting; the event loop runs callbacks from the task and microtask queues when the call stack is empty.
  • In real teams you will meet TypeScript almost everywhere. It compiles to JavaScript, so everything in this course still applies (lesson 7.3 introduces it).
  • Bookmark MDN Web Docs (developer.mozilla.org). It is the reference professionals use daily, including browser compatibility tables for every feature.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. In what order are the lines logged?

console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
console.log('C');
  • A 
    A
B
C
  • B 
    B
A
C
  • C 
    A
C
B
  • D 
    C
A
B

Snippet 2. What is logged?

console.log('5' + 3, '5' - 3);
  • A 8 2
  • B 53 2
  • C 53 NaN
  • D 8 8

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const lang = 'JavaScript';
console.log(lang.length, lang.includes('Java'), typeof lang);
  • A 10 true string
  • B 10 false string
  • C 11 true string
  • D 10 true object

Answers

  1. C. The script runs to the end first. The timer callback waits in the task queue until the call stack is empty, so B comes last even with a 0 ms delay.
  2. B. With a string, + joins text, so the result is "53". The - operator only works on numbers, so JavaScript converts "5" to 5 and gives 2. Lesson 1.2 covers these rules.
  3. A. "JavaScript" has 10 characters, it contains "Java", and a text value is the primitive type string. Java and JavaScript are still unrelated languages.

terms.definition: A high-level, dynamically typed language that runs in every browser and, through Node.js, on servers and in tools.
The official standard (ECMA-262) that defines the JavaScript language. A new edition such as ES2025 is published every year.
The Ecma technical committee of browser makers, companies and experts that designs new JavaScript features in stages 0 to 4.
The program that parses, compiles and runs JavaScript: V8 (Chrome, Edge, Node.js), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari, Bun).
What surrounds the engine and gives it extra APIs: the browser adds document and fetch, Node.js adds the file system and process.
The mechanism that takes finished work (timers, network replies, clicks) from queues and runs the callbacks one at a time on the single thread.
The panel where console.log output and errors appear: in DevTools, in the terminal for Node.js, and under every example on this site.

lessons.examTip: If an interviewer asks “Is JavaScript single-threaded?”, say: “The engine runs my code on one thread, but the host does timers, network and file work in the background and the event loop brings the results back.”

quiz.question: Which statement about JavaScript and ECMAScript is correct?
options: ECMAScript is the standard; JavaScript is the language that implements it in engines
ECMAScript is an older language that JavaScript replaced
ECMAScript is a framework written in JavaScript
They are two unrelated languages with similar syntax
quiz.explanation: ECMA-262 (ECMAScript) is the specification. Engines such as V8 implement it, and we call the result JavaScript. A new edition is published every year.

quiz.question: Your code calls setTimeout(fn, 0) and then runs a loop that takes 2 seconds. When does fn run?
options: Immediately, in parallel with the loop
After exactly 0 ms, interrupting the loop
After the loop finishes and the call stack is empty
Never, because the loop blocks the timer forever
quiz.explanation: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time. The timer callback waits in a queue until the current script finishes; only then can the event loop run it.

quiz.question: Which engine runs JavaScript inside Node.js?
options: SpiderMonkey
JavaScriptCore
Chakra
V8
quiz.explanation: Node.js is built on V8, the same engine as Chrome and Edge. Firefox uses SpiderMonkey and Safari uses JavaScriptCore.

quiz.question: Where does document.querySelector come from?
options: The ECMAScript language itself
The browser, as a host API (the DOM)
Node.js core modules
The V8 engine’s optimising compiler
quiz.explanation: The DOM is provided by the browser, not by the language. That is why document does not exist in Node.js, while things like arrays and Math exist everywhere.

lessons.title: Set up like a professional
lessons.summaryHtml:
A professional JavaScript setup has four parts: an editor (VS Code), a runtime (Node.js LTS, ideally installed with a version manager such as nvm or fnm), the browser DevTools, and a few project tools: npm, which comes with Node, plus Prettier and ESLint, which you install with npm.

You create a project with npm init, which writes a package.json. Prettier formats your code the same way every time, and ESLint finds likely bugs such as unused or undefined variables before you run anything.

You will also learn to read the console and a stack trace, set breakpoints in the Sources panel, and keep your work in git.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A carpenter does not start with wood; they start with a workbench and sharp tools. For a JavaScript developer the workbench is small and free: a code editor, the Node.js runtime to run files from the terminal, the browser DevTools to inspect and debug pages, and a couple of project tools that keep code clean.

This lesson sets up exactly what a professional team uses, so every later lab runs the same way on your machine as it does in a real job.

Why it matters

  • Consistency. When everyone uses the same Node.js version, formatter and linter, “works on my machine” problems mostly disappear.
  • Speed. Format on save, inline lint warnings and breakpoints save hours compared with hunting bugs by reading code.
  • Credibility. A take-home test with a package.json, clear scripts, a lint config and a clean git history tells a reviewer you already work like a team member.

How it works

The editor: VS Code

Visual Studio Code is the most common JavaScript editor. It is free, fast and understands JavaScript and TypeScript out of the box: autocomplete, “go to definition”, rename symbol (F2) and an integrated terminal (Terminal menu, New Terminal). Add a few extensions:

ExtensionWhat it does
ESLintShows lint problems as squiggles while you type.
Prettier - Code formatterFormats the file on save using the project’s Prettier settings.
Live Server (for the DOM course)Serves a folder and reloads the browser when you save.
Error Lens (optional)Prints errors and warnings at the end of the line.

Then turn on formatting on save in your user settings:

{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode",
  "editor.tabSize": 2
}

The runtime: Node.js LTS and a version manager

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser. Releases marked LTS (Long-Term Support) are stable and patched for a long time, so always install the version marked LTS on nodejs.org. This course needs Node.js 22 or newer.

You can use the installer, but professionals prefer a version manager, because different projects pin different versions:

# macOS / Linux with nvm
nvm install --lts
nvm use --lts

# Any OS with fnm (Windows too; nvm-windows is another option)
fnm install --lts
fnm use lts-latest

# Check what you have
node -v
npm -v

Run a file with node index.js. While you work, node --watch index.js reruns it every time you save. Typing just node opens the REPL, an interactive prompt that is handy for trying one line (Ctrl+D exits).

The browser console and DevTools

Every browser has DevTools. Open them with F12, or jump straight to the Console with Ctrl+Shift+J (Cmd+Option+J on a Mac) in Chrome and Edge. The Console both shows your logs and runs any expression you type, so it doubles as a scratchpad for the current page.

The console object has more than log. Log levels let you filter noise, table turns arrays of objects into a grid, group nests related lines, and time/timeEnd measures how long something took.

Try it: A console toolkit

JavaScript

console.log('log: normal output');
console.info('info: something worth knowing');
console.warn('warn: stock is low for Notebook');
console.error('error: payment failed (this one is on purpose)');

const cart = [
  { item: 'Notebook', price: 120, qty: 3 },
  { item: 'Gel pen', price: 25, qty: 4 },
];
console.table(cart);

console.group('Order R-1042');
console.log('Customer: Asha');
console.log('Items:', cart.length);
console.groupEnd();

console.time('build report');
const lines = cart.map((row) => `${row.item}: ${row.price * row.qty}`);
console.timeEnd('build report');
console.log(lines);

console.count('render');
console.count('render');
console.assert(cart.length === 3, 'Expected 3 items in the cart');

Different log levels, a table, a group and a timer. The red lines are on purpose: console.error and a failing console.assert.

A small habit makes console.log debugging much faster: wrap variables in braces. console.log({ subtotal, discount }) prints the names next to the values, so you never wonder which number is which.

Try it: Log with labels, not guesses

JavaScript

const subtotal = 460;
const discount = 46;
const gstRate = 0.18;
const total = (subtotal - discount) * (1 + gstRate);

// Hard to read: which number is which?
console.log(subtotal, discount, total);

// Better: log an object built from the variables
console.log({ subtotal, discount, total });

// Even better for a final answer: a clear sentence
console.log(`Total to pay: ${total.toFixed(2)}`);

Wrapping variables in { } prints their names with their values. It is the fastest way to debug with console.log.

Reading a stack trace

When code throws, the console shows an error type, a message and a stack trace: the chain of function calls that led to the crash, newest first, each with a file and line number.

Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'rate')
    at applyCoupon (app.js:15:36)
    at app.js:19:28

Read it in three steps. First, the type (TypeError: you used a value in a way its type does not allow). Second, the message (something was undefined and we tried to read .rate on it). Third, the top frame (line 15 in applyCoupon). Then ask “why was it undefined?” and follow the next frame to the caller, which forgot to pass a coupon.

Try it: Reading a stack trace

JavaScript

const order = {
  id: 'R-1042',
  items: [{ name: 'Notebook', price: 120, qty: 3 }],
};

function lineTotal(item) {
  return item.price * item.qty;
}

function orderTotal(order) {
  return order.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + lineTotal(item), 0);
}

function applyCoupon(total, coupon) {
  return total - total * coupon.rate; // coupon is undefined here
}

console.log('Subtotal:', orderTotal(order));
console.log('After coupon:', applyCoupon(orderTotal(order)));
console.log('This line never runs');

The error names the problem and the property. In DevTools (F12) the stack trace also lists applyCoupon, the function that crashed, then the line that called it.

Breakpoints in the Sources panel

Logging tells you what happened; a debugger lets you stop time. In the Sources panel, open your file and click a line number to set a breakpoint. When the code reaches it, execution pauses before that line runs. You can then:

  • hover any variable, or read the Scope pane for all local values;
  • see how you got here in the Call Stack pane;
  • step over (F10), step into (F11) or step out (Shift+F11) of functions;
  • right-click a line number for a conditional breakpoint (pause only when qty > 100) or a logpoint (log without editing the code).

Writing debugger; in your code does the same as a breakpoint, but only while DevTools is open. Remove it before committing. For Node.js, open a JavaScript Debug Terminal in VS Code and run your file there; breakpoints set in the editor then work too.

Your project: npm and package.json

npm comes with Node.js. npm init -y creates a package.json, the project’s manifest. Two fields matter from day one: "type": "module", which makes .js files use modern import/export, and "scripts", named commands you run with npm run <name> (npm start and npm test need no run).

{
  "name": "ralfiz-setup",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js",
    "dev": "node --watch index.js",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "format": "prettier . --write"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@eslint/js": "^9.0.0",
    "eslint": "^9.0.0",
    "globals": "^16.0.0",
    "prettier": "3.6.2"
  }
}

npm install --save-dev puts tools in devDependencies (needed to build and check the code, not to run it) and downloads them into node_modules. The generated package-lock.json records exact versions so every machine installs the same thing; commit it. npx runs a tool from node_modules without a global install. Lesson 6.2 covers versions and lockfiles in depth.

Prettier and ESLint

Prettier is a formatter: it reprints your code with consistent spacing, quotes and line breaks, and ends arguments about style. ESLint is a linter: it reads code without running it and reports likely bugs. They do different jobs:

PrettierESLint
AnswersHow should this look?Is this probably wrong?
ExampleAdds semicolons, uses single quotes“total is assigned but never used”
Config file.prettierrceslint.config.js (flat config)
Runnpx prettier . --writenpx eslint .

ESLint 9 uses a single eslint.config.js file that exports an array of config objects. The easiest start is npm init @eslint/config@latest, which asks a few questions and writes it for you. A minimal Node.js version looks like this:

import js from '@eslint/js';
import globals from 'globals';

export default [
  js.configs.recommended,
  {
    languageOptions: { globals: globals.node },
    rules: { eqeqeq: 'error', 'prefer-const': 'warn' },
  },
];

js.configs.recommended turns on rules such as no-unused-vars and no-undef. The globals line tells ESLint that names like process exist, so it does not flag them as undefined.

Try it: Where is my code running?

JavaScript

const inBrowser = typeof window !== 'undefined' && typeof document !== 'undefined';
const inNode = typeof process !== 'undefined' && Boolean(process.versions?.node);

console.log({ inBrowser, inNode });
console.log('globalThis is window here:', globalThis === window);
console.log('Browser language:', navigator.language);

// In Node.js you would see these instead:
// process.version  -> 'v22.x.x'
// process.platform -> 'win32', 'darwin' or 'linux'
// process.cwd()    -> the folder you ran node from

The same file can run in a browser or in Node.js. Feature checks with typeof are safe even when a name does not exist.

Folder conventions and git

Keep every project in its own folder with a predictable layout. For the labs in this course:

ralfiz-setup/
  .gitignore          node_modules, .env, dist
  .prettierrc
  eslint.config.js
  package.json
  package-lock.json
  README.md           what it is, how to run it
  index.js            or src/ for bigger projects

Use git from the first day: git init, a .gitignore containing node_modules, then small commits with clear messages (git add . and git commit -m "Add order formatter"). Push to GitHub to build a public portfolio.

Example: a professional starter project

Here is the whole setup for the lab, in the order you would do it:

mkdir ralfiz-setup && cd ralfiz-setup
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module scripts.start="node index.js"
npm install --save-dev --save-exact prettier
echo '{ "singleQuote": true }' > .prettierrc
npm init @eslint/config@latest
git init
echo "node_modules" > .gitignore
npm start

The program itself reads from the host and formats data, so it touches both Node.js APIs and plain language features:

function printEnvironment() {
  console.log('Node.js:', process.version);
  console.log('Platform:', process.platform);
  console.log('Folder:', process.cwd());
}

function formatOrder(order) {
  const total = order.price * order.qty;
  return `${order.id}: ${order.qty} x ${order.item} = ${total}`;
}

printEnvironment();
console.log(formatOrder({ id: 'R-1', item: 'Notebook', price: 120, qty: 3 }));

Run npm start to see the output, npx eslint . to check it and npx prettier . --write to format it. If ESLint reports nothing and Prettier changes nothing, the project is clean.

Common mistakes

1. Installing tools globally. npm install -g eslint ties the project to whatever version happens to be on your machine.

# Wrong: global install, different on every machine
npm install -g prettier

# Fix: a dev dependency, run with npx or an npm script
npm install --save-dev --save-exact prettier
npx prettier . --write

2. Committing node_modules. It is huge and rebuilt by npm install. Add it to .gitignore before the first commit.

3. Mixing module systems. Using import without "type": "module" in package.json (or a .mjs file) leaves Node.js guessing. Node.js 22 detects the import syntax and reruns the file as a module, but it does extra work and, inside a package without the field, prints a warning; older versions stop with a syntax error about import statements, and tools such as ESLint and bundlers may treat the file differently. Add the field, or use the .mjs extension.

4. Leaving debug code behind. Stray console.log and debugger lines in a pull request look careless. Many teams add the ESLint rule no-console as a warning for front-end code.

5. Ignoring the first error. One mistake often causes several errors. Fix the first one in the list (or the top of the stack trace) and run again.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain the difference between dependencies and devDependencies, and why the lockfile is committed.
  • Say that you debug with breakpoints as well as logs. Mention conditional breakpoints and the Network panel for API problems; interviewers like concrete tools.
  • Many companies pin the Node.js version in a .nvmrc or the engines field of package.json. Check it before running a new codebase.
  • Continuous integration (CI) usually runs npm ci, lint and tests on every push. If lint fails locally, it will fail in CI too, so run it before you push.

lessons.title: Values, variables and types
lessons.summaryHtml:
A program works with values: text, numbers, true or false, lists, objects. A variable is a name bound to a value. Use const when the name will not be reassigned (most of the time) and let when it will; the old var has function scope and surprising hoisting, so modern code avoids it.

JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Everything else, including arrays and functions, is an object. Primitives are immutable and compared by value; objects are compared by reference.

The language is dynamically typed: variables have no fixed type, values do. typeof tells you a value’s type, with two famous quirks: typeof null is 'object' and functions report 'function'. Finally, const stops reassignment, not change: a const array can still be pushed to.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Every program works with values: a customer’s name, a price, whether they are a member, a list of cart items. A variable is a label you stick on a value so you can refer to it later. const price = 120 means “the name price refers to the number 120”.

Values come in a few kinds called types. Text is a string, 120 is a number, true is a boolean, and so on. JavaScript does not ask you to declare types; it figures them out from the values while the program runs. That makes it quick to write, and also means you must know the rules, because the language will not stop you from mixing types.

Why it matters

Most beginner bugs come from three misunderstandings covered in this lesson:

  • a value was not the type you thought (a price from a form is the string "250", not the number 250);
  • two variables pointed to the same object, so changing one “changed” the other;
  • a variable was declared with var or in the wrong block, and was visible (or invisible) where you did not expect.

Get these right and invoices add up, carts do not mysteriously change, and your code reads clearly to the next developer.

How it works

Declaring variables: const, let and var

There are three keywords. Modern code uses the first two.

constletvar (legacy)
Reassign later?NoYesYes
ScopeBlock { }Block { }Whole function
Before its lineReferenceError (TDZ)ReferenceError (TDZ)undefined
Redeclare in same scopeSyntaxErrorSyntaxErrorAllowed
Top-level in a scriptNot on windowNot on windowBecomes window.name

All three are hoisted: the engine knows about them as soon as it enters their scope. The difference is what happens if you read one before its declaration line. A var has already been set to undefined, which hides bugs. A let or const is in the temporal dead zone (TDZ) until its line runs, and reading it throws a clear ReferenceError. Lesson 2.2 goes deeper into scope and hoisting.

Use const by default and switch to let only when you reassign, for example a running total in a loop.

Try it: const, let and the old var

JavaScript

const shopName = 'Ralfiz Store';
let itemsInCart = 0;
itemsInCart = itemsInCart + 2; // let can be reassigned
console.log(shopName, 'has', itemsInCart, 'items in the cart');

if (itemsInCart > 0) {
  var oldStyle = 'var ignores the block';
  let modern = 'let lives only in the block';
  console.log('inside:', modern);
}
console.log('outside:', oldStyle);
console.log('outside: typeof modern is', typeof modern);

// var is also hoisted as undefined, so this does not throw:
console.log('before declaration:', laterVar);
var laterVar = 'set later';

var leaks out of the if block; let stays inside it. Try changing const shopName to a new value and run again.

Naming. Names may contain letters, digits, _ and $, must not start with a digit, are case-sensitive (total and Total are different) and cannot be reserved words such as class or return. Conventions matter as much as rules:

  • camelCase for variables and functions: cartTotal, isMember, getInvoice.
  • UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for fixed configuration: GST_RATE, MAX_ITEMS.
  • PascalCase for classes: ShoppingCart.
  • Booleans read as questions: isPaid, hasCoupon, canCheckout. Avoid data, temp, x2.

The seven primitive types

A primitive is a simple, immutable value. JavaScript has exactly seven:

TypeExamplesUse it for
string'Asha', "R-1042", template literalsText
number120, 0.18, -3, NaN, InfinityAll ordinary numbers (64-bit floating point)
bigint9007199254740993nWhole numbers beyond about 9 quadrillion, exactly
booleantrue, falseYes/no facts
undefinedundefined“No value was given” (the engine’s default)
nullnull“Deliberately empty” (you set it)
symbolSymbol('id')Unique keys that cannot clash

A few details are worth knowing now. JavaScript has one number type for integers and decimals, stored as a 64-bit float, so integers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9,007,199,254,740,991). Beyond that, use BigInt by adding n; you cannot mix BigInt and number in arithmetic without converting. undefined and null both mean “nothing”, but by convention undefined is what the engine gives you (a missing property, a parameter nobody passed) and null is what you write to say “empty on purpose”, such as couponCode = null. Every call to Symbol() creates a brand-new value, which is why symbols are used as keys that no other code can accidentally reuse.

Everything else is an object

Arrays, plain objects, functions, dates, maps: all of them are objects. Primitives and objects behave differently in one crucial way. A variable holding a primitive holds the value itself; a variable holding an object holds a reference, an address pointing to the object somewhere in memory.

Strings look like objects because they have methods ('pen'.toUpperCase()). Behind the scenes the engine wraps the primitive in a temporary String object for the call and throws it away. The string itself never changes: methods return new strings.

typeof and its quirks

The typeof operator returns the type name as a string. It is safe even for names that were never declared (typeof missingName is 'undefined'). It has two famous quirks:

  • typeof null is 'object'. This is a bug from the first version of JavaScript that can never be fixed without breaking old websites. Check null with value === null.
  • typeof of a function is 'function', even though functions are objects. Arrays report 'object', so use Array.isArray(value).

Try it: The seven primitives and typeof

JavaScript

const samples = [
  ['string', 'Ralfiz'],
  ['number', 42.5],
  ['bigint', 9007199254740993n],
  ['boolean', true],
  ['undefined', undefined],
  ['null', null],
  ['symbol', Symbol('orderId')],
  ['object', { plan: 'pro' }],
  ['array', ['pen', 'book']],
  ['function', () => 'hi'],
];

const rows = samples.map(([kind, value]) => ({ kind, typeof: typeof value }));
console.table(rows);

console.log('Array.isArray([]):', Array.isArray([]));
console.log('null === null:', null === null);
console.log("Symbol('id') === Symbol('id'):", Symbol('id') === Symbol('id'));

Look at the null and function rows: those are the two typeof quirks. Array.isArray and === null are the reliable checks.

Dynamic typing

In JavaScript, values have types but variables do not. The same let can hold a number and later a string, and nothing complains until something goes wrong at run time:

let orderId = 1042;       // number
orderId = 'R-' + orderId; // now the string 'R-1042'
console.log(typeof orderId); // 'string'

This flexibility is useful for quick scripts and painful in large apps, which is why many teams add TypeScript (lesson 7.3). Until then, the discipline is simple: give each variable one type for its whole life and name it so the type is obvious.

Values vs references

Copying a primitive copies the value. Copying an object copies only the reference, so both names point to the same object. Comparison follows the same rule: primitives are equal if their values are equal; objects are equal only if they are the same object.

Try it: Values vs references

JavaScript

// Primitives are copied
let price = 120;
let salePrice = price;
salePrice = 99;
console.log({ price, salePrice });

// Objects are shared through references
const cart = { items: 2 };
const sameCart = cart;
sameCart.items = 5;
console.log(cart.items, sameCart.items, cart === sameCart);

// Two objects with the same content are still different objects
console.log({ a: 1 } === { a: 1 });
console.log('pen' === 'pen'); // primitives compare by value

Copying a primitive copies the value. Copying an object copies the reference, so both names see the same cart.

This is the root of many “why did my data change?” bugs. If you pass a cart object to a function that modifies it, the caller’s cart changes too. Lesson 3.2 shows how to make copies with spread and structuredClone.

const is not immutable

const protects the binding, the link between the name and the value. It does not protect the value. For primitives there is no difference, because primitives cannot change anyway. For objects and arrays, const still lets you push, pop and change properties; it only forbids pointing the name at a different object.

Try it: const is not immutable

JavaScript

const cart = ['Pen'];
cart.push('Notebook'); // allowed: we change the array
cart[0] = 'Gel pen';   // allowed too
console.log(cart);

const settings = Object.freeze({ currency: 'INR' });
settings.currency = 'USD'; // ignored (it would throw in strict mode)
console.log(settings.currency);

cart = ['Eraser']; // not allowed: reassigning a const

Pushing and changing items is allowed. Reassigning the name is the only thing const forbids, and that line throws.

If you really need a value that cannot change, Object.freeze(obj) blocks changes to its own properties. It is shallow: objects nested inside are still mutable. In strict mode (modules and classes) writing to a frozen property throws a TypeError; in a classic script the write is silently ignored, as you just saw.

Example: Shop Bill, version 1

The course’s first mini project is a console bill for the Ralfiz Store. This first version uses only constants, arithmetic and a few types; later lessons add formatting, arrays, functions and currency handling.

Start with configuration that never changes, in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Then the facts about this bill: the customer (a string), membership (a boolean) and the coupon (null: we know there is none). Then the cart lines as numbers. Finally, each step of the calculation gets its own well-named const, so a reviewer can check the maths line by line:

const subtotal = notebookPrice * notebookQty + penPrice * penQty;
const discount = isMember ? subtotal * MEMBER_DISCOUNT_RATE : 0;
const taxable = subtotal - discount;
const gst = taxable * GST_RATE;
const total = taxable + gst;

The ? : is the conditional operator: “if isMember then this, else that”. Notice there is no let at all: nothing is reassigned, each value is computed once. Run it, then change the inputs.

Try it: Shop Bill, version 1

JavaScript

const SHOP_NAME = 'Ralfiz Store';
const GST_RATE = 0.18;
const MEMBER_DISCOUNT_RATE = 0.1;

const customerName = 'Asha';
const isMember = true;
const couponCode = null; // no coupon yet

const notebookPrice = 120, notebookQty = 3;
const penPrice = 25, penQty = 4;

const subtotal = notebookPrice * notebookQty + penPrice * penQty;
const discount = isMember ? subtotal * MEMBER_DISCOUNT_RATE : 0;
const taxable = subtotal - discount;
const gst = taxable * GST_RATE;
const total = taxable + gst;

console.log(`${SHOP_NAME}: bill for ${customerName}`);
console.log('Subtotal:', subtotal);
console.log('Member discount:', discount);
console.log('GST (18%):', gst);
console.log('Total:', total);
console.log('Coupon:', couponCode === null ? 'none' : couponCode);

The start of the course’s Shop Bill. Try isMember = false or change a quantity and watch the total change.

In a real shop the numbers come from a form, and here the types bite. The value of every <input> is a string, even with type="number". The * operator converts strings to numbers, but + joins strings. The live bill below shows what happens and how Number() fixes it:

Try it: Form inputs are always strings

HTML

<main class="page">
  <form class="card" id="bill" autocomplete="off">
    <header>
      <h1>Quick bill</h1>
      <p>Ralfiz Store · counter 2</p>
    </header>
    <div class="grid">
      <label>Price (₹)<input id="price" type="number" value="250" min="0"></label>
      <label>Quantity<input id="qty" type="number" value="2" min="1"></label>
      <label>Delivery (₹)<input id="delivery" type="number" value="40" min="0"></label>
    </div>
    <label class="check"><input id="convert" type="checkbox"> Convert inputs with Number()</label>
    <div class="result">
      <span>Total</span>
      <strong id="total">–</strong>
    </div>
    <p class="types" id="types"></p>
  </form>
</main>

CSS

* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body {
  margin: 0; background: #f1f5f9; color: #0f172a;
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
}
.page { padding: 16px; display: grid; place-items: center; min-height: 100vh; }
.card {
  width: 100%; max-width: 460px; background: #fff; border-radius: 16px;
  border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; padding: 20px;
  box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.06);
}
header h1 { margin: 0; font-size: 20px; }
header p { margin: 4px 0 16px; color: #64748b; font-size: 13px; }
.grid { display: grid; gap: 12px; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(110px, 1fr)); }
label { display: grid; gap: 6px; font-size: 13px; font-weight: 600; color: #334155; }
input[type='number'] {
  font: inherit; font-weight: 500; padding: 10px 12px; border-radius: 10px;
  border: 1px solid #cbd5e1; background: #f8fafc; color: #0f172a; width: 100%;
}
input[type='number']:focus { outline: none; border-color: #0d9488; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px #ccfbf1; }
.check {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; margin: 16px 0;
  font-weight: 500; cursor: pointer;
}
.check input { width: 18px; height: 18px; accent-color: #0d9488; }
.result {
  display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: baseline;
  padding: 14px 16px; border-radius: 12px; background: #f0fdfa; border: 1px solid #99f6e4;
}
.result span { color: #115e59; font-weight: 600; }
.result strong { font-size: 24px; color: #0f766e; }
.result.bad { background: #fef2f2; border-color: #fecaca; }
.result.bad span, .result.bad strong { color: #b91c1c; }
.types { margin: 12px 0 0; font-size: 12px; color: #64748b; font-family: ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace; }

JavaScript

const form = document.querySelector('#bill');
const fields = ['#price', '#qty', '#delivery'].map((sel) =>
  document.querySelector(sel),
);
const convert = document.querySelector('#convert');
const totalEl = document.querySelector('#total');
const typesEl = document.querySelector('#types');

function update() {
  let [price, qty, delivery] = fields.map((input) => input.value); // strings!
  if (convert.checked) {
    [price, qty, delivery] = [price, qty, delivery].map(Number);
  }
  const total = price * qty + delivery;
  const looksWrong = typeof total === 'string';
  totalEl.textContent = looksWrong ? `"${total}"` : '₹' + total;
  totalEl.parentElement.classList.toggle('bad', looksWrong);
  typesEl.textContent = `typeof price: ${typeof price} · typeof total: ${typeof total}`;
  console.log({ price, qty, delivery, total });
}

form.addEventListener('input', update);
update();

Without Number(), price × qty works (the * operator converts), but + delivery joins text. Tick the box to convert the inputs.

Common mistakes

1. Forgetting the keyword. Assigning to an undeclared name creates a global variable in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode.

// Wrong
total = 500;          // accidental global (or ReferenceError in modules)

// Fix
const total = 500;

2. Using let everywhere “just in case”. It hides which values change. Start with const; the linter rule prefer-const tells you when let was not needed.

3. Checking for null with typeof.

// Wrong: also true for every object and array
if (typeof coupon === 'object') { applyCoupon(coupon); }

// Fix
if (coupon !== null && typeof coupon === 'object') { applyCoupon(coupon); }

4. Expecting const to freeze an object.

// Wrong assumption: const keeps the cart safe
const cart = ['Pen'];
addFreeGift(cart);    // this function pushes into cart!

// Fix: pass a copy when a function must not change your data
addFreeGift([...cart]);

5. Treating input values as numbers. '250' + 40 is '25040'. Convert with Number(input.value) (or input.valueAsNumber) as soon as you read a field.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Difference between let, const and var?” Scope (block vs function), reassignment, TDZ vs undefined before the declaration, and var creating properties on the global object in scripts.
  • “List the primitive types.” String, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol. Everything else is an object.
  • “Is JavaScript pass-by-reference?” No: it always passes a copy of the value, but for objects that value is a reference. That is why a function can change an object’s properties but cannot make the caller’s variable point to a new object.
  • “null vs undefined?” undefined means not assigned; null means intentionally empty. APIs often use null in JSON because JSON has no undefined.
  • In code review, a name like data or flag is a common comment. Descriptive names are the cheapest documentation you will ever write.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

console.log(typeof null, typeof undefined);
  • A null undefined
  • B object undefined
  • C object object
  • D undefined undefined

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const items = ['pen'];
items.push('book');
console.log(items.length);
  • A TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
  • B 1
  • C 2
  • D undefined

Snippet 3. What is logged?

let a = 5;
let b = a;
b = 10;
const x = { n: 1 };
const y = x;
y.n = 2;
console.log(a, x.n);
  • A 10 2
  • B 5 1
  • C 10 1
  • D 5 2

Snippet 4. What is logged?

console.log(typeof typeof 42);
  • A string
  • B number
  • C object
  • D undefined

Snippet 5. What is logged?

console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2);
console.log(9007199254740991n + 2n);
  • A 
    9007199254740993
9007199254740993n
  • B 
    9007199254740993
9007199254740993
  • C 
    9007199254740992
9007199254740993n
  • D 
    Infinity
9007199254740993n

Answers

  1. B. typeof undefined is 'undefined', but typeof null is 'object': a bug from 1995 that stays for compatibility. Test for null with value === null.
  2. C. push changes the array, it does not reassign items. const only forbids items = somethingElse.
  3. D. b got a copy of the number 5, so a is unchanged. y holds the same reference as x, so changing y.n changes the one shared object.
  4. A. typeof 42 is the string 'number', and typeof of any string is 'string'.
  5. C. Past MAX_SAFE_INTEGER a number cannot represent every integer, so the result rounds to the nearest double, 9007199254740992. BigInt is exact, and Node-style output adds the n suffix.

terms.definition: A name bound to a value. Declared with const (no reassignment) or let (can be reassigned); var is the legacy form.
One of seven immutable value types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol.
Any non-primitive value, such as an object literal, array, function or Date. Variables hold a reference to it, not a copy.
An operator that returns a string naming a value’s type, such as 'number' or 'object'. typeof null returns 'object' for historical reasons.
Types belong to values, not variables, so the same variable may hold a number now and a string later. Checks happen at run time.
let and const exist only inside the nearest { } block; var ignores blocks and is scoped to the whole function.
The time between entering a scope and the let or const line, when reading the variable throws a ReferenceError.

lessons.examTip: Default to const. When a reviewer sees let, it tells them “this value changes later”, so use it only when you really reassign.

lessons.title: Operators, comparison and coercion
lessons.summaryHtml:
Operators combine values: arithmetic (+ - * / % **), assignment (= += ??=), comparison (=== !== < >=) and logical (&& || ! ??). When an operator gets a type it does not expect, JavaScript silently converts the value: this is coercion.

Always compare with ===, which never converts. Know the eight falsy values (false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN); everything else, including '0' and [], is truthy.

|| and && return one of their operands, not just true or false. Use ?? for defaults when 0 or an empty string are valid values, ?. to read through data that may be missing, and parentheses whenever precedence is not obvious.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Operators are the verbs of a program: add these, compare those, pick this one if that one is missing. Most look like school maths, but JavaScript adds a twist. When an operator receives values of the wrong type, it does not stop with an error; it quietly converts them. This automatic conversion is called coercion.

Coercion is why '5' * 2 is 10 but '5' + 2 is '52'. Once you know the handful of rules underneath, these results stop being “JavaScript weirdness” and become predictable.

Why it matters

Real data is messy. Form fields are strings, APIs send null for missing values, and a quantity of 0 is a valid answer. Picture a checkout that treats a zero delivery fee as “missing” and charges the default ₹40, or a stock check that says '10' < '9'. These bugs come straight from coercion and from choosing || where ?? was needed. Interviewers love these questions for the same reason.

How it works

Arithmetic and assignment

The arithmetic operators are + - * /, % (remainder) and ** (exponent). A few behaviours are worth memorising:

  • % is a remainder, not a modulo: the result takes the sign of the left side, so -7 % 3 is -1. It is ideal for “every nth item” and even/odd checks.
  • Division by zero does not throw: 10 / 0 is Infinity and 0 / 0 is NaN (“not a number”).
  • x++ returns the old value and then increments; ++x increments first and returns the new value.
  • Compound assignment shortens updates: total += lineTotal, stock -= qty, price *= 1.18.

Try it: Arithmetic in a real bill

JavaScript

const unitPrice = 180;
const qty = 7;

// Buy 3, get the 3rd free: how many are free?
const freeItems = Math.floor(qty / 3);
const payable = (qty - freeItems) * unitPrice;
console.log({ freeItems, payable });

// % is the remainder, and keeps the sign of the left side
console.log(7 % 3, -7 % 3, 10 % 2 === 0 ? 'even' : 'odd');

// ** for compound growth: 5,000 saved at 8% a year for 3 years
const savings = 5000 * (1 + 0.08) ** 3;
console.log('After 3 years:', Math.round(savings));

// Increment: postfix returns the old value, prefix the new one
let ticket = 41;
console.log(ticket++, ticket, ++ticket);

// Division edge cases
console.log(10 / 0, -10 / 0, 0 / 0);

% gives the remainder (handy for “every 3rd item free” rules), ** raises to a power, and postfix ++ returns the old value.

How coercion works underneath

The specification defines a few conversion routines, and every operator uses one of them. You only need three:

  • ToNumber, used by - * / % **, unary +, and < > when at least one side is not a string.
  • ToString, used by + when either side is a string, and by template literals.
  • ToBoolean, used by if, while, !, &&, || and the ternary.

Objects first become primitives: an array joins its items ([5] becomes '5', [] becomes '') and a plain object becomes '[object Object]'. Then the rules below apply.

ValueNumber(v)String(v)Boolean(v)
''0''false
' 42 '42' 42 'true
'12px'NaN'12px'true
'0'0'0'true
true / false1 / 0'true' / 'false'true / false
null0'null'false
undefinedNaN'undefined'false
[]0''true
[5]5'5'true
{}NaN'[object Object]'true

Two rules explain most puzzles. The + rule: if either side of + is a string (after objects become primitives), both sides become strings and are joined; otherwise both become numbers. Left to right: 1 + 2 + '3' is 3 + '3', which is '33', while '1' + 2 + 3 is '123'.

Prefer explicit conversion in your own code: Number(value), String(value), Boolean(value). Number('12px') is NaN, while parseInt('12px', 10) reads the leading digits and gives 12; lesson 1.4 compares them.

Equality: === vs ==

Strict equality === compares type and value with no conversion: different types are never equal. Loose equality == converts first, following an algorithm with many branches. The results look random unless you have memorised them:

Try it: === vs == side by side

JavaScript

// Each pair: [label a, value a, label b, value b]
const pairs = [
  ['0', 0, "''", ''],
  ['0', 0, "'0'", '0'],
  ["''", '', "'0'", '0'],
  ['false', false, "'0'", '0'],
  ['null', null, 'undefined', undefined],
  ['null', null, '0', 0],
  ['NaN', NaN, 'NaN', NaN],
  ['1', 1, 'true', true],
  ["'1'", '1', '1', 1],
];

const rows = pairs.map(([la, a, lb, b]) => ({
  a: la,
  b: lb,
  '==': a == b,
  '===': a === b,
}));
console.table(rows);

console.log('Object.is(NaN, NaN):', Object.is(NaN, NaN));
console.log('Object.is(0, -0):', Object.is(0, -0));

Every row where the two columns differ is a place where == converted a value first. That is why teams ban == in their lint rules.

The rule for teams is simple: always use === and !== (the ESLint rule eqeqeq enforces it). There is one pattern some codebases allow: value == null is true for exactly null and undefined, so it checks “missing” in one test. Even there, value === null || value === undefined or ?? is clearer.

Two special cases: NaN is not equal to anything, including itself, so test it with Number.isNaN(x). And Object.is(a, b) is like === except that Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true and Object.is(0, -0) is false.

Relational operators (< > <= >=) compare two strings alphabetically, by UTF-16 code units, and compare anything else as numbers. So '10' < '9' is true (character 1 comes before 9), while '10' < 9 is false. Convert sizes and prices to numbers before comparing them.

Truthy, falsy and logical operators

Conditions convert values with ToBoolean. Exactly eight values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including '0', 'false', [] and {}. So if (cart.length) works (0 items is falsy), but if (cart) is always true for an array, even an empty one.

The logical operators do not return true/false; they return one of their operands, and they short-circuit (stop evaluating as soon as the answer is known):

OperatorReturnsTypical use
a || ba if truthy, else bFallback when any falsy value means “missing”
a && ba if falsy, else bGuard: user && user.name
a ?? ba unless it is null or undefined, else bDefaults where 0, '' and false are valid
!athe opposite boolean!!a converts to a real boolean

Try it: Truthy, falsy, || and ??

JavaScript

const samples = [
  ['false', false], ['0', 0], ['-0', -0], ['0n', 0n], ["''", ''],
  ['null', null], ['undefined', undefined], ['NaN', NaN],
  ["'0'", '0'], ["'false'", 'false'], ['[]', []], ['{}', {}],
];
for (const [label, value] of samples) {
  console.log(label.padEnd(10), Boolean(value) ? 'truthy' : 'falsy');
}

// A form where 0 and '' are valid answers
const form = { qty: 0, giftNote: '', express: undefined };

console.log('with ||:', form.qty || 1, JSON.stringify(form.giftNote || 'none'));
console.log('with ??:', form.qty ?? 1, JSON.stringify(form.giftNote ?? 'none'));
console.log('express:', form.express ?? false);

// && returns the first falsy operand, or the last one
console.log('Asha' && 'logged in', null && 'never evaluated');

The quantity 0 and the empty note are real answers, yet || throws them away. ?? keeps them.

The rule of thumb: use ?? for defaults. Reach for || only when an empty string or 0 really should be replaced, such as a display name where '' should become “Guest”.

Optional chaining and logical assignment

Reading order.customer.address.city throws a TypeError if any link in the chain is null or undefined. Optional chaining ?. stops at the first missing link and returns undefined instead. It has three forms: obj?.prop, obj?.[key] and fn?.(). Pair it with ?? for a default: order.customer?.address?.city ?? 'Pickup'.

Logical assignment combines a logical operator with = and assigns only when needed: a ||= b (if a is falsy), a &&= b (if a is truthy) and a ??= b (if a is nullish). They are handy for filling in defaults on settings objects.

Try it: Optional chaining and logical assignment

JavaScript

const user = {
  name: 'Asha',
  address: null,
  prefs: { theme: 'dark' },
};

console.log(user.address?.city);           // undefined, no crash
console.log(user.prefs?.theme ?? 'light'); // 'dark'
console.log(user.getPoints?.());           // method missing: undefined
console.log(user.orders?.[0]?.id);         // works with [ ] too

const settings = { pageSize: 0, currency: '', notify: true };
settings.pageSize ||= 20;     // 0 is falsy, so it is replaced (a bug?)
settings.currency ??= 'INR';  // '' is not nullish, so it is kept
settings.locale ??= 'en-IN';  // missing, so it is set
settings.notify &&= 'email';  // only assigns when already truthy
console.log(settings);

?. stops at null or undefined instead of crashing. ||=, &&= and ??= assign only when needed.

Watch out: use ?. where data is allowed to be missing. Sprinkling it everywhere hides real bugs: if an order must always have a customer, let the error surface.

Precedence: when to add parentheses

Operators have a precedence (which binds tighter) and an associativity (which side goes first). From high to low, roughly: ?. and calls, then unary (! typeof ++), **, * / %, + -, comparisons, equality, &&, || and ??, the ternary, then assignment. Two sharp edges are worth knowing:

  • ** is right-associative (2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** 9), and -2 ** 2 is a SyntaxError: write (-2) ** 2.
  • ?? cannot be mixed with || or && without parentheses: a || b ?? c is a SyntaxError.
// Hard to read: && binds tighter than ||, so this is NOT what it looks like
const freeShip = isMember || subtotal >= 999 && !isBulky;

// Clear: say exactly what you mean
const freeShipping = (isMember || subtotal >= 999) && !isBulky;

If a reader has to think about precedence, add parentheses. They cost nothing at run time.

Explore coercion yourself

This live page runs every combination for you. Choose values and an operator, and it shows the result with its type, plus how each side converts. Try [] + {}, null == 0 and '5' - 1.

Try it: Coercion explorer

JavaScript

const VALUES = {
  '0': 0, '1': 1, "''": '', "'0'": '0', "'5'": '5', "'abc'": 'abc',
  'true': true, 'false': false, 'null': null, 'undefined': undefined,
  'NaN': NaN, '[]': [], '[5]': [5], '{}': {},
};
const OPS = {
  '===': (a, b) => a === b, '==': (a, b) => a == b,
  '+': (a, b) => a + b, '-': (a, b) => a - b, '*': (a, b) => a * b,
  '||': (a, b) => a || b, '&&': (a, b) => a && b, '??': (a, b) => a ?? b,
};
const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const fill = (sel, keys, pick) => {
  for (const k of keys) sel.append(new Option(k, k, false, k === pick));
};
fill($('left'), Object.keys(VALUES), "'5'");
fill($('op'), Object.keys(OPS), '+');
fill($('right'), Object.keys(VALUES), '1');

const show = (v) => typeof v === 'string' ? `'${v}'`
  : Array.isArray(v) ? `[${v}]` : v && typeof v === 'object' ? '{}' : String(v);

function render() {
  const [l, op, r] = [$('left').value, $('op').value, $('right').value];
  const result = OPS[op](VALUES[l], VALUES[r]);
  $('expr').textContent = `${l} ${op} ${r}`;
  $('value').textContent = show(result);
  $('type').textContent = 'typeof → ' + typeof result;
  $('conv').replaceChildren(...[l, r].map((key) => {
    const v = VALUES[key];
    const tr = document.createElement('tr');
    for (const cell of [key, show(Number(v)), show(String(v)), show(Boolean(v))]) {
      tr.append(Object.assign(document.createElement('td'), { textContent: cell }));
    }
    return tr;
  }));
  console.log(`${l} ${op} ${r} →`, result);
}
document.querySelector('.controls').addEventListener('change', render);
render();

Pick two values and an operator. The panel shows the result, its type and how each side converts to a number and a boolean.

Example: Shop Bill, version 2 (checkout rules)

The lab upgrades the Shop Bill to handle orders that arrive from a web form: prices and quantities are strings, some orders have a coupon and some do not, and a delivery fee of 0 is a real value. Each rule uses one idea from this lesson:

const toNumber = (text) => (text === '' ? 0 : Number(text));

const lineTotal = (line) => toNumber(line.price) * toNumber(line.qty);

const deliveryFee = (order) => order.deliveryFee ?? 40;

const couponDiscount = (order, subtotal) =>
  subtotal * ((order.coupon?.percent ?? 0) / 100);

const isFreeShipping = (order, subtotal) =>
  (order.isMember || subtotal >= 999) && !order.isBulky;

Walk through an order with deliveryFee: 0 and no coupon. toNumber converts the form strings explicitly, so '250' times '2' is 500 and later additions stay numeric. ?? keeps the fee at 0 where || would have charged 40. order.coupon?.percent is undefined for orders without a coupon, and ?? 0 turns that into “no discount” instead of a crash or NaN. The parentheses in isFreeShipping make the business rule readable at a glance. (These are arrow functions; lesson 2.1 covers them properly.)

Common mistakes

1. Using == out of habit.

// Wrong: true for 0, '', '0', false and [] as well
if (qty == 0) { removeLine(); }

// Fix
if (qty === 0) { removeLine(); }

2. Defaults with || that erase valid values.

// Wrong: a free delivery (0) becomes 40
const fee = order.deliveryFee || 40;

// Fix
const fee = order.deliveryFee ?? 40;

3. Adding strings from inputs.

// Wrong: '250' + '40' is '25040'
const total = priceInput.value + deliveryInput.value;

// Fix: convert once, at the edge
const total = Number(priceInput.value) + Number(deliveryInput.value);

4. Testing for NaN with ===. x === NaN is always false. Use Number.isNaN(x). (The older global isNaN('abc') converts first and returns true for any non-numeric string, which is rarely what you want.)

5. Checking an empty array as a condition. if (items) is true for []. Use if (items.length > 0).

Interview and real-world notes

  • “== vs ===?” === compares without conversion; == converts types first. Use ===; mention Object.is for NaN and -0.
  • “What does || return?” The first truthy operand, or the last operand if none is truthy. && returns the first falsy operand, or the last one.
  • “?? vs ||?” ?? only falls back on null/undefined; || falls back on any falsy value, including 0 and ''.
  • Classic trick questions: [] + [] is '', [] + {} is '[object Object]', true + true is 2, 'b' + 'a' + +'a' + 'a' is 'baNaNa'. Explain them with the + rule rather than memorising.
  • In production code, convert at the boundaries (form input, API response, URL parameters) and keep real numbers and booleans inside your app. Then coercion rarely surprises you.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

console.log(1 + '2' + 3, 1 + 2 + '3');
  • A 6 6
  • B 123 123
  • C 15 33
  • D 123 33

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const qty = 0;
console.log(qty || 'guest', qty ?? 'guest');
  • A guest guest
  • B guest 0
  • C 0 guest
  • D 0 0

Snippet 3. What is logged?

console.log(null == 0, null == undefined, NaN === NaN);
  • A false true false
  • B true true false
  • C false true true
  • D true false false

Snippet 4. What is logged?

console.log('10' < '9', '10' < 9);
  • A false false
  • B true true
  • C false true
  • D true false

Snippet 5. What is logged?

let count = 5;
const next = count++;
const after = ++count;
console.log(next, count, after);
  • A 6 7 7
  • B 5 6 7
  • C 5 7 7
  • D 6 6 7

Answers

  1. D. + is evaluated left to right. 1 + '2' is '12', then '123'. In the second, 1 + 2 is the number 3 first, then 3 + '3' is '33'.
  2. B. || skips every falsy value, including 0. ?? only skips null and undefined, so it keeps 0.
  3. A. null loosely equals only undefined (and itself), so null == 0 is false. NaN is the only value not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN to test for it.
  4. D. Two strings compare character by character, and '1' comes before '9', so '10' < '9' is true. With a number on one side, '10' becomes 10, and 10 < 9 is false.
  5. C. Postfix count++ returns the old value (5) and then increments to 6. Prefix ++count increments first to 7 and returns 7.
