lessons.title: Strings and template literals
lessons.summaryHtml: A string is an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units: every method such as trim, slice or replaceAll returns a new string and leaves the original alone. Template literals (backtick strings) give you ${expressions}, real line breaks and tagged templates, where a function processes the pieces. You will learn the handful of methods that cover almost all real work: searching, slicing, splitting, padding, replacing and comparing. You will also see why '👍🏽'.length is 4, how to count what a user actually sees with Intl.Segmenter, and how Intl formats lists and money for any locale. The mini project is a receipt toolkit that turns messy shop data into a neat, aligned bill.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A string is text: a product name, an email address, a line on a receipt, a whole JSON document. In JavaScript a string is a primitive value, like a number. You cannot reach inside it and change one letter. Every tool you use on a string, such as trimming spaces or making it uppercase, hands you back a brand-new string.

Think of a string as a printed label. You can read it, cut a piece off a copy, or print a new label with different text. You never edit the ink on the original label. Keeping this picture in your head prevents the most common string bug of all.

A template literal is a string written with backticks. It lets you drop values straight into text with ${...} and write text over several lines, which makes receipts, emails and messages far easier to build.

Why it matters

Most of the data a front-end developer touches arrives as text: form inputs, URL query strings, CSV exports, API responses. Before you can calculate with it, store it or show it, you usually need to clean it (trim spaces, fix the case), take it apart (split a CSV line, read the last four digits of a card) and put it back together neatly (a receipt, a slug for a URL, a message for a customer).

Text also has traps. A tweet-style counter that uses .length tells a user that one emoji costs four characters. A sort that uses the default comparison puts “Émile” after “zara”. Building HTML by gluing strings together can open an XSS hole. This lesson shows the correct tool for each job so your code works for every customer, in every language.

How it works

Three ways to write a string, and why backticks win

Single quotes and double quotes behave exactly the same; pick one style (this course uses single quotes, which Prettier can enforce) and use the other when the text contains that quote. Backticks create a template literal. Inside it, ${expression} runs any JavaScript expression, converts the result with String() and inserts it. A line break in the source is a real line break in the string.

const name = 'Anu';
const qty = 3;
const plain = 'Hello, ' + name + '! You have ' + qty + ' items.';
const nicer = `Hello, ${name}! You have ${qty} items.`;
console.log(plain === nicer); // true

const email = `Hi ${name},
Your order of ${qty} ${qty === 1 ? 'item' : 'items'} has shipped.`;

Escape sequences such as \n (new line), \t (tab), \' and \\ work in all three kinds. Run the example and then change the total to see the ternary inside the template react.

Try it: Template literals: interpolation and real line breaks

JavaScript

const store = 'Ralfiz Store';
const customer = "Anu's Bakery";
const items = 3;
const total = 1249.5;

// Old style: + concatenation
const oldWay = 'Thanks for shopping at ' + store + ', ' + customer + '!';
// Template literal: expressions go inside ${ }
const newWay = `Thanks for shopping at ${store}, ${customer}!`;
console.log(oldWay === newWay);

// Any expression works: calls, maths, ternaries
const receipt = `${store.toUpperCase()}
Customer: ${customer}
Items: ${items} | Total: ₹${total.toFixed(2)}
Delivery: ${total >= 1000 ? 'free' : '₹49'}`;
console.log(receipt);

// Escapes still work in every kind of string
console.log('Tab:\there | Quote: \'ok\' | Backslash: \\');
console.log(`Values are converted with String(): ${null} ${[1, 2]} ${{}}`);

Change total to 800 and run again: the ternary inside ${} changes the delivery line.

Remember: ${} converts values with String(). An object becomes [object Object] and an array becomes its items joined by commas, so format objects yourself (or use JSON.stringify) before you interpolate them.

Immutability: every method returns a new string

Strings are stored as fixed sequences. When you call trim(), the engine builds a new sequence without the spaces and returns it. The original is untouched, so you must store the result. This is also why you can safely pass strings around: no function you call can change your copy.

You read characters with str[i] or str.at(i). The difference is that at accepts negative numbers, so at(-1) is the last character; an index past the end gives undefined in both. To search, use includes, startsWith and endsWith for yes/no questions and indexOf when you need the position (it returns -1 when nothing is found). To cut, use slice(start, end): the start is included, the end is not, and negative numbers count from the end.

Try it: Strings are immutable: methods return new strings

JavaScript

const sku = '  rz-Tshirt-0042  ';

sku.trim();                 // result thrown away
console.log(`[${sku}]`);   // still has spaces

const clean = sku.trim().toUpperCase();   // chain and store
console.log(`[${clean}]`, clean.length);

// Reading characters
console.log(clean[0], clean.at(0), clean.at(-1), clean[99]);

// Searching
console.log(clean.includes('TSHIRT'), clean.startsWith('RZ-'));
console.log(clean.indexOf('-'), clean.lastIndexOf('-'), clean.indexOf('X'));

// Slicing: start is included, end is not; negatives count from the end
console.log(clean.slice(0, 2), clean.slice(3, 9), clean.slice(-4));

// Trying to change a character does nothing (and throws in strict mode)
const word = 'cat';
try {
  (() => { 'use strict'; word[0] = 'b'; })();
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}

Notice that sku keeps its spaces and lowercase letters: only the returned value changes.

TaskMethodExample result
Remove outer spacestrim, trimStart, trimEnd' a '.trim() is 'a'
Change casetoUpperCase, toLowerCase'rz'.toUpperCase() is 'RZ'
Contains?includes, startsWith, endsWith'a.pdf'.endsWith('.pdf') is true
Where is it?indexOf, lastIndexOf'a-b'.indexOf('-') is 1
Cut a pieceslice (prefer it over substring)'invoice'.slice(-4) is 'oice'
One characterat, [i]'abc'.at(-1) is 'c'

Split, join, pad and replace

split(separator) turns a string into an array, and join(separator) turns an array back into a string. Together they are the workhorses of text processing: a CSV line becomes fields, a date becomes parts, a sentence becomes words. padStart and padEnd add characters until the string reaches a length, which is perfect for invoice numbers ('0042') and for aligning columns in plain-text receipts. repeat(n) builds divider lines.

replace with a string pattern changes only the first match. replaceAll changes every match. Both also accept a regular expression (you will master those in lesson 6.4); for now, reach for replaceAll when you mean “every”.

Try it: Split, pad and replace: an aligned receipt

JavaScript

const csv = `Notebook A5,3,89
Gel pen (blue),10,15
Steel bottle 1L,1,649`;

const rows = csv.split('\n').map((line) => {
  const [name, qty, price] = line.split(',');
  return { name, qty: Number(qty), price: Number(price) };
});
console.log(rows[0]);

const header = 'Item'.padEnd(18) + 'Qty'.padStart(5) + 'Amount'.padStart(11);
console.log(header);
console.log('-'.repeat(header.length));
for (const row of rows) {
  const amount = (row.qty * row.price).toFixed(2);
  console.log(
    row.name.padEnd(18) + String(row.qty).padStart(5) + amount.padStart(11)
  );
}

// replace changes the first match, replaceAll changes every match
const date = '2026-09-28';
console.log(date.replace('-', '/'), date.replaceAll('-', '/'));
console.log(date.split('-'), ['28', '09', '2026'].join('.'));
console.log('7'.padStart(3, '0'), 'ab'.repeat(3));

Try making the name column wider (padEnd(22)) and add a fourth product to the CSV text.

Text is harder than it looks: Unicode and comparison

JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units. Common letters fit in one unit, but many emoji and some scripts need a surrogate pair of two units. Some things users see as one character are several code points joined together: 👍🏽 is a thumbs-up plus a skin-tone modifier, and 🇮🇳 is two regional-indicator letters. So length counts code units, spreading [...str] counts code points, and only Intl.Segmenter counts graphemes, the characters a person actually sees.

This matters for character limits, for truncating names on a receipt (cutting inside a surrogate pair leaves a broken symbol) and for reversing strings. The same visible letter can also be stored in different ways: é can be one code point or an e plus a combining accent. Call normalize() on both sides before comparing text that came from different sources.

Sorting has the same problem. The default sort() compares code units, so every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one and accented letters land at the end. a.localeCompare(b) follows the rules of a language. For many comparisons, create one Intl.Collator and reuse its compare function; options such as numeric: true sort item2 before item10, and sensitivity: 'base' treats Anu and anu as equal.

Try it: Unicode: length, graphemes and fair comparison

JavaScript

const texts = ['hello', 'café', '👍', '👍🏽', '🇮🇳', 'Great tee 👍🏽'];
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
const graphemes = (s) => [...seg.segment(s)].length;

console.table(texts.map((t) => ({
  text: t,
  length: t.length,          // UTF-16 code units
  codePoints: [...t].length, // spreading iterates code points
  graphemes: graphemes(t),   // what a person sees
})));

// Cutting by code units can split an emoji in half
const broken = '👍🏽'.slice(0, 1);
console.log(broken.length, broken.isWellFormed());

// The same visible é can be stored in two ways
const composed = '\u00e9';     // one code point
const decomposed = 'e\u0301';  // e + combining accent
console.log(composed === decomposed);
console.log(composed.normalize() === decomposed.normalize());

// Sorting: default compares code units, localeCompare follows language rules
const names = ['zara', 'Arjun', 'émile', 'Bala', 'anu'];
console.log(names.toSorted());
console.log(names.toSorted((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)));
const byNumber = new Intl.Collator('en', { numeric: true });
console.log(['item10', 'item2', 'item1'].toSorted(byNumber.compare));

Add your own name or a flag emoji to the texts array and compare the three counts.

Tagged templates and Intl

If you put a function name directly before a template literal, JavaScript calls that function instead of building the string. The function receives an array of the literal pieces and then each value as a separate argument. There is always one more piece than there are values (the last piece may be an empty string). The tag can return anything: a formatted string, an escaped string, even an object. Libraries use tags for styled components, SQL builders and translations. The built-in String.raw is a tag that keeps backslashes exactly as typed.

The Intl family does locale-aware formatting so you never hand-build commas, currency symbols or “and” lists:

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
inr.format(123456.5);                // '₹1,23,456.50' (lakh grouping)

const list = new Intl.ListFormat('en', { type: 'conjunction' });
list.format(['Anu', 'Bala', 'Chitra']); // 'Anu, Bala, and Chitra'

const rules = new Intl.PluralRules('en');
rules.select(1);  // 'one'
rules.select(5);  // 'other'

Create a formatter once and reuse it: building one is much slower than calling format. The example below combines both ideas with an inr tag and a safeHtml tag that escapes every value before it reaches HTML.

Try it: Tagged templates: a money tag and an HTML-escaping tag

JavaScript

function show(strings, ...values) {
  console.log(strings, values);
}
show`Total ${3} items for ${'Anu'}`;

// A tag that formats every value as Indian rupees
const rupees = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR',
});
function inr(strings, ...values) {
  let out = strings[0];
  values.forEach((value, i) => {
    out += rupees.format(value) + strings[i + 1];
  });
  return out;
}
console.log(inr`Subtotal ${124950} minus ${5000} discount`);

// A tag that escapes values before they go into HTML
const escapeHtml = (value) => String(value)
  .replaceAll('&', '&').replaceAll('<', '<')
  .replaceAll('>', '>').replaceAll('"', '"')
  .replaceAll("'", ''');
function safeHtml(strings, ...values) {
  let out = strings[0];
  values.forEach((value, i) => {
    out += escapeHtml(value) + strings[i + 1];
  });
  return out;
}
const review = '<img src=x onerror="steal()"> Great tee!';
console.log(safeHtml`<p class="review">${review}</p>`);

// String.raw is a built-in tag: backslashes stay as typed
console.log(String.raw`C:\new\folder`, 'C:\new\folder'.length);

Look at how show() receives three string parts for two values. Then try safeHtml with your own script tag.

Watch out: a template literal on its own does not make HTML safe. `<p>${review}</p>` passed to innerHTML will run a script hidden in review. In the DOM track you will use textContent, and DOMPurify when HTML is truly needed. Escaping tags like safeHtml are a fallback, not a replacement.

Example: the receipt toolkit

The lab builds small, reusable text functions for the Ralfiz Store till. Each one takes a string, returns a new string and never changes its input, which makes them easy to test.

const formatName = (raw) => raw
  .trim()
  .split(' ')
  .filter((part) => part !== '')          // drop extra spaces
  .map((w) => w[0].toUpperCase() + w.slice(1).toLowerCase())
  .join(' ');

const makeSku = (category, id) =>
  `RZ-${category.slice(0, 3).toUpperCase()}-${String(id).padStart(4, '0')}`;

function receiptLine(name, qty, price) {
  const label = name.length > 18 ? name.slice(0, 17) + '…' : name;
  const amount = (qty * price).toFixed(2);
  return label.padEnd(18) + String(qty).padStart(5) + amount.padStart(11);
}

formatName('  anu   KRISHNAN ');   // 'Anu Krishnan'
makeSku('stationery', 42);        // 'RZ-STA-0042'

The same helpers power the live page below: a post composer for the Ralfiz Academy blog. It builds a URL slug from the title (normalising accents away) and counts graphemes for the title limit, while the footer shows how different .length would be. It writes with textContent, so whatever the user types is shown as text, never run as HTML.

Try it: Post composer: live slug and honest character count

HTML

<main class="card">
  <header>

  </header>

CSS

JavaScript

const title = document.querySelector('#title');
const body = document.querySelector('#body');
const counter = document.querySelector('#counter');
const slug = document.querySelector('#slug');
const stats = document.querySelector('#stats');

const LIMIT = 40;
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
const countGraphemes = (s) => [...seg.segment(s)].length;

function slugify(text) {
  return text
    .normalize('NFD')                 // é -> e + accent
    .replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, '')  // drop the accents
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')      // anything else becomes -
    .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '');         // no dashes at the ends
}

function countWords(text) {
  const trimmed = text.trim();
  return trimmed === '' ? 0 : trimmed.split(/\s+/).length;
}

function render() {
  const used = countGraphemes(title.value);
  counter.textContent = `${used}/${LIMIT}`;
  counter.classList.toggle('over', used > LIMIT);
  slug.textContent = slugify(title.value) || 'your-post-title';
  const words = countWords(body.value);
  const minutes = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(words / 200));
  stats.textContent = `${words} ${words === 1 ? 'word' : 'words'} · ` +
    `${minutes} min read · title .length is ${title.value.length}`;
}

title.addEventListener('input', render);
body.addEventListener('input', render);
render();
console.log('graphemes:', countGraphemes(title.value), '| length:', title.value.length);
console.log('slug:', slugify(title.value));

Type an emoji such as 👍🏽 in the title: the counter uses graphemes, while .length jumps by 4.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to store the result. email.trim(); does nothing useful. Write email = email.trim(); or better, const clean = email.trim();.
  • Using length for a user-facing limit. Wrong: if (bio.length > 160). Fix: count graphemes with [...new Intl.Segmenter().segment(bio)].length. (Servers and databases may still limit bytes or code units, so check both sides.)
  • Expecting replace to change every match. Wrong: '1-2-3'.replace('-', '') gives '12-3'. Fix: '1-2-3'.replaceAll('-', '').
  • Sorting names with the default sort. Wrong: names.sort(). Fix: names.toSorted((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)), which also leaves the original array untouched.
  • Case-sensitive checks on user input. Wrong: code === 'SAVE10' fails for ' save10'. Fix: code.trim().toUpperCase() === 'SAVE10'.
  • Interpolating objects. `User: ${user}` prints [object Object]. Pick the fields: `User: ${user.name}`.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Are strings mutable?” No. They are primitives; methods return new strings. Mention that const is about the binding, while immutability is about the value.
  • “Reverse a string.” The classic str.split('').reverse().join('') breaks emoji. A safer answer is [...str].reverse().join(''), and the fully correct one reverses graphemes from Intl.Segmenter. Saying this shows real-world awareness.
  • slice vs substring: slice supports negative indexes and is the one to prefer; substr is a legacy method you should not use.
  • Performance: building a big string with += in a loop is fine in modern engines; collecting parts in an array and calling join is also common and reads well.
  • Newer helpers: isWellFormed() and toWellFormed() detect and repair lone surrogates before you send text to an API. They are recent additions, so check the MDN compatibility table if you target older browsers.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

brand[0] = 'r';

console.log('👍'.length, [...'👍'].length);

  • B 1 1
  • C 2 2
  • D 4 1

const s = 'a-b-c';
console.log(s.replace('-', '+'), s.replaceAll('-', '+'));
  • A a+b+c a+b+c
  • B a-b-c a+b+c
  • C a+b-c a+b-c
  • D a+b-c a+b+c

const price = 5;
console.log(`Total: ${price * 2}` + 1);

  • C Total: 20
  • D Total: 10 1

Snippet 5. What is logged?

console.log('7'.padStart(3, '0'), 'shirt'.at(-1), '  hi  '.trim().length);

  • B 007 t 6
  • C 007 t 2
  • D 7 t 2

Answers

  1. C. Strings are immutable. The index assignment is silently ignored in sloppy mode and toLowerCase returns a new string that nobody stored.
  2. A. 👍 is one code point outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, so it is stored as a surrogate pair (2 code units). Spreading iterates by code point, giving 1.
  3. D. With a string pattern, replace changes only the first match; replaceAll changes every match.
  4. B. The template literal is evaluated first to the string Total: 10. Then + with a string concatenates, so 1 is appended as text.
  5. C. padStart fills on the left up to length 3, at(-1) reads the last character and trim removes the four spaces, leaving 2 characters.

terms.definition: A primitive value holding text as a sequence of UTF-16 code units. It is immutable: methods return new strings.
A string written with backticks that supports ${expression} interpolation and real line breaks.
A template literal preceded by a function name; the function receives the literal parts and the values and returns anything it likes.
The 16-bit unit JavaScript strings are made of. length counts these, so some emoji count as 2 or more.
One user-perceived character, such as 👍🏽 or 🇮🇳, which may be several code points. Intl.Segmenter splits text into graphemes.
A string method that compares two strings using the language rules of a locale, for human-friendly sorting.
The built-in internationalisation API: NumberFormat, DateTimeFormat, ListFormat, PluralRules, Collator and Segmenter.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers love asking why a string method did not change the string. Answer: strings are immutable primitives, so every method returns a new value you must store.

quiz.question: A teammate writes name.trim(); on its own line and the spaces are still there. Why?
options: trim only removes tabs
trim only works on template literals
Strings are immutable, so trim returns a new string that was thrown away
trim needs a regular expression argument
quiz.explanation: String methods never change the original string. You must use the returned value, for example name = name.trim().

quiz.question: Why does '👍🏽'.length return 4?

Emoji are stored as four bytes in UTF-8
length counts bytes
The skin tone modifier is a hidden space character

quiz.question: You need to sort customer names such as Émile, anu and Bala the way people expect. What should you use?
options: The default sort() with no comparator
A comparator that subtracts the strings
toUpperCase on every name and a less-than comparison
localeCompare or an Intl.Collator in the comparator
quiz.explanation: The default sort compares UTF-16 code units, so uppercase comes before lowercase and accented letters go to the end. localeCompare and Intl.Collator follow the language rules.

lessons.title: Numbers, Math and dates
lessons.summaryHtml: JavaScript has one everyday number type, a 64-bit floating-point double, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. You will learn how that storage works, why money should be kept in whole paise or cents, how to convert text to numbers safely (Number, parseFloat, Number.isNaN) and when you need BigInt. You will use Math for rounding, clamping and random values, and Intl.NumberFormat to show ₹1,23,456.50 or $1,234.50 correctly. Finally you will meet the Date object and its traps (months start at 0, time zones, mutation), format dates with Intl.DateTimeFormat, and hear about Temporal, the modern date API that is rolling out. The mini project is a GST invoice calculator that never loses a paisa.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Numbers look simple until real money, real measurements and real calendars show up. JavaScript stores almost every number in the same format, a 64-bit binary floating-point value (a “double”). It is fast and handles huge and tiny values, but it stores many decimal fractions only approximately, the way 1/3 can only be written approximately as 0.333… in decimal.

Dates are the second trap. A JavaScript Date is really just one number: milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. Everything else (the day, the month, the hour you see) is worked out from that number using a time zone. Once you understand these two ideas, most “weird” number and date bugs stop being weird.

Why it matters

An invoice that is off by one paisa fails reconciliation with the payment gateway. A due date that shows 30 January instead of 31 January because the server and the browser are in different time zones creates a support ticket. A dashboard that prints 1234567.891 instead of ₹12,34,567.89 looks unfinished. Getting numbers and dates right is one of the clearest signals that a developer is ready for production work, especially in billing, bookings and reporting apps.

How it works

One number type, stored in binary

A double has 52 bits for the digits (the mantissa), an exponent and a sign. Whole numbers are exact up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, which is 2 ** 53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991). Fractions are stored as sums of halves, quarters, eighths and so on. 0.5 fits perfectly; 0.1 does not, so the engine stores the nearest possible value. Add two approximations and the tiny errors can show: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004. This is not a JavaScript bug. Python, Java and C# doubles behave the same way.

Two practical rules follow. Never compare computed decimals with ===; compare with a small tolerance or, better, avoid decimals by working in integers. And when integers can exceed the safe range (database ids from some systems, cryptography, very large counters), use BigInt. A BigInt is written with an n suffix, has its own typeof, divides without decimals and cannot be mixed with ordinary numbers in arithmetic, which protects you from silently losing precision.

Try it: Floating point, safe integers and BigInt

JavaScript

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);

// Compare decimals with a small tolerance instead
const nearlyEqual = (a, b) => Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON * 4;
console.log(nearlyEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3));

// Integers are exact... up to a limit
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, 2 ** 53 - 1);
const big = 2 ** 53;
console.log(big + 1, big + 1 === big);   // precision lost!
console.log(Number.isSafeInteger(big - 1), Number.isSafeInteger(big + 1));

// BigInt: integers of any size (note the n suffix)
const orderId = 9007199254740993n;
console.log(orderId + 1n, typeof orderId);
console.log(10n / 3n);               // integer division, no decimals
try {
  console.log(orderId + 1);          // mixing BigInt and Number
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}
console.log(Number(10n) + 1, BigInt(42), 5n > 3);

Try 0.1 * 3, then change the big id to 2 ** 53 + 3. Where does Number stop being exact?

Rounding and money: work in paise

toFixed(n) is for display: it returns a string, and it rounds the stored binary value, so (1.005).toFixed(2) gives '1.00' because 1.005 is really stored as 1.00499999…. Multiplying by 100 and calling Math.round has the same problem for that value.

The professional pattern for money is minor units: convert rupees to whole paise once, at the edge (when reading input or an API), do every calculation on integers, round deliberately at defined steps (a discount, a tax line) and convert back only to format for display. Integer addition and multiplication are exact within the safe range, which covers amounts far bigger than any shop needs.

const toPaise = (rupees) => Math.round(Number(rupees) * 100);
const lineTotal = (unitPaise, qty) => unitPaise * qty;        // exact
const gst = (taxablePaise, rate) => Math.round(taxablePaise * rate / 100);

const unit = toPaise('249.99');       // 24999
const subtotal = lineTotal(unit, 3);  // 74997
const tax = gst(subtotal, 18);        // 13499 (rounded once)
const total = subtotal + tax;         // 88496 paise = ₹884.96

Try it: Rounding traps and money in paise

JavaScript

// toFixed returns a STRING and rounds the stored binary value
console.log((2.5).toFixed(0), (1.005).toFixed(2), typeof (1.5).toFixed(1));
console.log(Math.round(1.005 * 100) / 100); // 1.005 * 100 = 100.49999...

// Float version of a cart: errors creep in
const cart = [
  { name: 'Notebook', price: 49.9, qty: 1 },
  { name: 'Sticker', price: 0.1, qty: 3 },
  { name: 'Gel pen', price: 19.99, qty: 2 },
];
const floatTotal = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
console.log('float total:', floatTotal);

// Why toPaise needs Math.round: the multiplication is not exact either
console.log(4.35 * 100, Math.round(4.35 * 100));

// Paise version: convert once, then only integer maths
const toPaise = (rupees) => Math.round(rupees * 100);
const paiseTotal = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + toPaise(i.price) * i.qty, 0);
console.log('paise total:', paiseTotal, Number.isInteger(paiseTotal));

// 10% discount, rounded ONCE to the nearest paisa
const discount = Math.round(paiseTotal * 0.10);
const payable = paiseTotal - discount;

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
console.log('Subtotal', inr.format(paiseTotal / 100));
console.log('Discount', inr.format(-discount / 100));
console.log('Payable ', inr.format(payable / 100));

Change the cart prices and the discount. The paise version always adds up to the exact paisa.

Remember: agree on where rounding happens. Tax rules, payment gateways and accounting software each define their own rounding step (per line or per invoice). Your code should round exactly there, once, and nowhere else.

Converting text to numbers, NaN and Math

Form fields and query strings always give you strings. There are three main converters, and they disagree on edge cases:

InputNumber(s)parseFloat(s)parseInt(s, 10)
'42'424242
'3.99'3.993.993
'42px'NaN4242
''0NaNNaN
'1,299'NaN11

Number() is strict about the whole string, which is usually what you want for validation (but watch the empty string becoming 0). parseFloat and parseInt read from the start and stop at the first character they do not understand, which is handy for CSS values like '12px'. Always pass the radix 10 to parseInt.

NaN (“not a number”) is, confusingly, of type number. It spreads through calculations and is not equal to itself, so test with Number.isNaN(x). The older global isNaN converts its argument first, so isNaN('abc') is true. Number.isInteger, Number.isFinite and Number.isSafeInteger also avoid conversion.

The Math object holds the helpers. round, floor, ceil and trunc differ mainly for negative numbers; min and max take any number of arguments (spread an array into them); Math.random() returns a value from 0 up to but not including 1, which you scale for a range. It is not secure: use crypto.getRandomValues or crypto.randomUUID() for tokens and ids.

Try it: From text to numbers, NaN and Math

JavaScript

const samples = ['42', ' 42 ', '42px', '', '3.99', 'abc', '1,299'];
console.table(samples.map((s) => ({
  input: JSON.stringify(s),
  'Number()': Number(s),
  parseFloat: parseFloat(s),
  'parseInt(,10)': parseInt(s, 10),
})));

// NaN is a number that is not equal to itself
const qty = Number('two');
console.log(typeof qty, qty === qty, Number.isNaN(qty));
console.log(isNaN('abc'), Number.isNaN('abc'));   // global isNaN converts first
console.log(Number.isInteger(5.0), Number.isInteger(5.5), Number.isFinite('5'));

// Math rounds in different directions, especially for negatives
for (const n of [2.5, 2.4, -2.5, -2.7]) {
  console.log(n, Math.round(n), Math.floor(n), Math.ceil(n), Math.trunc(n));
}

const clamp = (n, min, max) => Math.min(Math.max(n, min), max);
console.log(clamp(12, 1, 10), clamp(-3, 1, 10), Math.max(...[4, 9, 2]));

// Random integer between min and max, both included
const randomInt = (min, max) => Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;
console.log('OTP:', String(randomInt(0, 999999)).padStart(6, '0'));
console.log(2 ** 10, Math.sqrt(144), Math.abs(-7), 17 % 5, -17 % 5);

Add your own inputs to the samples array, such as ' 42 ', '1e3' or '0x1F', and compare the columns.

Formatting with Intl.NumberFormat

Never hand-build separators or currency symbols. India groups digits in lakhs and crores (₹12,34,567.89), the US in thousands ($1,234,567.89), and other locales swap commas and points or use other digits. Intl.NumberFormat knows these rules. You choose a locale (how the reader expects numbers to look) and options such as style: 'currency' with a currency code, 'percent', 'unit' or notation: 'compact'. Create each formatter once and reuse it.

Try it: Intl.NumberFormat: currencies, compact and percent

JavaScript

const amount = 1234567.891;

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
const cad = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-CA', { style: 'currency', currency: 'CAD' });
const aed = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-AE', { style: 'currency', currency: 'AED' });
console.log(inr.format(amount));   // lakh and crore grouping
console.log(usd.format(amount));
console.log(cad.format(-amount));
console.log(aed.format(amount));

// Whole rupees for price tags
const tag = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});
console.log(tag.format(2499), tag.format(2499.5));

// Compact numbers for dashboards
const compactIN = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { notation: 'compact' });
const compactUS = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { notation: 'compact' });
console.log(compactIN.format(amount), compactUS.format(amount));

// Percent expects a fraction: 0.183 means 18.3%
const pct = new Intl.NumberFormat('en', { style: 'percent', maximumFractionDigits: 1 });
console.log(pct.format(0.183), pct.format(0.05));

// Units and plain grouping
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat('en', { style: 'unit', unit: 'kilogram' }).format(2.5));
console.log(amount.toLocaleString('en-IN', { maximumFractionDigits: 2 }));

Change the locale strings (try de-DE, ar-AE or ja-JP) and watch symbols, separators and digits change.

Notice that the locale and the currency are separate choices: a customer in Toronto paying in INR still expects Canadian formatting around the rupee amount. Percent style expects a fraction (0.18 prints 18%).

Dates: what the Date object really is

A Date wraps a single timestamp. Getters such as getHours() read it in the device’s local time zone; getUTCHours() reads it in UTC. Four traps catch almost everyone:

  • Months are 0-based in the constructor and in getMonth/setMonth (0 is January), but days of the month start at 1.
  • Dates are mutable. setDate changes the object in place, so copy with new Date(original) before changing it. Out-of-range values roll over (31 February becomes early March), which is handy for adding days but surprising when changing months.
  • Parsing depends on the format. A date-only ISO string ('2026-03-15') is read as UTC midnight, while '2026-03-15T09:30' without a Z is local time. Other formats such as '15/03/2026' are not reliable across engines. Send and store ISO 8601 strings in UTC.
  • Days are not always 24 hours in zones with daylight saving. For calendar maths, build dates with Date.UTC and subtract timestamps.

To display a date, use Intl.DateTimeFormat with a locale and, when it matters, an explicit timeZone such as 'Asia/Kolkata'. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat produces phrases like “yesterday” or “in 3 days”.

Try it: Dates: 0-based months, time zones and formatting

JavaScript

// Months are 0-based in the constructor: 0 = January
const invoiceDate = new Date(2026, 0, 31, 10, 30);   // 31 Jan 2026, local time
console.log(invoiceDate.getMonth(), invoiceDate.getDate(), invoiceDate.getDay());

// Date objects are MUTABLE: setters change the same object
const due = new Date(invoiceDate);        // copy first!
due.setDate(due.getDate() + 30);          // overflow rolls into March
console.log(due.getMonth(), due.getDate());
console.log(invoiceDate.getDate());        // original is unchanged

// A date-only ISO string is read as UTC; with a time but no Z, as local
console.log(new Date('2026-03-15').toISOString());
console.log(new Date('2026-03-15T09:30').getHours());

// Days between two calendar dates: use UTC to avoid DST surprises
const dayMs = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
const a = Date.UTC(2026, 2, 1);
const b = Date.UTC(2026, 3, 1);
console.log('days in March:', (b - a) / dayMs);

// One instant, shown in different zones
const meeting = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 8, 28, 4, 30));
const show = (locale, timeZone) => new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, {
  dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short', timeZone,
}).format(meeting);
console.log('Kochi  ', show('en-IN', 'Asia/Kolkata'));
console.log('Dubai  ', show('en-AE', 'Asia/Dubai'));
console.log('Toronto', show('en-CA', 'America/Toronto'));

const rtf = new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' });
console.log(rtf.format(-1, 'day'), '|', rtf.format(3, 'day'));
console.log('Temporal available here?', typeof Temporal !== 'undefined');

Change the timeZone values (try Asia/Dubai or Europe/London) and see the same instant printed differently.

Temporal: the new Temporal API (plain dates, zoned date-times, durations, immutable objects and 1-based months) is designed to replace Date. It is rolling out across engines, so check the MDN compatibility table or caniuse.com before relying on it. Until it is everywhere, use Date for storage and maths and Intl for display, as in this lesson.

Example: GST invoice calculator

The Ralfiz Billing quick-invoice screen takes a unit price, quantity, discount and GST rate. The whole calculation is one pure function that works in paise. The discount and the GST are each rounded once. To split GST into its central and state halves without losing a paisa, the code floors one half and gives the remainder to the other, so CGST + SGST always equals the rounded GST.

function calculate({ price, qty, discountPct, ratePct }) {
  const unit = Math.round(price * 100);             // rupees -> paise
  const subtotal = unit * qty;
  const discount = Math.round(subtotal * discountPct / 100);
  const taxable = subtotal - discount;
  const gst = Math.round(taxable * ratePct / 100);
  const cgst = Math.floor(gst / 2);
  const sgst = gst - cgst;                          // never off by one
  return { subtotal, discount, taxable, cgst, sgst, total: taxable + gst };
}

The page reads each input with Number(), clamps it to a sensible range, recalculates on every input event and shows every amount with one shared Intl.NumberFormat. The due date is today plus 15 days, copied before it is changed. The GST rates in the menu are examples for the demo; real rates depend on the goods and current rules.

Try it: GST invoice calculator in paise

HTML

<main class="card">
  <header><span class="logo">R</span><div><h1>Quick invoice</h1><p>Ralfiz Billing</p></div></header>

CSS

JavaScript

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const dateFmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-IN', { dateStyle: 'medium' });
const money = (paise) => inr.format(paise / 100);

function calculate({ price, qty, discountPct, ratePct }) {
  const unit = Math.round(price * 100);            // rupees -> paise, once
  const subtotal = unit * qty;
  const discount = Math.round(subtotal * discountPct / 100);
  const taxable = subtotal - discount;
  const gst = Math.round(taxable * ratePct / 100);
  const cgst = Math.floor(gst / 2);                 // halves that add up
  const sgst = gst - cgst;
  return { subtotal, discount, taxable, cgst, sgst, total: taxable + gst };
}

function render() {
  const input = {
    price: Math.max(0, Number($('price').value) || 0),
    qty: Math.max(1, Math.trunc(Number($('qty').value) || 1)),
    discountPct: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Number($('disc').value) || 0)),
    ratePct: Number($('rate').value),
  };
  const r = calculate(input);
  const rows = [
    ['Subtotal', money(r.subtotal)],
    [`Discount (${input.discountPct}%)`, '−' + money(r.discount)],
    ['Taxable value', money(r.taxable)],
    [`CGST ${input.ratePct / 2}%`, money(r.cgst)],
    [`SGST ${input.ratePct / 2}%`, money(r.sgst)],
    ['Total payable', money(r.total)],
  ];
  $('out').replaceChildren(...rows.map(([label, value], i) => {
    const row = document.createElement('div');
    if (i === rows.length - 1) row.className = 'total';
    const dt = document.createElement('dt');
    const dd = document.createElement('dd');
    dt.textContent = label;
    dd.textContent = value;
    row.append(dt, dd);
    return row;
  }));
  const due = new Date();
  due.setDate(due.getDate() + 15);
  $('due').textContent = `Payment due by ${dateFmt.format(due)} (15 days)`;
  console.log(r);
}

$('form').addEventListener('input', render);
render();

Try a price such as 199.99 with quantity 3, a 12.5% discount and 18% GST: the CGST and SGST halves always add up to the GST.

Common mistakes

  • Adding money as floats. Wrong: total += item.price * item.qty with price: 199.9. Fix: store pricePaise: 19990 and add integers.
  • Treating toFixed as maths. Wrong: const tax = (amount * 0.18).toFixed(2); total = amount + tax; which concatenates a string. Fix: round with Math.round on paise and format at the end.
  • Checking NaN with ===. Wrong: if (qty === NaN) is never true. Fix: if (Number.isNaN(qty)), or validate with Number.isFinite(qty).
  • Forgetting 0-based months. Wrong: new Date(2026, 3, 1) for 1 March (it is 1 April). Fix: subtract 1, or parse an ISO string such as '2026-03-01T00:00'.
  • Changing a shared date. Wrong: const due = invoice.date; due.setDate(due.getDate() + 30); changes the invoice date too. Fix: const due = new Date(invoice.date); first.
  • Using Math.random for OTPs or tokens. Fix: crypto.getRandomValues or crypto.randomUUID().

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not 0.3?” Explain binary fractions and IEEE 754, then give the fix: integers in minor units, or a tolerance for measurements.
  • “How would you store prices?” Integer paise or cents in the database and API, a currency code next to them, and formatting only in the UI. For arbitrary-precision decimals (exchange rates, crypto), use a decimal library or BigInt with a fixed scale.
  • Time zones: store and send instants as UTC ISO strings, show them in the user’s zone with Intl.DateTimeFormat, and store “calendar” values like a birthday as a plain YYYY-MM-DD string, not a timestamp.
  • Performance: constructing Intl formatters is relatively expensive; create them once per locale and reuse them in lists and tables.
  • BigInt limits: JSON.stringify throws on BigInt values, so convert them to strings for APIs.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, (0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2));
  • A true 0.30
  • B false 0.3
  • C false 0.30
  • D false 0.30000000000000004

Snippet 2. What is logged?

console.log(Number(''), Number('12px'), parseFloat('12px'));
  • A NaN NaN 12
  • B 0 NaN 12
  • C 0 12 12
  • D NaN 12 12

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const d = new Date(2026, 0, 31);
d.setMonth(1);
console.log(d.getMonth(), d.getDate());
  • A 1 28
  • B 1 31
  • C 2 31
  • D 2 3

Snippet 4. What is logged?

console.log(Math.round(-2.5), Math.trunc(-2.7), Math.floor(-2.7));
  • A -2 -2 -3
  • B -3 -2 -3
  • C -3 -3 -3
  • D -2 -3 -2

Snippet 5. What is logged?

console.log(typeof 10n, 10n / 3n, NaN === NaN);
  • A number 3.3333333333333335 false
  • B bigint 3n true
  • C bigint 3n false
  • D bigint 3.33n false

Answers

  1. C. The sum is 0.30000000000000004, so strict equality fails. toFixed(2) rounds it and returns the string 0.30, with the trailing zero.
  2. B. Number converts the whole string: an empty string becomes 0 and any stray character gives NaN. parseFloat reads as far as it can and stops at p.
  3. D. Setting the month to February keeps day 31. February 2026 has 28 days, so the date overflows by 3 days into 3 March, and March is month 2.
  4. A. Math.round rounds .5 towards +Infinity, so -2.5 becomes -2. trunc drops the decimals (towards zero) and floor always goes down.
  5. C. BigInt has its own typeof, and BigInt division drops the remainder. NaN is never equal to anything, even itself.

terms.definition: The 64-bit binary format every JavaScript number uses. It stores many decimals, such as 0.1, only approximately.
The smallest unit of a currency, such as paise for INR or cents for USD. Storing money as whole minor units avoids rounding errors.
Not a Number: the number value produced by invalid maths or failed conversions. It is not equal to anything, including itself.
An integer between -(2^53 - 1) and 2^53 - 1 that a double can represent exactly. Check with Number.isSafeInteger.
A separate numeric primitive for integers of any size, written with an n suffix such as 10n. It cannot be mixed with Number in arithmetic.
The built-in formatter for numbers, currencies, percentages, units and compact notation in any locale.
The number of milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. A Date object wraps one timestamp; time zones only matter when you read or display it.

lessons.examTip: In fintech and e-commerce interviews, say you store money as integer minor units (paise or cents), do all maths on integers, round once at a defined step, and format only for display.

quiz.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 return false?
options: JavaScript has a bug in its addition operator
0.1 and 0.2 are stored as the nearest binary fractions, so their sum is slightly more than 0.3
The numbers are converted to strings first
=== compares types, and the sum is a string
quiz.explanation: Like most languages, JavaScript uses IEEE 754 binary doubles. Many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly, so tiny errors appear. Compare with a tolerance, or use integers.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to store a product price of ₹249.99 for calculations?
options: As the string '249.99'
As the float 249.99 and call toFixed after every step
As the BigInt 249n
As the integer 24999 (paise), formatting it only for display
quiz.explanation: Integer arithmetic on paise is exact within the safe integer range. Format with Intl.NumberFormat only at the edge, when showing the value.

quiz.question: What date does new Date(2026, 1, 10) represent?
options: 10 February 2026, local time
1 October 2026
10 January 2026
10 February 2026, UTC
quiz.explanation: In the multi-argument constructor, months are 0-based (0 is January), so 1 is February, and the values are read as local time.

quiz.question: Which check returns true only for the actual NaN value, without converting its argument?
options: isNaN(value)
value === NaN
Number.isNaN(value)
typeof value === 'NaN'
quiz.explanation: The global isNaN converts first, so isNaN('abc') is true. Number.isNaN does not convert, and NaN === NaN is always false.

lessons.title: Control flow and loops
lessons.summaryHtml: Control flow decides which code runs and how many times. You will use if/else ladders, switch (with its strict matching and fall-through), and the conditional operator for small choices. You will write every kind of loop: the counting for, while and do…while, and the modern for…of, and learn why for…in is for object keys, not arrays. break and continue let you stop early or skip items, and guard clauses (early returns) keep functions flat and readable. The mini project is a console Grade Book for a Ralfiz Academy batch: grades, averages that skip absent marks, a topper, a grade chart and the first student who needs support.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

So far your programs have run top to bottom, one line after another. Real programs make decisions and repeat work. Control flow is the set of tools for that: branches (if this, do that; otherwise do something else) and loops (do this for every student, or keep trying until it works).

Think of a teacher marking a pile of answer sheets. For each sheet (a loop) they add up the marks, then decide the grade (a branch). If a sheet is blank they skip it (continue). If the bell rings they stop (break). Everything in this lesson is a precise way to write down those everyday instructions.

Why it matters

Every feature you will build is control flow wrapped around data: show a “Free delivery” badge when the cart is over ₹999, render one card per product, retry a payment up to three times, skip archived tasks, stop searching once you find a match. Choosing the right structure also decides how readable your code is. Deeply nested if blocks and loops that do five jobs are the most common reasons code reviews ask for a rewrite, and the most common source of off-by-one bugs.

How it works

if, else if and else

if (condition) runs its block when the condition is truthy. Remember the falsy values from lesson 1.2: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN. Everything else, including '0', [] and {}, is truthy. An else if ladder checks conditions in order and runs only the first one that matches, so put the most specific or highest band first. For grades, check 90 before 80; otherwise 95 would stop at the “80 or more” branch.

The conditional operator condition ? a : b is an expression: it produces a value. Use it for small either/or values inside a template literal or an assignment. Do not nest it several levels deep; an if ladder or a lookup object is easier to read.

Try it: if / else if: from marks to a grade

JavaScript

function gradeFor(marks) {
  // Guard clause: reject bad input first
  if (typeof marks !== 'number' || marks < 0 || marks > 100) {
    return 'Invalid';
  }
  // Order matters: check the highest band first
  if (marks >= 90) {
    return 'A+';
  } else if (marks >= 80) {
    return 'A';
  } else if (marks >= 70) {
    return 'B';
  } else if (marks >= 60) {
    return 'C';
  } else if (marks >= 50) {
    return 'D';
  } else {
    return 'F';
  }
}

for (const marks of [95, 80, 79.9, 64, 50, 12, 101]) {
  console.log(String(marks).padStart(5), '->', gradeFor(marks));
}

// Conditions use truthiness: '' 0 null undefined NaN are falsy
const note = '';
if (note) {
  console.log('Teacher note:', note);
} else {
  console.log('No teacher note');
}

// The conditional (ternary) operator for small either/or values
const attendance = 0.82;
const status = attendance >= 0.75 ? 'eligible' : 'not eligible';
console.log(`Attendance ${attendance * 100}% -> ${status} for the exam`);

Add 100, 39.5, -5 and '85' (a string) to the list. Which ones does the guard clause reject?

switch and lookup objects

switch (value) compares the value with each case using strict equality (===) and jumps to the first match. From there, execution continues downwards until it meets break or return. That is called fall-through. It is useful for grouping cases that share a body (case 'packed': case 'shipped':) and dangerous when you simply forget a break. default runs when nothing matches; put it last. Inside a function, return in each case is often cleaner than break.

When each case only maps a key to a value, a lookup object (or a Map) is shorter and can be loaded from data: const SHIPPING = { standard: 49, express: 99 }; then SHIPPING[method] ?? 49.

Try it: switch: strict matching, grouped cases and fall-through

JavaScript

function orderMessage(status) {
  switch (status) {
    case 'placed':
      return 'We have your order.';
    case 'packed':
    case 'shipped':          // grouped cases share one body
      return 'Your order is on its way.';
    case 'delivered':
      return 'Delivered. Enjoy!';
    default:
      return `Unknown status: ${status}`;
  }
}
for (const s of ['placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'lost']) {
  console.log(s.padEnd(10), orderMessage(s));
}

// Without return, you need break, or execution falls through
function perks(tier) {
  const list = [];
  switch (tier) {
    case 'gold':
      list.push('free delivery');
    case 'silver':           // intended fall-through: gold gets silver perks
      list.push('early sales');
      break;
    default:
      list.push('newsletter');
  }
  return list;
}
console.log(perks('gold'), perks('silver'), perks('bronze'));

// switch uses ===, so types must match
const fromUrl = '2';
switch (fromUrl) {
  case 2: console.log('number 2'); break;
  case '2': console.log('string "2"'); break;
}

// A lookup object is often cleaner than a long switch
const SHIPPING = { standard: 49, express: 99, pickup: 0 };
const method = 'express';
console.log(`Shipping: ₹${SHIPPING[method] ?? 49}`);

Delete the break after the silver case and run again: silver members fall through into the default newsletter too.

UseWhen
if / else ifRanges and different conditions (marks >= 90, isAdmin && isActive)
switchOne value against several exact cases, especially with grouped cases
Ternary ? :A single either/or value
Lookup object / MapPure key → value mapping, or data that may come from config

for, while and do…while

The classic for (init; condition; update) loop is best when you count: indexes, seat numbers, pages, a countdown. The let in the header creates a fresh binding for each iteration (lesson 2.2 shows why that matters for closures). The condition is checked before every iteration, so a loop may run zero times.

while (condition) repeats as long as the condition stays true. Use it when you do not know the number of iterations in advance: serving orders until stock runs out, or doubling savings until a goal is reached. Make sure something inside the loop changes the condition, or it will never end. do { … } while (condition) checks after the body, so the body always runs at least once, which fits “try once, then decide whether to try again”, such as an OTP attempt with a retry limit.

Try it: for, while and do…while

JavaScript

// for: when you know how many times (or need the index)
const seats = [];
for (let row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {
  for (let seat = 1; seat <= 4; seat++) {
    seats.push(`${String.fromCharCode(64 + row)}${seat}`);
  }
}
console.log(seats.join(' '));

// Counting down with a step
for (let i = 10; i > 0; i -= 3) {
  console.log('countdown', i);
}

// while: when you repeat until a condition changes
let stock = 7;
const orders = [3, 2, 4, 1];
let served = 0;
while (served < orders.length && stock >= orders[served]) {
  stock -= orders[served];
  served++;
}
console.log(`Served ${served} orders, ${stock} left in stock`);

// do…while: the body runs at least once
let attempt = 0;
let otpOk = false;
do {
  attempt++;
  otpOk = attempt === 2;          // pretend the 2nd try succeeds
  console.log(`OTP attempt ${attempt}: ${otpOk ? 'ok' : 'wrong'}`);
} while (!otpOk && attempt < 3);

// Doubling until a goal: how many months to reach 1 lakh?
let savings = 5000;
let months = 0;
while (savings < 100000) {
  savings *= 1.25;
  months++;
}
console.log(months, 'months, savings', Math.round(savings));

Change the stock to 0 in the while example: the loop body never runs, while do…while always runs once.

Watch out: an infinite loop freezes the page, because JavaScript runs on one thread and the browser cannot repaint or respond to clicks while your loop is busy. Always check that the loop variable moves towards the exit condition, and put a hard limit (like attempt < 3) on retries.

for…of versus for…in

for (const x of iterable) walks the values of anything iterable: arrays, strings (by code point, so emoji stay whole), Map, Set, the result of arr.entries() and more. It is the loop you will write most. Destructuring in the header gives you index and value together: for (const [i, item] of cart.entries()).

for (const key in object) walks the enumerable string keys of an object, including keys inherited through the prototype chain (lesson 4.1). On an array it gives '0', '1'… as strings, plus any extra properties someone added. So use for…in only for plain objects, and prefer Object.keys, Object.values or Object.entries with for…of, which list only the object’s own keys.

for…offor…in
Gives youValuesKeys (always strings)
Works onIterables: arrays, strings, Map, SetAny object
Inherited keysNot applicableIncluded if enumerable
Use it forArrays and collectionsPlain objects (or use Object.entries)

break, continue and guard clauses

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one: skip absent students, out-of-stock items or archived tasks. break leaves the loop at once: stop when you have found what you were looking for. break only exits the innermost loop; to stop an outer loop too, set a flag and check it, or move the search into a function and return (labels such as outer: exist but are rarely used). Both work in for, for…of, for…in, while and do…while, but not inside an array method callback such as forEach.

Try it: for…of vs for…in, break and continue

JavaScript

const cart = ['Chai mug', 'Coaster set', 'Tea caddy'];

// for…of gives VALUES of any iterable
for (const item of cart) console.log('of ->', item);

// entries() when you also need the index
for (const [i, item] of cart.entries()) console.log(`${i + 1}. ${item}`);

// for…in gives KEYS, as strings (avoid it for arrays)
for (const key in cart) console.log('in ->', key, typeof key);

// for…in is for plain objects; Object.entries is usually clearer
const prices = { mug: 299, coaster: 149, caddy: 899 };
for (const key in prices) console.log(key, prices[key]);
for (const [name, price] of Object.entries(prices)) {
  console.log(`${name}: ₹${price}`);
}

// for…of works on strings, Maps and Sets too
for (const ch of 'Hi👋') console.log(ch);
const stockBySku = new Map([['RZ-1', 4], ['RZ-2', 0], ['RZ-3', 9]]);

// continue skips one item, break stops the loop
for (const [sku, qty] of stockBySku) {
  if (qty === 0) {
    console.log(sku, 'out of stock, skipping');
    continue;
  }
  if (qty > 5) {
    console.log(sku, 'has plenty, stop checking');
    break;
  }
  console.log(sku, 'low stock:', qty);
}

Add Object.prototype.hacked = true at the top and run again: for…in picks up the inherited key.

A guard clause is an early return (or continue inside a loop) that handles an invalid or special case first. Compare these two versions of a refund check:

// Nested: the real rule is buried four levels deep
function canRefund(order) {
  if (order) {
    if (order.status === 'delivered') {
      if (order.daysSinceDelivery <= 7) {
        return order.total > 0;
      }
    }
  }
  return false;
}

// Guard clauses: each rule on its own line, happy path at the end
function canRefund(order) {
  if (!order) return false;
  if (order.status !== 'delivered') return false;
  if (order.daysSinceDelivery > 7) return false;
  return order.total > 0;
}

Example: Grade Book

The Ralfiz Academy Grade Book combines everything above. For each student (for…of) it averages the subject marks, skipping absent ones (continue) and returning null when there are none. A guard clause prints “Absent” and moves on. gradeFor uses guard clauses plus an ordered ladder. The loop also tracks the topper without sorting and counts grades in an object, which a for…in loop then prints as a small bar chart. Finally, nested loops find the first student with a subject below the pass mark, using break twice.

const counts = { 'A+': 0, A: 0, B: 0, C: 0, D: 0, F: 0 };
for (const s of students) {
  const avg = average(s.marks);
  if (avg === null) continue;               // guard
  const grade = gradeFor(avg);
  counts[grade]++;                          // count per grade
}
for (const grade in counts) {
  console.log(grade.padEnd(3), '#'.repeat(counts[grade]));
}

Run the full version and then change the data: make someone absent, give someone a 38, or add a new student.

Try it: Grade Book: the whole mini project

JavaScript

const students = [
  { name: 'Anu', marks: { maths: 92, science: 88, english: 95 } },
  { name: 'Bala', marks: { maths: 78, science: 65, english: 70 } },
  { name: 'Chitra', marks: { maths: 55, science: null, english: 61 } },
  { name: 'Dev', marks: { maths: 85, science: 91, english: 79 } },
  { name: 'Esha', marks: { maths: 40, science: 52, english: 38 } },
  { name: 'Gita', marks: { maths: null, science: null, english: null } },
];
const PASS_MARK = 40;

function gradeFor(score) {
  if (!Number.isFinite(score) || score < 0 || score > 100) return 'Invalid';
  if (score >= 90) return 'A+';
  if (score >= 80) return 'A';
  if (score >= 70) return 'B';
  if (score >= 60) return 'C';
  if (score >= 50) return 'D';
  return 'F';
}

function average(marks) {
  let total = 0;
  let count = 0;
  for (const mark of Object.values(marks)) {
    if (mark === null) continue;          // absent: skip it
    total += mark;
    count++;
  }
  return count === 0 ? null : total / count;
}

const counts = { 'A+': 0, A: 0, B: 0, C: 0, D: 0, F: 0 };
let topper = null;
console.log('Name'.padEnd(8) + 'Avg'.padStart(6) + '  Grade');
for (const s of students) {
  const avg = average(s.marks);
  if (avg === null) {                      // guard: nothing to grade
    console.log(s.name.padEnd(8) + 'Absent'.padStart(6));
    continue;
  }
  const grade = gradeFor(avg);
  counts[grade]++;
  if (topper === null || avg > topper.avg) topper = { name: s.name, avg };
  console.log(s.name.padEnd(8) + avg.toFixed(1).padStart(6) + '  ' + grade);
}

console.log(`Topper: ${topper.name} (${topper.avg.toFixed(1)})`);
for (const grade in counts) {
  console.log(grade.padEnd(3), '#'.repeat(counts[grade]), counts[grade]);
}

let needsSupport = null;
for (const s of students) {
  for (const [subject, mark] of Object.entries(s.marks)) {
    if (mark !== null && mark < PASS_MARK) {
      needsSupport = `${s.name} (${subject}: ${mark})`;
      break;
    }
  }
  if (needsSupport) break;               // stop the outer loop too
}
console.log('First student who needs support:', needsSupport ?? 'none');

Change a mark to null (absent) or below 40 and watch the average, the chart and the support list update.

The lab reads the same kind of data from students.json and adds a remark for each grade with a switch.

Common mistakes

  • Checking ranges in the wrong order. Wrong: if (m >= 50) 'D' else if (m >= 90) 'A+' gives D to everyone above 50. Fix: highest band first.
  • Forgetting break in a switch. Wrong: case 'gold': discount = 20; case 'silver': discount = 10; gives gold members 10. Fix: add break (or return), and comment any intended fall-through.
  • Using for…in on arrays. Wrong: for (const i in prices) total += prices[i] can pick up extra keys and gives string indexes. Fix: for (const price of prices) total += price;.
  • Off-by-one loops. Wrong: for (let i = 0; i <= items.length; i++) reads one past the end (undefined). Fix: i < items.length, or better, for…of.
  • Assignment instead of comparison. Wrong: if (status = 'paid') assigns and is always truthy. Fix: ===; ESLint’s no-cond-assign rule catches this.
  • Trying to break out of forEach. It is a syntax error there, and return only ends one callback. Fix: use for…of, or find/some (lesson 3.1).

Interview and real-world notes

  • “for…of vs for…in?” Values of iterables versus string keys of objects (including inherited enumerable ones). Mention Object.entries as the modern way to loop over an object.
  • “When would you use switch?” Many exact matches on one value, such as statuses or action types in a reducer. Mention strict matching and fall-through, and that a lookup object is often simpler.
  • FizzBuzz and its variants are loop-and-branch questions. Check the combined case (divisible by both) first, exactly like checking the highest grade band first.
  • Loops vs array methods: in lesson 3.1 you will replace many loops with map, filter and reduce. Plain loops remain the right choice when you need break, await inside the loop, or maximum clarity with several running totals.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const level = 2;
switch (level) {
  case 1:
    console.log('one');
  case 2:
    console.log('two');
  case 3:
    console.log('three');
    break;
  default:
    console.log('other');
}

three

const scores = [10, 20];
for (const k in scores) {
  console.log(typeof k);
}

1

let n = 5;
do {
  console.log(n);
  n++;
} while (n < 3);

  • D 
    1
2
3
4

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const input = '1';
switch (input) {
  case 1:
    console.log('number');
    break;
  case '1':
    console.log('string');
    break;
  default:
    console.log('none');
}
  • A number
  • B string
  • C 
    number
string
  • D none

Answers

  1. B. Execution starts at the matching case 2 and falls through into case 3 because there is no break, then stops at the break before default.
  2. D. for…in iterates property keys, and object keys are strings, even for array indexes. Use for…of for the values.
  3. A. The body of do…while runs once before the condition is checked. After that, 6 < 3 is false, so the loop ends.
  4. C. Even numbers are skipped by continue. At i = 5 the break runs before the log, so only 1 and 3 are printed.
  5. B. switch uses strict equality (===), so the string 1 does not match the number 1 but does match the string case.

terms.definition: An expression that is checked for truthiness to decide which branch runs, such as marks >= 40.
An early return at the top of a function that handles an invalid or special case, so the main logic is not nested.
A statement that compares one value against several case values with strict equality (===) and jumps to the first match.
In a switch, execution continues into the next case until it meets break or return.
A loop over the values of any iterable: arrays, strings, Maps, Sets and more.
A loop over the enumerable string keys of an object, including inherited ones. Not meant for arrays.
break leaves the loop (or switch) immediately; continue skips to the next iteration.

lessons.examTip: In code reviews, deeply nested if blocks are a red flag. Say you would invert the conditions into guard clauses so the happy path reads top to bottom.

quiz.question: A switch on the value '2' (a string) has case 2: and case '2':. Which one runs?
options: case 2:, because switch converts types like ==
Both of them
case '2':, because switch uses strict equality
Neither; switch only works with numbers
quiz.explanation: switch compares with ===, so the string only matches a string case. This is a common bug when values come from form inputs or URLs.

quiz.question: You want the values of an array, in order. Which loop fits best?
options: for…of
for…in
do…while
A switch inside a while(true)

quiz.question: What is special about do…while?
options: It can only count downwards
It checks its condition before the first run
It is faster than for
Its body always runs at least once, because the condition is checked after each run
quiz.explanation: do…while tests the condition at the end, so it suits cases like showing a menu or making a first attempt before deciding whether to repeat.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of guard clauses?

They handle invalid or special cases first and return early, so the main logic is not deeply nested
They replace all loops
They stop exceptions from being thrown
