lessons.title: Functions in depth
lessons.summaryHtml: Functions are the building blocks of every JavaScript program, and in JavaScript they are also values: you can store them, pass them and return them. You will compare the three ways to create one (declarations, expressions and arrow functions) and see how hoisting treats each. You will master parameters: missing and extra arguments, default values, the options object pattern, rest parameters and spread at the call site. You will learn what a function returns when you forget return, why pure functions are easier to test and reuse, and how to name and document functions with JSDoc so your editor can help. The mini project is a set of booking-quote functions for Ralfiz Stays, with a live quote page built on top.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A function is a named, reusable recipe. You give it ingredients (arguments), it follows its steps and it hands back a result (the return value). Writing calculateTotal(cart) once and calling it from the cart page, the checkout and the invoice email is how programs stay small and consistent.

JavaScript has a twist that many languages lack: functions are ordinary values. You can keep one in a variable, put it in an array, pass it to another function or return it from one. That idea powers event handlers, array methods such as map, and most modern frameworks. This lesson covers everything about writing a single function well; the next lessons cover scope, this and functions that work with other functions.

Why it matters

Most bugs hide in functions that do too much, change things they should not touch, or take five positional arguments that callers mix up. Well-designed functions have a clear name, a small number of well-named inputs, sensible defaults, one job and a predictable result. They are easy to test, easy to reuse and easy for the next developer (or you in six months) to understand. Interviewers also probe the details here: hoisting, arrow functions, default parameters and rest/spread appear in almost every JavaScript screening.

How it works

Declarations, expressions and arrow functions

A function declaration starts a statement with the function keyword and a name. A function expression creates a function inside an expression, usually assigned to a const. An arrow function is a compact expression: (a, b) => a + b. With one parameter the parentheses are optional (Prettier adds them by default); with no braces around the body, the expression is returned automatically. To return an object literal from a concise arrow, wrap it in parentheses, otherwise the braces are read as a function body.

Every function also has a name (inferred from the variable for anonymous expressions, which helps stack traces) and a length (the number of declared parameters before any default or rest). A function without a return, or with a bare return;, returns undefined.

Try it: Three ways to create a function

JavaScript

// 1. Function declaration
function subtotal(price, qty) {
  return price * qty;
}

// 2. Function expression (anonymous function stored in a const)
const withTax = function (amount, rate) {
  return Math.round(amount * (1 + rate));
};

// 3. Arrow function: short, implicit return without braces
const withTaxArrow = (amount, rate) => Math.round(amount * (1 + rate));
const double = (n) => n * 2;         // one parameter
const now = () => 'always the same'; // no parameters

console.log(subtotal(499, 3), withTax(1497, 0.18), withTaxArrow(1497, 0.18));
console.log(double(21), now());

// Functions are values: they have a type, a name and a length
console.log(typeof subtotal, subtotal.name, withTax.name, subtotal.length);

// ...and can be stored and passed like any value
const steps = [(n) => n + 100, double, (n) => n - 1];
let value = 50;
for (const step of steps) value = step(value);
console.log('after steps:', value);

// No return statement means the call returns undefined
function logOnly(msg) {
  console.log('LOG', msg);
}
console.log(logOnly('hi'));

// Returning an object from an arrow needs parentheses
const makeLine = (name, qty) => ({ name, qty });
console.log(makeLine('Chai mug', 2));

Rewrite the arrow version of withTax with curly braces. What do you have to add so it still returns a value?

DeclarationExpressionArrow
Hoisted with bodyYesNoNo
Own this and argumentsYesYesNo (uses the outer ones)
Can be used with newYesYesNo
Typical useTop-level helpers, main logicConditional or assigned functionsCallbacks, short utilities

A good default in modern code: declarations for named, top-level functions and arrows for callbacks and short helpers. Methods and this are the subject of lesson 2.3.

Hoisting: why declarations can be called early

Before running the code in a scope, the engine does a setup pass and registers every declaration it finds. Function declarations are created immediately, complete with their body, so you can call them above the line where they are written. That is handy for putting the main flow at the top of a file and the helpers below.

A const or let is registered too, but stays uninitialised until its line runs. Touching it earlier throws a ReferenceError; this gap is called the temporal dead zone (TDZ). An old-style var is initialised to undefined, so calling a function stored in a var too early throws a confusing TypeError: … is not a function. The example below ends with a deliberate TDZ error.

Try it: Hoisting: declarations versus expressions

JavaScript

// Function declarations are hoisted WITH their body
console.log(greet('Anu'));
function greet(name) {
  return `Welcome back, ${name}!`;
}

// A var holding a function expression is hoisted as undefined
try {
  legacyTotal(2, 3);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}
var legacyTotal = function (a, b) {
  return a + b;
};
console.log('after its line:', legacyTotal(2, 3));

// const/let are hoisted but uninitialised: the TDZ
console.log('About to call getRate before its line...');
console.log(getRate());

const getRate = () => 0.18;

This example throws on purpose. Move the call to getRate below the const line and it works.

Parameters, arguments and defaults

Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values passed in a call. JavaScript never complains about a mismatch: missing arguments become undefined and extra ones are ignored (though still visible through arguments in non-arrow functions). That flexibility is why defaults matter.

A default parameter (method = 'standard') is used when the argument is undefined, whether missing or passed explicitly. It is not used for null, 0 or ''. Defaults are evaluated at call time, left to right, so a later default can use an earlier parameter, and a default [] is a fresh array on every call.

Once a function needs more than about three inputs, or several optional flags, positional arguments become a trap: createOrder('Bala', items, true, false, '') is unreadable. The options object pattern takes one object and destructures it with defaults in the parameter list. Callers name what they pass, in any order, and you can add new options later without breaking anyone. The trailing = {} lets the function be called with no argument at all.

function createOrder({ customer, items = [], express = false } = {}) {
  // customer, items and express are ordinary local constants here
}
createOrder({ customer: 'Bala', express: true });   // self-explaining call

Try it: Parameters, defaults and the options object

JavaScript

// Missing arguments are undefined; extra ones are ignored
function describe(item, qty) {
  return `${item} x ${qty}`;
}
console.log(describe('Tea caddy'), '|', describe('Mug', 2, 'extra'));

// Defaults apply only when the value is undefined
function shipping(method = 'standard', fee = method === 'express' ? 99 : 49) {
  return `${method}: ₹${fee}`;   // a default can use earlier parameters
}
console.log(shipping(), '|', shipping('express'), '|', shipping(undefined, 0));
console.log(shipping(null));      // null is a value, so no default

// Defaults are evaluated on every call (a fresh array each time)
function addTag(tag, tags = []) {
  tags.push(tag);
  return tags;
}
console.log(addTag('new'), addTag('sale'));

// The options object pattern: one parameter, destructured with defaults
function createOrder({ customer, items = [], express = false, note = '' } = {}) {
  const fee = express ? 99 : 49;
  return { customer, count: items.length, fee, note: note || '(none)' };
}
console.log(createOrder({ customer: 'Bala', items: ['Mug', 'Coaster'] }));
console.log(createOrder({ express: true, customer: 'Chitra' }));
console.log(createOrder());       // works thanks to the = {} default

// Declared parameters vs arguments actually passed
function tally(a, b = 1, ...rest) {
  return `declared ${tally.length}, passed ${arguments.length}`;
}
console.log(tally(1, 2, 3, 4));

Call createOrder with only a customer name, then add express: true. Notice how readable the call sites are.

Rest parameters and spread

A rest parameter (...amounts) must come last and collects all remaining arguments into a real array, so you can loop over it or call array methods on it. It replaces the old arguments object, which is only array-like and does not exist in arrow functions.

Spread uses the same three dots at the other end: at a call site it expands an array (or any iterable, such as a string or a Set) into separate arguments, as in Math.max(...rates). Inside array literals it copies and merges arrays. The copy is shallow: the new array holds the same object references (lesson 3.2 goes deeper).

Try it: Rest parameters and spread arguments

JavaScript

// Rest: collect any number of arguments into a REAL array
function sumAll(...amounts) {
  let total = 0;
  for (const a of amounts) total += a;
  return total;
}
console.log(sumAll(), sumAll(450), sumAll(450, 1200, 900));

// Rest must be last, and can follow normal parameters
function invoiceLine(label, ...amounts) {
  return `${label}: ${amounts.length} charges, ₹${sumAll(...amounts)}`;
}
console.log(invoiceLine('Room 204', 3200, 3200, 450));

// Old style: the arguments object is array-LIKE, not an array
function oldSum() {
  console.log(Array.isArray(arguments), arguments.length);
  return Array.from(arguments).reduce((s, n) => s + n, 0);
}
console.log(oldSum(1, 2, 3));

// Spread: expand an array into separate arguments
const nightlyRates = [3200, 2800, 4100, 3600];
console.log(Math.max(...nightlyRates), Math.min(...nightlyRates));
console.log(sumAll(...nightlyRates, 500));

// Spread also copies and merges arrays (shallow copy)
const weekend = [4100, 3600];
const allRates = [...nightlyRates, ...weekend];
console.log(allRates.length, allRates === nightlyRates);

// Arrow functions have no arguments object of their own
const arrow = () => typeof arguments;
console.log(arrow());

Call sumAll with no arguments, then with a spread of an empty array. Both should return 0.

Remember: in a parameter list, ...x gathers (rest). In a call or an array literal, ...x spreads. Same syntax, opposite directions.

Pure and impure functions

A pure function has two properties: its result depends only on its arguments, and it has no side effects (it does not change its inputs, globals, the DOM, storage or the network, and it does not log). Give it the same input and you always get the same output. Pure functions are trivial to test, safe to call from anywhere, easy to cache and easy to reason about.

Programs still need side effects: saving data, showing things on screen, sending requests. The professional structure is a pure core and an impure shell: calculations live in pure functions, and a thin outer layer reads input, calls the core and performs the effects. Return new arrays and objects (with spread or copy methods such as toSorted) instead of mutating what you were given.

Try it: Pure versus impure functions

JavaScript

// IMPURE: reads and changes outside state
let cart = [];
let discountRate = 0.1;
function addToCartImpure(item) {
  cart.push(item);                                   // mutates shared state
  console.log('added', item.name);                   // side effect: I/O
  return cart.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0) * (1 - discountRate);
}
console.log(addToCartImpure({ name: 'Mug', price: 300 }));
discountRate = 0.5;                                  // someone changes a global
console.log(addToCartImpure({ name: 'Mug', price: 300 }));

// PURE: everything it needs comes in, a new value goes out
const addItem = (items, item) => [...items, item];
const cartTotal = (items, rate = 0) =>
  Math.round(items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0) * (1 - rate));

const empty = [];
const one = addItem(empty, { name: 'Mug', price: 300 });
const two = addItem(one, { name: 'Coaster', price: 150 });
console.log(empty.length, one.length, two.length);   // nothing was changed
console.log(cartTotal(two, 0.1), cartTotal(two, 0.1)); // same input, same output

// A tiny test is trivial for pure functions
const check = (label, actual, expected) =>
  console.log(actual === expected ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL', label, actual);
check('empty cart', cartTotal([]), 0);
check('10% off', cartTotal(two, 0.1), 405);

Call addToCartImpure a second time and look at the shared cart. Then do the same with the pure version.

Naming and JSDoc

Name functions with verbs that say what they return or do: calculateTotal, formatPrice, fetchProducts, isEligible or hasStock for booleans. Keep each function to one job; if the name needs “and”, split it. Document public functions with JSDoc. VS Code reads these comments and shows parameter hints and types on hover, and TypeScript can even type-check plain JavaScript that uses them (lesson 7.3).

/**
 * Price a stay, including weekend uplift and add-ons.
 * @param {object} options
 * @param {string} options.checkIn  ISO date, e.g. '2026-10-09'
 * @param {string} options.checkOut ISO date after checkIn
 * @param {number} [options.guests=2]
 * @returns {{ nights: number, total: number }} amounts in rupees
 */
function quote({ checkIn, checkOut, guests = 2 } = {}) { /* ... */ }

Example: Ralfiz Stays booking quote

The booking page for a Ralfiz Stays suite needs a price that updates as the guest changes dates, guests, add-ons and coupon. The design follows the lesson:

  • nightsBetween and countWeekendNights are function declarations that work in UTC, so time zones cannot shift a night.
  • sumAll(...amounts) uses a rest parameter, and quote spreads the add-on prices into it.
  • applyCoupon(amount, code = '') uses a default and a switch, and never returns a negative price.
  • quote(options) takes an options object with destructured defaults, is documented with JSDoc and returns a brand-new object. It is pure.
  • render() is the only impure function: it reads the form, calls quote and writes the lines with textContent.

Try it: Ralfiz Stays: live booking quote

HTML

JavaScript

const RATE = 3200;
const WEEKEND_UPLIFT = 0.2;      // Friday and Saturday nights
const EXTRA_GUEST_FEE = 800;     // per night, above 2 guests
const DAY_MS = 86_400_000;
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});

// ---------- pure core: inputs in, values out ----------
const toUtc = (iso) => Date.parse(`${iso}T00:00:00Z`);

function nightsBetween(checkIn, checkOut) {
  const nights = (toUtc(checkOut) - toUtc(checkIn)) / DAY_MS;
  return Number.isFinite(nights) && nights > 0 ? nights : 0;
}

function countWeekendNights(checkIn, nights) {
  let count = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < nights; i++) {
    const day = new Date(toUtc(checkIn) + i * DAY_MS).getUTCDay();
    if (day === 5 || day === 6) count++;
  }
  return count;
}

const sumAll = (...amounts) => amounts.reduce((s, a) => s + a, 0);

function applyCoupon(amount, code = '') {
  switch (code.trim().toUpperCase()) {
    case 'RALFIZ10': return Math.round(amount * 0.9);
    case 'STAY500': return Math.max(0, amount - 500);
    default: return amount;
  }
}

/**
 * Build a price quote. Pure: it never changes its input.
 * @param {{checkIn: string, checkOut: string, guests?: number,
 *   addOns?: number[], coupon?: string}} options
 * @returns {{nights: number, lines: Array<[string, number]>, total: number}}
 */
function quote({ checkIn, checkOut, guests = 2, addOns = [], coupon = '' } = {}) {
  const nights = nightsBetween(checkIn, checkOut);
  const weekend = countWeekendNights(checkIn, nights);
  const room = nights * RATE + Math.round(weekend * RATE * WEEKEND_UPLIFT);
  const extra = Math.max(0, guests - 2) * EXTRA_GUEST_FEE * nights;
  const before = sumAll(room, extra, ...addOns);
  const total = applyCoupon(before, coupon);
  const lines = [
    [`Room · ${nights} night${nights === 1 ? '' : 's'}`, nights * RATE],
    [`Weekend nights · ${weekend}`, Math.round(weekend * RATE * WEEKEND_UPLIFT)],
    ['Extra guests', extra],
    ['Add-ons', sumAll(...addOns)],
    ['Coupon', total - before],
  ].filter(([, amount]) => amount !== 0);
  return { nights, lines, total };
}

// ---------- impure shell: read the page, render the result ----------
const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(2, '0');
function isoInDays(days) {                  // local calendar date, n days ahead
  const d = new Date();
  d.setDate(d.getDate() + days);
  return `${d.getFullYear()}-${pad(d.getMonth() + 1)}-${pad(d.getDate())}`;
}
const untilFriday = ((5 - new Date().getDay() + 7) % 7) || 7;
$('checkIn').value = isoInDays(untilFriday);       // next Friday
$('checkOut').value = isoInDays(untilFriday + 3);  // Monday

function render() {
  const options = {
    checkIn: $('checkIn').value,
    checkOut: $('checkOut').value,
    guests: Number($('guests').value),
    addOns: [...document.querySelectorAll('fieldset input:checked')].map((c) => Number(c.value)),
    coupon: $('coupon').value,
  };
  const q = quote(options);
  const items = q.nights === 0 ? [] : [...q.lines, ['Total', q.total]];
  $('lines').replaceChildren(...items.map(([label, amount], i) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    const name = document.createElement('span');
    const value = document.createElement('span');
    name.textContent = label;
    value.textContent = (amount < 0 ? '−' : '') + inr.format(Math.abs(amount));
    if (i === items.length - 1) li.className = 'total';
    else if (amount < 0) li.className = 'save';
    li.append(name, value);
    return li;
  }));
  $('msg').className = q.nights === 0 ? 'msg error' : 'msg';
  $('msg').textContent = q.nights === 0
    ? 'Check-out must be after check-in.'
    : 'Taxes shown at checkout. Free cancellation up to 48 hours before check-in.';
}

$('form').addEventListener('input', render);
render();
console.log(quote({ checkIn: '2026-10-09', checkOut: '2026-10-12', addOns: [1200] }));

Change the dates, add guests and try the coupons RALFIZ10 and STAY500. The maths lives in pure functions; only render() touches the page.

The lab builds the same core in Node, prints two quotes, and proves purity by calling quote twice and comparing the input before and after.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting return in a braced arrow. Wrong: const total = (a, b) => { a + b; }; returns undefined. Fix: (a, b) => a + b or add return.
  • Returning an object literal without parentheses. Wrong: () => { id: 1 }. Fix: () => ({ id: 1 }).
  • Expecting defaults for null. Wrong: relying on limit = 10 when an API sends null. Fix: const size = limit ?? 10; inside the function.
  • Long positional parameter lists. Wrong: book('2026-10-09', '2026-10-12', 2, true, false, 'STAY500'). Fix: an options object with named properties.
  • Mutating arguments. Wrong: function addItem(cart, item) { cart.push(item); return cart; } changes the caller’s array. Fix: return [...cart, item];.
  • Calling an arrow before its const line. It throws a ReferenceError (TDZ). Fix: define it first, or use a function declaration for helpers you want to place below the main code.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Declaration vs expression vs arrow?” Cover hoisting, this/arguments, new, and when you use each.
  • “What is a pure function and why care?” Same input, same output, no side effects; mention testing, caching (memoisation, lesson 7.4) and React’s expectation that components render purely.
  • “Rest vs spread?” Gather in parameters, expand at call sites and in literals; arguments is legacy and array-like.
  • Function length ignores parameters from the first default or rest onwards, a favourite trick question.
  • In real projects, keep functions short, return early with guard clauses, prefer options objects for public APIs, and let ESLint flag unused parameters and missing returns.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

console.log(greet());

function greet() {
  return 'hi';
}
  • A undefined
  • B ReferenceError
  • C hi
  • D TypeError

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const pick = (size = 'M') => size;
console.log(pick(undefined), pick(null), pick(0));
  • A M null 0
  • B M M M
  • C M M 0
  • D undefined null 0

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const makeTotal = () => { total: 5 };
console.log(makeTotal());
  • A { total: 5 }
  • B 5
  • C SyntaxError
  • D undefined

Snippet 4. What is logged?

function book(room, nights = 1, ...extras) {}
console.log(book.length);
  • A 3
  • B 1
  • C 2
  • D 0

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const count = (...items) => items.length;
console.log(count(...[1, 2], 3, ...'ab'));
  • A 3
  • B 4
  • C 5
  • D 2

Answers

  1. C. Function declarations are hoisted together with their body, so greet can be called before the line where it is written.
  2. A. Defaults apply only to undefined, whether missing or passed explicitly. null and 0 are real values, so they are returned as they are.
  3. D. The braces are read as a function body, and total: is a statement label, so nothing is returned. Wrap an object literal in parentheses: () => ({ total: 5 }).
  4. B. length counts the parameters before the first one with a default value or a rest parameter, so only room is counted.
  5. C. Spread expands the array into 1 and 2 and the string into a and b. With the 3 in the middle, the rest parameter collects five arguments.

terms.definition: A statement such as function total(a, b) { … }. It is hoisted with its body, so it can be called before its line.
A function created inside an expression, usually assigned to a variable: const total = function (a, b) { … };
A shorter function expression, (a, b) => a + b, with no own this, arguments or prototype. It cannot be called with new.
A value used when the argument is missing or undefined: function greet(name = 'guest').
The last parameter written as ...items, which collects the remaining arguments into a real array.
A function whose result depends only on its inputs and which has no side effects, so the same input always gives the same output.
A comment format (/** … */ with @param and @returns) that documents a function and gives editors type hints.

lessons.examTip: When a function needs more than three inputs, or several optional ones, take a single options object with destructured defaults. Call sites become self-explaining and you can add options later without breaking anyone.

quiz.question: Which statement about arrow functions is true?
options: They are hoisted like function declarations
They have their own arguments object
They do not have their own this or arguments, and cannot be used with new
They always need curly braces and a return statement
quiz.explanation: Arrows take this and arguments from the surrounding scope and have no prototype, so new throws. A body without braces returns its expression automatically.

quiz.question: function ship(method = 'standard') { … } is called as ship(null). What is method?
options: null, because defaults only apply to undefined
'standard', because null is missing
undefined
It throws a TypeError
quiz.explanation: A default is used only when the argument is undefined (missing or passed as undefined). null is a real value, so it is kept. Use ?? inside the function if null should also fall back.

quiz.question: Which function is pure?
options: One that adds an item to a global cart array
One that returns the total of the items passed in, without changing them
One that logs the total to the console
One that returns Date.now() plus a delay
quiz.explanation: A pure function depends only on its arguments and has no side effects. Mutating globals, logging and reading the clock are all side effects or hidden inputs.

quiz.question: Why can you call a function declaration on a line above where it is written?
options: JavaScript reads files from the bottom up
The engine creates function declarations with their bodies when it sets up the scope, before running the code
Only in strict mode
Because declarations are stored in localStorage
quiz.explanation: Before any code in a scope runs, the engine registers its declarations. Function declarations are initialised with their full body; let and const bindings stay uninitialised (the TDZ) until their line runs.

lessons.title: Scope, hoisting and closures
lessons.summaryHtml:
Scope decides where a name can be used. JavaScript has global, module, function and block scope, and it is lexical: where you write a function in the source fixes which variables it can see, not where you call it.

Hoisting is what happens before a scope runs: the engine creates every binding first. var starts as undefined, function declarations are ready to call, and let/const exist but stay uninitialised until their line runs. That gap is the temporal dead zone.

A closure is a function together with the scope it was created in. Because the inner function keeps a reference to that environment, it can read and update variables long after the outer function returned. Closures give you private state, counters, once(), ID generators and most of the callbacks you will write, and they explain the classic loop bug with var.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Every variable lives somewhere. Scope is the answer to the question “from which lines of code can I use this name?”. Think of an office building: people in a cabin can see into the corridor, and people in the corridor can see the lobby, but the lobby cannot see inside the cabins. Inner code sees outward; outer code never sees inward.

Hoisting is the engine’s preparation step. Before a scope runs, the engine walks through it and creates a slot for every declared name. What goes into that slot at first depends on the keyword, which is why some variables read as undefined, some throw an error, and some functions can be called before the line that defines them.

A closure is what you get when a function is created inside another scope and then used somewhere else. The function carries a reference to the environment it came from, like a backpack it never takes off. Whenever it runs, it can open the backpack and use (or change) the variables inside.

Why it matters

Almost every bug report that says “the value is wrong, but I set it!” is a scope problem: a shadowed name, a variable read before it was set, or a callback that sees a later value than you expected. Understanding scope lets you read those bugs in seconds.

Closures are also everywhere in real code. Event handlers remember which product card they belong to. A debounce helper remembers its timer. React hooks, Express middleware, the module pattern, memoisation caches and rate limiters are all closures. In interviews, “what is a closure?” and the var loop question appear in nearly every junior front-end round.

How it works

When JavaScript runs code, it creates an environment record for each scope: a table of names and their current values. Each environment has a link to its outer environment. Looking up a name means checking the current table, then following the outer link, and so on up to the global environment. That chain of links is the scope chain. If the name is not found anywhere, you get ReferenceError: x is not defined.

Global, module, function and block scope

ScopeCreated byWhat lives there
GlobalA classic scriptTop-level let/const/class (shared by all classic scripts) and var/function declarations (which also become properties of globalThis)
ModuleEach ES module fileTop-level names of that file only; nothing leaks to globalThis
FunctionEvery function callParameters, var, and everything declared in the body
BlockAny { }: if, for, plain blockslet, const, class. Not var: it ignores blocks

Scope is lexical (also called static): it is decided by where you write a function, not where you call it. In the example below, show() is called from inside run(), which has its own label, yet it prints the outer one, because show was written at the top level.

Try it: Global, function and block scope

JavaScript

const shopName = 'Ralfiz Store';          // global (script) scope

function checkout(items) {
  const tax = 0.18;                         // function scope
  let total = 0;
  for (const item of items) {
    const line = item.price * item.qty;     // block scope: new each loop
    total += line;
  }
  // console.log(line);  // ReferenceError: line is not defined here
  return `${shopName}: ${(total * (1 + tax)).toFixed(2)}`;
}

console.log(checkout([{ price: 100, qty: 2 }, { price: 50, qty: 1 }]));
console.log('tax outside?', typeof tax);   // typeof is safe for undeclared names

// Shadowing: the inner name hides the outer one inside the block
const discount = 5;
{
  const discount = 20;
  console.log('inside block:', discount);
}
console.log('outside block:', discount);

// Lexical scope: where a function is WRITTEN decides what it sees
const label = 'outer';
function show() { return label; }
function run() {
  const label = 'inner';
  return show();          // show() still sees the outer label
}
console.log('lexical:', run());

Uncomment console.log(line) to see the ReferenceError. Then change const line to var and run again: the block no longer contains it.

The shadowing example also shows why you should avoid reusing names. An inner discount hides the outer one for the whole block. Linters flag this with the no-shadow rule because it is an easy way to read the wrong value.

Hoisting and the temporal dead zone

Before a scope’s first line runs, the engine creates all of its bindings. The keyword decides the starting state:

DeclarationScopeBefore its line
var xFunctionundefined
let x / const xBlockUninitialised: reading throws ReferenceError (TDZ)
function f() {}Function (block in strict code)Fully ready to call
class C {}BlockUninitialised (TDZ), like let
const f = () => {}BlockTDZ: the function does not exist until the line runs

“Hoisting” is a metaphor: nothing is physically moved to the top. It is simply that the bindings exist from the start of the scope. The temporal dead zone is temporal because it is about time, not position: the zone lasts from entering the scope until the declaration executes. Even typeof, which is normally safe on unknown names, throws inside the TDZ.

Try it: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone

JavaScript

// 1. var is hoisted and initialised to undefined
console.log('before var:', stock);
var stock = 12;
console.log('after var:', stock);

// 2. function declarations are hoisted whole
console.log(formatPrice(499));
function formatPrice(n) {
  return `₹${n}`;
}

// 3. let/const are hoisted but uninitialised: the TDZ
try {
  console.log(city);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}
let city = 'Kochi';
console.log('after let:', city);

// 4. function EXPRESSIONS follow their variable's rules
try {
  greet('Asha');
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}
const greet = (name) => `Hello ${name}`;
console.log(greet('Asha'));

// 5. typeof is not safe in the TDZ either
try {
  console.log(typeof secret);
  const secret = 42;
} catch (err) {
  console.log('typeof in TDZ ->', err.name);
}

Each try block shows what exists before its declaration line runs.

Why did the language designers add the TDZ? With var, reading a variable too early silently gave undefined and the bug surfaced much later. The TDZ turns that mistake into an immediate, clearly named error. It also makes const meaningful: a constant that could be observed as undefined and later as a value would not really be constant.

Closures: functions that remember

Normally, when a function returns, its local variables are no longer needed and the garbage collector can free them. But if an inner function that references those variables is still reachable (you returned it, stored it, or registered it as an event listener), the environment must stay alive. That surviving environment is the closure.

function makeCounter(start = 0) {
  let count = start;          // stored in makeCounter's environment
  return {
    increment: () => ++count, // all three functions point to
    decrement: () => --count, // the SAME environment
    value: () => count,
  };
}
const tickets = makeCounter(10); // environment #1: count = 10
const refunds = makeCounter();   // environment #2: count = 0

Picture memory after these two calls. There are two separate environment objects, each holding its own count. The three arrow functions in tickets all point to environment #1, so an increment is visible to value. refunds points to environment #2 and never sees those changes. Nothing else in the program has a reference to either environment, so count is truly private: tickets.count is simply undefined.

Try it: Closures remember by reference

JavaScript

function makeCounter(start = 0) {
  let count = start;            // lives in makeCounter's environment
  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    decrement: () => --count,
    value: () => count,
  };
}

const tickets = makeCounter(10);
const refunds = makeCounter();

tickets.increment();
tickets.increment();
refunds.increment();
console.log('tickets:', tickets.value(), 'refunds:', refunds.value());

// The three methods share ONE environment, so they see each other's changes
tickets.decrement();
console.log('after decrement:', tickets.value());

// count is private: there is no property to read or overwrite
console.log('tickets.count ->', tickets.count);

// Closures see the variable, not a snapshot of its value
function makeGreeter() {
  let name = 'guest';
  const greet = () => `Hi ${name}`;
  const setName = (n) => { name = n; };
  return { greet, setName };
}
const g = makeGreeter();
console.log(g.greet());
g.setName('Meera');
console.log(g.greet());   // sees the updated binding

Two counters from one factory: separate environments, shared by the functions inside each one.

Remember: a closure captures the variable (the binding), not its value at creation time. The greeter example proves it: after setName('Meera'), the old greet function prints the new name.

Useful closure patterns: once, ID generators and private state

Closures let a function keep a little memory between calls without a global variable. once(fn) keeps a called flag and the first result, which is perfect for “send the welcome email only once” or “initialise the analytics SDK only once”. An ID generator keeps a private next number so every invoice gets a unique, ordered ID and nobody can reset it by accident.

Try it: once(), ID generators and the loop bug

JavaScript

// once(): run a function the first time only
function once(fn) {
  let called = false;
  let result;
  return (...args) => {
    if (!called) {
      called = true;
      result = fn(...args);
    }
    return result;
  };
}
const sendWelcome = once((email) => {
  console.log('Sending welcome email to', email);
  return 'sent';
});
sendWelcome('asha@ralfiz.dev');
sendWelcome('asha@ralfiz.dev');
console.log('third call returns:', sendWelcome('someone@else.dev'));

// An ID generator: private, ever-increasing state
function makeIdGenerator(prefix) {
  let next = 1;
  return () => `${prefix}-${String(next++).padStart(4, '0')}`;
}
const invoiceId = makeIdGenerator('INV');
console.log(invoiceId(), invoiceId(), invoiceId());

// The classic loop bug: one shared var i
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('var loop:', i), 0);
}
// let makes a fresh binding for every iteration
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('let loop:', j), 0);
}

Watch the var loop print 3 three times, then the let loop print 0, 1, 2.

The same snippet ends with the most famous closure puzzle. A for loop with var i has a single i for the whole function. The three timer callbacks all close over that one binding and run after the loop has finished, so they print 3 three times. With let, the specification creates a fresh binding for each iteration and copies the current value into it, so each callback sees its own j. Before let existed, developers fixed this with an IIFE (an immediately invoked function) that took i as a parameter, and you will still meet that pattern in older code.

Closures in the browser

Each stepper in this basket is made by createStepper(product, onChange). Its qty lives only in that call’s environment; the plus and minus click handlers and the returned quantity() and subtotal() functions all share it. The coupon button uses once(), so the discount is applied a single time however often it is clicked, while a separate counter closure counts the clicks.

Try it: Basket steppers with private state

HTML

JavaScript

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN',
  { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0 });

const products = [
  { name: 'Notebook', emoji: '📓', price: 120, stock: 5 },
  { name: 'Gel pens (pack of 5)', emoji: '🖊️', price: 90, stock: 3 },
  { name: 'Laptop backpack', emoji: '🎒', price: 1499, stock: 2 },
];

// Each stepper keeps its own qty in a closure. Nothing else can touch it.
function createStepper(product, onChange) {
  let qty = 0;
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'item';
  li.innerHTML = '<span class="pic"></span><div class="info"><strong></strong>' +
    '<span class="muted"></span></div><div class="step">' +
    '<button aria-label="Remove one">−</button><output>0</output>' +
    '<button aria-label="Add one">+</button></div>';
  li.querySelector('.pic').textContent = product.emoji;   // data goes in as text
  li.querySelector('strong').textContent = product.name;
  li.querySelector('.muted').textContent = inr.format(product.price);
  const [minus, plus] = li.querySelectorAll('button');
  const out = li.querySelector('output');

  function set(next) {
    qty = Math.min(Math.max(next, 0), product.stock);
    out.textContent = qty;
    minus.disabled = qty === 0;
    plus.disabled = qty === product.stock;
    onChange();
  }
  minus.addEventListener('click', () => set(qty - 1));
  plus.addEventListener('click', () => set(qty + 1));

  return { el: li, add: () => set(qty + 1),
    quantity: () => qty, subtotal: () => qty * product.price };
}

function once(fn) {
  let called = false;
  let result;
  return (...args) => {
    if (!called) { called = true; result = fn(...args); }
    return result;
  };
}

function makeCounter() {
  let n = 0;
  return () => ++n;
}

let discount = 0;
const steppers = [];
const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);

function update() {
  const items = steppers.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.quantity(), 0);
  const gross = steppers.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.subtotal(), 0);
  const off = Math.round(gross * discount);
  $('count').textContent = `${items} item${items === 1 ? '' : 's'}`;
  $('total').textContent = inr.format(gross - off);
  $('save').textContent = off ? `You save ${inr.format(off)}` : '';
}

for (const p of products) {
  const stepper = createStepper(p, update);
  steppers.push(stepper);
  $('items').append(stepper.el);
}

const applyCoupon = once(() => {
  discount = 0.1;
  console.log('Coupon applied (this runs only once)');
});
const countClicks = makeCounter();

$('coupon').addEventListener('click', () => {
  applyCoupon();
  update();
  $('note').textContent =
    `WELCOME10 applied once · button clicked ${countClicks()} time(s)`;
});

steppers[0].add();
steppers[0].add();
steppers[1].add();
console.log('Can outside code see the qty variable?', 'qty' in steppers[0]);
console.log('Basket items:', steppers.map((s) => s.quantity()));

Notice how the card is built: a fixed HTML template, then the product data is inserted with textContent. Data should never be placed into innerHTML, even when it looks harmless today, because tomorrow it may come from an API or a user.

Memory implications

A closure keeps its environment alive for as long as the function is reachable. That is the point, but it can also retain more than you meant. In V8 (Chrome and Node), all closures created in the same scope share one context object, so a large array used by one inner function stays in memory while any of the functions from that scope is still referenced. Typical leaks are event listeners or timers that are never removed and hold closures over big data or DOM nodes.

function attachReport(button, rows) {   // rows: 50,000 objects
  const summary = `${rows.length} rows`;
  // Only summary is needed, but if the handler used rows, all 50,000
  // objects would live as long as the listener does.
  const onClick = () => console.log(summary);
  button.addEventListener('click', onClick);
  return () => button.removeEventListener('click', onClick); // cleanup
}

Good habits: copy only what you need into the closure, return a cleanup function, and remove listeners with an AbortController signal when a component goes away. You will measure leaks with DevTools heap snapshots in js30.

Example: Ticket Desk utilities

The lab builds a small toolbox that a help-desk or billing app would really use. Each tool is a factory that returns functions sharing private state.

function makeIdGenerator(prefix, start = 1) {
  let next = start;
  return () => `${prefix}-${String(next++).padStart(4, '0')}`;
}

function makeRateLimiter(limit) {
  let used = 0;
  return () => {
    if (used >= limit) return false;   // guard clause
    used += 1;
    return true;
  };
}

const nextInvoice = makeIdGenerator('INV');
const nextReceipt = makeIdGenerator('REC', 100);
console.log(nextInvoice(), nextInvoice()); // INV-0001 INV-0002
console.log(nextReceipt());                // REC-0100

const allowOtp = makeRateLimiter(3);
console.log([1, 2, 3, 4].map(() => allowOtp())); // [ true, true, true, false ]
  1. Each factory call creates a new environment, so nextInvoice and nextReceipt count independently.
  2. The state (next, used) cannot be changed from outside, which is exactly what you want for IDs and limits.
  3. The reminders task fixes a var loop so each reminder keeps its own hour.

Common mistakes

1. Using var in a loop with callbacks. All callbacks share one variable.

// Wrong: logs 3, 3, 3
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));
// Fix: let gives each iteration its own binding
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));

2. Reading a let before its declaration. Often hidden by shadowing: an inner let total makes every earlier line in that block refer to the inner, uninitialised one.

// Wrong: ReferenceError, the inner total is in the TDZ
let total = 0;
function add(n) { total = total + n; let total = 1; }
// Fix: use a different name, and declare before use
function add(n) { total = total + n; }

3. Accidental globals. Assigning to an undeclared name in sloppy mode creates a global property. Modules and strict mode throw instead, which is one more reason to use them.

// Wrong (sloppy script): creates globalThis.count
function reset() { count = 0; }
// Fix: declare it where it belongs
let count = 0;
function reset() { count = 0; }

4. Expecting a closure to freeze a value. It sees later changes. If you need the value at a moment in time, copy it into a new const inside the function.

// Wrong: the log shows the price at click time, not creation time
let price = 100;
const logPrice = () => console.log(price);
// Fix: capture a snapshot
const snapshot = price;
const logOriginal = () => console.log(snapshot);

Interview and real-world notes

  • Define it crisply: “A closure is a function bundled with references to the variables in the scope where it was created. It lets the function use those variables after that scope has finished.”
  • Every function in JavaScript is a closure technically; the term matters when the function outlives its outer scope.
  • Explain hoisting with states, not movement: “all bindings are created on entry; var is undefined, let/const/class are in the TDZ, function declarations are initialised.”
  • Private state today: closures were the original way to get privacy. Classes now also have #private fields (js17); both are valid, and closures remain the simplest choice for small factories.
  • Real-world: debounce and throttle helpers (js30), memoisation caches, React’s useState and useEffect, and middleware chains are all closures. When a React effect shows an old value, it is a “stale closure”: the function captured an older render’s variables.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

console.log(a);
var a = 5;
function hi() {
  return 'hi';
}
console.log(hi());
  • A 
    5
hi
  • B ReferenceError
  • C 
    undefined
hi
  • D 
    undefined
undefined

Snippet 2. What is logged after the timers fire?

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
}
  • A 
    0
1
2
  • B 
    3
3
3
  • C 
    2
2
2

0

Snippet 3. What is logged?

function makeCounter() {
  let n = 0;
  return () => ++n;
}
const a = makeCounter();
const b = makeCounter();
a();
a();
console.log(a(), b());
  • A 3 3
  • B 1 1
  • C 2 1
  • D 3 1

Snippet 4. What is logged?

let price = 100;
function checkout() {
  try {
    console.log(price);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(err.name);
  }
  let price = 80;
  return price;
}
console.log(checkout());
  • A 
    ReferenceError

  • B

Answers

  1. C. var a is hoisted and initialised to undefined, so the first log prints undefined. The function declaration is hoisted whole, so hi() works.
  2. B. With var there is one i for the whole loop. The callbacks run after the loop finished, when i is 3.
  3. D. Each call to makeCounter creates a new n. a was called twice before, so the third call returns 3; b is fresh and returns 1.
  4. A. The inner let price shadows the outer one for the whole function body, so reading it before its line is in the TDZ and throws a ReferenceError. The function then returns 80.

quiz.question: What does a closure keep hold of?
options: A copy of the outer variables’ values at the moment the function was created
A live reference to the environment where the function was created, so it sees later changes
Only the global variables
Nothing: variables are always destroyed when the outer function returns
quiz.explanation: Closures capture the environment (the bindings), not a snapshot of the values. If the outer variable changes, the closure sees the new value.

quiz.question: Why does reading a let variable before its declaration line throw, while a var variable gives undefined?
options: let is not hoisted at all
var is block scoped
Both are hoisted, but let stays uninitialised (the temporal dead zone) until its declaration runs, while var is initialised to undefined
The engine reads let variables from the global object
quiz.explanation: Every declaration is hoisted. The difference is initialisation: var gets undefined at once; let and const stay in the TDZ until their line runs.

quiz.question: A for loop with var i creates three setTimeout callbacks that log i. Why do they all log 3?
options: setTimeout copies the value when the loop ends
Arrow functions cannot see loop variables
The loop runs three times too many
There is one function-scoped i shared by all callbacks, and by the time they run the loop has set it to 3
quiz.explanation: var creates a single binding for the whole function. let creates a fresh binding per iteration, so each callback closes over its own value.

quiz.question: Which is the best reason to use a closure-based factory like makeCounter() instead of a global variable?
options: The state is private, so only the returned functions can change it, and each call to the factory gets its own independent state
It runs faster in every engine
It lets you use var safely
It stops the garbage collector from running
quiz.explanation: Closures give encapsulation: no other code can reach the variable, and each factory call creates a separate environment.

lessons.title: this, call, apply and bind
lessons.summaryHtml:
this is a hidden parameter that every regular function receives. Unlike other variables, its value is not fixed where the function is written: it is decided each time the function is called, by how it is called.

Four rules cover almost every case: a plain call gets undefined in strict code (or globalThis in sloppy scripts); a call like cart.total() gets the object before the dot; call, apply and bind set it explicitly; and new creates a fresh object for it. Arrow functions are the exception: they have no this of their own and use the one from the surrounding code.

Knowing these rules fixes the most common bug in object-oriented JavaScript: passing obj.method as a callback and losing this. You fix it with bind, an arrow wrapper or an arrow class field.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In everyday speech, “this” means “the thing I am pointing at right now”. JavaScript’s this works the same way: it is the object a function is working on for this particular call. The same function can be pointed at different objects on different calls.

That is the key difference from ordinary variables. A variable’s meaning is fixed by where you write it (lexical scope, from js9). this is fixed by how you call the function. Think of a cashier’s script: “Please pay the total on this bill.” The script is written once, and “this bill” changes with every customer who walks up.

Why it matters

Objects and classes use this to reach their own data: this.items, this.total, this.user. The moment you hand one of those methods to someone else (a click listener, setTimeout, array.map, a promise’s then), the caller changes, and so does this. The result is the famous error Cannot read properties of undefined, which beginners often “fix” with random rewrites. Once you know the rules, you can predict this for any line of code, and you will understand code in React class components, Node event emitters, Express and older jQuery projects.

How it works

Every call to a regular (non-arrow) function creates a new execution context with a this value. The engine picks it by looking at the call site, the exact expression that invoked the function. Four rules, checked from strongest to weakest, decide the value.

The four binding rules

RuleCall site looks likethis is
1. new bindingnew Invoice('INV-1')A brand-new object linked to Invoice.prototype
2. Explicit bindingfn.call(obj), fn.apply(obj), fn.bind(obj)()obj
3. Implicit bindingcart.total()The object before the dot: cart
4. Default bindingtotal()undefined in strict code; globalThis in sloppy code

Priority runs from top to bottom: new beats a bound function, a bound function beats the dot, and the dot beats a plain call. Arrow functions are outside the table entirely; they are covered below.

Try it: The four binding rules

JavaScript

function whoAmI() {
  'use strict';
  return this;
}
const invoice = { id: 'INV-7', whoAmI };

// 1. Default binding: a plain call. Strict code gets undefined.
console.log('1 default :', whoAmI());

// 2. Implicit binding: the object before the dot
console.log('2 implicit:', invoice.whoAmI().id);

// 3. Explicit binding: call / apply / bind choose this
console.log('3 explicit:', whoAmI.call({ id: 'INV-9' }).id);

// 4. new binding: this is a brand-new object
function Invoice(id, amount) {
  this.id = id;
  this.amount = amount;
}
console.log('4 new     :', new Invoice('INV-12', 2500));

// Priority: new > bind/call > implicit > default
const bound = whoAmI.bind({ id: 'BOUND' });
const holder = { id: 'HOLDER', bound };
console.log('bind beats the dot:', holder.bound().id);

function Tag(label) { this.label = label; }
const BoundTag = Tag.bind({ label: 'ignored' });
console.log('new beats bind:', new BoundTag('fresh'));

// Sloppy (non-strict) code swaps undefined for the global object
function sloppy() { return this === globalThis; }
console.log('sloppy plain call gets globalThis:', sloppy());

Same function, four ways to call it, four different values of this.

Implicit binding looks only at the last dot. In order.customer.greet(), this is order.customer, not order. And only the call itself counts: (cart.total)() still has the dot, but const t = cart.total; t() does not.

The method extraction bug

A method is just a function stored in a property. It has no permanent link to its object. When you read cart.total without calling it, you get the bare function. Whoever calls it later decides this.

Try it: The method extraction bug

JavaScript

const cart = {
  owner: 'Asha',
  items: [
    { name: 'Notebook', price: 120, qty: 2 },
    { name: 'Pen', price: 30, qty: 3 },
  ],
  total() {
    return this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  },
  summary() {
    return `${this.owner} owes ₹${this.total()}`;
  },
};
console.log('method call:', cart.summary());

// The bug: take the method off the object, and the dot is gone
const getTotal = cart.total;
try {
  console.log(getTotal());
} catch (err) {
  console.log('extracted :', err.message);
}

// Same bug when you pass a method as a callback
function runLater(fn) {
  return fn();          // called plainly: no object before the dot
}
try {
  console.log(runLater(cart.summary));
} catch (err) {
  console.log('callback  :', err.message);
}

// Fix 1: bind creates a function with this fixed to cart
console.log('fix bind  :', runLater(cart.summary.bind(cart)));

// Fix 2: an arrow wrapper keeps the dot inside it
console.log('fix arrow :', runLater(() => cart.summary()));

Passing cart.total on its own loses cart. Try each fix.

Both failures are the same bug: runLater calls fn() plainly, so the default rule applies. The playground runs a classic (sloppy) script, so this became the global object, which has no items. Inside a class or a module the code is strict, this is undefined, and you get “Cannot read properties of undefined”. Either way, the two fixes are the same:

  • bind returns a new function whose this is locked to the object. Good when you pass the same handler many times, or need to remove the listener later (keep the bound reference).
  • An arrow wrapper, () => cart.summary(), keeps the call site with its dot inside the arrow. It is short, readable and lets you pass extra arguments.

Arrow functions and lexical this

Arrow functions do not get their own this. Inside an arrow, this is looked up like any other variable, in the surrounding scope. That makes arrows perfect for callbacks inside methods, and a bad choice as methods.

Try it: Arrow functions and this

JavaScript

const timer = {
  label: 'Checkout timer',
  startRegular() {
    setTimeout(function () {
      // a regular callback: setTimeout decides this (not timer)
      console.log('regular callback sees timer?', this === timer);
    }, 0);
  },
  startArrow() {
    setTimeout(() => {
      // an arrow uses startArrow's this, which is timer
      console.log('arrow callback label:', this.label);
    }, 0);
  },
};
timer.startRegular();
timer.startArrow();

// Arrows make poor object methods: they ignore the dot
const product = {
  name: 'Pen',
  isMeArrow: () => this === product,
  isMeRegular() { return this === product; },
};
console.log('arrow method:', product.isMeArrow(),
  '| regular method:', product.isMeRegular());

// call/bind cannot change an arrow's this
const arrow = () => this;
const target = { id: 1 };
console.log('arrow.call(target) === target ?', arrow.call(target) === target);

// Class fields with arrows: this is fixed per instance
class Counter {
  count = 0;
  inc = () => ++this.count;               // own property, bound
  dec() { return --this.count; }           // on the prototype, not bound
}
const { inc, dec } = new Counter();
console.log('inc():', inc(), inc());
try {
  dec();
} catch (err) {
  console.log('dec():', err.message);
}

Arrows borrow this from the method around them, which is perfect for callbacks and wrong for object methods.

Regular functionArrow function
Own thisYes, chosen by the call siteNo, uses the outer scope’s
call/apply/bind change thisYesNo (arguments still pass through)
Can be used with newYes (declarations and expressions)No, throws TypeError
Best forObject and class methods, constructorsCallbacks: map, timers, promise handlers, listeners inside classes

The class example shows a common professional pattern. inc = () => ++this.count is a class field holding an arrow function. Fields are created in the constructor, where this is the new instance, so the arrow captures that instance forever. You can destructure it or pass it to a listener safely. The trade-off: each instance gets its own copy of the function, instead of sharing one on the prototype. For a handful of UI objects that does not matter; for 100,000 objects it would.

call, apply and bind

All three let you choose this yourself. They differ in when the function runs and how you pass arguments:

MethodRuns now?ArgumentsReturns
fn.call(obj, a, b)YesOne by oneThe function’s result
fn.apply(obj, [a, b])YesOne arrayThe function’s result
fn.bind(obj, a)NoOptional first ones, fixedA new bound function

Try it: call, apply and bind in practice

JavaScript

function priceTag(currency, locale) {
  const money = new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: 'currency', currency });
  return `${this.name}: ${money.format(this.price)}`;
}
const pen = { name: 'Pen', price: 30 };

// call: this, then arguments one by one
console.log(priceTag.call(pen, 'INR', 'en-IN'));

// apply: this, then ONE array of arguments
console.log(priceTag.apply(pen, ['AED', 'en-AE']));

// bind: returns a new function for later, with this and args fixed
const mugInCanada = priceTag.bind({ name: 'Mug', price: 12.5 }, 'CAD', 'en-CA');
console.log(mugInCanada());

// Partial application with bind: fix the first argument only
function withTax(rate, amount) {
  return Math.round(amount * (1 + rate));
}
const withGst = withTax.bind(null, 0.18);   // this is not used: pass null
console.log('₹1000 with GST:', withGst(1000));

// apply before spread existed; spread is clearer today
const prices = [499, 1299, 89];
console.log('max (apply) :', Math.max.apply(null, prices));
console.log('max (spread):', Math.max(...prices));

// Borrowing a method for an array-like object
const arrayLike = { 0: 'a', 1: 'b', 2: 'c', length: 3 };
console.log(Array.prototype.map.call(arrayLike, (s) => s.toUpperCase()));

Formatting prices for different countries by choosing this and the arguments.

A memory aid: apply takes an array, call takes commas. Since ES2015, spread syntax (Math.max(...prices)) replaced most uses of apply. bind is still everywhere, including for partial application: withTax.bind(null, 0.18) fixes the first argument and returns a GST calculator. You will build more of these in js11. Two rules to remember: binding a bound function again cannot change its this, and calling a bound function with new ignores the bound this (the new object wins).

this in the browser: event handlers and classes

When the browser calls a listener added with addEventListener, it sets this to the element the listener is attached to (the same as event.currentTarget). That is handy in small scripts, but inside a class you usually want this to be the class instance. The stopwatch shows the three standard ways to get that: this.toggle.bind(this) in the constructor, an arrow class field (lap), and an inline arrow wrapper for reset.

Try it: Stopwatch class with bound handlers

HTML

<main class="watch">
  <p class="eyebrow">Ralfiz Tools</p>
  <h1>Stopwatch</h1>
  <output class="time" id="time">00:00.00</output>
  <div class="row">
    <button class="primary" id="toggle">Start</button>
    <button id="lap" disabled>Lap</button>
    <button id="reset">Reset</button>
  </div>
  <ol class="laps" id="laps"></ol>
  <button class="link" id="who">Which this does a regular handler get?</button>
</main>

CSS

JavaScript

class Stopwatch {
  elapsed = 0;
  startedAt = 0;
  intervalId = null;
  laps = [];

  constructor(root) {
    this.display = root.querySelector('#time');
    this.toggleBtn = root.querySelector('#toggle');
    this.lapBtn = root.querySelector('#lap');
    this.list = root.querySelector('#laps');
    // Methods on the prototype lose this when passed as callbacks: bind once.
    this.tick = this.tick.bind(this);
    this.toggleBtn.addEventListener('click', this.toggle.bind(this));
    // An arrow class field (below) is already bound, so pass it directly.
    this.lapBtn.addEventListener('click', this.lap);
    root.querySelector('#reset').addEventListener('click', () => this.reset());
  }

  now() {
    return this.elapsed + (this.intervalId ? performance.now() - this.startedAt : 0);
  }

  toggle() {
    if (this.intervalId) {
      this.elapsed = this.now();
      clearInterval(this.intervalId);
      this.intervalId = null;
    } else {
      this.startedAt = performance.now();
      this.intervalId = setInterval(this.tick, 31);   // tick is bound
    }
    const running = Boolean(this.intervalId);
    this.toggleBtn.textContent = running ? 'Stop' : 'Start';
    this.toggleBtn.classList.toggle('running', running);
    this.lapBtn.disabled = !running;
    this.tick();
  }

  tick() {
    this.display.textContent = Stopwatch.format(this.now());
  }

  lap = () => {
    const total = this.now();
    const prev = this.laps.at(-1) ?? 0;
    this.laps.push(total);
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    const name = document.createElement('span');
    const split = document.createElement('span');
    name.textContent = `Lap ${this.laps.length} · ${Stopwatch.format(total)}`;
    split.textContent = `+${Stopwatch.format(total - prev)}`;
    li.append(name, split);
    this.list.prepend(li);
  };

  reset() {
    if (this.intervalId) this.toggle();
    this.elapsed = 0;
    this.laps = [];
    this.list.replaceChildren();
    this.tick();
  }

  static format(ms) {
    const cs = Math.floor(ms / 10) % 100;
    const s = Math.floor(ms / 1000) % 60;
    const m = Math.floor(ms / 60000);
    const pad = (n) => String(n).padStart(2, '0');
    return `${pad(m)}:${pad(s)}.${pad(cs)}`;
  }
}

const watch = new Stopwatch(document.querySelector('.watch'));

// A regular function handler: the browser sets this to the element.
document.querySelector('#who').addEventListener('click', function () {
  console.log('regular handler: this is the', this.tagName, 'with id', this.id);
});
// An arrow handler would keep the outer this instead.
document.querySelector('#who').addEventListener('click', () => {
  console.log('arrow handler: this is still the outer this, window?', this === globalThis);
});

// Demo run: start, record two laps, stop.
watch.toggle();
setTimeout(watch.lap, 400);
setTimeout(watch.lap, 900);
setTimeout(() => {
  watch.toggle();
  document.querySelector('#who').click();
}, 1200);

The demo clicks the link button at the end. The regular handler logs the BUTTON; the arrow handler logs whatever this was at the top of the script. Notice also that setInterval(this.tick, 31) only works because tick was bound in the constructor. Without that line, the timer would call tick with the global object as this, and the display would never update.

Watch out: removeEventListener needs the same function reference. el.removeEventListener('click', this.toggle.bind(this)) does nothing, because bind creates a new function each time. Store the bound function once, or use an AbortController signal to remove listeners (dm5).

globalThis and strict mode

The global object has different names in different places: window (and self) in browsers, global in Node. globalThis is the standard name that works everywhere. The value of this at the top level, outside any function, also depends on where code runs:

WhereTop-level this
Classic browser scriptwindow (the global object)
ES module (browser or Node)undefined
Node CommonJS filemodule.exports (an empty object at first)
A regular setTimeout callbackwindow in browsers; a Timeout object in Node

Strict mode changes the default rule. In sloppy code, a plain call with no this silently gets the global object, so a lost this writes to global variables instead of failing. Strict mode leaves this as undefined, so the bug throws immediately. Modules and class bodies are always strict; in a classic script you opt in with 'use strict'; at the top of the file or function. Prefer modules and classes, and the safer behaviour comes for free.

Example: fixing the Booking Desk

The lab gives you a BookingDesk class for a venue booking app. It works when you call methods directly, but breaks whenever a method is handed to someone else. A small safely() helper catches each failure and prints a BUG line so the script keeps running.

class BookingDesk {
  constructor(venue) {
    this.venue = venue;
    this.bookings = [];
  }
  describeAll() {
    // Bug: a regular callback gets its own this (undefined in a class)
    // return this.bookings.map(function (b) { return b.name + this.venue; });
    // Fix: the arrow uses describeAll's this
    return this.bookings.map((b) => `${b.name} x${b.seats} at ${this.venue}`);
  }
  remind() {
    console.log(`Reminder: ${this.bookings.length} bookings at ${this.venue}`);
  }
}
const desk = new BookingDesk('Ralfiz Hall A');
// Bug: setTimeout(desk.remind, 10) loses desk
setTimeout(() => desk.remind(), 10);         // fix with an arrow
const seats = desk.seatsTaken.bind(desk);   // or with bind
  1. Run the starter and read each BUG line: every message mentions undefined, the signature of a lost this.
  2. Find the call site for each one: a callback inside map, a method stored in a variable, a method passed to setTimeout.
  3. Pick the fix that reads best: an arrow for inline callbacks, bind for a reference you keep, call to borrow a method once.

Common mistakes

1. An arrow function as an object method. It ignores the dot, so this is the outer scope.

// Wrong: this is not the account
const account = { balance: 500, show: () => this.balance };
// Fix: method shorthand gets implicit binding
const account = { balance: 500, show() { return this.balance; } };

2. A regular function callback inside a method.

// Wrong: the inner function has its own this
total() { return this.items.reduce(function (s, i) { return s + i.price * this.rate; }, 0); }
// Fix: an arrow shares the method's this
total() { return this.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * this.rate, 0); }

3. Passing a method directly as a listener or timer.

// Wrong: the browser calls save with this = the button
button.addEventListener('click', form.save);
// Fix: wrap it, or bind it once and keep the reference
button.addEventListener('click', () => form.save());

4. Binding inside a loop or render and then trying to remove it.

// Wrong: two different bound functions, so nothing is removed
el.addEventListener('click', this.open.bind(this));
el.removeEventListener('click', this.open.bind(this));
// Fix: bind once in the constructor
this.open = this.open.bind(this);

Interview and real-world notes

  • Answer with the rules in order: “Is it an arrow? Use the outer this. Called with new? The new object. call/apply/bind? That object. A dot? The object before it. Otherwise undefined in strict mode, the global object in sloppy mode.”
  • Classic question: “What is the difference between call, apply and bind?” Call and apply run now (commas vs array); bind returns a new function for later.
  • Implement bind: a common exercise. function myBind(fn, ctx, ...a) { return (...b) => fn.apply(ctx, [...a, ...b]); } covers the core idea (the real one also handles new).
  • Modern code uses fewer this tricks: React function components and hooks avoid this entirely, and many teams prefer closures and plain functions. You still need these rules for classes, Web Components (dm23), event emitters and older codebases.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const shop = {
  name: 'Ralfiz Store',
  getName() {
    return this.name;
  },
};
const getName = shop.getName;
console.log(shop.getName());
console.log(getName.call({ name: 'Ralfiz Academy' }));
  • A 
    Ralfiz Store
undefined
  • B 
    Ralfiz Store
Ralfiz Store
  • C 
    Ralfiz Store
Ralfiz Academy
  • D 
    undefined
Ralfiz Academy

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const team = {
  lead: 'Asha',
  members: ['Ravi', 'Meera'],
  list() {
    return this.members.map((m) => `${m} reports to ${this.lead}`);
  },
};
console.log(team.list()[1]);
  • A Meera reports to undefined
  • B Meera reports to Asha
  • C TypeError
  • D Ravi reports to Asha

Snippet 3. What is logged?

function label() {
  return this.code;
}
const a = label.bind({ code: 'A' });
const b = a.bind({ code: 'B' });
console.log(b(), a.call({ code: 'C' }));
  • A A A
  • B B C
  • C B A
  • D A C

Snippet 4. What is logged? (classic script, not a module)

function strictCall() {
  'use strict';
  return this === undefined;
}
function looseCall() {
  return this === globalThis;
}
console.log(strictCall(), looseCall());
  • A false true
  • B true false
  • C false false
  • D true true

Answers

  1. C. shop.getName() binds this to shop. The extracted function is then called with call(), which sets this explicitly to the other object.
  2. B. The arrow callback inside map has no own this, so it uses list()’s this, which is team. Index 1 is Meera.
  3. A. A bound function’s this is permanent: binding it again or calling it with call() cannot change it.
  4. D. In strict code a plain call gets undefined. In sloppy code, undefined is replaced by the global object.

terms.definition: A value every regular function call receives implicitly; it depends on how the function is called, not where it is defined.
Calling a function as obj.method() sets this to obj, the object before the dot.
Choosing this yourself with fn.call(thisArg, ...args), fn.apply(thisArg, argsArray) or fn.bind(thisArg).
A new function returned by bind whose this (and optionally first arguments) are fixed permanently.
Arrow functions have no own this; they use the this of the scope they were written in.
The standard name for the global object in every environment: window in browsers, global in Node.
A stricter set of rules (automatic in modules and classes) in which a plain function call gets this as undefined instead of the global object.

lessons.examTip: When a callback says “Cannot read properties of undefined”, check whether you passed obj.method without its object. The quick fix is () => obj.method().
