lessons.title: Higher-order functions and functional patterns
lessons.summaryHtml:
In JavaScript, functions are values: you can store them in variables and objects, pass them to other functions and return them. A higher-order function is one that takes a function as an argument (a callback) or returns a function. map, filter, addEventListener and setTimeout are all higher-order functions.

Returning functions, together with closures, gives you partial application and currying: make a specialised function such as gst18 from a general one such as makeTax. Composition (pipe and compose) chains small functions into a pipeline, like an invoice going through subtotal, coupon, tax and rounding.

These patterns work best with pure functions and immutable data: functions that return new arrays and objects instead of changing shared ones. That avoids a whole family of bugs where one part of the app silently changes data another part is using. You will build Tip and Bill Splitter utilities in this style.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A higher-order function is a function that works with other functions: it takes one as an input, returns one as an output, or both. You already use them. cart.map(item => item.price) hands map a small function and says “do this to every item”. button.addEventListener('click', save) hands the browser a function and says “call this later”.

A kitchen analogy: a head chef does not cook every dish. They hand recipes (functions) to cooks (other functions) and say “apply this to every order”. Some recipes even produce new recipes: “give me a spice level and I will write you a curry recipe with that level”. That is a function returning a function.

Functional patterns add two habits: keep functions pure (same input, same output, no side effects) and treat data as immutable (make a new array instead of changing the old one). Together they make code easy to test, reuse and reason about.

Why it matters

Real applications repeat the same shapes: apply a discount, add tax, round, format as INR; filter a list, sort it, show the top five. Higher-order functions let you write each small step once and combine them in different orders, instead of copying loops everywhere. Frameworks are built on these ideas: React components are functions of state, Redux reducers must be pure and immutable, Express middleware is a chain of callbacks, and array methods replace most hand-written loops. Shared mutable state is one of the most common causes of “it changed by itself” bugs in front-end apps, and immutability is the standard cure.

How it works

Functions in JavaScript are first-class: they are objects like any other value, so anything you can do with a number or an array, you can do with a function. Combined with closures (js9), this gives three building blocks: callbacks (pass behaviour in), factories (return configured behaviour) and composition (connect behaviours together).

Functions as values and callbacks

The checkout function below does not know which discount rule it will run. It just calls the callback it receives. This is called the strategy pattern: you swap behaviour by passing a different function, without editing checkout.

Try it: Functions as values and callbacks

JavaScript

// 1. Functions are values: store them in an object
const discounts = {
  none: (total) => total,
  flat100: (total) => Math.max(total - 100, 0),
  festive15: (total) => total * 0.85,
};

// 2. Pass one in as a callback: checkout does not care which
function checkout(total, applyDiscount) {
  return Math.round(applyDiscount(total));
}
for (const [name, fn] of Object.entries(discounts)) {
  console.log(name.padEnd(10), checkout(1200, fn));
}

// 3. Write your own higher-order function
function times(n, makeItem) {
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out.push(makeItem(i));
  return out;
}
console.log(times(3, (i) => `Seat A${i + 1}`));

// 4. Array methods are higher-order functions you already use
const orders = [
  { id: 101, total: 450, paid: true },
  { id: 102, total: 1200, paid: false },
  { id: 103, total: 300, paid: false },
];
const isUnpaid = (o) => !o.paid;          // named callbacks read well
const toTotal = (o) => o.total;
const sum = (a, b) => a + b;
console.log('unpaid:', orders.filter(isUnpaid).map(toTotal).reduce(sum, 0));

// 5. Wrap a function to add behaviour (a "decorator")
function withLogging(fn) {
  return (...args) => {
    const result = fn(...args);
    console.log(`${fn.name}(${args.join(', ')}) -> ${result}`);
    return result;
  };
}
function lineTotal(price, qty) { return price * qty; }
const loggedLineTotal = withLogging(lineTotal);
loggedLineTotal(250, 4);

Swap the discount strategy passed to checkout without changing checkout itself.

Look at the unpaid-orders line: orders.filter(isUnpaid).map(toTotal).reduce(sum, 0). Giving callbacks names turns the chain into a sentence. The last example, withLogging, is a decorator: it takes a function and returns a new function that does the same job plus something extra (logging here; caching, timing or retrying in real apps). Notice it uses rest parameters and spread so it works for functions with any number of arguments.

Functions that return functions

When a function returns another function, the inner one closes over the outer arguments. makeTax(0.18) returns a function that remembers rate = 0.18. Each call to makeTax makes an independent, specialised function.

Try it: Functions that return functions

JavaScript

// A function factory: the returned function closes over rate
const makeTax = (rate) => (amount) => Math.round(amount * rate);
const gst18 = makeTax(0.18);
const gst5 = makeTax(0.05);
console.log('GST on ₹1000:', gst18(1000), 'vs', gst5(1000));

// Partial application: fix the first arguments now, the rest later
function formatMoney(locale, currency, amount) {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: 'currency', currency })
    .format(amount);
}
const partial = (fn, ...preset) => (...rest) => fn(...preset, ...rest);
const inr = partial(formatMoney, 'en-IN', 'INR');
const cad = partial(formatMoney, 'en-CA', 'CAD');
console.log(inr(125000), '|', cad(89.9));

// Currying: collect arguments until there are enough (fn.length)
const curry = (fn) => {
  const curried = (...args) =>
    args.length >= fn.length
      ? fn(...args)
      : (...more) => curried(...args, ...more);
  return curried;
};
const linePrice = (qty, unit, discount) => qty * unit * (1 - discount);
const price = curry(linePrice);
console.log(price(2)(500)(0.1), price(2, 500)(0), price(2, 500, 0.5));

// Real use: configurable callbacks for sort and filter
const byField = (field) => (a, b) => a[field] - b[field];
const above = (min) => (item) => item.price > min;
const products = [
  { name: 'Mouse', price: 699 },
  { name: 'Keyboard', price: 1499 },
  { name: 'Cable', price: 199 },
];
console.log(products.toSorted(byField('price')).map((p) => p.name));
console.log(products.filter(above(500)).map((p) => p.name));

makeTax, partial and curry all build specialised functions from general ones.

Two related techniques build on this:

TechniqueShapeExampleUse it when
Partial applicationFix some arguments now, pass the rest later in one goinr = partial(formatMoney, 'en-IN', 'INR')The same settings repeat on every call
CurryingOne argument per call: f(a)(b)(c)addPercent(10)(amount)You want to build callbacks for map, filter or pipe
bind (js10)Partial application that also fixes thiswithTax.bind(null, 0.18)Working with existing functions

The generic curry helper relies on fn.length, the number of declared parameters (parameters with defaults and rest parameters do not count). In day-to-day code, hand-written curried arrows like byField('price') and above(500) are more common than a generic curry, because they read clearly and fit straight into toSorted and filter.

Composition with pipe and compose

If every step takes one value and returns one value, you can chain steps. pipe(f, g, h)(x) means h(g(f(x))): data flows left to right, the way you read. compose is the same idea right to left, matching the mathematical notation. Both are one line of reduce.

Try it: An invoice pipeline with pipe and compose

JavaScript

const pipe = (...fns) => (input) => fns.reduce((value, fn) => fn(value), input);
const compose = (...fns) => (input) =>
  fns.reduceRight((value, fn) => fn(value), input);

// Small, pure steps: each takes one value and returns one value
const subtotal = (items) => items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
const applyCoupon = (pct) => (amount) => amount * (1 - pct / 100);
const addGst = (amount) => amount * 1.18;
const roundRupees = (amount) => Math.round(amount);
const tap = (label) => (value) => {
  console.log(`  ${label}:`, value);   // look inside the pipeline
  return value;
};

const invoiceTotal = pipe(
  subtotal, tap('subtotal'),
  applyCoupon(10), tap('after 10% coupon'),
  addGst, tap('with 18% GST'),
  roundRupees,
);

const cart = [
  { name: 'Course: JavaScript', price: 2999, qty: 1 },
  { name: 'Workbook', price: 450, qty: 2 },
];
console.log('Invoice total: ₹' + invoiceTotal(cart));

// compose reads right to left, like maths: f(g(h(x)))
const slugify = compose(
  (s) => s.replaceAll(/\s+/g, '-'),
  (s) => s.toLowerCase(),
  (s) => s.trim(),
);
console.log(slugify('  Ralfiz Winter   Sale '));

tap() logs the value between steps without changing it. Reorder the steps and compare.

This is why curried helpers matter: applyCoupon(10) returns a one-argument function, so it slots straight into a pipeline. The tap helper is a debugging trick worth remembering: it logs the value flowing through and returns it unchanged. Because every step is small and pure, you can test each one with a single line, reorder them (does the coupon apply before or after GST?) and reuse them in other pipelines. The long decimal after the GST step is floating-point arithmetic at work (js6); rounding once, as the final step, keeps the error out of the result, and the lab goes further by working in whole paise. A proposal for a native pipe operator (|>) exists at TC39, but it is not part of the language yet, so libraries and helpers like this one fill the gap.

Immutability and shared mutable state

Arrays and objects are passed by reference: a function receives a pointer to the caller’s data, not a copy. If the function changes it, every other part of the program holding that pointer sees the change. That is shared mutable state, and it is why a “read-only” helper that calls sort can reorder a cart on screen.

Try it: Immutability versus shared mutable state

JavaScript

// The bug: a helper that mutates the array it was given
function cheapestFirstBad(items) {
  return items.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price);   // sorts IN PLACE
}
const cart = [
  { name: 'Bag', price: 1499 },
  { name: 'Pen', price: 30 },
  { name: 'Ink', price: 90 },
];
const shown = cheapestFirstBad(cart);
console.log('cart after "read-only" helper:', cart.map((i) => i.name));
console.log('same array?', shown === cart);

// The fix: return new data and leave the input alone
const basket = [
  { name: 'Bag', price: 1499 },
  { name: 'Pen', price: 30 },
  { name: 'Ink', price: 90 },
];
const cheapestFirst = (items) => items.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
console.log('sorted:', cheapestFirst(basket).map((i) => i.name),
  '| original:', basket.map((i) => i.name));

// Immutable updates: add, change and remove without mutation
const addItem = (items, item) => [...items, item];
const setPrice = (items, name, price) =>
  items.map((i) => (i.name === name ? { ...i, price } : i));
const removeItem = (items, name) => items.filter((i) => i.name !== name);

const v1 = basket;
const v2 = addItem(v1, { name: 'Diary', price: 220 });
const v3 = setPrice(v2, 'Pen', 25);
const v4 = removeItem(v3, 'Ink');
console.log('v1 prices:', v1.map((i) => i.price));
console.log('v4 prices:', v4.map((i) => i.price));
console.log('unchanged Bag object reused?', v1[0] === v4[0]);

// Object.freeze is shallow
const settings = Object.freeze({ currency: 'INR', tips: [5, 10] });
settings.currency = 'USD';     // ignored (throws in strict mode)
settings.tips.push(15);        // the inner array is NOT frozen
console.log(settings);

The first helper changes the caller’s cart. The immutable versions return new data and reuse unchanged items.

Mutating (changes the original)Non-mutating (returns new data)
push, pop, shift, unshift[...items, x], items.slice(1), items.slice(0, -1)
sort, reverse, splicetoSorted, toReversed, toSpliced (ES2023)
items[i] = xitems.with(i, x)
obj.price = 25{ ...obj, price: 25 }
delete obj.couponconst { coupon, ...rest } = obj

Immutable updates are cheaper than they sound, because of structural sharing: setPrice creates a new array and a new Pen object, but the Bag object is reused (v1[0] === v4[0] is true). Only the changed path is copied. Spread copies are shallow; when you really need a full independent copy of nested data, use structuredClone (js13). Object.freeze can guard against accidental writes, but it is shallow too, as the last line shows.

Remember: a pure function has no side effects and returns the same result for the same input. Keep your calculation code pure, and do the impure parts (DOM updates, network, storage, logging) at the edges. That split is called “pure core, impure shell” (js27).

Putting it together in a UI

The bill splitter below is a small version of the lab. All the maths lives in pure, curried helpers: pipe(toPaise, addPercent(tip)) computes the total, splitEvenly(people) divides it into whole paise, and roundUpTo(1000) is mapped over the shares when rounding is on. The UI state is a single object that is replaced, never mutated: state = { ...state, ...patch }, followed by render(state). You will see this same “update state, then render” loop in dm10 and in every modern framework.

Try it: Tip and bill splitter

HTML

<main class="split">
  <header>
    <p class="eyebrow">Ralfiz Tools</p>
    <h1>Split the bill</h1>
  </header>
  <label class="field">
    <span>Bill amount (₹)</span>
    <input id="bill" type="number" min="0" step="1" inputmode="decimal" value="2450">
  </label>
  <div class="field">
    <span id="tipLabel">Tip</span>
    <div class="chips" id="tips" role="group" aria-labelledby="tipLabel"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="row">
    <div class="field">
      <span>People</span>
      <div class="step">
        <button id="less" aria-label="One person fewer">−</button>
        <output id="people">3</output>
        <button id="more" aria-label="One person more">+</button>
      </div>
    </div>
    <label class="toggle"><input id="round" type="checkbox"> Round each share up to ₹10</label>
  </div>
  <section class="result" aria-live="polite">
    <p class="muted">Each person pays</p>
    <p class="big" id="each">₹0</p>
    <p class="muted" id="detail"></p>
    <dl id="lines"></dl>
  </section>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #b45309; --ink: #1f2937; --muted: #6b7280;
  --line: #e5e7eb; --bg: #f6f7fb; }
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; background: var(--bg); color: var(--ink);
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif; }
.split { max-width: 460px; margin: 0 auto; background: #fff; display: grid; gap: 14px;

  box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgba(17, 24, 39, .06); }

  border-radius: 10px; overflow: hidden; width: max-content; }
.step button { width: 38px; height: 38px; border: 0; background: #fff; font-size: 18px;
  cursor: pointer; color: var(--ink); }

  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

  font-size: 14px; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

JavaScript

// ---- Pure, reusable helpers (money in integer paise) ----
const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x);
const toPaise = (rupees) => Math.round(rupees * 100);
const addPercent = (pct) => (paise) => Math.round(paise * (1 + pct / 100));
const roundUpTo = (step) => (paise) => Math.ceil(paise / step) * step;
const splitEvenly = (people) => (total) => {
  const base = Math.floor(total / people);
  const leftover = total - base * people;           // spare paise
  return Array.from({ length: people }, (_, i) => base + (i < leftover ? 1 : 0));
};
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const money = (paise) => inr.format(paise / 100);

// calculate(state) is pure: same state in, same numbers out
function calculate({ bill, tip, people, roundUp }) {
  const total = pipe(toPaise, addPercent(tip))(bill);
  let shares = splitEvenly(people)(total);
  if (roundUp) shares = shares.map(roundUpTo(1000));  // ₹10 = 1000 paise
  const paid = shares.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return { bill: toPaise(bill), tipAmount: total - toPaise(bill), total, shares, paid };
}

// ---- State is replaced, never mutated ----
let state = { bill: 2450, tip: 10, people: 3, roundUp: false };
const update = (patch) => {
  state = { ...state, ...patch };
  render(state);
};

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const TIP_OPTIONS = [0, 5, 10, 15, 20];
for (const pct of TIP_OPTIONS) {
  const b = document.createElement('button');
  b.textContent = pct + '%';
  b.addEventListener('click', () => update({ tip: pct }));
  $('tips').append(b);
}

function render(s) {
  const r = calculate(s);
  $('people').textContent = s.people;
  $('less').disabled = s.people === 1;
  [...$('tips').children].forEach((b, i) =>
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(TIP_OPTIONS[i] === s.tip)));
  const high = Math.max(...r.shares);
  const low = Math.min(...r.shares);
  $('each').textContent = money(high);
  $('detail').textContent = high === low ? 'Everyone pays the same'
    : `${r.shares.filter((x) => x === low).length} of you pay ${money(low)} (paise split fairly)`;
  const lines = [['Bill', r.bill], [`Tip (${s.tip}%)`, r.tipAmount], ['Total', r.total]];
  if (r.paid !== r.total) lines.push(['Extra from rounding', r.paid - r.total]);
  $('lines').replaceChildren(...lines.flatMap(([label, value]) => {
    const dt = document.createElement('dt');
    const dd = document.createElement('dd');
    dt.textContent = label;
    dd.textContent = money(value);
    return [dt, dd];
  }));
}

$('bill').addEventListener('input', (e) => update({ bill: Math.max(Number(e.target.value) || 0, 0) }));
$('less').addEventListener('click', () => update({ people: Math.max(state.people - 1, 1) }));
$('more').addEventListener('click', () => update({ people: state.people + 1 }));
$('round').addEventListener('change', (e) => update({ roundUp: e.target.checked }));

render(state);
console.log('shares in paise:', calculate(state).shares);
console.log('with rounding  :', calculate({ ...state, roundUp: true }).shares);

Try 3 people with a ₹2,450 bill and a 10% tip: the total is ₹2,695.00, which does not divide evenly into paise. One person pays one paisa more than the other two, so the shares always add up exactly to the total. Splitting money by dividing a float and rounding each share would lose or invent paise.

Example: Tip and Bill Splitter utilities

The lab builds these helpers for a restaurant billing tool, working in integer paise (js6) to avoid floating-point errors.

const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x);
const addPercent = (pct) => (paise) => Math.round(paise * (1 + pct / 100));
const discountFlat = (off) => (paise) => Math.max(paise - off, 0);
const roundUpTo = (step) => (paise) => Math.ceil(paise / step) * step;

function makeBillCalculator({ tip = 10, service = 0, discount = 0, roundTo = 0 } = {}) {
  const steps = [discountFlat(discount), addPercent(service), addPercent(tip)];
  if (roundTo) steps.push(roundUpTo(roundTo));
  return pipe(...steps);          // a new, configured function
}

const dinner = makeBillCalculator({ tip: 10, service: 5, discount: 10000, roundTo: 1000 });
console.log(dinner(120000));      // 128000 paise = ₹1,280.00
  1. makeBillCalculator is a higher-order function: it takes options and returns a pipeline.
  2. Each step is curried, so it fits in pipe and can be tested alone: addPercent(10)(1000) is 1100.
  3. The order is data, never mutated. At the end the script compares it with a structuredClone snapshot to prove it.

Common mistakes

1. Calling the callback instead of passing it.

// Wrong: save() runs now, and its return value is passed
button.addEventListener('click', save());
// Fix: pass the function itself (or wrap it)
button.addEventListener('click', save);

2. Passing a callback that takes extra arguments. map passes (item, index, array), so functions with optional second parameters misbehave.

// Wrong: parseInt('10', 1) and parseInt('7', 2) -> [ 12, NaN, NaN ]
['12', '10', '7'].map(parseInt);
// Fix: say exactly what you mean
['12', '10', '7'].map((s) => Number.parseInt(s, 10));

3. Mutating inside map or a "pure" helper.

// Wrong: changes the original items too
const discounted = items.map((i) => { i.price *= 0.9; return i; });
// Fix: return new objects
const discounted = items.map((i) => ({ ...i, price: i.price * 0.9 }));

4. Forgetting to return in a multi-line arrow.

// Wrong: braces start a block, so this returns undefined
const totals = orders.map((o) => { o.price * o.qty; });
// Fix: return explicitly, or drop the braces
const totals = orders.map((o) => o.price * o.qty);

Interview and real-world notes

  • Common tasks: implement pipe/compose, curry, once, memoize and your own map or filter using a loop and a callback. Practise saying why each works (closures).
  • Currying vs partial application: currying always produces one-argument functions; partial application fixes any number of arguments at once.
  • Do not over-abstract. Point-free chains of ten tiny functions can be harder to read than a clear loop. Use these tools where they make the code simpler, and name your steps.
  • Performance: chaining filter().map() loops the data twice, which is fine for hundreds or thousands of items. For very large data, a single reduce or loop may be better; measure first (js30).
  • In React: state updates must be immutable (setItems([...items, x])), because React compares references to decide what to re-render. Mutating and setting the same array does nothing.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const add = (a) => (b) => a + b;
const add5 = add(5);
console.log(add5(2), add(1)(1));
  • A 5 2
  • B 7 1
  • C 7 2
  • D NaN 2

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x);
const compose = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduceRight((v, f) => f(v), x);
const double = (n) => n * 2;
const inc = (n) => n + 1;
console.log(pipe(double, inc)(5), compose(double, inc)(5));
  • A 11 12
  • B 12 11
  • C 11 11
  • D 12 12

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const prices = [300, 100, 200];
const cheapest = prices.sort((a, b) => a - b)[0];
console.log(cheapest, prices[0], prices.length);
  • A 100 300 3
  • B 100 100 3
  • C 300 100 3
  • D 100 100 2

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const order = Object.freeze({ id: 7, items: ['pen'] });
order.id = 8;
order.items.push('book');
console.log(order.id, order.items.length);
  • A 8 2
  • B 7 1
  • C 8 1
  • D 7 2

Answers

  1. C. add(5) returns a function that remembers a = 5, so add5(2) is 7. add(1)(1) is 2.
  2. A. pipe doubles first then adds 1: 5 * 2 + 1 = 11. compose runs right to left, adding 1 first: (5 + 1) * 2 = 12.
  3. B. sort sorts in place and returns the same array, so prices itself is now [100, 200, 300].
  4. D. freeze blocks reassigning id (silently in sloppy code), but it is shallow: the items array inside can still be pushed to.

terms.definition: Functions are ordinary values: they can be stored, passed as arguments and returned from other functions.
A function that takes a function as an argument or returns a function, such as map, filter or makeTax.
A function you pass to another function so it can call it later or for each item.
Fixing some of a function’s arguments now and returning a function that takes the rest later.
Turning a function of several arguments into a chain of functions that each take one argument: f(a)(b)(c).
Combining functions so the output of one becomes the input of the next; pipe runs left to right, compose right to left.
Never changing existing data; instead creating new arrays and objects with the change, so earlier versions stay valid.

lessons.title: Arrays in depth
lessons.summaryHtml:
An array is an ordered list of values with a numeric index starting at 0. Arrays are objects with a special length and a large toolbox of methods. You create them with literals, Array.from or Array.of, read items with [i] or at(-1), and use push/pop/shift/unshift as stacks and queues.

The most important split is mutating vs non-mutating. splice, sort and reverse change the array in place; slice, map, filter and the ES2023 copy methods toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with return a new one.

The search and transform methods (map, filter, reduce, find, findLast, some, every, includes, flat, flatMap) replace most loops. Sorting needs a comparator for numbers, and localeCompare for names. Destructuring pulls items out by position. You will use all of them in the Student Records Analyser.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An array is a numbered list: a class register, a shopping cart, the rows of an invoice. Each slot has a position called an index, starting at 0. Arrays can hold anything (numbers, strings, objects, even other arrays) and they grow and shrink as you add and remove items.

Under the hood, an array is an object whose keys are the indexes, plus a length that is always one more than the highest index. Engines store arrays of similar values very efficiently, but in JavaScript you can think of them as ordered objects with a large, powerful toolbox of methods.

Why it matters

Almost every screen you build is an array rendered as a list: products, orders, notifications, students, messages. Every API response you fetch has arrays inside it. Filtering, sorting, totalling and grouping those lists is the daily work of a front-end developer, and the array methods in this lesson let you write each of those jobs in one clear line instead of a ten-line loop. They also show up in every coding interview.

How it works

Two questions unlock every array method: does it change the original array? and what does it return? Keep them in mind as you go through the sections below; the summary table at the end of this section answers both for every method.

Creating arrays, reading items, stacks and queues

Use a literal ([]) most of the time. Array.from builds an array from anything iterable or array-like and takes a mapping function, which makes it the easiest way to generate sequences. Avoid new Array(n) unless you immediately fill it: it creates empty slots (holes), which many methods skip.

Try it: Creating arrays, indexing and stack or queue methods

JavaScript

// Four ways to create arrays
const seats = ['A1', 'A2', 'A3'];                      // literal
const zeros = new Array(3).fill(0);                    // length 3, filled
const squares = Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i * i);
const letters = Array.from('RALFIZ');                  // any iterable
console.log(seats, zeros, squares, letters);

// Array.of(7) vs new Array(7): a classic trap
console.log(Array.of(7), 'vs length', new Array(7).length, '(empty slots)');

// Reading items
console.log(seats[0], seats[seats.length - 1], seats.at(-1), seats[10]);

// Stack (last in, first out): push and pop at the END
const undo = [];
console.log('push returns new length:', undo.push('type'), undo.push('bold'));
console.log('pop returns the item:', undo.pop(), '| left:', undo);

// Queue (first in, first out): push at the end, shift from the FRONT
const queue = ['Asha', 'Ravi'];
queue.push('Meera');
console.log('serving', queue.shift(), '| waiting', queue);
queue.unshift('VIP guest');                            // jump the queue
console.log('after unshift:', queue);

// Arrays are objects; length is writable
console.log(typeof seats, Array.isArray(seats));
const recent = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
recent.length = 2;                                     // truncates!
console.log('after length = 2:', recent);

Note what push, pop, shift and unshift return: not always the array.

at(-1) reads from the end without the length - 1 arithmetic. Reading past the end gives undefined, never an error. The four end methods turn arrays into the two most common data structures: a stack (last in, first out: undo history, the browser’s back button) with push/pop, and a queue (first in, first out: a support ticket line) with push/shift. Watch the return values: push and unshift return the new length, not the array. shift and unshift must renumber every item, so on very large arrays they are slower than push and pop.

slice vs splice, and the copy methods

These two names differ by one letter and behave completely differently:

slice(start, end)splice(start, count, ...items)
Changes the original?NoYes
ReturnsA new array with the copied partAn array of the removed items
end / second argumentIndex to stop before (not included)How many items to remove
Typical usePagination, “first 5”, copyingRemove or insert in place

Try it: slice vs splice, and the copy methods

JavaScript

const queue = ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Meera', 'Joel', 'Irfan'];

// slice(start, end): copies a part, end not included, original untouched
console.log('slice(1, 3):', queue.slice(1, 3));
console.log('slice(-2)  :', queue.slice(-2));
console.log('original   :', queue);

// splice(start, deleteCount, ...newItems): edits IN PLACE
const removed = queue.splice(1, 2, 'Nikhil');
console.log('splice returned:', removed);
console.log('queue is now   :', queue);

// ES2023 copy methods: the same jobs, but they return new arrays
const marks = [72, 45, 90, 61];
console.log('toSorted  :', marks.toSorted((a, b) => a - b));
console.log('toReversed:', marks.toReversed());
console.log('toSpliced :', marks.toSpliced(1, 1));     // remove index 1
console.log('with      :', marks.with(0, 75));          // replace index 0
console.log('marks untouched:', marks);

// Copying a whole array (shallow)
const copyA = [...marks];
const copyB = marks.slice();
console.log(copyA !== marks, copyB !== marks);

slice copies, splice edits in place. The to… methods and with() never touch the original.

ES2023 added copy methods for the old mutating ones: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with(index, value). They take the same arguments and return a new array, so you no longer need [...arr].sort(). They are supported in all current browsers and in Node 20 and newer; for older targets, check caniuse.com or the MDN compatibility table. Use them whenever the array is shared (state, props, cached API data), as you saw in js11.

Transform and search: map, filter, reduce, find and friends

All of these take a callback that receives (item, index, array) and none of them change the array. Pick the method by what you want back:

You wantMethodReturns
A changed version of every itemmapA new array, same length
Only some itemsfilterA new array, same or shorter
One combined valuereduceAnything: a number, object, array
The first / last matching itemfind / findLastThe item or undefined
Its positionfindIndex / findLastIndexThe index or -1
Does any / every item pass?some / everytrue or false
Is this exact value present?includestrue or false

Try it: map, filter, reduce, find and friends

JavaScript

const orders = [
  { id: 'ORD-1', customer: 'Asha', total: 1250, status: 'paid' },
  { id: 'ORD-2', customer: 'Ravi', total: 480, status: 'pending' },
  { id: 'ORD-3', customer: 'Meera', total: 3200, status: 'paid' },
  { id: 'ORD-4', customer: 'Asha', total: 150, status: 'cancelled' },
  { id: 'ORD-5', customer: 'Joel', total: 990, status: 'paid' },
];

// map: one output per input
console.log(orders.map((o) => o.id));

// filter: keep the items that pass a test
const paid = orders.filter((o) => o.status === 'paid');
console.log('paid:', paid.length);

// reduce: many items into one value
const revenue = paid.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0);
console.log('revenue:', revenue);

const byStatus = orders.reduce((acc, o) => {
  acc[o.status] = (acc[o.status] ?? 0) + 1;
  return acc;
}, {});
console.log(byStatus);

// find / findLast / findIndex: the first or last match
console.log(orders.find((o) => o.total > 1000).id);
console.log(orders.findLast((o) => o.customer === 'Asha').id);
console.log(orders.findIndex((o) => o.status === 'refunded'));

// some / every: yes-or-no questions
console.log('any pending?', orders.some((o) => o.status === 'pending'));
console.log('all above ₹100?', orders.every((o) => o.total > 100));

// includes: is this exact value in the list?
const customers = orders.map((o) => o.customer);
console.log(customers.includes('Meera'), customers.includes('meera'));

An order list analysed without a single for loop.

reduce deserves a closer look. It calls your function with an accumulator and the current item, and whatever you return becomes the accumulator for the next item. Always pass the initial value (the 0 or {} after the callback). Without it, reduce uses the first item as the start value, which breaks for arrays of objects and throws a TypeError on an empty array. The byStatus example is the classic counting pattern; in js14 you will meet Object.groupBy, which does grouping in one call.

some, every and find short-circuit: they stop at the first item that decides the answer. Note also that every on an empty array returns true (there is no item that fails), which can surprise you in validation code.

flat, flatMap and destructuring

Nested data is common: orders contain items, students contain marks, posts contain tags. flat(depth) removes levels of nesting (one by default, Infinity for all). flatMap maps and then flattens one level in a single pass, and because returning [] contributes nothing, it can filter and transform at the same time.

Try it: flat, flatMap and destructuring

JavaScript

const orders = [
  { id: 1, items: ['notebook', 'pen'] },
  { id: 2, items: ['backpack'] },
  { id: 3, items: [] },
];

// map gives nested arrays; flat() removes one level
console.log(orders.map((o) => o.items));
console.log(orders.map((o) => o.items).flat());

// flatMap = map + flat(1) in one pass
console.log(orders.flatMap((o) => o.items));

// flatMap can also filter: return [] to drop an item
const bigOrders = orders.flatMap((o) => (o.items.length > 1 ? [o.id] : []));
console.log('orders with 2+ items:', bigOrders);

// flat with a depth
const nested = [1, [2, [3, [4]]]];
console.log(nested.flat(), nested.flat(Infinity));

// Array destructuring: by position
const podium = ['Fathima', 'Nikhil', 'Aisha', 'Irfan', 'Meera'];
const [gold, silver, bronze, ...others] = podium;
console.log(gold, silver, bronze, others);

const [, second, , fourth = 'nobody'] = ['a', 'b', 'c'];   // skip and default
console.log(second, fourth);

let left = 'Kochi';
let right = 'Thrissur';
[left, right] = [right, left];                         // swap
console.log(left, right);

// Destructuring in loops: entries() gives [index, value]
for (const [i, name] of podium.slice(0, 3).entries()) {
  console.log(`#${i + 1} ${name}`);
}

flatMap can map and filter in one step by returning an empty array to skip an item.

Array destructuring unpacks items by position. Commas skip positions, = value sets a default used when the item is undefined, and ...rest collects what remains into a new array. The swap trick, [a, b] = [b, a], needs no temporary variable. Combined with entries(), destructuring gives you both the index and the value in a for...of loop.

Sorting with comparators

Without a comparator, sort converts items to strings and compares UTF-16 code units. That is why [10, 9, 1, 100] sorts to [1, 10, 100, 9], and why capital letters come before lowercase ones. A comparator (a, b) => returns a negative number to put a first, a positive number to put b first, and 0 to leave them.

Try it: Sorting with comparators

JavaScript

// 1. The default sort compares STRINGS
console.log([10, 9, 1, 100].sort());

// 2. Numbers need a comparator: negative = a first, positive = b first
const prices = [499, 89, 1299, 250];
console.log('low to high:', prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b));
console.log('high to low:', prices.toSorted((a, b) => b - a));

// 3. Text: localeCompare knows about case and accents
const names = ['zara', 'Émile', 'Aisha', 'ben'];
console.log('default :', names.toSorted());
console.log('locale  :', names.toSorted((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)));

// 4. Several keys: batch A..Z, then average high to low
const students = [
  { name: 'Ravi', batch: 'B', avg: 72 },
  { name: 'Asha', batch: 'A', avg: 85 },
  { name: 'Joel', batch: 'B', avg: 88 },
  { name: 'Meera', batch: 'A', avg: 91 },
];
const ranked = students.toSorted(
  (a, b) => a.batch.localeCompare(b.batch) || b.avg - a.avg,
);
console.log(ranked.map((s) => `${s.batch} ${s.name} ${s.avg}`));

// 5. Sort is stable: equal items keep their original order
const tickets = [
  { id: 1, priority: 'high' },
  { id: 2, priority: 'low' },
  { id: 3, priority: 'high' },
  { id: 4, priority: 'low' },
];
const rank = { high: 0, low: 1 };
console.log(tickets.toSorted((a, b) => rank[a.priority] - rank[b.priority])
  .map((t) => t.id));

The default sort compares strings. Numbers need a comparator; names need localeCompare.

  • Numbers: (a, b) => a - b ascending, b - a descending.
  • Text: a.localeCompare(b) sorts the way people expect, handling case and accents. For a large list, create one Intl.Collator and use its compare method.
  • Several keys: chain comparisons with ||. If the first key is equal (0), the second decides.
  • Stability: since ES2019, sort is guaranteed stable, so items that compare equal keep their original order.

Everything together: a records dashboard

This page is the browser version of the lab. map derives an average and a pass flag for each student (without touching the original objects), every decides the pass rule, filter handles the chips and the search box, toSorted applies the chosen comparator, and reduce finds the top student. The filters and sorts are stored as objects of functions, so switching behaviour is a lookup, not an if/else chain.

Try it: Student records dashboard

JavaScript

const students = [
  { name: 'Aisha Rahman', city: 'Kochi', marks: [78, 85, 92], attendance: 0.93 },
  { name: 'Rahul Menon', city: 'Thrissur', marks: [65, 58, 71], attendance: 0.88 },
  { name: 'Fathima Nazar', city: 'Malappuram', marks: [92, 88, 95], attendance: 0.97 },
  { name: 'Arjun Das', city: 'Kozhikode', marks: [35, 52, 48], attendance: 0.81 },
  { name: 'Sneha Pillai', city: 'Kochi', marks: [88, 79, 84], attendance: 0.72 },
  { name: 'Mohammed Ashik', city: 'Perinthalmanna', marks: [72, 69, 80], attendance: 0.9 },
  { name: 'Divya Krishnan', city: 'Thrissur', marks: [55, 61, 47], attendance: 0.85 },
  { name: 'Nikhil Varghese', city: 'Kochi', marks: [90, 94, 89], attendance: 0.95 },
];

// Derived data: computed once with map, never stored by hand
const average = (nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / nums.length;
const records = students.map((s) => ({
  ...s,
  avg: Math.round(average(s.marks) * 10) / 10,
  passed: s.marks.every((m) => m >= 40) && s.attendance >= 0.75,
}));

const FILTERS = {
  all: () => true,
  passed: (r) => r.passed,
  help: (r) => !r.passed,
};
const SORTS = {
  avg: (a, b) => b.avg - a.avg,
  name: (a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name),
  att: (a, b) => a.attendance - b.attendance,
};
const state = { filter: 'all', sort: 'avg', query: '' };
const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);

function visibleRecords() {
  const q = state.query.trim().toLowerCase();
  return records
    .filter(FILTERS[state.filter])
    .filter((r) => r.name.toLowerCase().includes(q))
    .toSorted(SORTS[state.sort]);
}

function stat(label, value) {
  const div = document.createElement('div');
  div.className = 'stat';
  const span = document.createElement('span');
  const strong = document.createElement('strong');
  span.textContent = label;
  strong.textContent = value;
  div.append(span, strong);
  return div;
}

function render() {
  const list = visibleRecords();
  const top = list.length ? list.reduce((best, r) => (r.avg > best.avg ? r : best)) : null;
  const passRate = list.length ? list.filter((r) => r.passed).length / list.length : 0;
  $('stats').replaceChildren(
    stat('Students shown', list.length),
    stat('Class average', list.length ? average(list.map((r) => r.avg)).toFixed(1) : '–'),
    stat('Pass rate', Math.round(passRate * 100) + '%'),
    stat('Top student', top ? top.name.split(' ')[0] : '–'),
  );
  $('rows').replaceChildren(...list.map((r) => {
    const tr = document.createElement('tr');
    const name = document.createElement('td');
    name.textContent = r.name;
    const sub = document.createElement('small');
    sub.textContent = `${r.city} · ${Math.round(r.attendance * 100)}% attendance`;
    name.append(sub);
    const markCells = r.marks.map((m) => {
      const td = document.createElement('td');
      td.textContent = m;
      if (m < 40) td.className = 'low';
      return td;
    });
    const avg = document.createElement('td');
    avg.textContent = r.avg;
    const status = document.createElement('td');
    const pill = document.createElement('span');
    pill.className = 'pill ' + (r.passed ? 'pass' : 'help');
    pill.textContent = r.passed ? 'Passed' : 'Needs help';
    status.append(pill);
    tr.append(name, ...markCells, avg, status);
    return tr;
  }));
  $('empty').hidden = list.length > 0;
  [...$('chips').children].forEach((b) =>
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b.dataset.f === state.filter)));
}

for (const [key, label] of [['all', 'All'], ['passed', 'Passed'], ['help', 'Needs help']]) {
  const b = document.createElement('button');
  b.dataset.f = key;
  b.textContent = label;
  b.addEventListener('click', () => { state.filter = key; render(); });
  $('chips').append(b);
}
$('sort').addEventListener('change', (e) => { state.sort = e.target.value; render(); });
$('q').addEventListener('input', (e) => { state.query = e.target.value; render(); });

render();
console.log('Needs help:', records.filter(FILTERS.help).map((r) => r.name));
console.log('Original data untouched?', !('avg' in students[0]));

Every render starts from the original records and derives the visible list again. Nothing is removed from or reordered in the source data, which is why clearing the search box brings every student back.

Method summary

Mutates the arrayReturns a new arrayReturns something else
push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill, copyWithinslice, map, filter, flat, flatMap, concat, toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, withreduce, find, findLast, findIndex, indexOf, includes, some, every, join, at, forEach (undefined)

Example: Student Records Analyser

The lab loads students.json (twelve records, each with three subject marks and an attendance ratio) and answers the questions a course coordinator would ask.

const SUBJECTS = ['JavaScript', 'DOM', 'SQL'];
const round1 = (n) => Math.round(n * 10) / 10;
const average = (nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / nums.length;

const withAvg = students.map((s) => ({ ...s, average: round1(average(s.marks)) }));
const passed = withAvg.filter((s) => s.marks.every((m) => m >= 40)
  && s.attendance >= 0.75);
const top3 = withAvg.toSorted((a, b) => b.average - a.average).slice(0, 3);

const toppers = SUBJECTS.map((subject, i) => {
  const best = students.reduce((a, b) => (b.marks[i] > a.marks[i] ? b : a));
  return `${subject}: ${best.name} (${best.marks[i]})`;
});
  1. map with spread adds average to a copy of each student; the loaded data stays as it was.
  2. filter plus every expresses the pass rule almost in plain English.
  3. toSorted then slice(0, 3) gives the top three without reordering the source.
  4. The subject toppers use the index i that map passes as its second argument.

Common mistakes

1. Sorting numbers without a comparator.

// Wrong: [ 1, 10, 100, 9 ]
[10, 9, 1, 100].sort();
// Fix
[10, 9, 1, 100].toSorted((a, b) => a - b);

2. Using map when you mean forEach (or the reverse). map builds a new array; if you ignore it, use forEach or for...of. And forEach returns undefined, so it cannot be chained.

// Wrong: totals is undefined
const totals = orders.forEach((o) => o.price * o.qty);
// Fix
const totals = orders.map((o) => o.price * o.qty);

3. reduce without an initial value.

// Wrong: starts with the first OBJECT, and throws on []
const sum = cart.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price);
// Fix: always pass the start value
const sum = cart.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0);

4. Checking for an object with includes. includes and indexOf compare objects by reference, not by content.

// Wrong: false, it is a different object with the same content
cart.includes({ id: 3 });
// Fix: search by a field
cart.some((item) => item.id === 3);

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the mutators by heart: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill. Interviewers love “what is arr after this line?”.
  • Explain reduce by writing sum, then a counting object, then implementing map with reduce.
  • Complexity: includes, find and indexOf scan the array (O(n)). For many lookups, build a Set or Map once (js14, js30).
  • In React and other frameworks, prefer toSorted, map, filter and spread for state, because mutating arrays in state breaks change detection.
  • Empty slots: new Array(3) and [1, , 3] create holes that map and forEach skip. Use Array.from({ length: n }) or fill to avoid them.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const nums = [10, 9, 1, 100];
nums.sort();
console.log(nums.join(','));
  • A 1,9,10,100
  • B 100,10,9,1
  • C 1,10,100,9
  • D 9,10,100,1

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const seats = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E'];
const x = seats.slice(1, 3);
const y = seats.splice(1, 2);
console.log(x.join(''), y.join(''), seats.join(''));
  • A BC BC ADE
  • B BC BCD ADE
  • C BC BC ABCDE
  • D BCD BC ADE

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const marks = [45, 82, 67, 90];
console.log(
  marks.find((m) => m > 60),
  marks.findLast((m) => m > 60),
  marks.findIndex((m) => m > 95),
);
  • A 67 90 -1
  • B 82 82 -1
  • C 82 90 undefined
  • D 82 90 -1

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const readings = [3, NaN, 7];
console.log(readings.indexOf(NaN), readings.includes(NaN), readings.at(-1));
  • A 1 true 7
  • B -1 true 7
  • C -1 false 7
  • D 1 false undefined

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const scores = [3, 1, 2];
const sorted = scores.toSorted();
const fixed = scores.with(0, 9);
console.log(scores.join(), sorted.join(), fixed.join());
  • A 1,2,3 1,2,3 9,2,3
  • B 9,1,2 1,2,3 9,1,2
  • C 3,1,2 1,2,3 9,1,2
  • D 3,1,2 3,2,1 9,1,2

Answers

  1. C. Without a comparator, sort compares the items as strings, so "100" comes before "9".
  2. A. slice(1, 3) copies indexes 1 and 2. splice(1, 2) removes two items starting at index 1 and returns them, changing seats to A, D, E.
  3. D. find returns the first match (82), findLast the last match (90). findIndex returns -1, not undefined, when nothing matches.
  4. B. indexOf uses strict equality and NaN is not equal to itself, so it returns -1. includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to NaN.
  5. C. toSorted and with return new arrays, so scores keeps its original order. with(0, 9) replaces index 0 in the copy.

terms.definition: The position of an item, starting at 0; the last item is at length - 1, or at(-1).
A method that changes the array it is called on, such as push, splice, sort and reverse.
An ES2023 method that returns a changed copy and leaves the original alone: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with.
Array methods call your function with (item, index, array); reduce adds the accumulator first.
A function (a, b) for sort that returns a negative number if a comes first, positive if b comes first, and 0 to keep their order.
Combines all items into one value (a total, an object, a map) by carrying an accumulator through the array.
Unpacking items by position into variables: const [first, , third, ...rest] = list.

lessons.examTip: Before calling an array method, ask two questions: does it change the original, and what does it return? Most array bugs come from getting one of those wrong.

lessons.title: Objects in depth
lessons.summaryHtml:
Objects are how JavaScript groups related data and behaviour: a product, a booking, an invoice, a user profile. In this lesson you go beyond { name: 'Pen' } to the tools professionals use every day: shorthand properties, computed keys, methods, destructuring with defaults and renaming, and spread and rest.

You learn to treat objects as data you can transform with Object.keys, values, entries and fromEntries, and you learn the single most important idea about objects: variables hold references, not copies. That is why spread gives a shallow copy, why structuredClone exists, and why Object.freeze only protects the top level.

The mini project is an Invoice Builder that normalises messy order data without ever mutating the original.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An object is a labelled box of values. A product has a title, a price and a stock count; a booking has a guest, a date and a seat count. Each label is a key (a string or a symbol) and each label points to a value (any value, including another object or a function).

That sounds simple, and it is. The hard part, and the part that causes real bugs in real apps, is this: a variable does not contain an object. It contains a reference to one, like a delivery address written on a slip of paper. Copy the slip and you have two slips pointing to the same house. Paint the house through one slip and the other slip sees the new colour. Most of this lesson is about working confidently with that fact.

Why it matters

Nearly all data in a front-end or Node app is objects: API responses, form values, cart lines, settings and state. You constantly read nested fields, fill in missing ones with defaults, build new objects from old ones and pass objects between functions. When a teammate says “the cart total changed on its own” or “the defaults got overwritten”, it is almost always a shared reference that someone mutated. Frameworks such as React also compare objects by reference to decide what to re-render, so an in-place mutation can mean the screen does not update. Knowing how to copy and update objects without mutation is a daily, practical skill.

How it works

Literals, shorthand, computed keys and methods

The object literal {} creates a plain object. Modern syntax adds three shortcuts. Shorthand properties turn { title: title } into { title } when a variable has the same name. Computed keys put any expression inside square brackets, which is how you build keys from variables. Method shorthand writes total() { … } instead of total: function () { … }.

const field = 'category';
const product = {
  title,                 // same as title: title
  [field]: 'stationery', // key comes from the variable
  priceWithTax(rate = 0.18) {
    return Math.round(this.price * (1 + rate));
  },
};

Use dot access (product.title) when you know the key while writing the code, and bracket access (product[field]) when the key is in a variable or is not a valid identifier, such as 'order-id'. Keys are always strings or symbols: obj[1] and obj['1'] are the same property. To check whether a property exists, prefer Object.hasOwn(obj, key) (own properties only) or key in obj (includes inherited ones). Comparing with undefined fails when a property exists but holds undefined.

Try it: Literals, shorthand, computed keys and methods

JavaScript

const title = 'Ralfiz Notebook';
const price = 149;
const field = 'category';

const product = {
  title,                      // shorthand for title: title
  price,
  [field]: 'stationery',      // computed key
  ['tag_' + 1]: 'bestseller', // any expression works
  priceWithTax(rate = 0.18) { // method shorthand
    return Math.round(this.price * (1 + rate));
  },
};

console.log(product);
console.log('With GST:', product.priceWithTax());

// Dot vs bracket access
console.log(product.title, product['tag_1'], product[field]);

// Adding, updating and deleting properties
product.stock = 40;
product.price = 139;
delete product.tag_1;
console.log(Object.keys(product));
console.log('stock' in product, Object.hasOwn(product, 'color'));

Change field to 'sku' and run again: the computed key follows the variable. Notice the method uses this to reach its own object.

Destructuring with defaults, renaming and rest

Destructuring unpacks properties into variables in one statement. The pattern on the left mirrors the shape of the object. You can rename with a colon (id: bookingId), give a default with =, reach into nested objects, and collect the remaining properties with rest (...others).

The most useful place for destructuring is a function’s parameter list. An options object lets callers pass named settings in any order, and defaults document the behaviour right in the signature. Always add = {} after the pattern, or calling the function with no argument throws, because you cannot destructure undefined.

function createBooking({ show = 'Evening', seats = 1, vip = false } = {}) {
  // ...
}
createBooking({ seats: 3 }); // show and vip use their defaults
createBooking();             // works thanks to = {}
Watch out: defaults kick in only for undefined. An API that sends null or 0 keeps those values. If null should also fall back, write const seats = input.seats ?? 1;.

Try it: Destructuring with defaults, renaming and rest

JavaScript

const booking = {
  id: 'BK-104',
  guest: { name: 'Anu', phone: '98470 12345' },
  seats: 2,
  extras: undefined,
};

// Rename + default + nested
const {
  id: bookingId,
  seats = 1,
  extras = [],
  guest: { name: guestName, email = 'not given' },
} = booking;
console.log(bookingId, seats, extras, guestName, email);

// Rest collects everything else
const { id, ...withoutId } = booking;
console.log(withoutId);

// Options object in a parameter, with a default for the whole thing
function createBooking({ show = 'Evening', seats = 1, vip = false } = {}) {
  return `${show} show, ${seats} seat(s)${vip ? ', VIP' : ''}`;
}
console.log(createBooking({ seats: 3, vip: true }));
console.log(createBooking());
console.log(createBooking({ seats: null })); // null is NOT undefined

Try calling createBooking({}) or passing seats: null and see which defaults apply.

Treating objects as data: keys, values, entries, fromEntries

Arrays have map, filter and reduce. Objects do not, but you can borrow them. Object.keys(obj), Object.values(obj) and Object.entries(obj) give arrays of the own, enumerable, string-keyed properties. Object.fromEntries(pairs) goes the other way and builds an object from [key, value] pairs. Together they give you a pipeline: object → pairs → transform → new object.

MethodReturns for { pen: 20, bag: 899 }Typical use
Object.keys['pen', 'bag']Counting fields, checking what exists
Object.values[20, 899]Totals and averages
Object.entries[['pen', 20], ['bag', 899]]Looping with both key and value
Object.fromEntriesobject from pairsBuilding the transformed result

Key order is predictable but surprising: integer-like keys ('2', '10') come first in ascending order, then other string keys in insertion order. If order matters for numeric ids, use an array or a Map (next lesson).

Try it: Transform objects with entries and fromEntries

JavaScript

const prices = { pen: 20, notebook: 149, bag: 899, bottle: 349 };

console.log(Object.keys(prices));
console.log(Object.values(prices));
console.log(Object.entries(prices));

// Apply 10% off to every item
const sale = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(prices).map(([item, p]) => [item, Math.round(p * 0.9)])
);
console.log('Sale:', sale);

// Keep only items under 400
const cheap = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(prices).filter(([, p]) => p < 400)
);
console.log('Under 400:', cheap);

// Total of all values
const total = Object.values(prices).reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
console.log('Total:', total);

// Build an object from any list of pairs, e.g. a Map or form fields
const fields = [['name', 'Anu'], ['city', 'Kochi']];
console.log(Object.fromEntries(fields));
console.log('Original untouched:', prices);

The price list is never mutated: every step returns a new object. Change the discount to 0.25 and run.

References, shallow copies and deep copies

Primitives (numbers, strings, booleans and so on) are copied by value. Objects, arrays, dates and functions are not: assigning or passing them copies the reference. JavaScript passes arguments “by sharing”: the function receives a copy of the reference, so it can mutate the caller’s object, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

There are three levels of copying:

  • Same reference: const b = a. One object, two names.
  • Shallow copy: { ...a } or Object.assign({}, a). A new top-level object, but nested objects and arrays are shared.
  • Deep copy: structuredClone(a). Every level is new. It handles nested objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set and even circular references. It throws a DataCloneError for functions and DOM nodes, and class instances come back as plain objects.

The old trick JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) is weaker: it turns dates into strings and drops undefined, functions, Map and Set. Prefer structuredClone.

Often you do not need a deep copy at all. An immutable update copies only the path you change and shares the rest, which is cheaper and is exactly how state updates work in React and Redux:

const updated = {
  ...order,
  customer: { ...order.customer, city: 'Perinthalmanna' },
};
// order is untouched; updated.items is still shared (not changed)

Try it: References, shallow copy and structuredClone

JavaScript

const order = {
  id: 7,
  customer: { name: 'Rahul', city: 'Malappuram' },
  items: [{ sku: 'PEN', qty: 2 }],
  placedAt: new Date('2026-09-01T10:00:00Z'),
};

const same = order;                 // copies the reference
same.id = 8;
console.log('same === order:', same === order, 'order.id =', order.id);

const shallow = { ...order };       // new top level, shared nested
shallow.id = 9;                     // safe
shallow.customer.city = 'Kochi';    // changes order too!
console.log('order.id:', order.id, 'order city:', order.customer.city);

const deep = structuredClone(order); // nothing shared
deep.items[0].qty = 99;
deep.customer.city = 'Thrissur';
console.log('order qty:', order.items[0].qty, 'city:', order.customer.city);
console.log('Date survives:', deep.placedAt instanceof Date);

// Immutable update: copy each level you change
const updated = {
  ...order,
  customer: { ...order.customer, city: 'Perinthalmanna' },
};
console.log(updated.customer === order.customer, order.customer.city);

try {
  structuredClone({ total: 10, print() {} });
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', 'functions cannot be cloned');
}

Watch which line changes the original order. Only structuredClone gives a fully independent copy.

Optional chaining and freezing

Real data has gaps. user.address.city throws a TypeError if address is missing. user.address?.city stops and returns undefined as soon as it hits null or undefined. Pair it with ?? for a fallback. It also works for calls (obj.method?.()) and brackets (list?.[0]). Use it where a value may legitimately be missing, not everywhere: hiding a bug behind ?. just moves the crash somewhere harder to find.

Object.freeze(obj) makes the object’s own properties read-only and blocks adding or deleting properties. In strict mode (modules, classes) a write throws a TypeError; in a classic script it fails silently. Freezing is shallow, so constants such as tax tables often use a small recursive deepFreeze. Related helpers: Object.seal allows changing values but not adding or removing keys, and Object.preventExtensions only blocks new keys.

Try it: Optional chaining and freezing

JavaScript

const users = [
  { name: 'Anu', address: { city: 'Kochi' }, getBadge: () => 'Gold' },
  { name: 'Faris' },
];

for (const u of users) {
  const city = u.address?.city ?? 'Unknown city';
  const badge = u.getBadge?.() ?? 'No badge';
  console.log(`${u.name}: ${city}, ${badge}`);
}
console.log(users[5]?.name); // undefined, no crash

const TAX = Object.freeze({ gst: 0.18, slabs: { food: 0.05 } });
TAX.gst = 0;                 // ignored (throws in strict mode)
TAX.slabs.food = 0.12;       // nested object is NOT frozen
console.log(TAX.gst, TAX.slabs.food, Object.isFrozen(TAX));

function deepFreeze(obj) {
  for (const value of Object.values(obj)) {
    if (value && typeof value === 'object') deepFreeze(value);
  }
  return Object.freeze(obj);
}
const RATES = deepFreeze({ gst: 0.18, slabs: { food: 0.05 } });
RATES.slabs.food = 0.12;
console.log('After deepFreeze:', RATES.slabs.food);

The frozen config silently ignores the write in a classic script. Add 'use strict'; as the first line and run again to see the TypeError.

The saved preferences override the frozen defaults with a two-level merge: a single spread would replace the whole channels object and lose the default channels the user never touched. Every toggle produces a new state object, and Object.entries computes which settings differ from the defaults.

JavaScript

const DEFAULTS = Object.freeze({
  channels: Object.freeze({ email: true, sms: false, push: true }),
  digest: 'weekly',
});

function load() {
  try { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('prefs')) ?? {}; }
  catch { return {}; }
}

// Merge two levels: a plain spread would drop default channels
function merge(defaults, saved) {
  return {
    ...defaults,
    ...saved,
    channels: { ...defaults.channels, ...saved.channels },
  };
}

let state = merge(DEFAULTS, load());

function changes(current) {
  const flat = (o) => ({ ...o.channels, digest: o.digest });
  const base = flat(DEFAULTS);
  return Object.entries(flat(current)).filter(([k, v]) => base[k] !== v);
}

function render() {
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-channel]').forEach((box) => {
    box.checked = state.channels[box.dataset.channel];
  });
  document.querySelector('#digest').value = state.digest;
  const diff = changes(state);
  document.querySelector('#badge').textContent =
    `${diff.length} change${diff.length === 1 ? '' : 's'}`;
  document.querySelector('#preview').textContent =
    JSON.stringify(state, null, 2);
}

document.querySelector('.rows').addEventListener('change', (e) => {
  const ch = e.target.dataset.channel;
  state = ch
    ? { ...state, channels: { ...state.channels, [ch]: e.target.checked } }
    : { ...state, digest: e.target.value };
  render();
});

document.querySelector('#save').addEventListener('click', () => {
  localStorage.setItem('prefs', JSON.stringify(state));
  console.log('Saved changes:', Object.fromEntries(changes(state)));
});

document.querySelector('#reset').addEventListener('click', () => {
  state = structuredClone(DEFAULTS); // a fresh, unfrozen copy
  localStorage.removeItem('prefs');
  render();
  console.log('Back to defaults. Frozen original:', Object.isFrozen(DEFAULTS));
});

render();
console.log('Loaded state:', state);

Example: Invoice Builder

The lab turns raw orders from a shop into clean invoices. The raw data is messy: some lines have no quantity, one customer has no address, and a discount must be applied without changing the original orders (the finance team still needs them).

  1. Freeze the tax configuration so nothing can change it by accident.
  2. Build a price lookup with Object.fromEntries from the catalogue array.
  3. Normalise each line with destructuring and defaults.
  4. Read optional fields with ?. and ??.
  5. Apply a discount to a structuredClone, then prove the original is unchanged.
const TAX = Object.freeze({ rate: 0.18 });
const priceOf = Object.fromEntries(catalogue.map((p) => [p.sku, p.price]));

function buildInvoice({ id, customer, lines = [] }) {
  const items = lines.map(({ sku, qty = 1 }) => ({
    sku, qty, amount: priceOf[sku] * qty,
  }));
  const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.amount, 0);
  return {
    id,
    billTo: customer?.name ?? 'Walk-in customer',
    city: customer?.address?.city ?? '-',
    items,
    subtotal,
    tax: Math.round(subtotal * TAX.rate),
    total: Math.round(subtotal * (1 + TAX.rate)),
  };
}

Common mistakes

1. Thinking spread is a deep copy.

// Wrong: the nested address is shared, the original changes too
const draft = { ...user };
draft.address.city = 'Kochi';

// Fix: copy the level you change, or clone everything
const draft2 = { ...user, address: { ...user.address, city: 'Kochi' } };
const draft3 = structuredClone(user);

2. Mutating a function argument.

// Wrong: the caller's cart is changed behind its back
function addItem(cart, item) { cart.items.push(item); return cart; }

// Fix: return a new object
function addItem2(cart, item) {
  return { ...cart, items: [...cart.items, item] };
}

3. Forgetting the default for the whole options object.

// Wrong: createBooking() throws "Cannot destructure ... undefined"
function createBooking({ seats = 1 }) {}
// Fix
function createBooking2({ seats = 1 } = {}) {}

4. Using a default where ?? is needed. An API sends discount: null, the default does not apply, and price * null quietly becomes 0. Write const discount = data.discount ?? 0;.

// Wrong: the default only applies to undefined, not null
const { discount = 0 } = { discount: null }; // discount is null
// Fix
const discount2 = data.discount ?? 0;

5. Comparing objects with ===. { a: 1 } === { a: 1 } is false because they are two different objects. Compare the fields you care about, or compare a stable id.

// Wrong: always false for two separate objects
if (cartItem === { sku: 'PEN' }) { /* never runs */ }
// Fix: compare a field
if (cartItem.sku === 'PEN') { /* runs */ }

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Is JavaScript pass-by-reference?” No: it is pass-by-value, where the value of an object variable is a reference (often called pass-by-sharing). Show both mutation (visible outside) and reassignment (not visible).
  • Deep copy question: answer structuredClone first, mention its limits (functions, DOM nodes, class prototypes), and mention why the JSON trick is lossy.
  • const is not immutability: const fixes the binding; Object.freeze fixes the object’s top level. They are independent.
  • In code review, look for mutations of props, state or function arguments. Prefer returning new objects, and copy only the path you change.
  • Performance: spreading a large object on every keystroke is fine for normal UI state. If a profiler shows it matters, restructure the data rather than giving up immutability.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

const b = a;
b.total = 250;

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const order = { id: 1, customer: { city: 'Kochi' } };
const copy = { ...order };
copy.id = 2;
copy.customer.city = 'Delhi';

Snippet 3. What is logged?

console.log(Object.keys(row).join(','));

const { qty = 1, note = 'none', gift = false } =
  { qty: null, note: undefined, gift: 0 };

  • B null undefined 0

Snippet 5. What is logged?

cfg.name = 'VAT';
cfg.tax.rate = 18;

  • B VAT 18
  • C GST 5
  • D TypeError

Answers

  1. C. b = a copies the reference, so a and b point at the same object. Changing b.total changes the only object there is.
  2. C. Spread makes a new top-level object, so id is independent. customer is still the same nested object, so the city change shows through.
  3. B. Integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order. Do not rely on object key order for numeric ids: use a Map or an array.
  4. D. Defaults apply only for undefined. null and 0 are real values, so qty stays null and gift stays 0; only note falls back to the default.
  5. A. freeze is shallow. The write to name is ignored (no error outside strict mode), but tax is a separate, unfrozen object.

A property name written as [expression] in a literal; the expression is evaluated and converted to a string or symbol key.
Syntax that unpacks properties into variables, with optional defaults and renaming: const { price: cost = 0 } = item.
The value a variable holds for an object: a pointer to one object in memory. Copying the variable copies the pointer, not the object.
A new top-level object whose nested objects are still shared with the original, as made by spread or Object.assign.
A copy with no shared nested objects, made with structuredClone for plain data.
Makes an object’s own properties read-only and stops adding or removing them. It is shallow.

quiz.question: What does const copy = { ...order } give you when order.customer is an object?
options: A deep copy: changing copy.customer.city leaves order untouched

options: undefined
null

quiz.question: Which statement about Object.freeze(config) is true?
options: It freezes config and every nested object inside it
It makes the variable config impossible to reassign
It stops changes to config’s own properties, but nested objects can still be changed
It throws immediately if config contains an array
