quiz.question: Why does Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(prices).map(...)) appear so often in real code?
options: It is the idiomatic way to transform an object’s values or keys into a new object without mutating it
It is the only way to loop over an object
It makes the object faster to read
It converts an object into a Map
quiz.explanation: entries turns the object into an array of pairs, you use map or filter on the array, and fromEntries builds a fresh object. The original is never changed.

lessons.title: Map, Set, JSON and grouping
lessons.summaryHtml:
Plain objects and arrays are not the only collections. A Map is a key–value store where keys can be any value, it keeps insertion order and knows its size. A Set holds unique values, with fast membership checks, and ES2025 adds set algebra such as union, intersection and difference. WeakMap attaches data to objects without keeping them alive.

You also learn JSON properly: what JSON.stringify keeps and silently drops, how replacers and revivers work, and how to round-trip dates. Finally you group data with Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy, and put it all together in an Order Report that a shop owner could actually use.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

You already know two containers: arrays (ordered lists) and objects (records with named fields). This lesson adds specialised containers that fit common jobs better. A Map is a lookup table: give it a key, get a value back, and the key can be anything, even an object. A Set is a bag that refuses duplicates. A WeakMap is a sticky note you attach to an object: when the object is thrown away, the note goes with it.

Then there is JSON, the text format every API speaks. Converting objects to JSON and back looks trivial, but it silently drops values and turns dates into strings. Finally, grouping answers the everyday question “show me these orders by category”.

Why it matters

Reports, dashboards and carts are built from exactly these operations. “Revenue by category” is a group-and-sum. “How many unique customers?” is a Set. “Which customers bought in both months?” is an intersection. “Cache the total for this cart” is a WeakMap. And every save to localStorage or send to a server goes through JSON.stringify, so knowing what it loses prevents the classic bug where a date turns into a string and order.placedAt.getFullYear() crashes after a page reload.

How it works

Map: a real lookup table

A plain object used as a dictionary has three hidden problems. Every key is converted to a string, so the number 1 and the string '1' collide, and every object key becomes '[object Object]'. It has no size. And it inherits properties such as toString from Object.prototype, so a user-supplied key such as 'constructor' can clash. A Map fixes all three.

const stock = new Map();
stock.set('PEN', 120).set('NB', 40);   // set returns the map, so it chains
stock.get('PEN');     // 120
stock.has('BAG');     // false
stock.delete('NB');
stock.size;           // 1
for (const [sku, qty] of stock) { /* insertion order */ }
Plain objectMap
Key typesStrings and symbols (others converted)Any value, including objects
SizeObject.keys(o).lengthmap.size
OrderInteger-like keys first, then insertionAlways insertion order
Frequent add and deleteWorks, not optimised for itDesigned for it
JSONSerialises directlyConvert first: Object.fromEntries(map)
Best forFixed-shape records (a user, an order)Dynamic dictionaries, counters, caches

Convert freely between them: new Map(Object.entries(obj)) and Object.fromEntries(map). Remember the second one turns every key into a string.

Try it: Map vs plain object

JavaScript

// Counting with a Map: numbers stay numbers, order is kept
const views = [101, 204, 101, 330, 204, 101];
const count = new Map();
for (const id of views) count.set(id, (count.get(id) ?? 0) + 1);
console.log(count);
console.log('size:', count.size, '| 101 viewed', count.get(101), 'times');

// Keys can be objects
const anu = { name: 'Anu' };
const faris = { name: 'Faris' };
const cart = new Map([[anu, 3], [faris, 1]]);
console.log(cart.get(anu), cart.has(faris));

// The same thing with a plain object breaks
const broken = {};
broken[anu] = 3;
broken[faris] = 1;               // same key "[object Object]"!
console.log(broken);

// Iterate and convert
for (const [id, n] of count) console.log(`product ${id}: ${n}`);
const asObject = Object.fromEntries(count);
console.log(asObject);           // keys became strings
console.log(new Map(Object.entries({ a: 1, b: 2 })));

Objects turn every key into a string, so two different objects collide. Try deleting a key and logging size.

Set: uniqueness and set algebra

A Set stores each value once. Equality uses the SameValueZero rule: like ===, except NaN equals NaN. Objects are compared by reference, so two objects with the same content are two different members. The two big uses are removing duplicates ([...new Set(list)]) and fast membership tests: set.has(x) stays fast as the set grows, while array.includes(x) scans the whole array. For a list of thousands of blocked ids checked in a loop, that difference is real.

ES2025 added set algebra methods that return new sets and never change the original: union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, plus the checks isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf and isDisjointFrom. They shipped in all major browsers in 2024 and in Node 22. For older targets, check the MDN compatibility table or caniuse.com, and fall back to a filter:

const both = new Set([...a].filter((x) => b.has(x)));   // intersection
const onlyA = new Set([...a].filter((x) => !b.has(x))); // difference

Try it: Set for uniqueness, plus ES2025 Set methods

JavaScript

const tags = ['js', 'web', 'js', 'api', 'web', 'css'];
const unique = new Set(tags);
console.log(unique, unique.size);
console.log([...unique]);                 // back to an array
console.log(unique.has('api'), unique.has('php'));

unique.add('html').delete('css');
console.log(unique);

// Objects are unique by reference, not by content
const s = new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]);
console.log('object set size:', s.size);

// Set algebra (ES2025)
const augBuyers = new Set(['Anu', 'Faris', 'Meera', 'John']);
const sepBuyers = new Set(['Faris', 'John', 'Zara']);
console.log('Either month:', augBuyers.union(sepBuyers));
console.log('Both months:', augBuyers.intersection(sepBuyers));
console.log('Lost in Sep:', augBuyers.difference(sepBuyers));
console.log('Only one month:', augBuyers.symmetricDifference(sepBuyers));
console.log(new Set(['Faris']).isSubsetOf(sepBuyers));

// Fallback for older runtimes
const both = [...augBuyers].filter((name) => sepBuyers.has(name));
console.log('Fallback:', both);

Change the course lists and rerun. The Set methods need a 2024+ browser or Node 22; check MDN compatibility for your targets.

WeakMap and WeakSet: data that does not leak

A normal Map holds its keys strongly: as long as the map exists, every key object stays in memory, even if the rest of your app forgot it. For a cache keyed by objects, that is a memory leak. A WeakMap holds its keys weakly. If the only remaining reference to an object is the WeakMap key, the garbage collector may remove the object and its entry.

The trade-off: keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols), and you cannot iterate a WeakMap or read its size, because entries can vanish at any time. Typical uses are caching results per object, storing extra data about DOM elements you do not own, and keeping private data for objects created by a library. WeakSet is the same idea for marking objects, for example “this form has already been initialised”.

Try it: WeakMap: data attached to objects

JavaScript

const totals = new WeakMap();
let computeCount = 0;

function cartTotal(cart) {
  if (totals.has(cart)) return totals.get(cart);
  computeCount++;
  const total = cart.items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  totals.set(cart, total);
  return total;
}

let cart = { items: [{ price: 149, qty: 2 }, { price: 20, qty: 5 }] };
console.log(cartTotal(cart), cartTotal(cart), cartTotal(cart));
console.log('computed', computeCount, 'time(s)');

// Immutable update = new object = fresh cache entry
cart = { ...cart, items: [...cart.items, { price: 899, qty: 1 }] };
console.log(cartTotal(cart), '| computed', computeCount, 'times');
// The old cart has no references left, so its entry can be collected.

try {
  totals.set('not-an-object', 1);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}
console.log(typeof totals.size, typeof totals.keys);

The cache never holds a cart alive. You cannot list a WeakMap: it has get, set, has and delete only.

JSON: what survives the trip

JSON.stringify walks your value and writes text. JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and objects, so everything else needs a rule:

ValueAs a propertyInside an array
undefined, functions, symbolsSkippednull
NaN, Infinitynullnull
DateISO string (via toJSON)ISO string
Map, Set{} (data lost){}
BigIntThrows TypeErrorThrows

The second argument, the replacer, controls the output. An array of key names acts as a whitelist. A function (key, value) => newValue is called for every value; return undefined to drop it. The third argument indents the output for humans (2 is common). Any object with a toJSON() method decides its own representation, which is how Date works.

JSON.parse takes an optional reviver with the same shape. It runs bottom-up after parsing, which makes it the right place to turn ISO strings back into Date objects. Also remember that JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid input, so wrap it in try/catch whenever the text comes from storage or the network.

Try it: JSON: replacers, revivers and dates

JavaScript

const order = {
  id: 42,
  placedAt: new Date('2026-09-15T09:30:00Z'),
  customer: { name: 'Meera', password: 'secret123' },
  note: undefined,
  print() {},
  tags: new Set(['gift']),
  total: 1249.5,
};

console.log(JSON.stringify(order));

// Replacer function: hide secrets, convert Sets
const safe = JSON.stringify(order, (key, value) => {
  if (key === 'password') return undefined;       // drop it
  if (value instanceof Set) return [...value];    // Set -> array
  return value;
}, 2);
console.log(safe);

// Replacer array: whitelist keys (applies at every level)
console.log(JSON.stringify(order, ['id', 'total']));

// Reviver: turn ISO date strings back into Date objects
const ISO = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/;
const back = JSON.parse(safe, (key, value) =>
  typeof value === 'string' && ISO.test(value) ? new Date(value) : value);
console.log(back.placedAt instanceof Date, back.placedAt.getUTCHours());

try {
  JSON.parse("{ id: 1 }");                         // keys need "quotes"
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name);
}

Look at what disappears in the first line. Then see how the reviver turns the ISO string back into a real Date.

Grouping with Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy

Before ES2024 everyone wrote the same reduce to group items. Now Object.groupBy(items, callback) does it: the callback returns a key for each item, and you get an object whose keys are the groups and whose values are arrays of items, in their original order. The result has a null prototype, so it has no toString or hasOwnProperty, and a group named 'constructor' is safe. Map.groupBy does the same but returns a Map, so keys can be numbers, booleans or objects without being converted to strings.

// What groupBy replaces
const byCategory = orders.reduce((acc, o) => {
  (acc[o.category] ??= []).push(o);
  return acc;
}, {});

Grouping gives you arrays; totals are one more step with Object.entries and reduce. Both functions are ES2024, available in current browsers and Node 21 and later.

Try it: Object.groupBy and Map.groupBy

JavaScript

const orders = [
  { id: 1, category: 'stationery', total: 180, city: 'Kochi' },
  { id: 2, category: 'bags', total: 899, city: 'Calicut' },
  { id: 3, category: 'stationery', total: 60, city: 'Kochi' },
  { id: 4, category: 'bottles', total: 698, city: 'Thrissur' },
  { id: 5, category: 'bags', total: 1798, city: 'Kochi' },
];

const byCategory = Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.category);
console.log(Object.keys(byCategory));
console.log(byCategory.bags.map((o) => o.id));

// Totals per group
const revenue = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(byCategory).map(([cat, list]) =>
    [cat, list.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0)])
);
console.table(revenue);

// Bucket by a computed label
const bySize = Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => (o.total >= 500 ? 'large' : 'small'));
console.log(bySize.large.length, 'large,', bySize.small.length, 'small');

// Map.groupBy keeps non-string keys (here: booleans)
const isKochi = Map.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.city === 'Kochi');
console.log(isKochi.get(true).length, 'Kochi orders');

// Result has no prototype: no toString, no hasOwnProperty
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(byCategory));

groupBy returns arrays per group. Add an order with category 'bags' and a new group appears.

JavaScript

const orders = [
  { id: 1, customer: 'Anu', city: 'Kochi', category: 'Stationery', total: 954 },
  { id: 2, customer: 'Faris', city: 'Calicut', category: 'Bags', total: 899 },
  { id: 3, customer: 'Anu', city: 'Kochi', category: 'Bottles', total: 698 },
  { id: 4, customer: 'Meera', city: 'Thrissur', category: 'Stationery', total: 340 },
  { id: 5, customer: 'John', city: 'Kochi', category: 'Bags', total: 1798 },
  { id: 6, customer: 'Zara', city: 'Calicut', category: 'Electronics', total: 2499 },
  { id: 7, customer: 'Faris', city: 'Calicut', category: 'Stationery', total: 120 },
  { id: 8, customer: 'Meera', city: 'Thrissur', category: 'Bottles', total: 349 },
];
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});
const cities = ['All', ...new Set(orders.map((o) => o.city))]; // unique, in order
let city = 'All';

function render() {
  const list = city === 'All' ? orders : orders.filter((o) => o.city === city);

  // Map: customer -> spend, to find the top customer
  const spend = new Map();
  for (const o of list) {
    spend.set(o.customer, (spend.get(o.customer) ?? 0) + o.total);
  }
  const [topName, topSpend] = [...spend].toSorted((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0];

  const revenue = list.reduce((s, o) => s + o.total, 0);
  const stats = [
    ['Revenue', inr.format(revenue)],
    ['Orders', list.length],
    ['Customers', new Set(list.map((o) => o.customer)).size],
    ['Top customer', `${topName} (${inr.format(topSpend)})`],
  ];
  document.querySelector('#stats').replaceChildren(...stats.map(([label, value]) => {
    const div = document.createElement('div');
    div.className = 'stat';
    const b = document.createElement('b');
    b.textContent = value;
    const span = document.createElement('span');
    span.textContent = label;
    div.append(b, span);
    return div;
  }));

  const groups = Object.groupBy(list, (o) => o.category);
  const rows = Object.entries(groups)
    .map(([cat, items]) => [cat, items.reduce((s, o) => s + o.total, 0)])
    .toSorted((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
  const max = rows[0][1];
  document.querySelector('#bars').replaceChildren(...rows.map(([cat, sum]) => {
    const row = document.createElement('div');
    row.className = 'bar';
    row.innerHTML = '<span></span><div class="track"><div class="fill"></div></div><span class="amt"></span>';
    row.children[0].textContent = cat;
    row.querySelector('.fill').style.width = (sum / max) * 100 + '%';
    row.children[2].textContent = inr.format(sum);
    return row;
  }));
  document.querySelector('#meta').textContent =
    `${Object.keys(groups).length} categories · ${city === 'All' ? 'all cities' : city}`;
  document.querySelectorAll('.chip').forEach((c) =>
    c.setAttribute('aria-pressed', c.textContent === city));
}

document.querySelector('#chips').append(...cities.map((name) => {
  const b = document.createElement('button');
  b.className = 'chip';
  b.textContent = name;
  b.addEventListener('click', () => { city = name; render(); });
  return b;
}));
render();
console.log('Cities from a Set:', cities);
console.log('Grouped:', Object.keys(Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.category)));

Example: Order Report

The lab builds the report a shop owner asks for at the end of the month. Given August and September orders, it prints:

  1. Revenue per category, sorted from highest to lowest, using Object.groupBy.
  2. Spend per customer in a Map, and the top three customers.
  3. Unique customers per month as Sets, then repeat customers (intersection), new customers (difference) and lost customers.
  4. A JSON export with a replacer that converts the Map and Sets and rounds money, then a reviver that restores the generatedAt date.
const report = {
  generatedAt: new Date(),
  spend,                       // a Map
  repeat,                      // a Set
};
const json = JSON.stringify(report, (key, value) => {
  if (value instanceof Map) return Object.fromEntries(value);
  if (value instanceof Set) return [...value].sort();
  return value;
}, 2);
const restored = JSON.parse(json, (key, value) =>
  key === 'generatedAt' ? new Date(value) : value);

Common mistakes

1. Using an object as a dictionary with object keys.

// Wrong: both keys become "[object Object]"
const seen = {};
seen[userA] = true;
// Fix
const seen2 = new Set();
seen2.add(userA);

2. Saving a Map or Set with JSON.stringify.

// Wrong: prints {} and the data is gone
localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(cartMap));
// Fix: convert to entries, and back when loading
localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify([...cartMap]));
const cart = new Map(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('cart') ?? '[]'));

3. Forgetting that dates come back as strings.

// Wrong: TypeError, placedAt is a string after parse
JSON.parse(text).placedAt.getFullYear();
// Fix: revive it (or wrap it with new Date(...) where you read it)
const order = JSON.parse(text, (k, v) => k === 'placedAt' ? new Date(v) : v);

4. Parsing without try/catch. Corrupted localStorage or an HTML error page from a server makes JSON.parse throw and can stop your whole app from starting. Catch it and fall back to a default.

// Wrong: one bad value crashes start-up
const prefs = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('prefs'));
// Fix
let prefs2;
try { prefs2 = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('prefs')) ?? {}; }
catch { prefs2 = {}; }

5. Using map.key = value. That sets a normal property on the Map object, not an entry. map.get('key') returns undefined and size does not change. Always use set and get.

// Wrong: a plain property, not an entry
stock.pen = 40;
console.log(stock.get('pen'), stock.size); // undefined 0
// Fix
stock.set('pen', 40);
console.log(stock.get('pen'), stock.size); // 40 1

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Remove duplicates from an array”: [...new Set(arr)]. Then mention it compares objects by reference, so for objects you dedupe by a key with a Map: [...new Map(list.map((x) => [x.id, x])).values()].
  • “Why is Set.has faster than includes?” Sets are hash-based, so a lookup does not scan every element. Say “roughly constant time versus linear time”, not invented numbers.
  • “What is a WeakMap for?” Associating data with objects without preventing garbage collection: caches, private data, DOM metadata.
  • “Deep copy with JSON?” Explain what is lost (dates, undefined, Map, Set, functions) and recommend structuredClone.
  • Security: JSON is data, never code. Never turn JSON text into code with eval; JSON.parse is safe and fast.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const ids = new Set([1, '1', 1, NaN, NaN]);
console.log(ids.size);
  • A 5
  • B 2
  • C 3
  • D 4

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const m = new Map();
m.set(1, 'number').set('1', 'string');
const o = {};
o[1] = 'number';
o['1'] = 'string';
console.log(m.size, Object.keys(o).length);
  • A 2 1
  • B 1 1
  • C 2 2
  • D 1 2

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const data = { a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: null, d: [undefined, NaN] };
console.log(JSON.stringify(data));
  • A {"a":null,"b":null,"c":null,"d":[null,null]}
  • B {"c":null,"d":[]}
  • C {"c":null,"d":[undefined,NaN]}
  • D {"c":null,"d":[null,null]}

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const text = JSON.stringify({ at: new Date(0) });
const back = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(typeof back.at, back.at.slice(0, 4));
  • A object 1970
  • B string 1970
  • C number 0
  • D TypeError

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const g = Object.groupBy([3, 8, 5, 2], (n) => (n > 4 ? 'big' : 'small'));
console.log(Object.keys(g).join(','), g.big.length);
  • A big,small 2
  • B small,big 1
  • C small,big 2
  • D big,small 1

Answers

  1. C. 1 and '1' are different values, the second 1 is a duplicate, and Set treats NaN as equal to NaN. That leaves 1, '1' and NaN.
  2. A. Map keeps 1 and '1' as different keys. A plain object converts the key 1 to the string '1', so the second write overwrites the first.
  3. D. Properties holding undefined or functions are skipped. Inside arrays they cannot be skipped (it would shift the indexes), so they become null, and NaN always becomes null.
  4. B. Date.prototype.toJSON turns the date into an ISO string, and JSON.parse has no idea it was a date. Use a reviver to turn it back into a Date.
  5. C. Groups are created in the order their first member appears: 3 is small, so small comes first. big holds 8 and 5.

terms.definition: A keyed collection where keys can be any value (objects included), iteration follows insertion order and size is a property.
A collection of unique values; has() checks membership quickly. Uniqueness uses SameValueZero, so NaN equals NaN.
A Map whose keys must be objects and are held weakly: when nothing else references the key, the entry can be garbage-collected. It cannot be iterated.
JavaScript Object Notation: a text format for data with strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and objects only.
A function or key list passed to JSON.stringify that filters or transforms values while serialising.
A function passed to JSON.parse that can transform each value while parsing, for example turning ISO strings back into Date objects.
ES2024 function that splits an iterable into a null-prototype object of arrays, keyed by the string your callback returns.

lessons.examTip: When an interviewer asks “object or Map?”, answer: Map for dynamic keys, non-string keys, frequent adds and deletes, and when you need size or order; plain objects for fixed-shape records and JSON.

quiz.question: You need to count how many times each product id (a number) appears, then list them in first-seen order with a total count. Which structure fits best?
options: A Map from id to count
A Set of ids
A WeakMap from id to count
An array of ids, searched with indexOf each time
quiz.explanation: Map keeps number keys as numbers, keeps insertion order and has size. A Set cannot store counts, and WeakMap keys must be objects.

quiz.question: What does JSON.stringify({ at: new Date(0), fn() {}, note: undefined }) contain?
options: All three properties
Only fn and note
Only at, as an ISO date string
An error, because functions cannot be serialised
quiz.explanation: Date has a toJSON method that returns an ISO string. Functions and undefined properties are skipped silently, which is a common source of lost data.

quiz.question: Why would you choose a WeakMap to cache a computed total for each cart object?
options: WeakMap lookups are faster than Map lookups
WeakMap can be serialised to JSON
WeakMap sorts its keys automatically
When a cart object is no longer used anywhere, its cache entry can be garbage-collected too
quiz.explanation: A normal Map would keep every cart alive forever through its keys, which is a memory leak. WeakMap holds keys weakly, so the cache never outlives the objects.

quiz.question: setA.intersection(setB) is part of ES2025. What is the professional way to use it in a product?
options: Never use new features until they are ten years old
Check support on MDN or caniuse.com for your target browsers and Node version, and fall back to filter with has() if needed
Assume it works everywhere because it is in the standard
Only use it inside try/catch
quiz.explanation: New standard features arrive in runtimes at different times. Check the compatibility tables for your targets; a filter over one set with has() on the other is a simple fallback.

lessons.title: Iterators, generators and symbols
lessons.summaryHtml:
Why does for…of work on arrays, strings, Maps and Sets but not on plain objects? Because of the iteration protocol: any object with a [Symbol.iterator] method that returns an iterator (an object with next()) can be looped, spread and destructured. In this lesson you learn that protocol and make your own classes iterable.

Generators (function* and yield) are the easy way to write iterators. They pause and resume, which makes lazy and even infinite sequences possible. ES2025 iterator helpers add map, filter and take directly on iterators. Finally you meet symbols: unique keys, plus the well-known symbols that let your objects plug into built-in language behaviour.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a ticket counter with a queue. The counter does not need to see the whole queue at once; it just calls “next!” and one person steps forward, until nobody is left. That is an iterator: something you can keep asking for the next value until it says “done”.

A generator is a function that can pause in the middle, hand you a value, and continue later from exactly where it stopped. And a symbol is a special kind of key that can never clash with any other key, which is how JavaScript itself adds hooks such as “this is how you iterate me” to objects without breaking your property names.

Why it matters

You use iteration every day: for…of, spread [...set], destructuring, Array.from, Promise.all and new Map(entries) all run on the same protocol. When you understand it, your own classes (a cart, a playlist, a paginated API client) can work with all of those features for free. Generators make it easy to produce data on demand: invoice numbers, pages of results, steps of a wizard or an endless feed. Lazy pipelines avoid building huge temporary arrays. And symbols explain how Symbol.iterator, Symbol.toPrimitive and friends let objects customise built-in behaviour, a common interview topic.

How it works

The iteration protocol

The protocol has two parts:

  • An iterable is any object with a method under the key Symbol.iterator. Calling it returns an iterator.
  • An iterator is an object with a next() method. Each call returns { value, done }. When done is true, the sequence is over.

So for (const x of list) is roughly this:

const iterator = list[Symbol.iterator]();
let step = iterator.next();
while (!step.done) {
  const x = step.value;
  // ...loop body...
  step = iterator.next();
}
// if the loop exits early (break, return, throw),
// for...of calls iterator.return?.() so the source can clean up

Arrays, strings, Map, Set, arguments, NodeList and typed arrays are iterable. Plain objects are not, on purpose: should a loop give you keys, values or both? You choose with Object.keys, Object.values or Object.entries, which return arrays. Strings iterate by code point, so [...'Hi👋'] has three items even though 'Hi👋'.length is 4.

Try it: The iteration protocol by hand

JavaScript

const seats = ['A1', 'A2', 'A3'];

// What for...of does behind the scenes
const it = seats[Symbol.iterator]();
console.log(it.next());
console.log(it.next());
console.log(it.next());
console.log(it.next()); // done: true

// Every consumer uses the same protocol
const [first, ...others] = seats;          // destructuring
console.log(first, others);
console.log([...'Hi👋']);                  // strings iterate by code point
console.log(Math.max(...new Set([3, 9, 4])));
console.log(Array.from(new Map([['a', 1]])));

// Plain objects are NOT iterable
const prices = { pen: 20, bag: 899 };
try {
  for (const p of prices) console.log(p);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}
for (const [item, price] of Object.entries(prices)) {
  console.log(item, price);                // entries() gives an iterable array
}

for…of does exactly what the manual loop does. Try the same code with a string that contains an emoji.

Making your own objects iterable

To make an object iterable, give it a [Symbol.iterator]() method. You can write the iterator by hand, returning an object with next() that tracks its own position. That works, but it is easy to get the done flag wrong. The usual professional shortcut is to make the method a generator by putting * in front of it: the generator object it returns already is an iterator.

class Cart {
  #lines = [];
  *[Symbol.iterator]() {
    yield* this.#lines;    // delegate to the array's own iterator
  }
}
for (const line of new Cart()) { /* works */ }

A class can also offer several named iterators, like Map does with keys(), values() and entries(). Keep the private data private: callers get the values one by one but never the internal array, so they cannot mutate it.

Try it: Make your own class iterable

JavaScript

// 1. A hand-written iterator: a range of seat numbers
const range = {
  from: 1,
  to: 4,
  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    let current = this.from;
    const last = this.to;
    return {
      next: () => current <= last
        ? { value: current++, done: false }
        : { value: undefined, done: true },
    };
  },
};
console.log([...range]);

// 2. A class whose iterator is a generator method
class Cart {
  #lines = [];
  add(title, price, qty = 1) {
    this.#lines.push({ title, price, qty });
    return this;
  }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() {              // generator method
    for (const line of this.#lines) yield line;
  }
  *titles() {                          // extra, named iterator
    for (const { title } of this) yield title;
  }
}

const cart = new Cart()
  .add('Notebook', 149, 2)
  .add('Gel pen', 20, 5)
  .add('Bottle', 349);

for (const { title, price, qty } of cart) {
  console.log(`${title.padEnd(9)} ${qty} x ${price}`);
}
console.log([...cart.titles()]);
const total = [...cart].reduce((s, l) => s + l.price * l.qty, 0);
console.log('Total:', total);

Both approaches work with for…of and spread. The generator version is shorter and handles the done flag for you.

Generators: functions that pause

A generator function is declared with function*. Calling it does not run the body; it returns a generator object. Each next() runs the body until the next yield, hands that value out, and freezes the function with all its local variables intact. A return ends the sequence with done: true. Because nothing runs until it is asked for, a generator can safely contain an infinite loop: the caller decides how many values to take.

SyntaxMeaning
function* name() {}Declares a generator function
yield valuePause and produce value
yield* iterableProduce every value from another iterable
return valueFinish; value appears with done: true (spread and for…of ignore it)
gen.return()Stop early; finally blocks still run

Real uses: id and invoice-number sequences, splitting data into pages or chunks, walking a tree (a category menu, a folder structure) with yield* for the children, and step-by-step flows. You will meet async generators (async function* with for await…of) in the async module; they are perfect for paginated APIs:

async function* allProducts(pageSize = 30) {
  for (let skip = 0; ; skip += pageSize) {
    const res = await fetch(
      `https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=${pageSize}&skip=${skip}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const { products, total } = await res.json();
    yield* products;
    if (skip + pageSize >= total) return;
  }
}
// for await (const p of allProducts()) { ... }

Try it: Generators pause and resume

JavaScript

function* checkout() {
  console.log('  -> validating cart');
  yield 'validated';
  console.log('  -> charging card');
  yield 'paid';
  console.log('  -> sending email');
  return 'done';
}

const steps = checkout();          // nothing runs yet
console.log('created');
console.log(steps.next());
console.log(steps.next());
console.log(steps.next());
console.log(steps.next());         // finished: stays done

// Infinite and lazy: invoice numbers
function* invoiceNumbers(prefix = 'INV', start = 1) {
  for (let n = start; ; n++) yield `${prefix}-${String(n).padStart(4, '0')}`;
}
const ids = invoiceNumbers('INV-2026', 41);
console.log(ids.next().value, ids.next().value, ids.next().value);

// yield* delegates to another iterable
function* allSeats() {
  yield* ['A1', 'A2'];
  yield* ['B1', 'B2'];
}
console.log([...allSeats()]);

// break calls return(), so finally blocks run
function* withCleanup() {
  try { yield 1; yield 2; yield 3; }
  finally { console.log('cleanup ran'); }
}
for (const n of withCleanup()) { if (n === 2) break; console.log(n); }

Read the log order: the body only runs when next() is called. The infinite generator is safe because nothing asks for more than 3 values.

Lazy pipelines and iterator helpers (ES2025)

Array methods are eager: list.filter(a).map(b).slice(0, 4) filters the whole list, maps every survivor into a new array, and only then keeps four. ES2025 adds iterator helpers, methods that live on every iterator (generators included) and work lazily, one value at a time: map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, plus the consumers toArray, reduce, forEach, some, every and find. Iterator.from(x) wraps any iterable, such as a Set, so you can use them there too.

With take(4) at the end, the pipeline pulls values only until it has four results, so it works even on an infinite generator. They are supported in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, and in Node 22, but they are recent, so older phones and browsers may lack them. Check the MDN compatibility table or caniuse.com for your exact targets; for older ones, write the loop with for…of and break.

Remember: an iterator can be consumed only once. After toArray() it is finished. If you need the values again, call the generator function again for a fresh iterator.

Try it: Lazy pipelines with iterator helpers (ES2025)

JavaScript

let made = 0;
function* products() {                  // pretend this is a huge catalogue
  for (let id = 1; ; id++) {
    made++;
    yield { id, price: (id * 137) % 1000, inStock: id % 3 !== 0 };
  }
}

const cheapInStock = products()
  .filter((p) => p.inStock)
  .filter((p) => p.price < 500)
  .map((p) => `#${p.id} Rs ${p.price}`)
  .take(4)
  .toArray();
console.log(cheapInStock);
console.log('products made:', made);

// Iterator.from wraps any iterable or iterator
const tags = new Set(['js', 'dom', 'css', 'api']);
console.log(Iterator.from(tags).drop(1).map((t) => t.toUpperCase()).toArray());

// Other helpers
console.log(products().take(5).reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0));
console.log(products().some((p) => p.price > 900));
console.log([...products().take(3).flatMap((p) => [p.id, -p.id])]);

// Arrays have map too, but eagerly: a full new array at every step.
// Helpers work on one value at a time.

Only the products needed are generated: count the “made” lines. Iterator helpers are recent (Node 22 and current browsers); check the MDN compatibility table for your targets.

Symbols and the well-known symbols

Symbol('label') creates a new, unique primitive. The label is only a description for debugging; two symbols with the same label are still different. Symbol keys never clash with string keys, and they are skipped by Object.keys, for…in and JSON.stringify. That makes them useful for metadata that libraries attach to your objects. They are not private: Object.getOwnPropertySymbols reveals them. For real privacy, use #private class fields. Symbol.for('key') returns a shared symbol from a global registry, the same one everywhere in your app.

The language uses well-known symbols as hooks you can implement:

SymbolLets your object…
Symbol.iteratorwork with for…of, spread and destructuring
Symbol.asyncIteratorwork with for await…of
Symbol.toPrimitivedecide how it converts to a string or number
Symbol.toStringTagset the name in Object.prototype.toString output
Symbol.hasInstancecustomise instanceof (rarely needed)

Try it: Symbols and well-known symbols

JavaScript

const id = Symbol('id');
const id2 = Symbol('id');
console.log(id === id2, id.description);

const user = { name: 'Anu', [id]: 7 };
console.log(Object.keys(user), JSON.stringify(user));
console.log(user[id], Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(user));

// A shared symbol from the global registry
console.log(Symbol.for('app.id') === Symbol.for('app.id'));

class Money {
  constructor(paise) { this.paise = paise; }
  [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) {
    if (hint === 'number') return this.paise / 100;
    return new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
      style: 'currency', currency: 'INR',
    }).format(this.paise / 100);
  }
  get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return 'Money'; }
}

const price = new Money(124950);
console.log(`Price: ${price}`);         // hint "string"
console.log(+price, price * 2);           // hint "number"
console.log(Object.prototype.toString.call(price));
console.log(typeof Symbol.iterator, typeof Symbol.asyncIterator);

Symbol keys never clash and stay out of keys and JSON. Symbol.toPrimitive decides how Money turns into a string or a number.

Finally, a generator driving a real UI. The pages generator slices the catalogue into pages of four, and the Load more button pulls exactly one page per click with feed.next(). The generator remembers its position between clicks, so there is no page counter to manage.

Try it: Paged catalogue with a generator

HTML

<main class="shop">
  <header>
    <h1>Ralfiz Store</h1>
    <p id="status" class="muted" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </header>
  <ul id="grid" class="grid"></ul>
  <button id="more" class="more">Load more</button>
</main>

CSS

*{box-sizing:border-box}
body{margin:0;padding:16px;background:#f6f7fb;color:#1c2030;font:14px/1.45 system-ui,-apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif}
.shop{max-width:760px;margin:0 auto}
header{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:12px}
h1{font-size:18px;margin:0}

JavaScript

const catalogue = [
  ['Notebook', 149, 4.6, '📓'], ['Gel pen', 20, 4.2, '🖊️'],
  ['Laptop bag', 899, 4.8, '💼'], ['Steel bottle', 349, 4.5, '🧴'],
  ['Desk lamp', 1299, 4.4, '💡'], ['Headphones', 2499, 4.7, '🎧'],
  ['Backpack', 1199, 4.3, '🎒'], ['Sticky notes', 60, 4.1, '🗒️'],
  ['Mouse', 599, 4.5, '🖱️'], ['Keyboard', 1499, 4.6, '⌨️'],
  ['Mug', 249, 4.0, '☕'], ['Planner', 399, 4.4, '📅'],
  ['Calculator', 699, 4.2, '🧮'], ['Scissors', 99, 3.9, '✂️'],
].map(([title, price, rating, icon], i) =>
  ({ id: i + 1, title, price, rating, icon }));

// A generator that hands out one page at a time
function* pages(items, size) {
  for (let start = 0; start < items.length; start += size) {
    yield items.slice(start, start + size);
  }
}

const feed = pages(catalogue, 4);
const grid = document.querySelector('#grid');
const button = document.querySelector('#more');
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
  style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
});
let shown = 0;

function card({ title, price, rating, icon }) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'card';
  li.innerHTML = '<span class="icon" aria-hidden="true"></span><h2></h2>' +
    '<div class="row"><span class="price"></span><span class="rating"></span></div>';
  li.querySelector('.icon').textContent = icon;
  li.querySelector('h2').textContent = title;
  li.querySelector('.price').textContent = inr.format(price);
  li.querySelector('.rating').textContent = '★ ' + rating;
  return li;
}

function loadMore() {
  const { value: page, done } = feed.next();   // pull ONE page
  if (done) return;
  grid.append(...page.map(card));
  shown += page.length;
  status.textContent = `Showing ${shown} of ${catalogue.length}`;
  if (shown === catalogue.length) {
    button.disabled = true;
    button.textContent = 'All products loaded';
  }
  console.log('Loaded page:', page.map((p) => p.id));
}

button.addEventListener('click', loadMore);
loadMore();
loadMore(); // two pages to start

Example: Store catalogue toolkit

In the lab you build four small tools for the Ralfiz Store:

  1. invoiceNumbers(prefix, start): an infinite generator that yields INV-2026-0041, INV-2026-0042 and so on.
  2. A Catalogue class whose [Symbol.iterator] yields only in-stock products, plus a *byCategory(name) generator.
  3. chunk(iterable, size): a generator that groups any iterable into arrays of size, for printing a catalogue three per row.
  4. A lazy query with iterator helpers: the first three in-stock products under ₹500 with a rating of at least 4.
function* chunk(iterable, size) {
  let batch = [];
  for (const item of iterable) {
    batch.push(item);
    if (batch.length === size) { yield batch; batch = []; }
  }
  if (batch.length) yield batch;   // the last, shorter batch
}

Common mistakes

1. Reusing a finished iterator.

// Wrong: the second spread is empty
const it = cart[Symbol.iterator]();
console.log([...it], [...it]);   // [ ... ] [ ]
// Fix: ask the iterable for a fresh iterator each time
console.log([...cart], [...cart]);

2. Spreading an infinite generator.

// Wrong: never finishes and freezes the tab
const all = [...invoiceNumbers()];
// Fix: limit it first
const firstFive = invoiceNumbers().take(5).toArray();

3. Expecting the body to run on call. const g = loadSteps(); does nothing until g.next(). If a generator “does not work”, check that something consumes it.

// Wrong: nothing logs, the body has not started
const g = loadSteps();
// Fix: consume it
for (const step of loadSteps()) console.log(step);

4. Forgetting the * on a generator method.

// Wrong: SyntaxError, yield is not allowed in a normal method
[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* this.items; }
// Fix
*[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* this.items; }

5. Treating symbols as private. Symbol keys are hidden from casual listing but are fully readable with Object.getOwnPropertySymbols. Use #fields for privacy.

// Wrong: anyone can read it
const secret = Symbol('secret');
const acc = { [secret]: 'pin-1234' };
console.log(acc[Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(acc)[0]]); // pin-1234
// Fix: a private field
class Account { #pin = 'pin-1234'; }

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Iterable vs iterator?” An iterable can produce iterators (it has Symbol.iterator); an iterator is the cursor with next(). Arrays are iterable; arr.values() is an iterator. Generator objects are both.
  • “Why generators?” Lazy and infinite sequences, pausable logic, and the simplest way to implement iterators. Libraries such as Redux-Saga are built on them.
  • “Array-like vs iterable?” Array-like has length and indexes; iterable has Symbol.iterator. Array.from accepts both; spread needs an iterable.
  • Performance: for small arrays, plain array methods are simplest and fast. Reach for generators and iterator helpers when data is large, streamed, paginated or potentially endless.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

function* g() {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
  return 3;
}
console.log([...g()].join(','));
  • A 1,2,3
  • B 1,2
  • C 3
  • D 1,2,undefined

Snippet 2. What is logged?

function* nums() {
  for (let i = 1; ; i++) {
    console.log('make ' + i);
    yield i;
  }
}
const it = nums();
console.log('start');
it.next();
  • A 
    make 1
start
  • B start
  • C 
    start
make 1
make 2
  • D 
    start
make 1

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const it = [10, 20][Symbol.iterator]();
it.next();
it.next();
console.log(JSON.stringify(it.next()));
  • A {"done":true}
  • B {"value":undefined,"done":true}
  • C {"value":null,"done":true}
  • D {"value":20,"done":false}

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const id = Symbol('id');
const user = { name: 'Ana', [id]: 7 };
console.log(Object.keys(user).length, JSON.stringify(user));
  • A 2 {"name":"Ana","id":7}
  • B 2 {"name":"Ana"}
  • C 1 {"name":"Ana"}
  • D 1 {"name":"Ana","Symbol(id)":7}

Snippet 5. What is logged?

console.log(
  Symbol('a') === Symbol('a'),
  Symbol.for('a') === Symbol.for('a')
);
  • A true true
  • B false true
  • C false false
  • D true false

Answers

  1. B. Spread and for…of stop when done becomes true, and the return value arrives in the same object as done: true, so it is ignored. Only yielded values are collected.
  2. D. Calling nums() runs nothing. The first next() runs the body up to the first yield, so exactly one “make” line appears, after “start”.
  3. A. The third call finds no more items and returns { value: undefined, done: true }. JSON.stringify skips properties whose value is undefined.
  4. C. Symbol-keyed properties are skipped by Object.keys and by JSON.stringify. They are still there: user[id] is 7.
  5. B. Every Symbol() call creates a new, unique symbol. Symbol.for looks the key up in a global registry and returns the same symbol each time.

terms.definition: An object with a [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an iterator. Arrays, strings, Map, Set and NodeList are iterable.
An object with a next() method that returns { value, done } each time it is called.
A function declared with function* that returns a generator; its body runs only when next() is called and pauses at each yield.
Pauses a generator and hands a value to the caller; yield* delegates to another iterable.
Computing each value only when it is asked for, so long or infinite sequences cost nothing until used.
ES2025 methods on iterators such as map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, reduce and toArray, plus Iterator.from.
A primitive that is always unique, used as a property key that cannot clash; well-known symbols such as Symbol.iterator customise language behaviour.

lessons.examTip: If an interviewer asks how for…of works, say: it calls obj[Symbol.iterator](), then calls next() until done is true, and calls return() if you break early.

quiz.question: What makes an object usable in for…of?
options: It has a length property
It is an instance of Array
It has a [Symbol.iterator] method that returns an object with next()
It has only numeric keys
quiz.explanation: for…of relies only on the iteration protocol. length and numeric keys make an object array-like, which Array.from understands, but for…of needs Symbol.iterator.

quiz.question: You call const gen = makeIds(); on a generator function that logs “start” in its first line. When does “start” appear?
options: On the first gen.next() call
Immediately, when makeIds() is called
Never: generators cannot log
Only after the generator finishes
quiz.explanation: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object. The body starts running at the first next() and pauses at each yield.

quiz.question: Why is Iterator.from(allProducts()).filter(inStock).take(5).toArray() efficient even if allProducts() is an infinite generator?
options: toArray sorts the values first
filter and take are lazy: values are pulled one at a time and it stops after five matches
The engine converts the generator to an array in the background
It is not efficient: it runs forever
quiz.explanation: Iterator helpers are lazy. take(5) stops pulling as soon as it has five values, so only as many products as needed are ever generated.

quiz.question: Which statement about symbols is correct?
options: Symbol('id') === Symbol('id') is true
Symbol-keyed properties appear in Object.keys and JSON.stringify
Symbols are objects created with new Symbol()
Every Symbol() call creates a unique value, and symbol keys are skipped by Object.keys, for…in and JSON.stringify
quiz.explanation: Symbols are unique primitives (new Symbol() throws). Symbol keys are hidden from the usual key listings; Object.getOwnPropertySymbols or Reflect.ownKeys reveal them. Use Symbol.for for a shared, registry-wide symbol.

lessons.title: Prototypes and inheritance
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every JavaScript object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype. When you read a property that the object does not have, JavaScript follows that link and looks there, then on that object’s prototype, and so on until it reaches null. This prototype chain is how arrays get map, how every object gets toString, and how inheritance works in JavaScript.

You learn Object.create, constructor functions and the .prototype property, the difference between __proto__, prototype and Object.getPrototypeOf, and how to tell own properties from inherited ones. Then you see that class is mostly a cleaner syntax for exactly the same machinery, which prepares you for the next lesson.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Imagine a new employee at the Ralfiz Store. When a customer asks something they do not know, they ask their team lead. If the team lead does not know, the team lead asks the manager, and so on up to the owner. If nobody knows, the answer is “we don’t have that”. Nobody copies all the knowledge into the new employee; they delegate questions upward.

JavaScript objects work the same way. Each object has a hidden link, called [[Prototype]], to another object. When you read obj.x and obj has no x, the engine asks its prototype, then that object’s prototype, and so on. The line of objects is the prototype chain. It ends at null, and if nobody had x, you get undefined.

Why it matters

Prototypes are not an old curiosity; they are how the language works today. Every array method, every string method and every class method you call is found by walking a prototype chain. Understanding it explains many everyday puzzles: why for…in shows keys you did not add, why 'constructor' in {} is true, why a method “lost” its data, what instanceof actually checks, and why class behaves the way it does. It is also one of the most common interview topics for front-end roles, and reading library code or older codebases (full of constructor functions) requires it.

How it works

Property lookup walks the chain

Reading a property follows a simple algorithm:

  1. Does the object have an own property with this key? Return it.
  2. Otherwise, move to Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) and repeat.
  3. If the prototype is null, stop and return undefined.

A method found up the chain still runs with this set to the object you called it on (the thing left of the dot). That is why one shared describe function on a prototype can describe many different objects.

Writing is different: an assignment such as obj.x = 5 creates or updates an own property on obj. It never changes the prototype. That own property now shadows the inherited one for this object only. (The exception is an inherited setter or a read-only inherited property, which you will meet with classes.)

phone  { model: 'R1' }
  -> device  { brand, describe }
    -> Object.prototype  { toString, hasOwnProperty, ... }
      -> null

Try it: Property lookup walks the chain

JavaScript

const device = {
  brand: 'Ralfiz',
  describe() {
    return `${this.brand} ${this.model}`;
  },
};

const phone = Object.create(device);  // phone's prototype is device
phone.model = 'R1';

console.log(phone.describe());          // found on device, this = phone
console.log(phone.brand, phone.color);  // inherited, then missing

// Walk the chain by hand
let level = phone;
while (level) {
  console.log(Object.keys(level));
  level = Object.getPrototypeOf(level);
}

// Shadowing: an own property hides the inherited one
phone.brand = 'Ralfiz Pro';
console.log(phone.brand, '| device still says', device.brand);
delete phone.brand;
console.log(phone.brand);

// Writes never go up the chain; they create own properties
console.log(Object.hasOwn(phone, 'model'), Object.hasOwn(phone, 'describe'));
console.log(typeof phone.toString);     // from Object.prototype

Add a sound property to phone and run again: the own property shadows the one on device. Then delete it and the inherited value comes back.

Object.create: choose the prototype directly

Object.create(proto) makes a new empty object whose prototype is proto. It is the most direct way to see delegation: put shared methods in one object, and create many objects that point to it. The methods exist once in memory, and adding a method to the prototype later makes it available to every object immediately, because they look it up at call time rather than copying it.

Object.create(null) makes an object with no prototype. It has no toString, no hasOwnProperty and no constructor, which makes it a safe dictionary when keys come from users: a key named '__proto__' or 'constructor' cannot collide with anything. (Object.groupBy from the previous lesson returns exactly this kind of object. A Map is often the even better choice.)

Try it: Object.create and shared methods

JavaScript

const accountMethods = {
  deposit(amount) {
    this.balance += amount;
    return this;
  },
  statement() {
    return `${this.owner}: Rs ${this.balance}`;
  },
};

function createAccount(owner, balance = 0) {
  const acc = Object.create(accountMethods);
  acc.owner = owner;
  acc.balance = balance;
  return acc;
}

const accounts = [
  createAccount('Anu', 500),
  createAccount('Faris'),
  createAccount('Meera', 90),
];
accounts[1].deposit(250).deposit(100);
accounts.forEach((a) => console.log(a.statement()));
console.log('Shared method:', accounts[0].deposit === accounts[2].deposit);

// Add a method later: every account gets it instantly
accountMethods.isEmpty = function () { return this.balance === 0; };
console.log(accounts.map((a) => a.isEmpty()));

// A dictionary with no prototype
const plain = {};
const dict = Object.create(null);
console.log('constructor' in plain, 'constructor' in dict);
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(dict));
try {
  console.log(dict.toString());
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ': no toString on a null-prototype object');
}

All three accounts share one deposit function. Object.create(null) makes a safe dictionary with no inherited keys.

Constructor functions and .prototype

Before classes existed, reusable “types” were written as constructor functions: normal functions, capitalised by convention, called with new. Every normal function has a .prototype property holding a plain object. new Product('Pen', 20) does four things:

  1. Creates a new empty object.
  2. Sets its prototype to Product.prototype.
  3. Runs Product with this bound to the new object, so it can set fields.
  4. Returns the new object (unless the function explicitly returns another object).

So fields such as title become own properties of each instance, and methods placed on Product.prototype are shared by all instances. Inheritance links two prototypes: DigitalProduct.prototype = Object.create(Product.prototype), plus calling the parent with Product.call(this, …) inside the child constructor. It works, but it is easy to forget a step, which is one reason classes were added.

Watch out: calling a constructor function without new in a classic (non-strict) script runs it with this set to the global object, silently creating global variables. In strict mode this is undefined and it throws. Classes always throw if called without new.

Try it: Constructor functions, .prototype and new

JavaScript

function Product(title, price) {
  this.title = title;
  this.price = price;
}
Product.prototype.withTax = function (rate = 0.18) {
  return Math.round(this.price * (1 + rate));
};

const pen = new Product('Gel pen', 20);
console.log(pen, pen.withTax());
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(pen) === Product.prototype);
console.log(pen.constructor === Product);

// What "new" does, in four steps
function construct(Ctor, ...args) {
  const obj = Object.create(Ctor.prototype); // 1-2. new object, linked
  const result = Ctor.apply(obj, args);      // 3. run with this = obj
  return result instanceof Object ? result : obj; // 4. return it
}
console.log(construct(Product, 'Bag', 899).withTax());

// Inheritance the old way
function DigitalProduct(title, price, sizeMb) {
  Product.call(this, title, price);          // parent sets its fields
  this.sizeMb = sizeMb;
}
DigitalProduct.prototype = Object.create(Product.prototype);
DigitalProduct.prototype.constructor = DigitalProduct;
DigitalProduct.prototype.withTax = function () {
  return Product.prototype.withTax.call(this, 0.12); // "super" call
};

const course = new DigitalProduct('JS course', 999, 850);
console.log(course.withTax(), course instanceof Product);

const oops = Product('Mug', 249);            // forgot new!
console.log(oops, typeof globalThis.title);  // leaked a global

This is how inheritance was written before classes, and how classes still work underneath. Try calling Product without new.

__proto__ vs prototype vs Object.getPrototypeOf

These three names confuse almost everyone at first, so learn them as a table:

NameExists onMeansUse it?
Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)Any objectThis object’s own prototype (what lookups use)Yes, the standard way to read it
Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, p)Any objectChanges the prototype of an existing objectRarely: slow in engines; prefer Object.create
obj.__proto__Objects inheriting from Object.prototypeLegacy getter/setter for the same linkAvoid in code; fine in the console
Fn.prototypeFunctions and classesThe object future new Fn() instances will inherit fromYes, when working with constructors

The key insight: Product.prototype is not the prototype of Product. It is the prototype of instances. The prototype of the function Product itself is Function.prototype, which is where call, apply and bind come from.

Own vs inherited properties

ToolOwnInheritedNon-enumerableSymbols
Object.hasOwn(obj, k)YesNoYesYes
k in objYesYesYesYes
Object.keys(obj)YesNoNoNo
for (k in obj)YesYesNoNo
Reflect.ownKeys(obj)YesNoYesYes

Object.hasOwn (ES2022) replaces obj.hasOwnProperty(k), which breaks on null-prototype objects and on objects that define their own hasOwnProperty. instanceof is also a chain walk: x instanceof Fn asks “is Fn.prototype anywhere in x’s chain?”

Try it: __proto__ vs prototype, own vs inherited

JavaScript

function Booking(guest) { this.guest = guest; }
Booking.prototype.status = 'pending';       // inherited data
Booking.prototype.confirm = function () { this.status = 'confirmed'; };

const b = new Booking('Anu');

// Three names, two different things
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(b) === Booking.prototype); // the link
console.log(b.__proto__ === Booking.prototype);       // legacy accessor
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Booking) === Function.prototype);
console.log(b.prototype);                    // instances have no .prototype

// Own vs inherited
console.log(Object.hasOwn(b, 'guest'), Object.hasOwn(b, 'status'));
console.log('status' in b);                  // in walks the chain
const forIn = [];
for (const key in b) forIn.push(key);
console.log('for...in:', forIn, '| keys:', Object.keys(b));

b.confirm();                                 // creates an OWN status
console.log(Object.hasOwn(b, 'status'), b.status, Booking.prototype.status);

// instanceof checks whether Booking.prototype is anywhere in the chain
console.log(b instanceof Booking, b instanceof Object, [] instanceof Object);
console.log(Object.create(null) instanceof Object);

for…in includes inherited enumerable keys; Object.keys does not. Use Object.getPrototypeOf in real code, not __proto__.

Classes are syntax over prototypes

The class keyword (ES2015) builds the same structure with less ceremony. typeof a class is 'function'; its methods are stored on Class.prototype; extends sets Child.prototype’s prototype to Parent.prototype; and super.method() calls the parent’s version. extends also links a second chain, from Child to Parent itself, which is how static methods are inherited.

Classes are not only sugar. They add real guarantees: class bodies are always strict mode, calling a class without new throws, methods are non-enumerable (so they do not show up in for…in), and classes support #private fields, static blocks and a correctly ordered super(). You will use them in the next lesson. But when something odd happens with a class, the prototype chain is still where the answer is.

Try it: Classes are syntax over prototypes

JavaScript

class Product {
  constructor(title, price) {
    this.title = title;
    this.price = price;
  }
  withTax(rate = 0.18) {
    return Math.round(this.price * (1 + rate));
  }
  static compare(a, b) {
    return a.price - b.price;
  }
}

class DigitalProduct extends Product {
  constructor(title, price, sizeMb) {
    super(title, price);
    this.sizeMb = sizeMb;
  }
  withTax() {
    return super.withTax(0.12);
  }
}

const course = new DigitalProduct('JS course', 999, 850);
console.log(typeof Product, typeof DigitalProduct);
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Product.prototype));
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(course) === DigitalProduct.prototype);
const parentProto = Object.getPrototypeOf(DigitalProduct.prototype);
console.log(parentProto === Product.prototype);
console.log(course.withTax(), Object.keys(course));

// Chain for static members: DigitalProduct -> Product
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(DigitalProduct) === Product);
console.log(typeof DigitalProduct.compare);

// Class methods are non-enumerable; classes require new
console.log(Object.keys(Product.prototype));
try {
  Product('Pen', 20);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}

The class version builds exactly the chain you built by hand. Notice that static methods are inherited too, through a second chain.

class Product {

}
class DigitalProduct extends Product {

const samples = {
  'Object literal': { id: 1, name: 'Anu' },

let current = 'DigitalProduct';

function labelFor(obj, isTarget) {
  if (isTarget) return 'your value';
  const ctor = Object.hasOwn(obj, 'constructor') ? obj.constructor : null;
  return ctor ? `${ctor.name}.prototype` : 'object';

function render() {
  const key = document.querySelector('#prop').value.trim();

Example: products by hand, then with class

The lab builds the same small product hierarchy twice so you can see they are equivalent:

  1. A Product constructor function with a shared label() method on Product.prototype.
  2. A DigitalProduct constructor that inherits from it, overriding label() and calling the parent version.
  3. A chainOf(obj) helper that walks the chain and returns names such as ['DigitalProduct', 'Product', 'Object'].
  4. A whereIs(obj, key) helper that returns 'own', 'inherited' or 'missing'.
  5. The same two types rewritten with class and extends, and proof that both versions produce the same chain shape.
function chainOf(obj) {
  const names = [];
  for (let p = Object.getPrototypeOf(obj); p; p = Object.getPrototypeOf(p)) {
    names.push(Object.hasOwn(p, 'constructor') ? p.constructor.name : '?');
  }
  return names;
}

function whereIs(obj, key) {
  if (Object.hasOwn(obj, key)) return 'own';
  return key in obj ? 'inherited' : 'missing';
}

Common mistakes

1. Putting methods inside the constructor.

// Wrong: every product gets its own copy of the function
function Product(title) {
  this.title = title;
  this.label = function () { return this.title; };
}
// Fix: share one function through the prototype (or use a class)
Product.prototype.label = function () { return this.title; };

2. Linking prototypes by assignment.

// Wrong: both names point to ONE object, so child methods leak to Product
DigitalProduct.prototype = Product.prototype;
// Fix: a new object whose prototype is the parent's
DigitalProduct.prototype = Object.create(Product.prototype);
DigitalProduct.prototype.constructor = DigitalProduct;

3. Using for…in to copy or count an object’s data. It includes inherited enumerable keys. Use Object.keys or Object.entries, which only list own properties.

// Wrong: also counts inherited enumerable keys
let count = 0;
for (const key in product) count++;
// Fix: own keys only
const count2 = Object.keys(product).length;

4. Shared mutable data on the prototype.

// Wrong: every cart shares ONE items array
Cart.prototype.items = [];
// Fix: create per-instance data in the constructor
function Cart() { this.items = []; }

5. Extending built-in prototypes. Adding Array.prototype.sum affects every array in the app and every library, and can clash with a future standard method. Write a helper function instead.

// Wrong: changes every array everywhere
Array.prototype.sum = function () { return this.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); };
// Fix: a plain helper
const sum = (nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);

Interview and real-world notes

  • “Explain prototypal inheritance.” Objects delegate missing property lookups to their prototype; the chain ends at null; methods are shared, data is usually own; classes are built on this.
  • “Difference between __proto__ and prototype?” __proto__ (better: Object.getPrototypeOf) is an object’s actual prototype. prototype is a property of functions that becomes the prototype of instances created with new.
  • “What does new do?” Be ready to write the four-step construct function from memory.
  • Security: merging untrusted JSON into objects with a naive deep merge can set __proto__ and change Object.prototype for the whole app (prototype pollution). Use Object.create(null) or Map for user-keyed data, and skip __proto__, constructor and prototype keys when merging.
  • Performance: engines optimise objects whose prototype does not change. Set the prototype when you create the object, not later with Object.setPrototypeOf.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const base = { greet() { return 'hi ' + this.name; } };
const user = Object.create(base);
user.name = 'Ana';
console.log(user.greet(), Object.hasOwn(user, 'greet'));
  • A hi undefined false
  • B hi Ana true
  • C TypeError
  • D hi Ana false

Snippet 2. What is logged?

function Car() {}
Car.prototype.wheels = 4;
const car = new Car();
Car.prototype = { wheels: 8 };
console.log(car.wheels, new Car().wheels);
  • A 8 8
  • B 4 8
  • C 4 4
  • D undefined 8

Snippet 3. What is logged?

class Account {}
const acc = new Account();
console.log(typeof Account, Object.getPrototypeOf(acc) === Account.prototype);
  • A function true
  • B class true
  • C object true
  • D function false

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const shop = { count: 1 };
const branch = Object.create(shop);
branch.count++;
console.log(shop.count, branch.count);
  • A 2 2
  • B 1 1
  • C 1 2
  • D 2 1

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const proto = { a: 1 };
const obj = Object.create(proto);
obj.b = 2;
const keys = [];
for (const k in obj) keys.push(k);
console.log(keys.join(','), Object.keys(obj).join(','));
  • A b b
  • B a,b b
  • C b,a a,b
  • D b,a b

Answers

  1. D. greet is found on base through the chain, and this is user because greet was called as user.greet(). It is inherited, so hasOwn is false.
  2. B. car was linked to the original prototype object when it was created. Replacing Car.prototype affects only instances created afterwards. (Mutating the old object would have changed car.)
  3. A. A class is a special kind of function, so typeof says function. Instances are linked to Account.prototype, exactly as with constructor functions.
  4. C. branch.count++ reads 1 through the chain, then writes 2 as a new own property on branch. Writes never change the prototype, so shop keeps 1.
  5. D. for…in visits own enumerable keys first, then inherited enumerable ones, so it sees b and a. Object.keys lists only own enumerable keys.

terms.definition: The object another object delegates to for properties it does not have itself. Read it with Object.getPrototypeOf(obj).
The linked series of prototypes that a property lookup walks, ending at Object.prototype and then null.
A property stored directly on the object, as reported by Object.hasOwn(obj, key).
Creating an own property with the same name as an inherited one, which hides the inherited one for that object.
A normal function called with new; the new object’s prototype is set to the function’s .prototype property.
A property of functions (and classes) holding the object that instances made with new will inherit from. It is not the function’s own prototype.
Creates a new, empty object whose prototype is proto; Object.create(null) makes an object with no prototype at all.
