undefined
false, because toString is inherited from Object.prototype
quiz.explanation: toString is found through the chain, but it is not an own property. The in operator would return true; hasOwn only looks at the object itself.

quiz.question: In function Product() {}, what is Product.prototype?
options: The object that instances created with new Product() will use as their prototype
The prototype of the Product function itself
A copy of Object.prototype that each instance receives
The same thing as Product.__proto__
quiz.explanation: .prototype is the blueprint for instances. The function’s own prototype is Function.prototype, which is what Object.getPrototypeOf(Product) returns.

quiz.question: Which statement about class in JavaScript is accurate?
options: Classes copy methods into every instance, unlike prototypes
Classes replace the prototype system with a separate class system
Classes build on prototypes: methods live on Class.prototype, and extends links the prototype chains, with extra safety such as requiring new
Classes cannot be inspected with Object.getPrototypeOf
quiz.explanation: typeof a class is function and its methods sit on Class.prototype. Classes add real improvements (strict mode, required new, non-enumerable methods, private fields, super), but lookups still walk the same chain.

lessons.title: Classes in depth
lessons.summaryHtml:
A class is a blueprint for objects that share the same data shape and behaviour. Under the hood it is the same prototype machinery you met in the last lesson, with cleaner syntax and a few powers of its own: public fields, truly private #fields and #methods, getters and setters, static members and static blocks.

With extends and super one class can build on another, and instanceof checks the prototype chain. You will also learn when not to inherit: most real designs are easier to change when objects are composed from small parts.

The mini project is a Ralfiz Bank account with a private balance, plus a small library system that lends books with a swappable fine policy.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A class is a blueprint for objects that share the same shape and the same behaviour. Think of Ralfiz Bank opening thousands of savings accounts. Every account has an owner and a balance, and every account can take a deposit, allow a withdrawal and print a statement. You describe that once, in a class, and new SavingsAccount('Anu') stamps out a fresh account whenever you need one.

In the previous lesson you saw how objects inherit through the prototype chain. The class keyword does not replace that system: it is a cleaner way to write it. It also adds features the old constructor-function style never had, such as truly private #fields, static blocks and a safe super keyword.

Why it matters

  • Rules live in one place. "A balance can never go below zero" is written once, inside withdraw(), instead of being repeated in every button handler that touches money.
  • You will meet classes everywhere. Custom errors (class ValidationError extends Error), Web Components (class RatingStars extends HTMLElement), Node's EventEmitter, many SDKs, and back-end frameworks such as NestJS are all built on classes.
  • Encapsulation prevents bugs. When the balance is private, no other file can set it to a random number by accident. The only way in is through methods that validate.
  • Knowing the limits matters as much. Deep inheritance trees are a common source of pain in real projects. Senior developers are expected to know when a plain object, a closure or composition is the better tool.

How it works

Anatomy of a class

A class body can contain five kinds of member. Each one ends up in a different place, and knowing where each lives explains most class behaviour.

MemberWritten asLives onTypical use
Public fieldcategory = 'general';each instanceper-object data with a default
Methodlabel() { … }the prototype (shared)behaviour
Getter / setterget total() { … }the prototypecomputed values, validation
Private field / method#balance = 0;each instance, hiddeninternal state and helpers
Static memberstatic fromJSON() { … }the class itselffactories, counters, constants

When you write new Product('Gel Pen', 40), the engine does four things:

  1. Creates an empty object whose [[Prototype]] is Product.prototype.
  2. Initialises the class fields on it, top to bottom (in a base class this happens before the constructor body).
  3. Runs the constructor body with this pointing at the new object.
  4. Returns the object.

Class code is always in strict mode. A class must be called with new, and a class declaration is hoisted but stays in the temporal dead zone, so you cannot use it above the line where it is declared.

Try it: Anatomy of a class

JavaScript

class Product {
  category = 'general'; // public field: every instance gets its own

  constructor(title, price) {
    this.title = title;
    this.price = price;
  }

  label() {
    // a method: stored once on Product.prototype
    return `${this.title} (₹${this.price})`;
  }

  get isExpensive() {
    // a getter: read like a property, computed on demand
    return this.price > 1000;
  }
}

const pen = new Product('Gel Pen', 40);
const bag = new Product('Laptop Bag', 1899);

console.log(pen);
console.log(pen.label(), '|', bag.label());
console.log('Is the bag expensive?', bag.isExpensive);
console.log('typeof Product:', typeof Product);
console.log('Own keys:', Object.keys(pen));
console.log('Shared method?', pen.label === bag.label);
console.log('On the prototype:', Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Product.prototype));

Fields are listed first in the output because they are set before the constructor body runs. Methods do not appear: they live once on the prototype.

Private fields and methods

Before 2022, developers marked "private" data with an underscore: this._balance. That is only a polite request, because any code can still read and change _balance. A name that starts with # is different: the engine itself refuses access from outside the class body. Writing acc.#balance outside the class is a SyntaxError, so the whole file fails to load. The error is caught before any code runs.

class BankAccount {
  #balance = 0;              // must be declared in the class body
  #log(msg) { /* private method */ }
  static isAccount(obj) {
    return #balance in obj;  // "brand check": was obj made by this class?
  }
}
const acc = new BankAccount();
acc.#balance = 1e9;          // SyntaxError: the file does not even run

Private members do not show up in Object.keys, JSON.stringify, for…in or a spread copy. They are not inherited by subclasses either: a SavingsAccount method cannot read the parent's #balance. It must use a public getter or a method, which is exactly the point.

Try it: Private fields and methods

JavaScript

class BankAccount {
  #balance = 0;
  #history = [];

  constructor(owner) {
    this.owner = owner;
  }

  deposit(amount) {
    this.#assertPositive(amount);
    this.#balance += amount;
    this.#history.push(`+${amount}`);
    return this; // returning this allows chaining
  }

  withdraw(amount) {
    this.#assertPositive(amount);
    if (amount > this.#balance) {
      throw new RangeError(`Insufficient funds: balance is ${this.#balance}`);
    }
    this.#balance -= amount;
    this.#history.push(`-${amount}`);
    return this;
  }

  get balance() {
    return this.#balance;
  }

  get statement() {
    return [...this.#history]; // a copy: callers cannot edit the history
  }

  #assertPositive(amount) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(amount) || amount <= 0) {
      throw new TypeError(`Amount must be a positive integer, got ${amount}`);
    }
  }

  static isAccount(value) {
    return #balance in value; // brand check (ES2022)
  }
}

const acc = new BankAccount('Anu').deposit(5000).withdraw(1200);
console.log('Balance:', acc.balance);
console.log('Statement:', acc.statement);
console.log(acc); // private fields are not listed

acc.balance = 1_000_000; // getter only: ignored here, a TypeError in strict mode
console.log('After tampering:', acc.balance);
console.log('acc["#balance"] is', acc['#balance']); // a different, normal key

for (const bad of [99999, -50]) {
  try {
    acc.withdraw(bad);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`${err.name}: ${err.message}`);
  }
}
console.log(BankAccount.isAccount(acc), BankAccount.isAccount({ balance: 1 }));

Try adding console.log(acc.#balance) at the bottom: the whole script fails to parse, because private names are checked before any code runs.

Watch out: private means "hidden from other code", not "secret". Anyone can open DevTools and see the value, and all front-end code is downloadable. Never keep API keys or passwords in browser JavaScript, private or not.

Getters, setters and static members

A getter is a method that is read like a property: student.grade, with no brackets. Use it for values that are computed from other data, so they can never be out of date. A setter runs when someone assigns to the property, which makes it the perfect place for validation. Assigning in the constructor (this.marks = marks) goes through the setter too, so bad data is rejected on the way in.

Static members belong to the class, not to each object. Common uses:

  • Factory methods that build instances from other formats: Student.fromJSON(text), Invoice.fromCsvRow(row).
  • Shared counters and caches: a static #nextId that hands out ids.
  • Constants: Student.passMark.

A static block, static { … }, runs once when the class is defined. Use it when static setup needs more than one expression, for example reading settings or filling a lookup table. Inside a static method or block, this is the class, which is why new this(name, marks) also works correctly for subclasses.

Try it: Getters, setters, static members and a static block

JavaScript

class Student {
  static passMark;
  static #nextId = 1;

  static {
    // Runs once, when the class is defined.
    // Imagine these settings were read from a config file.
    const settings = { passMark: 40, school: 'Ralfiz Academy' };
    Student.passMark = settings.passMark;
    Student.school = settings.school;
  }

  id = Student.#nextId++;
  #marks = 0;

  constructor(name, marks) {
    this.name = name;
    this.marks = marks; // uses the setter below
  }

  get marks() {
    return this.#marks;
  }

  set marks(value) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 0 || value > 100) {
      throw new RangeError(`Invalid marks for ${this.name}: ${value}`);
    }
    this.#marks = value;
  }

  get grade() {
    const m = this.#marks;
    if (m >= 90) return 'A';
    if (m >= 75) return 'B';
    return m >= Student.passMark ? 'C' : 'F';
  }

  static fromJSON(json) {
    const { name, marks } = JSON.parse(json);
    return new this(name, marks); // in a static method, this is the class
  }
}

const rows = [
  '{"name":"Anu","marks":92}',
  '{"name":"Rahul","marks":67}',
  '{"name":"Fathima","marks":38}',
];
const students = rows.map((row) => Student.fromJSON(row));
console.table(students.map(({ id, name, marks, grade }) => ({ id, name, marks, grade })));
console.log(Student.school, '| pass mark:', Student.passMark);

students[1].marks = 81;
console.log(`${students[1].name} now has grade ${students[1].grade}`);

try {
  students[2].marks = 140;
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.message);
}
console.log('passMark on an instance?', 'passMark' in students[0]);

The constructor assigns this.marks, which goes through the setter, so invalid data can never get in. Change 67 to 670 in rows and run again.

extends and super

class SavingsAccount extends Account links two prototype chains. Instances of SavingsAccount inherit from SavingsAccount.prototype, which inherits from Account.prototype. The constructor functions are linked as well, so static members are inherited too.

current ──▶ CurrentAccount.prototype ──▶ Account.prototype ──▶ Object.prototype ──▶ null
             available(), describe()      deposit(), withdraw()

The rules you need to remember:

  1. In a subclass constructor you must call super(...) before using this. The parent constructor is what creates the object. If you touch this first, you get a ReferenceError.
  2. If you leave the constructor out, JavaScript writes one for you: constructor(...args) { super(...args); }.
  3. super.method() calls the parent's version of a method. Use it to extend behaviour instead of copying it.
  4. Subclass fields are initialised right after super() returns. That is why a parent constructor that calls an overridden method sees the subclass fields as undefined (see the second Predict snippet).
  5. obj instanceof Account walks obj's prototype chain looking for Account.prototype.

Try it: extends, super and overriding

JavaScript

class Account {
  #balance = 0;

  constructor(owner) {
    this.owner = owner;
  }

  get balance() {
    return this.#balance;
  }

  available() {
    return this.#balance;
  }

  deposit(amount) {
    this.#balance += amount;
    return this;
  }

  withdraw(amount) {
    if (amount > this.available()) {
      throw new RangeError(`${this.owner}: cannot withdraw ₹${amount}`);
    }
    this.#balance -= amount;
    return this;
  }

  describe() {
    return `${this.constructor.name} of ${this.owner}: ₹${this.#balance}`;
  }
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
  constructor(owner, monthlyRate) {
    super(owner); // must run before we touch this
    this.monthlyRate = monthlyRate;
  }

  addInterest() {
    return this.deposit(Math.round(this.balance * this.monthlyRate));
  }
}

class CurrentAccount extends Account {
  constructor(owner, overdraft) {
    super(owner);
    this.overdraft = overdraft;
  }

  available() {
    return super.available() + this.overdraft; // extend, don't copy
  }

  describe() {
    return `${super.describe()} (overdraft ₹${this.overdraft})`;
  }
}

const savings = new SavingsAccount('Anu', 0.005).deposit(20000).addInterest();
const current = new CurrentAccount('Ralfiz Traders', 10000).deposit(5000);
current.withdraw(12000); // allowed: 5000 balance + 10000 overdraft

for (const acc of [savings, current]) console.log(acc.describe());

try {
  savings.withdraw(50000);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.message);
}

console.log(current instanceof CurrentAccount, current instanceof Account);
console.log('current instanceof SavingsAccount:', current instanceof SavingsAccount);
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(CurrentAccount.prototype) === Account.prototype);

CurrentAccount overrides available() and still reuses the parent version with super.available(). The parent withdraw() calls this.available(), so it picks up the override automatically.

You can also extend built-ins: class ValidationError extends Error (next lesson), class Stack extends Array, or class ProductCard extends HTMLElement in the DOM track.

Composition over inheritance

Inheritance models an is-a relationship: a savings account is an account. It works well for one level. Trouble starts when several things vary independently. Imagine a library with printed and digital books, some books that can be borrowed and some that cannot, and fine rules that differ by branch. With inheritance you soon have LendableEBook, ReferenceAudioBook and a tree nobody wants to touch.

Composition models has-a: the library has a fine policy, a catalogue and members. Each part is small, and you change behaviour by passing in a different part.

// Inheritance: one subclass per rule
class WeekendLibrary extends Library { fine(days) { return days * 2; } }

// Composition: pass the rule in
const perDay = (rupees) => (daysLate) => Math.max(0, daysLate) * rupees;
const branch = new Library({ fine: perDay(2) });
const campus = new Library({ fine: perDay(5), loanDays: 21 });
Inheritance (extends)Composition (has-a)
Best fora true, stable is-a relationshipbehaviours that vary or combine
Couplingtight: subclasses depend on parent internalsloose: parts meet through small interfaces
Changing behaviourwrite a new subclasspass a different object or function
Testingneeds the whole hierarchytest each part alone, inject fakes

A good rule of thumb: inherit at most one or two levels, for true is-a cases such as custom errors. Compose everything else.

Example: Bank Account and Library system

The mini project has two parts. First, the library. Book knows only whether it is on loan. Member knows only their own loans and limit. Library coordinates them and owns a fine policy, which is just a function passed to its constructor. Notice two design choices in lend():

  • It checks everything before changing anything. If the member is over their limit, the book is not left half checked out.
  • It returns a message instead of printing it, so the class does not care whether it runs in a console, a web page or a test.

Try it: Mini project: a library built by composition

JavaScript

class Book {
  #onLoan = false;

  constructor(isbn, title) {
    this.isbn = isbn;
    this.title = title;
  }

  get available() {
    return !this.#onLoan;
  }

  checkOut() {
    if (this.#onLoan) throw new Error(`"${this.title}" is already on loan`);
    this.#onLoan = true;
  }

  checkIn() {
    this.#onLoan = false;
  }
}

class Member {
  #loans = new Map(); // isbn -> due day

  constructor(id, name, limit = 2) {
    Object.assign(this, { id, name, limit });
  }

  canBorrow() {
    return this.#loans.size < this.limit;
  }

  addLoan(isbn, dueDay) {
    this.#loans.set(isbn, dueDay);
  }

  removeLoan(isbn) {
    if (!this.#loans.has(isbn)) throw new Error(`${this.name} does not have ${isbn}`);
    const due = this.#loans.get(isbn);
    this.#loans.delete(isbn);
    return due;
  }
}

// Fine policies are plain functions: easy to swap and to test
const perDay = (rupees) => (daysLate) => Math.max(0, daysLate) * rupees;
const capped = (policy, max) => (daysLate) => Math.min(policy(daysLate), max);

class Library {
  #books = new Map();
  #members = new Map();

  constructor({ loanDays = 14, fine = perDay(5) } = {}) {
    this.loanDays = loanDays;
    this.fine = fine; // the library HAS a fine policy
  }

  add(...items) {
    for (const item of items) {
      if (item instanceof Book) this.#books.set(item.isbn, item);
      else if (item instanceof Member) this.#members.set(item.id, item);
    }
    return this;
  }

  lend(isbn, memberId, today) {
    const book = this.#find(this.#books, isbn, 'Book');
    const member = this.#find(this.#members, memberId, 'Member');
    // check everything first, change state last
    if (!book.available) throw new Error(`"${book.title}" is already on loan`);
    if (!member.canBorrow()) {
      throw new Error(`${member.name} has reached their loan limit (${member.limit})`);
    }
    book.checkOut();
    member.addLoan(isbn, today + this.loanDays);
    return `${member.name} borrowed "${book.title}" (due day ${today + this.loanDays})`;
  }

  giveBack(isbn, memberId, today) {
    const member = this.#find(this.#members, memberId, 'Member');
    const due = member.removeLoan(isbn);
    this.#find(this.#books, isbn, 'Book').checkIn();
    return this.fine(today - due);
  }

  get shelf() {
    return [...this.#books.values()].map(({ title, available }) => ({ title, available }));
  }

  #find(map, key, kind) {
    const item = map.get(key);
    if (!item) throw new Error(`${kind} ${key} not found`);
    return item;
  }
}

const lib = new Library({ fine: capped(perDay(5), 50) }).add(
  new Book('B1', 'Clean Code'),
  new Book('B2', 'Eloquent JavaScript'),
  new Book('B3', 'Refactoring'),
  new Member('M1', 'Anu'),
  new Member('M2', 'Rahul', 1),
);

console.log(lib.lend('B1', 'M1', 1));
for (const [isbn, who, day] of [['B1', 'M2', 2], ['B2', 'M2', 3], ['B3', 'M2', 4]]) {
  try {
    console.log(lib.lend(isbn, who, day));
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('Refused:', err.message);
  }
}
console.table(lib.shelf);
console.log('Anu returns on day 21, fine ₹' + lib.giveBack('B1', 'M1', 21));
console.log('Rahul returns on day 40, fine ₹' + lib.giveBack('B2', 'M2', 40));

Library does not inherit from anything. It HAS books, members and a fine policy. Swap capped(perDay(5), 50) for perDay(10) and run again.

Second, the bank account as a real page. The balance is kept in paise (integers), as you learned in the numbers lesson, and formatted with Intl.NumberFormat only for display. The account class has no idea that a web page exists. It exposes deposit(), withdraw(), getters and an onChange() subscription, and the UI code re-renders when it is notified. This split between a pure model and a thin UI layer is the same one frameworks use.

Try it: Ralfiz Bank: a class-powered account

HTML

<main class="bank">
  <header class="top">
    <div class="logo" aria-hidden="true">R</div>
    <div>
      <h1>Ralfiz Bank</h1>

    </div>

CSS

JavaScript

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const rupees = (paise) => inr.format(paise / 100);

class Account {
  #balance = 0; // in paise, so we never add 0.1 + 0.2
  #history = [];
  #listeners = new Set();

  constructor(owner) {
    this.owner = owner;
  }

  get balance() {
    return this.#balance;
  }

  get recent() {
    return this.#history.slice(-5).reverse();
  }

  onChange(fn) {
    this.#listeners.add(fn);
    return () => this.#listeners.delete(fn); // call it to unsubscribe
  }

  deposit(paise, note = 'Deposit') {
    this.#check(paise);
    this.#apply(paise, note);
  }

  withdraw(paise, note = 'Withdrawal') {
    this.#check(paise);
    if (paise > this.#balance) {
      throw new RangeError(`Insufficient funds. You can withdraw up to ${rupees(this.#balance)}.`);
    }
    this.#apply(-paise, note);
  }

  #check(paise) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(paise) || paise <= 0) {
      throw new TypeError('Enter an amount greater than zero.');
    }
  }

  #apply(delta, note) {
    this.#balance += delta;
    this.#history.push({ delta, note, at: new Date() });
    this.#listeners.forEach((fn) => fn(this));
  }
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
  constructor(owner, annualRate) {
    super(owner);
    this.annualRate = annualRate;
  }

  addMonthlyInterest() {
    const interest = Math.round((this.balance * this.annualRate) / 12);
    if (interest > 0) this.deposit(interest, 'Interest credited');
    return interest;
  }
}

// ---- UI: talks to the account only through its public API ----
const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
const clock = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-IN', { hour: '2-digit', minute: '2-digit' });
const account = new SavingsAccount('Anu Mathew', 0.04);

function row({ delta, note, at }) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  const text = document.createElement('span');
  const when = document.createElement('small');
  const amount = document.createElement('span');
  text.textContent = note;
  when.textContent = clock.format(at);
  text.append(when);
  amount.className = delta > 0 ? 'in' : 'out';
  amount.textContent = (delta > 0 ? '+ ' : '− ') + rupees(Math.abs(delta));
  li.append(text, amount);
  return li;
}

function render(acc) {
  $('#bal').textContent = rupees(acc.balance);
  $('#hist').replaceChildren(...acc.recent.map(row));
}

function say(text, ok = true) {
  $('#msg').textContent = text;
  $('#msg').className = `msg ${ok ? 'ok' : 'err'}`;
}

account.onChange(render);

$('#tx').addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const action = event.submitter?.value ?? 'deposit'; // Enter key = first button
  const paise = Math.round(Number($('#amt').value) * 100);
  try {
    account[action](paise);
    say(`${action === 'deposit' ? 'Deposited' : 'Withdrew'} ${rupees(paise)}.`);
    $('#amt').value = '';
  } catch (err) {
    say(err.message, false);
    console.warn(`${err.name}: ${err.message}`);
  }
});

$('#interest').addEventListener('click', () => {
  const paid = account.addMonthlyInterest();
  say(`Interest of ${rupees(paid)} credited.`);
});

account.deposit(2500000, 'Salary');
account.withdraw(120000, 'Electricity bill');
account.deposit(50000, 'UPI from Rahul');
console.log('Balance in paise:', account.balance);
console.log('instanceof SavingsAccount:', account instanceof SavingsAccount);
console.log('Own keys (no #balance):', Object.keys(account));

The UI only talks to the account through deposit(), withdraw() and getters. Try withdrawing more than the balance, a negative amount, or adding interest.

Common mistakes

1. Calling a class without new. Classes refuse to run as plain functions.

const acc = BankAccount('Anu');     // TypeError: Class constructor BankAccount
                                    // cannot be invoked without 'new'
const acc = new BankAccount('Anu'); // fix

2. Using this before super().

class Savings extends Account {
  constructor(owner, rate) {
    this.rate = rate;  // ReferenceError: must call super constructor first
    super(owner);
  }
}
// fix: call super(owner) on the first line, then set this.rate

3. Losing this when you pass a method as a callback. A method is a normal function. Passed on its own, it forgets its object.

button.addEventListener('click', cart.clear);        // this is the button!
button.addEventListener('click', () => cart.clear()); // fix 1: arrow wrapper
button.addEventListener('click', cart.clear.bind(cart)); // fix 2: bind
class Cart { clear = () => { this.items = []; }; }    // fix 3: arrow field

Arrow-function fields are handy for event handlers, but each instance gets its own copy of the function. Keep them for callbacks, not for every method.

4. A getter that reads itself. This recurses until the stack overflows.

class User {
  get name() { return this.name; }       // RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
}
class User {
  #name = '';
  get name() { return this.#name; }      // fix: store the value in a private field
}

5. Reading a private field from an object of another class. A method like equals(other) throws a TypeError when other is a plain object. Guard it with a brand check.

equals(other) { return this.#id === other.#id; }       // TypeError for {id: 1}
equals(other) { return #id in other && this.#id === other.#id; } // fix

6. Inheriting just to reuse code. class Invoice extends Array "because it has a list of items" drags every array method into your public API. Use a private #items = [] field and expose only what callers need.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "Are JavaScript classes real classes?" They are syntax over prototypes and constructor functions. typeof MyClass is 'function', and methods live on MyClass.prototype. The syntax adds real features, though: private members, static blocks, super, and mandatory new.
  • Privacy options: #private fields (enforced by the engine), closures (a factory function with local variables), and _convention (not enforced). TypeScript's private keyword is checked only at compile time; at runtime the property is still public.
  • Method or arrow field? Methods are shared on the prototype, which is cheaper in memory. Arrow fields capture this for callbacks but are copied per instance.
  • Explain super clearly: super(...) runs the parent constructor, which creates this. super.x() calls the parent's method with the current this.
  • Design answer that impresses: "I keep hierarchies shallow and inject behaviour, such as a pricing strategy or a clock, through the constructor. That makes the class easy to test with fakes."
  • In real code bases you will see classes in models and services, and plain functions plus objects everywhere else. Neither style is "more professional". Pick the one that makes the rules easiest to find.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

class Counter {
  static created = 0;
  constructor() {
    Counter.created++;
  }
}
new Counter();
new Counter();
const c = new Counter();
console.log(Counter.created, c.created);
  • A 3 3
  • B 3 undefined
  • C 1 undefined
  • D 0 undefined

Snippet 2. What is logged?

class Base {
  constructor() {
    console.log(this.describe());
  }
  describe() {
    return 'base';
  }
}
class Child extends Base {
  label = 'child';
  describe() {
    return this.label ?? 'not ready';
  }
}
new Child();
  • A base
  • B child
  • C not ready
  • D undefined

Snippet 3. What is logged?

class Temperature {
  #celsius = 0;
  get fahrenheit() {
    return (this.#celsius * 9) / 5 + 32;
  }
  set fahrenheit(f) {
    this.#celsius = ((f - 32) * 5) / 9;
  }
}
const t = new Temperature();
t.fahrenheit = 212;
console.log(t.fahrenheit, Object.keys(t));
  • A 212 []
  • B 212 [ 'fahrenheit' ]
  • C 100 []
  • D 32 []

Snippet 4. What is logged?

class Shape {}
class Circle extends Shape {}
const c = new Circle();
console.log(typeof Circle, c instanceof Shape, Object.getPrototypeOf(Circle) === Shape);
  • A class true false
  • B object true true
  • C function true false
  • D function true true

Answers

  1. B. created is static, so it lives on the Counter class and is shared. Instances do not see static members, so c.created is undefined.
  2. C. The overridden describe() runs, because this is a Child. But Child fields are initialised only after super() returns, so this.label is still undefined inside the Base constructor.
  3. A. The setter stores 100 °C privately and the getter converts it back to 212. The accessor lives on the prototype and #celsius is private, so the instance has no own enumerable keys.
  4. D. A class is a special kind of function, so typeof gives function. extends links both chains: Circle.prototype inherits from Shape.prototype, and the Circle constructor itself inherits from Shape (that is how static members are inherited).

terms.definition: A template for creating objects. It is syntax over constructor functions and prototypes, and it must be called with new.
The special method that runs once for every new instance, after the fields are initialised (in a base class).
A property declared in the class body, such as count = 0, that every instance gets as its own property.
A field or method whose name starts with #. Only code inside the class body can read it; the engine enforces this.
Methods declared with get and set that look like a normal property from outside, for computed values and validation.
A property or method that belongs to the class itself, not to its instances, such as Student.fromJSON().
Calls the parent class constructor, super(...), or a parent method, super.method(), from a subclass.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say that JavaScript classes are syntax over prototypes, that methods live once on the prototype, and that #private fields are enforced by the engine while _underscore names are only a convention.

quiz.question: What does the # in #balance mean inside a class body?
options: It is a naming convention that tells other developers not to touch the property
It declares a private field that only code inside the class body can access, enforced by the engine
It makes the property read-only for everyone
It creates a static property shared by all instances
quiz.explanation: A # name is a private class member. Code outside the class body cannot even mention it: obj.#balance outside the class is a SyntaxError. An underscore prefix is only a convention.

quiz.question: In the constructor of class Savings extends Account, when can you use this?
options: Anywhere, because this always exists in a constructor
Only after the class fields of Savings are declared
Only inside arrow functions
Only after super(...) has been called
quiz.explanation: In a derived class, the parent constructor creates the object. Until super() returns there is no this, and touching it throws a ReferenceError. The subclass fields are initialised right after super() returns.

quiz.question: Where is a method such as deposit() { … } written in a class body stored?
options: Once, on the class prototype, and shared by every instance
As a copy on every instance
On the class itself as a static function
In a hidden private slot of each instance
quiz.explanation: Methods go on ClassName.prototype, so a thousand accounts share one deposit function. Arrow-function fields (handle = () => {}) are the exception: each instance gets its own copy.

quiz.question: A library app needs e-books, audiobooks, reference books that cannot be borrowed, and different fine rules per branch. Which design is usually easiest to change?
options: A deep hierarchy: Book → LendableBook → EBook → LendableEBook, and so on
One giant class with a type string and many if statements
Small classes composed together, with behaviours such as the fine policy passed in as objects or functions
Copying the Book class for every kind of book
quiz.explanation: Inheritance fixes one axis of variation. When several things vary independently, composing objects (the library HAS a fine policy) avoids a combinatorial explosion of subclasses.

lessons.title: Errors and debugging
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every program meets bad input, broken networks and plain bugs. JavaScript reports them with Error objects: built-in types such as TypeError and SyntaxError, or your own classes such as ValidationError. You throw an error to stop normal flow, and try…catch…finally decides where it is handled and what always runs.

Good error handling is a design skill. You validate at the boundaries, throw specific errors, keep the original problem with { cause }, handle only the errors you expect, and let real bugs surface loudly.

You will also learn to debug like a professional: the console toolbox, the debugger statement, DevTools breakpoints and reading stack traces. The mini project is an order importer with a checkout form that shows friendly field errors.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An error is JavaScript's way of saying "I cannot continue from here". When something goes wrong, code throws an Error object. The engine then stops running the current function and walks back up the call stack, looking for a catch block that wants to handle it. If none does, the error is uncaught: the browser prints a red line in the console and that piece of work stops.

Debugging is the other half of the story. Errors tell you that something went wrong. The console, breakpoints and stack traces tell you why.

Why it matters

  • Users see your error handling. "Something went wrong" with a spinner that never stops is an error handling bug. "The PIN code must have 6 digits" is good error handling.
  • Money and data are at stake. A checkout that half-completes, or an import that silently skips bad rows, costs real money and trust.
  • Bugs you hide are the most expensive. An empty catch {} turns a crash you would fix in five minutes into wrong data that nobody notices for weeks.
  • Debugging speed is a job skill. In interviews and on the job, people notice whether you read the stack trace and set a breakpoint, or add console.log everywhere and guess.

How it works

Error objects and the built-in types

Every error object has a name, a message and, in all modern engines, a stack string that records where it was created. The engine throws these built-in types for you:

TypeThrown whenExample
TypeErrora value is the wrong type for the operationnull.total, calling a non-function
ReferenceErrora variable name does not exist (or is in the TDZ)totl + 1
SyntaxErrorcode or data cannot be parsedJSON.parse('{bad')
RangeErrora number is outside the allowed range(1).toFixed(200), infinite recursion
URIErrorbad URI encodingdecodeURIComponent('%')
AggregateErrorseveral errors at oncePromise.any when all fail

You can throw any value, even a string, but you should only throw Error objects. A string has no stack trace, no name and no way to be recognised with instanceof.

Try it: The built-in error types

JavaScript

const experiments = [
  ['null.total', () => null.total],
  ['totl + 1', () => totl + 1],
  ["JSON.parse('{bad')", () => JSON.parse('{bad')],
  ['(12.5).toFixed(200)', () => (12.5).toFixed(200)],
  ["decodeURIComponent('%')", () => decodeURIComponent('%')],
  ["throw 'oops'", () => { throw 'oops'; }],
];

const rows = experiments.map(([code, run]) => {
  try {
    run();
    return { code, name: '(no error)' };
  } catch (err) {
    const isError = err instanceof Error;
    const message = isError ? err.message : String(err);
    return {
      code,
      name: isError ? err.name : `a ${typeof err}`,
      stack: isError && typeof err.stack === 'string' ? 'yes' : 'no',
      message: message.length > 30 ? message.slice(0, 30) + '…' : message,
    };
  }
});

console.table(rows);
console.log('Every built-in type extends Error:', new RangeError('x') instanceof Error);

Each row triggers a different kind of error. The last one throws a plain string: notice that it has no name and no stack, which is why you should always throw Error objects.

throw, try, catch and finally

throw stops the current function immediately. The engine unwinds the call stack, frame by frame, until it finds an enclosing try with a catch. Code between the throw and that catch never runs.

  • try { … } wraps the code that might fail.
  • catch (err) { … } receives the thrown value. If you do not need it, write catch { … } (optional catch binding).
  • finally { … } always runs last: after success, after a return, and after an error, whether or not it was caught. It is the place to hide a spinner, close a file or release a lock.

The most important habit is to catch narrowly. Handle the errors you expected, and rethrow everything else so real bugs are not disguised as bad input.

Try it: try, catch and finally in order

JavaScript

let spinnerVisible = false;

function placeOrder(cart) {
  spinnerVisible = true;
  console.log('1. spinner on');
  try {
    if (cart.length === 0) throw new Error('Cart is empty');
    const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0);
    console.log('2. total is', total);
    return total; // finally still runs before the caller gets this
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('2. caught:', err.message);
    return null;
  } finally {
    spinnerVisible = false;
    console.log('3. finally: spinner off');
  }
}

console.log('Result:', placeOrder([{ price: 250, qty: 2 }]));
console.log('Result:', placeOrder([]));
console.log('Spinner visible?', spinnerVisible);
console.log('---');

// Handle only what you expect; rethrow the rest
function readQty(text) {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(text).value; // hidden bug: text may be "null"
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof SyntaxError) return 1; // bad input: default to 1
    throw err; // anything else is a bug: let it surface
  }
}

console.log(readQty('{"value":3}'), readQty('three'));
try {
  readQty('null');
} catch (err) {
  console.log('A real bug surfaced instead of hiding:', err.name);
}

finally runs even when try returns. The second half shows the habit that separates juniors from seniors: handle the error you expected, rethrow everything else.

Remember: try/catch is not free protection for "everything below". Wrap the smallest block that can fail for a reason you understand, and decide what the user should see when it does.

Custom error classes and error cause

Built-in types describe technical problems. Your app has business problems: invalid input, payment declined, out of stock. Give each one a class, and callers can react with instanceof instead of comparing message strings, which break the moment someone rewords a message.

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, options) {
    super(message, options);       // options may contain { cause }
    this.name = new.target.name;   // the name of the class used with new
  }
}
class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.field = field;            // extra data for the UI
  }
}
class NotFoundError extends AppError {}

When you catch a low-level error and throw a higher-level one, pass the original as the cause (ES2022): throw new PaymentError('Payment failed', { cause: err }). The user sees a clear message, and your logs keep the whole chain, down to "Gateway timeout (504)". Without cause, wrapping an error throws away the most useful debugging information.

Try it: Custom error classes and cause

JavaScript

class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, options) {
    super(message, options); // passes { cause } through
    this.name = new.target.name; // 'ValidationError', 'PaymentError', ...
  }
}

class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.field = field;
  }
}

class PaymentError extends AppError {}

function chargeCard(amount) {
  // pretend the payment gateway timed out
  throw new Error(`Gateway timeout (504) while charging ₹${amount}`);
}

function checkout(order) {
  if (!order.email?.includes('@')) {
    throw new ValidationError('email', 'Please enter a valid email address');
  }
  try {
    chargeCard(order.total);
  } catch (err) {
    throw new PaymentError(`Payment of ₹${order.total} failed`, { cause: err });
  }
}

function causeChain(err) {
  const parts = [];
  for (let e = err; e; e = e.cause) parts.push(`${e.name}: ${e.message}`);
  return parts.join('\n   caused by ');
}

function handle(order) {
  try {
    checkout(order);
    console.log('Order placed');
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof ValidationError) {
      console.log(`Show under the ${err.field} field: ${err.message}`);
    } else if (err instanceof PaymentError) {
      console.log('Tell the user:', err.message);
      console.log('Log for developers:', causeChain(err));
    } else {
      throw err; // unknown problem: do not swallow it
    }
  }
}

handle({ email: 'anu.example.com', total: 1499 });
handle({ email: 'anu@example.com', total: 1499 });

const e = new PaymentError('demo');
console.log(e.name, e instanceof PaymentError, e instanceof AppError, e instanceof Error);

new.target.name gives every subclass the right name automatically. The UI shows err.message; logs follow err.cause down to the root problem.

Errors in asynchronous code (a preview)

A try block only protects code that runs while the try block is running. Callbacks run later, in a new task, when the try block has long finished. You will meet this properly in the next module.

try {
  setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('late'); }, 0); // NOT caught below
} catch (err) {
  console.log('never runs');
}

fetch('/api/orders')
  .then((res) => res.json())
  .catch((err) => showToast('Could not load orders'));  // promises: .catch

async function load() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/orders');                 // await: try/catch works again
  } catch (err) { /* handle */ }
}

Errors that nobody catches can still be noticed globally: window.addEventListener('error', …) and 'unhandledrejection' in browsers, and process.on('uncaughtException') in Node. Use these for logging and error-tracking services, not as your main handling strategy.

Defensive coding and validation

Validate data where it enters your program: form input, JSON from an API, a file, URL parameters. Inside your own well-tested functions you can then trust the data, instead of sprinkling checks everywhere.

  • Fail fast with a clear error at the boundary (validateOrder(order)), not three functions later with Cannot read properties of undefined.
  • Collect all problems for forms, so the user fixes everything in one go. AggregateError is a natural container for several ValidationErrors.
  • Use guard clauses and ?? for genuinely optional data, but do not use ?. to hide data that must be there.
  • Expected versus exceptional: a user typing a bad email is expected, so some teams return { ok: false, errors } instead of throwing. A database that is down is exceptional, so throw. Pick one style per layer and be consistent.

The console toolbox and the debugger

console.log is only the start. console.table shows arrays of objects as a grid, group and groupEnd indent related lines, count counts calls per label, time and timeEnd measure roughly, and assert logs only when a condition is false. warn and error are highlighted and can be filtered in DevTools.

Try it: The console toolbox

JavaScript

const orders = [
  { id: 'A-101', customer: 'Anu', total: 1499, status: 'paid' },
  { id: 'A-102', customer: 'Rahul', total: 0, status: 'paid' },
  { id: 'A-103', customer: 'Fathima', total: 3200, status: 'refunded' },
];

console.table(orders, ['id', 'total', 'status']); // pick the columns

console.group('Checking orders');
for (const order of orders) {
  console.count(order.status); // how many times each status was seen
  console.assert(order.total > 0, `${order.id} has a zero total`);
}
console.groupEnd();

console.time('sum a million numbers');
let sum = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) sum += i % 7;
console.timeEnd('sum a million numbers');

console.info('info: routine detail');
console.warn('warn: looks odd, but the app keeps working');
console.error('error: something failed and needs attention');
console.log({ sum }); // wrap variables in {} to see their names

console.error and failed asserts show in red (this example expects that). Use table for arrays of objects, group to indent related lines, count for "how often", and time for rough timings.

For anything harder, pause the program instead of printing it. Add a debugger; statement, or click a line number in DevTools Sources (Chrome) or Debugger (Firefox). When execution pauses you can hover over variables, look at the call stack and step through lines. In Node, run node --inspect-brk index.js and open chrome://inspect, or use the VS Code debugger.

Breakpoint typeUse it when
Line breakpointyou know roughly where it goes wrong
Conditional breakpointa loop of 5,000 orders fails only for order.id === 'A-4312'
Logpointyou want a log line without editing and reloading the code
Pause on exceptionsyou want to stop at the exact line that throws (optionally including caught ones)
Event listener / DOM / fetch breakpointsyou do not know which code runs on a click, a DOM change or a request
function applyCoupon(cart, code) {
  debugger; // pauses here only while DevTools is open; remove before committing
  return cart.total - discounts[code];
}

Reading a stack trace

A stack trace is read top to bottom, newest call first. The first line is the error; the next line is where it was created, and each following line is the function that called the one above it.

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'price')
    at lineTotal (cart.js:14:22)       <- where it broke
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at cartTotal (cart.js:20:28)       <- who called it
    at HTMLButtonElement.onCheckout (app.js:41:17)

Start at the first line that points to your code, open that file and line, and ask: "which value is undefined here, and why?" Here lineTotal received an item without a product, so the real bug is probably in how the cart was built. In production the code is usually minified, so stack traces point to app.4f3c.js:1:20391. Source maps let DevTools and error trackers translate those back to your original files.

Example: an order importer and a checkout form

The lab builds a Node order importer. It receives a batch of orders as JSON text, just as you would from an upload or an API. parseBatch wraps JSON.parse and turns a SyntaxError into an ImportError with the original as its cause. validateOrder throws a ValidationError naming the field. importOrders collects every failure instead of stopping at the first one, and uses finally to always print a summary line.

for (const order of orders) {
  try {
    validateOrder(order);
    accepted.push(order);
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof ValidationError)) throw err; // a bug, not bad data
    rejected.push({ id: order.id ?? '(none)', field: err.field, message: err.message });
  }
}

The same ideas power the checkout page below. Validation throws an AggregateError of field errors, which the UI turns into messages under each input with aria-invalid set. A payment failure becomes a PaymentError whose message is safe to show, while the technical cause goes to the console. Any other error is a bug, so it is rethrown.

Try it: Checkout with friendly errors

HTML

<main class="wrap">
  <form id="checkout" class="card" novalidate>
    <header>
      <h1>Checkout</h1>
      <p class="muted">Ralfiz Store · 2 items · <strong>₹2,998</strong></p>
    </header>
    <label for="name">Full name</label>
    <input id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name" aria-describedby="name-err">
    <p class="err" id="name-err"></p>
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" aria-describedby="email-err">
    <p class="err" id="email-err"></p>
    <label for="pin">PIN code</label>
    <input id="pin" name="pin" inputmode="numeric" maxlength="6" aria-describedby="pin-err">
    <p class="err" id="pin-err"></p>
    <label class="check"><input type="checkbox" name="outage"> Simulate a payment gateway outage</label>
    <button class="btn">Pay ₹2,998</button>
    <div id="banner" class="banner" role="alert" hidden></div>
  </form>
</main>

CSS

JavaScript

// ---- Errors: specific classes that carry data ----
class AppError extends Error {
  constructor(message, options) {
    super(message, options);
    this.name = new.target.name;
  }
}
class ValidationError extends AppError {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.field = field;
  }
}
class PaymentError extends AppError {}

// ---- Business logic: no DOM in here ----
function validate({ name, email, pin }) {
  const errors = [];
  if (name.trim().length < 2) {
    errors.push(new ValidationError('name', 'Enter your full name.'));
  }
  if (!/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(email)) {
    errors.push(new ValidationError('email', 'Enter an email like anu@example.com.'));
  }
  if (!/^[1-9]\d{5}$/.test(pin)) {
    errors.push(new ValidationError('pin', 'A PIN code has 6 digits and does not start with 0.'));
  }
  if (errors.length) throw new AggregateError(errors, 'Please fix the highlighted fields');
}

function chargeCard(amount, simulateOutage) {
  if (simulateOutage) throw new Error('Gateway timeout (504) from payments.ralfiz.dev');
  return { ref: 'PAY-' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8).toUpperCase(), amount };
}

function pay(data) {
  validate(data);
  try {
    return chargeCard(2998, data.outage);
  } catch (err) {
    throw new PaymentError('We could not reach your bank. You have not been charged.', {
      cause: err,
    });
  }
}

// ---- UI: turns errors into friendly messages ----
const form = document.querySelector('#checkout');
const banner = document.querySelector('#banner');

function reset() {
  form.querySelectorAll('[aria-invalid]').forEach((el) => el.removeAttribute('aria-invalid'));
  form.querySelectorAll('.err').forEach((p) => (p.textContent = ''));
  banner.hidden = true;
}

function showBanner(text, kind) {
  banner.textContent = text;
  banner.className = `banner ${kind}`;
  banner.hidden = false;
}

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  reset();
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  data.outage = form.elements.outage.checked;
  try {
    const receipt = pay(data);
    showBanner(`Payment successful. Reference ${receipt.ref}`, 'ok');
    console.log('Paid', receipt);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof AggregateError) {
      for (const { field, message } of err.errors) {
        form.elements[field].setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
        document.getElementById(`${field}-err`).textContent = message;
      }
      form.elements[err.errors[0].field].focus();
      console.warn(`${err.message}: ${err.errors.map((e) => e.field).join(', ')}`);
    } else if (err instanceof PaymentError) {
      showBanner(err.message, 'bad');
      console.warn(`${err.name}: ${err.message}\n  caused by ${err.cause.message}`);
    } else {
      showBanner('Something went wrong on our side. Please try again.', 'bad');
      throw err; // a real bug: let it reach the console and error tracking
    }
  }
});

form.requestSubmit(); // show the empty-form errors straight away

The form is submitted once on load so you can see the error state. Fill it in, then tick the outage box to see how a PaymentError with a cause is shown to the user and to the developer.

Common mistakes

1. Swallowing errors.

try { saveCart(cart); } catch (err) {}            // the bug vanishes
try { saveCart(cart); } catch (err) {              // fix: handle it or report it
  showToast('Could not save your cart');
  reportError(err);
}

2. Throwing strings.

throw 'Out of stock';                              // no stack, no instanceof
throw new StockError('Out of stock', { cause: err }); // fix

3. Checking message text instead of the type. Messages are for humans and change.

if (err.message === 'Invalid email') { … }        // breaks after a copy edit
if (err instanceof ValidationError && err.field === 'email') { … } // fix

4. Losing the original error when wrapping.

catch (err) { throw new Error('Import failed'); }                  // root cause gone
catch (err) { throw new ImportError('Import failed', { cause: err }); } // fix

5. Returning from finally. It overrides the try or catch result and can hide a thrown error (see the Predict snippets). Use finally only for clean-up.

6. Showing err.message from the server or the engine directly to users. "Cannot read properties of undefined" means nothing to a customer and can leak internals. Map errors to friendly messages, and log the details.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "How do you handle errors in a front-end app?" Validate at boundaries, use specific error classes, show friendly messages, keep causes, report unexpected errors to a tracking service with source maps, and add global error and unhandledrejection listeners as a safety net.
  • Operational versus programmer errors: a timeout or bad input is operational, so handle and recover. A TypeError from your own code is a programmer error, so fix the bug; do not catch and continue.
  • Know finally semantics exactly: it runs after return and throw, and a return inside it wins.
  • Error.captureStackTrace exists in V8 (Chrome and Node) but is not standard. With new.target.name and super(message, options) you rarely need it.
  • Explain your debugging process in interviews: reproduce, read the stack trace, form a hypothesis, set a breakpoint, inspect, fix, and add a test so the bug cannot return.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

function f() {
  try {
    return 'from try';
  } finally {
    console.log('finally runs');
  }
}
console.log(f());
  • A from try
  • B 
    finally runs
from try
  • C 
    from try
finally runs
  • D finally runs

Snippet 2. What is logged?

function g() {
  try {
    throw new Error('boom');
  } catch {
    return 'catch';
  } finally {
    return 'finally';
  }
}
console.log(g());
  • A catch
  • B boom
  • C finally
  • D undefined

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const names = [];
try { JSON.parse('{oops'); } catch (e) { names.push(e.name); }
try { null.length; } catch (e) { names.push(e.name); }
try { missingFn(); } catch (e) { names.push(e.name); }
console.log(names.join(' '));
  • A SyntaxError TypeError TypeError
  • B Error Error Error
  • C SyntaxError ReferenceError ReferenceError
  • D SyntaxError TypeError ReferenceError

Snippet 4. What is logged?

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
    this.field = field;
  }
}
const err = new ValidationError('email', 'Required');
console.log(err instanceof Error, err.field, String(err));
  • A true email ValidationError: Required
  • B false email Error: Required
  • C true email Error: Required
  • D true undefined ValidationError: Required

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const low = new Error('ECONNRESET');
const high = new Error('Could not load orders', { cause: low });
console.log(high.message + ' <- ' + high.cause.message, high.cause === low);
  • A Could not load orders <- undefined false
  • B Could not load orders <- ECONNRESET true
  • C ECONNRESET <- Could not load orders true
  • D Could not load orders <- ECONNRESET false

Answers

  1. B. The return value is computed first, then finally runs, and only then does the function actually return to the caller, which logs the value.
  2. C. A return inside finally replaces the pending return from catch (and would even swallow a thrown error). That is why you should never return from finally.
  3. D. Invalid JSON is a SyntaxError, reading a property of null is a TypeError, and using a name that was never declared is a ReferenceError.
  4. A. The subclass is still an Error. String(err) uses Error.prototype.toString, which prints name, a colon and the message, and we set name ourselves.
  5. B. The options object sets high.cause to the very same error object, so the chain keeps the original message and stack for debugging.

terms.definition: An instance of Error (or a subclass) with name, message, stack and optionally cause. Always throw these, not strings.
Stops the current function and unwinds the call stack until a matching catch is found. Uncaught, it ends the current task.
try runs code that may fail, catch handles a thrown value, and finally always runs afterwards, even after return.
A subclass such as class ValidationError extends Error that carries a clear name and extra data such as field.
The second argument new Error(message, { cause }) that links a high-level error to the lower-level error that caused it (ES2022).
The list of function calls active when the error was created, newest first, with file names and line numbers.
A marker in DevTools (or a debugger statement) that pauses execution so you can inspect variables and step through code.

lessons.examTip: Catch errors where you can do something useful (show a message, retry, fall back) and rethrow the rest. An empty catch block that hides a bug is one of the most expensive lines in any code base.

quiz.question: Which statement about finally is correct?
options: finally runs only when no error was thrown
finally runs after try or catch, even if one of them returns or throws
finally runs before catch so it can log the error
finally prevents the error from reaching the caller

quiz.question: A payment call fails with a low-level network error. What is the best thing to throw to the UI layer?
options: The raw network error, unchanged
A string such as 'payment failed'
Nothing: log it and return undefined
new PaymentError('Payment failed', { cause: err }), keeping the original as the cause
quiz.explanation: A specific error class tells the caller what failed in business terms, and cause keeps the technical detail for logs and debugging. Strings have no stack, and silently returning undefined hides the failure.

quiz.question: Why is throw 'Invalid email' worse than throw new ValidationError('Invalid email')?
options: A string has no stack trace, no name and fails instanceof checks
Strings cannot be caught by catch
It is a SyntaxError to throw a string
There is no difference
quiz.explanation: You can throw any value, but only Error objects capture a stack trace and support instanceof, name and cause. Handlers and logging tools rely on those.

quiz.question: setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('x'); }, 0) is inside a try block. What happens?
options: The catch block handles it
finally catches it
The error is uncaught, because the callback runs later in a new task, after the try block has finished
The timer is cancelled
quiz.explanation: try/catch only covers code that runs synchronously inside it. The callback runs later on an empty call stack, so the error must be handled inside the callback, or with promises and await (next module).

domains.name: Asynchronous JavaScript
domains.blurb: The event loop, promises, async and await, fetch and real APIs.

lessons.title: The event loop
lessons.summaryHtml:
JavaScript runs your code on one main thread with one call stack. It still handles timers, clicks and network responses without freezing because the host (the browser or Node) does the waiting, and the event loop feeds finished work back to JavaScript one piece at a time.

The loop has a strict order: run one task (a script, a timer, an event), then drain every microtask (promise callbacks, code after await, queueMicrotask), then, in browsers, maybe render a frame. Then it takes the next task.

Knowing this order explains why setTimeout(fn, 0) runs after promise callbacks, why a long loop freezes the page, and how to split heavy work so the interface stays smooth.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Picture a small restaurant with one chef. The chef can only cook one dish at a time. That is JavaScript's single main thread. But the chef does not stand by the oven waiting for bread to bake. They set a timer, hand the delivery order to a courier, and start the next dish. Kitchen helpers do the waiting. When the bread is ready, a ticket goes onto a rail, and the chef picks it up when the current dish is done.

In JavaScript, the helpers are the host APIs (timers, network, the DOM, the file system), the ticket rail is the task queue, and the rule for which ticket comes next is the event loop. There is also a short "urgent notes" list, the microtask queue: the chef always clears every urgent note before picking the next ticket.

Why it matters

  • Frozen pages. A heavy calculation in a click handler blocks everything: no typing, no scrolling updates, no painting. Google's Interaction to Next Paint (INP) metric measures exactly this.
  • Ordering bugs. "Why is my value still empty?" is usually code that reads a result before the callback that sets it has run.
  • Everything async builds on it. Promises, async/await, fetch, events and animations are all scheduled by the event loop. The next three lessons assume you understand it.
  • Interviews. "What order does this log?" is one of the most common JavaScript interview questions.

How it works

The call stack

When a function is called, a frame with its local variables is pushed onto the call stack. When it returns, the frame is popped. JavaScript only ever runs the frame at the top.

function lineTotal(item) { return item.price * item.qty; }
function cartTotal(cart) { return cart.reduce((s, i) => s + lineTotal(i), 0); }
function checkout(cart) { console.log(cartTotal(cart)); }
checkout([{ price: 250, qty: 2 }]);
// stack while lineTotal runs (top first):
// lineTotal → (reduce callback) → Array.reduce → cartTotal → checkout → (script)

The key fact: nothing else can run until the stack is empty. A callback, however urgent, has to wait for the current code to finish.

Host APIs do the waiting

The JavaScript engine (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) only knows how to run code. It has no idea what a timer or a network request is. Those come from the host: the browser gives you setTimeout, fetch and DOM events, and Node gives you timers, fs and sockets. When you call setTimeout(fn, 1000), the host starts a timer outside the main thread, and your code continues at once. When the time is up, the host puts a task that will call fn into a queue. JavaScript is non-blocking because the waiting happens in the host, not on your stack.

Tasks and microtasks

Tasks (macrotasks)Microtasks
Created byrunning a script, setTimeout/setInterval, DOM events, postMessage, I/O callbacks in Nodepromise then/catch/finally callbacks, code after await, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver
How many per turnoneall of them, including ones added while draining
Rendering in between?yes, the browser may render between tasksno, never in the middle of a drain

The rule to remember: after every task, the engine runs microtasks until the microtask queue is empty. Only then can the loop render or pick the next task. That is why a promise callback always beats a setTimeout(…, 0) scheduled at the same time.

Try it: Sync first, then microtasks, then tasks

JavaScript

console.log('1. script starts (sync)');

setTimeout(() => console.log('7. setTimeout 0 (task)'), 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('4. promise.then (microtask)'));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log('5. queueMicrotask (microtask)'));

(async () => {
  console.log('2. async function body runs sync until await');
  await null;
  console.log('6. code after await (microtask)');
})();

console.log('3. script ends (sync)');

The numbers show the real order. The async function runs synchronously until its first await, and the part after await joins the microtask queue behind the two callbacks queued earlier.

"Until the queue is empty" includes microtasks queued by other microtasks. A promise chain adds its next step only when the previous step runs, so separate chains interleave, while a timer waits patiently for the whole drain.

Try it: Microtasks drain completely

JavaScript

setTimeout(() => console.log('timer: finally my turn'), 0);

let n = 0;
function again() {
  n++;
  console.log('microtask', n);
  if (n < 5) queueMicrotask(again); // each one queues another
}
queueMicrotask(again);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('  then A'))
  .then(() => console.log('  then B (queued only after A ran)'))
  .then(() => console.log('  then C'));

console.log('script done: now the microtask queue drains');

Each microtask here queues another one, and the promise chain queues its next step only after the previous one runs, so the two interleave. The timer waits until the queue is completely empty.

Watch out: a microtask that always queues another microtask never lets the queue empty. The page freezes exactly as with while (true) {}, because no task and no rendering can happen. This is called starving the event loop.

The rendering step

In a browser, the loop looks roughly like this (simplified from the HTML specification):

while (true) {
  const task = pickOldestRunnableTask(); // timers, events, messages, …
  run(task);
  while (microtaskQueue.length > 0) runNext(microtaskQueue);
  if (isTimeToRender()) {                // usually once per display refresh
    runAnimationFrameCallbacks();        // requestAnimationFrame
    recalculateStyles(); layout(); paint();
  }
}

A 60 Hz screen refreshes about every 16.7 ms. If one task takes 300 ms, the browser misses about 18 frames in a row, and the page visibly freezes. Browsers treat any task that runs longer than 50 ms as a "long task". requestAnimationFrame(cb) is the right tool for visual updates, because cb runs just before the next paint.

setTimeout(fn, 0) and timer accuracy

The delay is a minimum, not a promise. setTimeout(fn, 0) means "run fn as a new task as soon as possible after 0 ms". It still waits for the current task and all microtasks, and for any earlier tasks in the queue. A few more facts:

  • When timers are nested more than five levels deep, the HTML spec requires a delay of at least 4 ms.
  • Node treats a delay of 0 as 1 ms.
  • Browsers throttle timers in background tabs heavily, often to once per second or less, to save battery.
  • Never use timers to "wait until something is ready". Use the event or promise that signals it.

Try it: setTimeout(0) is a minimum, not a promise

JavaScript

const start = performance.now();
const at = () => `${Math.round(performance.now() - start)} ms`;

setTimeout(() => console.log('setTimeout(0) callback ran at', at()), 0);

// Keep the main thread busy for 200 ms
while (performance.now() - start < 200) {}
console.log('busy loop finished at', at());

// Nested zero-delay timers
const gaps = [];
let last;
function nested(level) {
  const now = performance.now();
  if (last !== undefined) gaps.push(Number((now - last).toFixed(1)));
  last = now;
  if (level < 10) setTimeout(() => nested(level + 1), 0);
  else console.log('gaps between nested setTimeout(0) calls (ms):', gaps);
}
setTimeout(() => nested(1), 250);

The zero-delay timer cannot run until the busy loop gives the thread back. Nested zero-delay timers are also clamped: from about the fifth level, browsers wait at least 4 ms. Your numbers will vary slightly.

await is a microtask checkpoint

An async function runs synchronously until its first await. At that point it pauses only itself and returns a promise to the caller, which carries on. When the awaited value is ready, the rest of the function is queued as a microtask. So several async functions can take turns, one step each, without any threads.

Try it: await hands control back

JavaScript

async function brew(drink) {
  console.log(`${drink}: start`);
  await null; // pause this function; the rest resumes as a microtask
  console.log(`${drink}: step 2`);
  await null;
  console.log(`${drink}: done`);
  return drink;
}

setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout: after every microtask'), 0);

const tea = brew('Tea');
brew('Coffee');
console.log('sync code finished, tea is a', tea.constructor.name);

tea.then((d) => console.log(`${d} promise fulfilled`));

Two async functions take turns at every await, like two customers being served one step at a time. Neither blocks the other, and the timer still waits for all microtasks.

Blocking the main thread, and how to avoid it

"Non-blocking" only describes waiting. Heavy computation still blocks: parsing a 50 MB JSON file, sorting a million rows or resizing an image in JavaScript all hold the one thread. You have three tools:

  1. Do less: paginate, filter on the server, use a Map instead of repeated searches (performance lesson, js30).
  2. Chunk the work: process a slice for a few milliseconds, then give the thread back with setTimeout or await scheduler.yield(), so input and rendering can happen between slices. scheduler.yield() is a newer API that also ends the current task, but your continuation is queued ahead of other waiting tasks, so a long job is not pushed to the back of the line. It shipped in Chromium-based browsers first: check the MDN compatibility table and keep a setTimeout fallback.
  3. Move it off the main thread with a Web Worker (browser) or worker_threads (Node). Workers run in parallel on another thread and talk to the page with messages.
const yieldToMain = () =>
  globalThis.scheduler?.yield ? scheduler.yield() : new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0));

async function processAll(invoices) {
  let sliceStart = performance.now();
  for (const invoice of invoices) {
    calculateGst(invoice);
    if (performance.now() - sliceStart > 8) {  // about half a frame
      await yieldToMain();                      // input and paint can happen here
      sliceStart = performance.now();
    }
  }
}

Note that await Promise.resolve() does not help: it only creates a microtask, and microtasks never let the browser render. You need a real task boundary.

The event loop in Node.js

Node uses the same model of one thread, tasks and microtasks, but its loop runs in phases, powered by the libuv library:

PhaseRuns
timerssetTimeout / setInterval callbacks that are due
pollI/O callbacks (files, sockets); waits for new events
checksetImmediate callbacks
closeclose events, such as a socket closing

Between every callback, Node first runs the process.nextTick queue and then the promise microtask queue. At the top level of a script, whether setTimeout(fn, 0) or setImmediate(fn) runs first depends on timing, but inside an I/O or timer callback setImmediate always comes first. Prefer queueMicrotask and promises over process.nextTick in new code: they work the same way in browsers.

Example: the main thread lab

This page makes the event loop visible. The ball is moved by JavaScript on every animation frame, and the page records the longest gap between two frames. Each button runs the same 1.2 seconds of invoice calculations in a different way:

  • Block runs everything in one task. The ball stops, typing does nothing, and the frame gap is about 1,200 ms.
  • Chunked works in slices of about 8 ms and yields with setTimeout, a real task boundary, between slices. The ball keeps moving, you can type, and the gap stays small.
  • Microtask flood slices the work too, but "yields" with await Promise.resolve(). Since microtasks drain before rendering, the page freezes just like the blocking version. This is the most surprising result, and the most important one.

Try it: Main thread lab

HTML

<main class="lab">
  <header>
    <h1>Main thread lab</h1>
    <p class="muted">Each button runs about 1.2 s of invoice calculations.</p>
  </header>
  <section class="card">
    <div class="track"><div id="ball" class="ball"></div></div>
    <div class="stats">

JavaScript

const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
const ball = $('#ball');
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('[data-mode]');

// ---- 1. A JavaScript-driven animation that measures frame gaps ----
let lastFrame = performance.now();
let windowStart = lastFrame;
let frames = 0;
let maxGap = 0;

function frame(now) {
  maxGap = Math.max(maxGap, now - lastFrame);
  lastFrame = now;
  frames++;
  if (now - windowStart >= 500) {
    $('#fps').textContent = Math.round((frames * 1000) / (now - windowStart));
    $('#gap').textContent = `${Math.round(maxGap)} ms`;
    frames = 0;
    windowStart = now;
  }
  const room = ball.parentElement.clientWidth - 28;
  ball.style.transform = `translateX(${((Math.sin(now / 350) + 1) / 2) * room}px)`;
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
}
requestAnimationFrame(frame);

// ---- 2. The "work": pretend to calculate GST for one invoice ----
function processInvoice(i) {
  let total = 0;
  for (let k = 0; k < 300; k++) total += ((i * 31 + k) % 997) * 1.18;
  return total;
}

const BUDGET_MS = 1200;
// A new task via setTimeout: input and rendering can happen before we continue.
// (scheduler.yield() is the newer option; see the lesson text.)
const yieldToMain = () => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));

// ---- 3. Three ways to run the same amount of work ----
const modes = {
  blocking() {
    let n = 0;
    const end = performance.now() + BUDGET_MS;
    while (performance.now() < end) processInvoice(n++);
    return n;
  },

  async chunked() {
    let n = 0;
    let spent = 0;
    while (spent < BUDGET_MS) {
      const sliceStart = performance.now();
      while (performance.now() - sliceStart < 8) processInvoice(n++);
      spent += performance.now() - sliceStart;
      $('#done').textContent = n.toLocaleString('en-IN');
      await yieldToMain(); // a real task boundary: input and rendering can happen
    }
    return n;
  },

  async microtasks() {
    let n = 0;
    let spent = 0;
    while (spent < BUDGET_MS) {
      const sliceStart = performance.now();
      while (performance.now() - sliceStart < 8) processInvoice(n++);
      spent += performance.now() - sliceStart;
      $('#done').textContent = n.toLocaleString('en-IN');
      await Promise.resolve(); // only a microtask: no rendering in between
    }
    return n;
  },
};

async function start(mode) {
  buttons.forEach((b) => (b.disabled = true));
  $('#status').textContent = `Running "${mode}"…`;
  $('#done').textContent = '0';
  await new Promise(requestAnimationFrame); // let the "Running" text paint first
  maxGap = 0;
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const count = await modes[mode]();
  const took = Math.round(performance.now() - t0);
  $('#done').textContent = count.toLocaleString('en-IN');
  // wait two frames so the frame loop can record the gap this work caused
  requestAnimationFrame(() => requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    const gap = Math.round(maxGap);
    $('#status').textContent = `${mode}: ${count.toLocaleString('en-IN')} invoices in ${took} ms, longest frame gap ${gap} ms.`;
    console.log(`${mode.padEnd(10)} → longest frame gap ${gap} ms`);
    buttons.forEach((b) => (b.disabled = false));
  }));
}

buttons.forEach((b) => b.addEventListener('click', () => start(b.dataset.mode)));
console.log('A smooth 60 Hz screen draws a frame about every 16.7 ms.');

The ball is moved by JavaScript on every animation frame. Press each button and watch the ball, the frame gap and the text box. Microtasks never give the browser a chance to render, just like one long task.

The lab repeats the experiment in Node. A heartbeat setInterval counts ticks while invoices are processed. The blocking version lets it tick zero times; the chunked version, which yields with setImmediate, keeps it ticking.

Common mistakes

1. Expecting a zero-delay timer to run "now".

let user;
setTimeout(() => { user = loadUser(); }, 0);
console.log(user.name);                 // TypeError: user is undefined
// fix: use the value inside the callback, or await a promise that returns it

2. Using microtasks to "yield".

for (const chunk of chunks) { work(chunk); await Promise.resolve(); } // still frozen
for (const chunk of chunks) { work(chunk); await yieldToMain(); }      // fix

3. Thinking async code runs in parallel. Marking a CPU-heavy function async does not move it off the main thread. Only waiting is concurrent. Use a Web Worker for real parallel computation.

4. Animating with setInterval.

setInterval(() => move(box), 16);       // drifts, runs in background tabs, may skip
function tick(t) { move(box, t); requestAnimationFrame(tick); } // fix
requestAnimationFrame(tick);

5. Relying on setTimeout versus setImmediate order at the top level of a Node script. It can change from run to run. If order matters, chain the steps explicitly.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Explain the loop in one breath: "One task runs to completion, then all microtasks drain, then the browser may render, then the next task."
  • Why is JavaScript single-threaded but non-blocking? The engine has one call stack, but the host does the waiting for timers, network and I/O in the background and queues callbacks when they are ready.
  • Classify callbacks quickly: promises, await and queueMicrotask are microtasks; timers, events and messages are tasks; requestAnimationFrame runs in the rendering step.
  • Real-world performance: long tasks hurt INP. Break them up, move heavy work to workers, and measure with the DevTools Performance panel, which marks long tasks with a red corner.
  • Know the Node extras: process.nextTick runs before promise callbacks, and setImmediate runs in the check phase.

terms.definition: The list of functions currently running. JavaScript can only run the function at the top; everything else waits.
A unit of work taken from a task queue: running a script, a timer callback, a DOM event, a message or an I/O callback.
A small callback that runs right after the current task, before rendering or the next task: promise reactions, await continuations and queueMicrotask.
The host algorithm that repeatedly takes one task, drains the microtask queue, and gives the browser a chance to render.
Features provided by the browser or Node, not by the JavaScript engine: timers, fetch, DOM events, file system. They do the waiting off the main thread.
A task that keeps the main thread busy for longer than 50 ms. During it the page cannot respond to input or paint.
A point between tasks where the browser may run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, recalculate styles and layout, and paint a new frame.

quiz.question: The current script schedules setTimeout(a, 0) and then Promise.resolve().then(b). Which runs first after the script ends, and why?
options: a, because it was scheduled first
