quiz.explanation: The script itself is a task. When it finishes, the engine drains the microtask queue (b) before the event loop picks the next task, the timer (a).

quiz.question: A click handler runs a loop that takes 2 seconds. What does the user experience?
options: The loop runs in the background while the page stays responsive
Only animations freeze; typing still works
The browser automatically splits the loop into chunks
The page freezes: no painting, no typing and no other handlers until the loop ends
quiz.explanation: There is one main thread. While a task runs, the event loop cannot take other tasks or render, so the page looks frozen. (CSS animations that run on the compositor may continue, but nothing driven by JavaScript does.)

quiz.question: What does await do inside an async function?
options: It pauses only that async function; the caller continues, and the rest of the function resumes later as a microtask
It blocks the whole thread until the promise settles
It creates a new thread
It turns the promise into a synchronous value immediately
quiz.explanation: await returns control to the caller at once. When the awaited promise settles, the rest of the function is queued as a microtask. Nothing else is blocked.

quiz.question: When does a browser get a chance to render a new frame?
options: In the middle of a microtask drain, whenever 16 ms have passed
Whenever a promise resolves
Between tasks, after the microtask queue is empty, typically in step with the display refresh rate
Only when setTimeout is called
quiz.explanation: Rendering happens between tasks. A never-ending chain of microtasks blocks rendering just as much as a long loop does.

lessons.title: Callbacks and Promises
lessons.summaryHtml:
Asynchronous work finishes later, so you need a way to say "when this is done, do that". The oldest way is a callback: you pass a function and the API calls it later. Nested callbacks quickly become the "pyramid of doom", with error handling repeated at every level.

A Promise is an object that stands for a future result. It starts pending and settles exactly once, as fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. then, catch and finally return new promises, so steps form a flat chain, and one catch handles an error from any step.

You will also combine promises with Promise.all, allSettled, race and any, turn callback APIs into promises, and use Promise.withResolvers. The live page loads a Ralfiz Store dashboard from several endpoints in parallel.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

At a busy food court you order a dosa, pay, and get a buzzer. You do not stand at the counter blocking the queue. You sit down, and when the buzzer goes off you collect your food, or you are told they have run out. A promise is that buzzer: an object you get now that stands for a result you will get later, or a failure.

Before promises, JavaScript used callbacks: "here is my phone number, call me when it is ready". That works for one step. With several dependent steps, callbacks nest inside callbacks, and the code becomes hard to read, hard to change and easy to break.

Why it matters

  • Everything async in modern JavaScript returns promises: fetch, response.json(), Node's fs/promises, database drivers, navigator.clipboard, and every async function.
  • async/await (next lesson) is built on promises. If you understand chains, error propagation and combinators, await becomes easy. If you do not, await bugs are baffling.
  • Real screens load several things at once. A dashboard that loads five widgets one after another is five times slower than it needs to be, and one broken widget should not blank the whole page.
  • You will still meet callbacks in older Node code, event listeners and some libraries, and you need to wrap them in promises.

How it works

Callbacks and the pyramid of doom

A callback API takes a function and calls it when the work is done. Node standardised the error-first style: callback(err, result). When step two needs the result of step one, step two must start inside step one's callback, and so on.

Try it: Callbacks and the pyramid of doom

JavaScript

// A fake API with error-first callbacks, like older Node.js code
const db = {
  users: { 7: { id: 7, name: 'Anu' } },
  orders: { 7: [{ id: 'A-101', total: 1499 }, { id: 'A-102', total: 650 }] },
};

function getUser(id, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    const user = db.users[id];
    if (!user) callback(new Error(`User ${id} not found`));
    else callback(null, user);
  }, 100);
}

function getOrders(user, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => callback(null, db.orders[user.id] ?? []), 100);
}

function getInvoice(order, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => callback(null, `Invoice ${order.id}: ₹${order.total}`), 100);
}

// The pyramid of doom
getUser(7, (err, user) => {
  if (err) return console.log('Error:', err.message);
  getOrders(user, (err, orders) => {
    if (err) return console.log('Error:', err.message);
    getInvoice(orders[0], (err, invoice) => {
      if (err) return console.log('Error:', err.message);
      console.log(`${user.name} → ${invoice}`);
    });
  });
});

getUser(99, (err, user) => {
  if (err) return console.log('Error:', err.message);
  console.log('never reached', user);
});

console.log('Requests sent; nothing has come back yet.');

Each step can only start inside the previous callback, and every level repeats if (err). The error for user 99 arrives first because it needs one step, not three.

The problems go beyond indentation:

  • Error handling is repeated at every level, and it is easy to forget one if (err).
  • Inversion of control: you hand your function to someone else's code and trust it to call you exactly once, not zero times or twice.
  • Composition is hard: "run these three in parallel and continue when all are done" needs counters and flags.
  • try/catch does not help, because callbacks run later, in a different task.

Creating a promise

new Promise(executor) calls the executor function immediately and synchronously, passing it two functions: resolve(value) and reject(error). Your executor starts the async work and calls one of them when it finishes. If the executor throws, the promise is rejected.

StateMeaningCan it change?
pendingthe work is not finishedyes, once
fulfilledit succeeded, with a valuenever
rejectedit failed, with a reason (an Error)never

A promise settles exactly once. Extra calls to resolve or reject are ignored, which fixes the "called twice" problem of callbacks. Handlers always run asynchronously, as microtasks, even when the promise is already settled. And a handler added after settling still runs with the stored result.

Try it: Creating a promise: executor, states and settle-once

JavaScript

function payWithUpi(amount) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    console.log(`Requesting ₹${amount}…`); // runs right away
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (amount > 10000) reject(new Error(`₹${amount} is over the demo limit`));
      else resolve({ ref: `UPI-${amount}`, amount });
    }, 150);
  });
}

const ok = payWithUpi(499);
const bad = payWithUpi(25000);
console.log('Right after the calls, ok is a', ok.constructor.name, '(still pending)');

ok.then((receipt) => console.log('fulfilled with', receipt));
bad.catch((err) => console.log('rejected with:', err.message));

// A promise settles exactly once
const once = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  resolve('first');
  resolve('second'); // ignored
  reject(new Error('too late')); // ignored
});
once.then((value) => console.log('once:', value));

// Handlers added after settling still run (asynchronously)
setTimeout(() => {
  ok.then((receipt) => console.log('late handler still gets', receipt.ref));
}, 300);

The executor runs immediately and synchronously. The promise can only settle once, so the later resolve and reject calls are ignored.

If you call resolve with another promise (or any "thenable"), the outer promise adopts it: it waits and settles the same way. That rule is what makes chaining work.

then, catch and finally: chaining

promise.then(onFulfilled, onRejected) registers handlers and returns a new promise. What that new promise does depends on what your handler does:

Inside the handler you…The next promise in the chain…
return a valuefulfils with that value
return a promisewaits for it and settles the same way
throw an errorrejects with that error
return nothingfulfils with undefined

.catch(fn) is short for .then(undefined, fn). .finally(fn) runs on both outcomes, receives no argument, and passes the original value or error through unchanged. That makes it the place to hide a spinner.

Error propagation is the big win. A rejection skips every then fulfilment handler until it reaches a catch. One catch at the end handles a failure in any step, and a catch that returns a value recovers, so the chain continues as fulfilled.

Try it: Chaining: return values and error propagation

JavaScript

const db = {
  users: { 7: { id: 7, name: 'Anu' } },
  orders: { 7: [{ id: 'A-101', total: 1499 }, { id: 'A-102', total: 650 }] },
};
const later = (fn, ms = 100) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) => setTimeout(() => {
    try { resolve(fn()); } catch (err) { reject(err); }
  }, ms));

const getUser = (id) => later(() => {
  if (!db.users[id]) throw new Error(`User ${id} not found`);
  return db.users[id];
});
const getOrders = (user) => later(() => db.orders[user.id] ?? []);

getUser(7)
  .then((user) => {
    console.log('1. got user', user.name);
    return getOrders(user); // a promise: the chain waits for it
  })
  .then((orders) => {
    console.log('2. got', orders.length, 'orders');
    return orders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0); // a value: passed on
  })
  .then((total) => {
    console.log(`3. lifetime spend ₹${total}`);
    if (total < 5000) throw new Error('not a gold member yet'); // jumps to catch
    return 'gold';
  })
  .then((tier) => console.log('4. skipped when step 3 throws', tier))
  .catch((err) => {
    console.log('caught:', err.message);
    return 'silver'; // recover: the chain continues fulfilled
  })
  .then((tier) => console.log('5. final tier:', tier))
  .finally(() => console.log('6. finally: hide the spinner'));

Returning a promise makes the chain wait; returning a value passes it on; throwing skips to the next catch. Change the 5000 threshold to 1000 and run again.

Remember: if a then callback starts async work, return its promise. Without return, the chain moves on at once and any error in that work escapes your catch.

Combining promises

When the tasks do not depend on each other, start them all at once and combine the promises. The total time is then roughly the time of the slowest request, not the sum of all of them.

CombinatorFulfils whenRejects whenUse it for
Promise.allall fulfil (array of values, in input order)the first one rejects (fail-fast)everything is required: order + items + customer
Promise.allSettledall have settled (array of {status, value | reason})neverindependent widgets where partial success is fine
Promise.racethe first to settle fulfilsthe first to settle rejectstimeouts
Promise.anythe first one fulfilsall reject (AggregateError)mirrors, fallbacks, "whichever works first"

Try it: Combinators: all, allSettled, race and any

JavaScript

const fakeFetch = (name, ms, fail = false) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => (fail ? reject(new Error(`${name} failed`)) : resolve(name)), ms));

const t0 = performance.now();
const after = () => `~${Math.round((performance.now() - t0) / 50) * 50} ms`;

Promise.all([fakeFetch('products', 300), fakeFetch('users', 200), fakeFetch('orders', 100)])
  .then((values) => console.log('all:', values, after()));

Promise.all([fakeFetch('products', 300), fakeFetch('reviews', 150, true)])
  .then((values) => console.log('never logged', values))
  .catch((err) => console.log('all rejected fast:', err.message, after()));

Promise.allSettled([fakeFetch('stock', 250), fakeFetch('reviews', 150, true)])
  .then((results) => {
    const summary = results.map((r) => (r.status === 'fulfilled' ? r.value : r.reason.message));
    console.log('allSettled:', summary, after());
  });

Promise.race([fakeFetch('mirror A', 220), fakeFetch('mirror B', 120)])
  .then((winner) => console.log('race winner:', winner, after()));

Promise.any([fakeFetch('cdn 1', 80, true), fakeFetch('cdn 2', 160)])
  .then((first) => console.log('any: first success is', first, after()));

Promise.any([fakeFetch('x', 50, true), fakeFetch('y', 60, true)])
  .catch((err) => console.log('any when all fail:', err.name, err.errors.length, 'errors'));

Lines appear in time order. all fails fast on the first rejection, allSettled always reports everything, race takes the first to settle, and any takes the first success.

Promises cannot be cancelled. When Promise.all rejects early, or race picks a winner, the other operations keep running and their results are ignored. To really cancel a fetch, you use an AbortController (next lesson).

Promisifying callback APIs and Promise.withResolvers

To use an old callback API in a promise chain, wrap it once. A generic promisify does this for any error-first function. Node ships one as util.promisify, and most core modules also have promise versions, such as node:fs/promises and node:timers/promises.

import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { setTimeout as sleep } from 'node:timers/promises';

readFile('orders.json', 'utf8')
  .then((text) => JSON.parse(text))
  .then((orders) => sleep(100, orders))   // resolves with orders after 100 ms
  .then((orders) => console.log(orders.length, 'orders'))
  .catch((err) => console.log('Could not read orders:', err.message));

Sometimes the code that creates a promise is not the code that settles it: a modal that resolves when the user clicks OK, or a queue item confirmed later. Promise.withResolvers() (ES2024) returns { promise, resolve, reject } so you do not have to smuggle resolve out of an executor. It is available in Node 22 and all current evergreen browsers; check the MDN compatibility table if you support older ones.

Try it: Promisify, sleep, timeouts and withResolvers

JavaScript

// 1. Promisify an error-first callback function
function promisify(fn) {
  return (...args) =>
    new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      fn(...args, (err, result) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve(result)));
    });
}

function readSettings(name, callback) {
  setTimeout(() => callback(null, { name, theme: 'dark', currency: 'INR' }), 80);
}

const readSettingsAsync = promisify(readSettings);
readSettingsAsync('store').then((settings) => console.log('settings:', settings));

// 2. sleep: the classic promisified setTimeout
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

// 3. withTimeout: race the work against a timer that rejects
function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  let timer;
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`Timed out after ${ms} ms`)), ms);
  });
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

withTimeout(sleep(100).then(() => 'fast report'), 300)
  .then((report) => console.log('withTimeout ok:', report));
withTimeout(sleep(500).then(() => 'slow report'), 200)
  .catch((err) => console.log('withTimeout:', err.message));

// 4. Promise.withResolvers: resolve it from somewhere else
function createApproval() {
  const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
  return { approved: promise, approve: resolve, decline: reject };
}

const refund = createApproval();
refund.approved.then((manager) => console.log('refund approved by', manager));
setTimeout(() => refund.approve('Meera (store manager)'), 350);

promisify turns any error-first callback API into a promise API. withTimeout is built from race. Promise.withResolvers (ES2024) hands you resolve and reject to call from elsewhere.

Unhandled rejections

A rejected promise with no catch anywhere is an unhandled rejection. Browsers log "Uncaught (in promise)" and fire an unhandledrejection event. Node, by default, prints the error and exits the process. Every chain needs an end: a catch, or a caller that the promise is returned to.

Example: Ralfiz Store dashboard

The dashboard needs product, customer, task and blog numbers from four DummyJSON endpoints, plus a "Refunds" endpoint that does not exist, to show a failure. The design:

  1. getJSON(path) wraps fetch and always checks response.ok. fetch only rejects on network failure, so a 404 must be turned into an error by you.
  2. loadTile(t) renders its own tile when its request settles, with textContent because the data comes from an API. It rethrows errors so the caller can count them.
  3. loadParallel() starts every request at once and waits with Promise.allSettled, so one broken endpoint shows an error tile instead of blanking the page.
  4. loadOneByOne() chains the same requests with reduce, so each waits for the previous one. It exists only to show how much slower that is.
  5. .finally() re-enables the buttons however it ended.

Try it: Ralfiz Store dashboard: parallel requests

JavaScript

const API = 'https://dummyjson.com';
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

// fetch + simulated latency + the response.ok check you must always do
function getJSON(path, latency) {
  return sleep(latency)
    .then(() => fetch(API + path))
    .then((res) => {
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status} for ${path}`);
      return res.json();
    });
}

const TILES = [
  { id: 'products', icon: '🛍️', label: 'Products', latency: 450,
    path: '/products?limit=1&sortBy=rating&order=desc&select=title,rating',
    read: (d) => [d.total.toLocaleString('en-IN'), `Top rated: ${d.products[0].title}`] },
  { id: 'users', icon: '👥', label: 'Customers', latency: 300,
    path: '/users?limit=1&select=firstName',
    read: (d) => [d.total.toLocaleString('en-IN'), 'registered accounts'] },
  { id: 'todos', icon: '✅', label: 'Open tasks', latency: 350,
    path: '/todos?limit=30',
    read: (d) => [String(d.todos.filter((t) => !t.completed).length), 'in the latest 30'] },
  { id: 'posts', icon: '📝', label: 'Blog posts', latency: 250,
    path: '/posts?limit=1&select=title',
    read: (d) => [d.total.toLocaleString('en-IN'), 'published'] },
];
const BROKEN = { id: 'refunds', icon: '↩️', label: 'Refunds', latency: 200,
  path: '/refunds', read: (d) => [String(d.total), 'this week'] };

const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
const grid = $('#grid');
const buttons = [$('#seq'), $('#par')];

function tile(t) {
  const el = document.createElement('article');
  el.className = 'tile loading';
  el.id = `tile-${t.id}`;
  const head = document.createElement('div');
  head.className = 'head';
  head.textContent = `${t.icon} ${t.label}`;
  const value = document.createElement('div');
  value.className = 'value';
  value.textContent = '000';
  const note = document.createElement('div');
  note.className = 'note';
  note.textContent = 'Loading…';
  el.append(head, value, note);
  return el;
}

function show(t, value, note, isError = false) {
  const el = document.getElementById(`tile-${t.id}`);
  el.className = isError ? 'tile error' : 'tile';
  el.querySelector('.value').textContent = value; // API data: always textContent
  el.querySelector('.note').textContent = note;
}

function loadTile(t) {
  return getJSON(t.path, t.latency).then(
    (data) => {
      show(t, ...t.read(data));
      return t.label;
    },
    (err) => {
      show(t, 'Could not load', err.message, true);
      throw err; // keep it rejected so the caller can count failures
    },
  );
}

function report(results, t0, how) {
  const ms = Math.round(performance.now() - t0);
  const failed = results.filter((r) => r.status === 'rejected').length;
  const text = `${results.length - failed} loaded · ${failed} failed · ${ms} ms (${how})`;
  $('#status').textContent = text;
  console.log(text);
}

function start() {
  const list = $('#broken').checked ? [...TILES, BROKEN] : TILES;
  buttons.forEach((b) => (b.disabled = true));
  $('#status').textContent = 'Loading…';
  grid.replaceChildren(...list.map(tile));
  return { list, t0: performance.now() };
}

const done = () => buttons.forEach((b) => (b.disabled = false));

function loadParallel() {
  const { list, t0 } = start();
  return Promise.allSettled(list.map(loadTile))
    .then((results) => report(results, t0, 'parallel'))
    .finally(done);
}

function loadOneByOne() {
  const { list, t0 } = start();
  const results = [];
  return list
    .reduce(
      (chain, t) =>
        chain.then(() =>
          loadTile(t).then(
            (value) => results.push({ status: 'fulfilled', value }),
            (reason) => results.push({ status: 'rejected', reason }),
          ),
        ),
      Promise.resolve(),
    )
    .then(() => report(results, t0, 'one by one'))
    .finally(done);
}

$('#par').addEventListener('click', loadParallel);
$('#seq').addEventListener('click', loadOneByOne);
loadParallel();

Each request has a little simulated latency so the timing is visible. Compare "one by one" with "in parallel", and untick the broken request to see every tile succeed.

In parallel mode the total time is close to the slowest request. One by one, it is the sum of all of them. The lab brings the same patterns to a callback-based "legacy" store API in Node: promisify it, chain it, run it in parallel, survive a failing service, and add a timeout.

Common mistakes

1. Forgetting to return inside then.

getUser(7)
  .then((user) => { getOrders(user); })       // not returned: the chain does not wait
  .then((orders) => console.log(orders));      // undefined
getUser(7)
  .then((user) => getOrders(user))            // fix: return the promise
  .then((orders) => console.log(orders));

2. Nesting thens (callback hell with promises).

getUser(7).then((user) => {
  getOrders(user).then((orders) => { /* … */ });  // nested again
});
getUser(7).then(getOrders).then(render).catch(showError);  // fix: flat chain

3. Wrapping a promise in new Promise for no reason (the "explicit construction" anti-pattern). It adds code and often loses errors.

const load = () => new Promise((resolve) => {
  fetch(url).then((res) => resolve(res.json()));   // a rejection is lost
});
const load = () => fetch(url).then((res) => res.json()); // fix

4. Waiting one by one when requests are independent. Start them together and combine with Promise.all or allSettled.

5. Using Promise.all when partial success is acceptable. One failed widget rejects everything. Choose allSettled for independent parts.

6. Assuming fetch rejects on 404 or 500. It does not. Check res.ok and throw.

Interview and real-world notes

  • "What is a promise?" An object representing the eventual result of an async operation. It is pending, then fulfilled or rejected, exactly once. Handlers run as microtasks.
  • Know all four combinators and when each rejects. "Build withTimeout with race" and "implement Promise.all yourself" are classic exercises. The key is a counter of fulfilled promises and results stored by index.
  • Explain the microtask timing: then callbacks never run synchronously, even on an already settled promise.
  • Parallel versus sequential is a performance question in disguise. Mention dependent steps (sequential), independent ones (parallel), and limiting concurrency for large batches.
  • In real code you mostly consume promises with await. You create them with new Promise only to wrap callback or event APIs.

  2. B. The first then returns 6. The second logs it but returns nothing, so the third receives undefined.

  4. D. allSettled waits for every promise, including the slower one, and never rejects. Each result has a status of fulfilled or rejected, in the original order.
  5. B. race settles like the first promise to settle, which is the rejection after 10 ms. any ignores rejections while a success is still possible, so it fulfils with slow at 30 ms.

terms.definition: A function passed to another function to be called later, for example when a timer ends or data arrives.
The Node.js convention callback(err, result): the first argument is an error or null.
An object representing a value that will be available later. It is pending, then fulfilled or rejected, exactly once.
A promise that is no longer pending: it has been fulfilled or rejected, and it can never change again.
Calls to then/catch/finally linked together. Each returns a new promise that follows whatever the handler returned or threw.
A function that combines several promises into one: Promise.all, allSettled, race and any.
Wrapping a callback-based function so it returns a promise instead.

quiz.question: A then callback runs some code but has no return statement. What does the next then in the chain receive?
options: The same value the previous then received
undefined
The promise itself
Nothing: the chain stops
quiz.explanation: Each then returns a new promise that fulfils with whatever the handler returned. No return means undefined. This is also why forgetting to return an inner promise breaks the chain.

quiz.question: Promise.all([a, b, c]) is used and b rejects after 100 ms while a and c are still pending. What happens?
options: It waits for a and c, then resolves with the two successful values
It resolves with [a, undefined, c]
It rejects immediately with b's error; a and c keep running but their results are ignored
It retries b automatically
quiz.explanation: Promise.all is fail-fast: the first rejection rejects the combined promise. Promises cannot be cancelled, so the others still run. Use allSettled when you want every outcome.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Promise.race and Promise.any?
options: race settles like the first promise to settle, success or failure; any fulfils with the first success and rejects only if all fail
They are aliases
any settles with the first failure
race waits for all promises and returns the fastest value
quiz.explanation: race is about speed, whatever the outcome, which makes it good for timeouts. any is about the first success, which suits mirrors and fallbacks. When every promise rejects, any rejects with an AggregateError.

quiz.question: Why are deeply nested callbacks hard to maintain?
options: Callbacks are slower than promises
JavaScript limits nesting to three levels
Callbacks cannot pass data
Error handling is repeated at every level, the code drifts further right with each step, and you trust each API to call you exactly once
quiz.explanation: With callbacks you hand control to other code (inversion of control). Promises give you an object you control: it settles once, errors propagate to one catch, and steps compose in a flat chain.

lessons.title: async and await
lessons.summaryHtml:
async and await let you write promise-based code that reads top to bottom like ordinary code. An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses only that function until a promise settles, while the rest of the page keeps running.

You will handle failures with try/catch/finally, run independent work in parallel with Promise.all instead of one after another, and use await correctly inside loops. You will also add the three habits of production code: timeouts, cancellation with AbortController, and retry with exponential backoff.

The mini project is an order-dashboard loader for Ralfiz Store that loads data in parallel, survives a slow service and a flaky one, and reports exactly what happened.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of ordering at a busy café. You place your order, get a token, and step aside. You do not stand frozen at the counter: you check your phone, and when your token is called you collect the coffee. A promise is that token. await is you saying “I will continue this particular task when the token is called”, while the café (the event loop) keeps serving everyone else.

In the last lesson you chained promises with .then(). async/await is the same machinery with friendlier syntax. It lets you write asynchronous steps top to bottom, use normal try/catch for errors, and use normal loops. Nothing about the event loop changes: await never blocks the page. It only pauses the one function it is written in.

Why it matters

Almost every real front-end screen waits for something: a product list, a login, a payment, a file upload. Code that waits badly is slow (steps run one after another for no reason), fragile (one failed request blanks the whole dashboard), or stuck (a request hangs for a minute with a spinner and no way out). Interviewers know this, so questions about await in loops, Promise.all and error handling are among the most common in junior front-end interviews. The patterns in this lesson are exactly what you will write in your first job: load in parallel, show partial results, time out, allow cancel, and retry gently.

How it works

An async function always returns a promise

Put async before any function (declaration, expression, arrow or method) and two things change. First, the function always returns a promise. If you return 1499, callers get a promise that fulfils with 1499. If you throw, callers get a rejected promise; the error does not fly out synchronously. Second, you may use await inside it.

The body runs synchronously until the first await. At that point the function is suspended: its local variables are saved, and control returns to the caller, which carries on. When the awaited promise settles, the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask and continues from where it stopped. Run the example and follow the numbers.

Try it: An async function always returns a promise

JavaScript

async function getTotal() {
  return 1499;                            // a plain value...
}
async function getUser() {
  throw new Error('Session expired');     // ...or a thrown error
}

const p = getTotal();
console.log('is a promise?', p instanceof Promise);
p.then((total) => console.log('total:', total));
getUser().catch((err) => console.log('caught:', err.message));

async function checkout() {
  console.log('2. checkout starts (runs synchronously)');
  const total = await getTotal();         // pause this function only
  console.log('4. resumed with', total);
  return total + 99;                      // fulfils checkout's promise
}

console.log('1. before');
checkout().then((amount) => console.log('5. checkout result:', amount));
console.log('3. after: the caller did not wait');

Read the numbers, then run it. The caller keeps going while checkout() is paused at await.

// These two functions behave the same way
async function getPrice() {
  const res = await fetch('https://dummyjson.com/products/1');
  const product = await res.json();
  return product.price;
}

function getPriceThen() {
  return fetch('https://dummyjson.com/products/1')
    .then((res) => res.json())
    .then((product) => product.price);
}

You can await any value. A non-promise is wrapped with Promise.resolve, which is why await null still pauses for one microtask. Awaiting a rejected promise throws the rejection reason at that line, exactly like a throw statement.

Errors: try, catch and finally

Because a rejected await throws, ordinary try/catch handles async failures. finally runs whether the work succeeded or failed, which makes it the right place to hide a spinner or re-enable a button. For several independent requests, Promise.allSettled waits for all of them and tells you, per item, whether it was 'fulfilled' (with value) or 'rejected' (with reason). A dashboard can then show the widgets that loaded and an error card for the one that did not.

Try it: try, catch and finally with await

JavaScript

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
const STOCK = { 'TEE-01': 12, 'CAP-03': 0 };

async function getStock(sku) {
  await sleep(50);                        // pretend network call
  if (!(sku in STOCK)) throw new Error(sku + ': warehouse offline');
  return { sku, qty: STOCK[sku] };
}

async function showStock(sku) {
  console.log('spinner on for', sku);
  try {
    const item = await getStock(sku);     // a rejection throws here
    console.log('  in stock:', item);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('  could not load:', err.message);
  } finally {
    console.log('  spinner off for', sku); // success or failure
  }
}

await showStock('TEE-01');
await showStock('MUG-02');

// Many at once: one failure must not hide the others
const skus = ['TEE-01', 'MUG-02', 'CAP-03'];
const results = await Promise.allSettled(skus.map(getStock));
results.forEach((r, i) => {
  const detail = r.status === 'fulfilled' ? 'qty ' + r.value.qty : r.reason.message;
  console.log(skus[i], r.status, '-', detail);
});

The MUG-02 lookup fails. See that finally runs both times, and that allSettled reports every result.

Watch out: try { return fail(); } does not catch a rejection from fail(). The promise is returned before it rejects, so the try block is already over. Write return await fail(); whenever the call sits inside try. Outside a try, plain return is fine.

Sequential vs parallel

This is the most important performance idea in the lesson. A promise-returning function starts its work when you call it, not when you await it. If you write three await lines in a row, the second call does not even start until the first finishes, so the times add up. When the calls do not depend on each other, start them all first and wait once with Promise.all. The total time then equals the slowest call.

Try it: Sequential vs parallel

JavaScript

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

// Three independent "API calls", about 300 ms each
async function getProfile() { await sleep(300); return { name: 'Asha' }; }
async function getOrders() { await sleep(300); return [101, 102, 103]; }
async function getOffers() { await sleep(300); return ['FEST10']; }

// Round to the nearest 100 ms so the output is stable
const since = (t0) => Math.round((performance.now() - t0) / 100) * 100 + ' ms';

let t0 = performance.now();
const profile = await getProfile();       // wait...
const orders = await getOrders();         // ...then wait again
const offers = await getOffers();         // ...and again
console.log('sequential:', since(t0), profile.name, orders.length, offers[0]);

t0 = performance.now();
const [p2, o2, f2] = await Promise.all([
  getProfile(), getOrders(), getOffers(),  // all three start right now
]);
console.log('parallel:  ', since(t0), p2.name, o2.length, f2[0]);

// Start early, await late: same speed-up without Promise.all
t0 = performance.now();
const ordersPromise = getOrders();        // started, not awaited yet
const who = await getProfile();
const list = await ordersPromise;
console.log('start early:', since(t0), who.name, list.length);

Each fake call takes 300 ms. Sequential awaits add up; Promise.all waits only for the slowest.

PatternTotal time (3 calls of 300 ms)Use when
await a(); await b(); await c();about 900 msEach step needs the previous result (log in, then load the cart for that user)
await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()])about 300 msIndependent calls, and any failure should fail the whole screen
await Promise.allSettled([...])about 300 msIndependent calls, and partial results are useful
Start early, await laterabout 300 msYou want one result sooner but can still overlap the rest

Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects, but it does not cancel the other calls: they keep running and their results are ignored. If you need them stopped, pass them an AbortSignal and abort it in your catch.

await inside loops

Loops are where most async bugs live. for...of with await processes items one at a time, in order. That is correct when order matters or when an API has a rate limit. items.map(fn) calls the async function for every item immediately and gives you an array of promises; wrap it in Promise.all to wait for them together. Results come back in input order, even if they finish in a different order.

forEach is the trap. It calls your async callback, receives a promise, and throws it away. Nothing waits, errors become unhandled rejections, and the code after the loop runs immediately. The same applies to filter, some and reduce with async callbacks.

Try it: await inside loops

JavaScript

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
const ms = (t0) => Math.round((performance.now() - t0) / 100) * 100 + ' ms';

const invoices = [
  { id: 'INV-1', delay: 300 },
  { id: 'INV-2', delay: 100 },
  { id: 'INV-3', delay: 200 },
];
async function sendReminder(inv) {
  await sleep(inv.delay);                 // pretend email API
  return inv.id;
}

// 1. for...of + await: one at a time, in order
let t0 = performance.now();
const order = [];
for (const inv of invoices) {
  order.push(await sendReminder(inv));
}
console.log('for...of   ', order, ms(t0));

// 2. map + Promise.all: all at once, results keep input order
t0 = performance.now();
const ids = await Promise.all(invoices.map(sendReminder));
console.log('Promise.all', ids, ms(t0));

// 3. forEach ignores the promises your callback returns
const sent = [];
invoices.forEach(async (inv) => {
  sent.push(await sendReminder(inv));
});
console.log('right after forEach:', sent);
await sleep(400);
console.log('400 ms later:       ', sent, '(finish order)');

for...of waits for each item, Promise.all runs them together, and forEach does not wait at all.

Between “one at a time” and “everything at once” there is a middle path for large lists, such as sending 500 emails: a concurrency limit. A few workers pull from a shared queue, so at most N requests are in flight.

async function mapLimit(items, limit, fn) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  async function worker() {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const i = next++;                  // claim the next index
      results[i] = await fn(items[i]);
    }
  }
  const workers = Array.from({ length: limit }, worker);
  await Promise.all(workers);
  return results;
}

// At most 3 requests at a time
const receipts = await mapLimit(orders, 3, sendReceipt);

Top-level await in modules

Inside an ES module you can use await directly at the top level, with no wrapper function. Scripts loaded with <script type="module">, .mjs files and files in a package with "type": "module" are all modules. Most playground examples in this lesson run as modules for that reason.

// config.js (an ES module)
const res = await fetch('/config.json');
export const config = await res.json();

// main.js: this import waits until config.js has finished
import { config } from './config.js';
console.log(config.currency);

Top-level await pauses the whole module graph that imports this module. That makes it perfect for one-off setup, such as loading configuration or a translations file, but a slow request here delays your whole app. In a classic script, top-level await is a syntax error; use an async function instead.

Timeouts and cancellation

fetch has no default timeout that you control. A request to a struggling server can hang for a long time. The web platform answers with AbortController. The controller owns a signal. You pass the signal to fetch (or to your own functions), and calling controller.abort() makes them reject with an AbortError. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) creates a signal that aborts itself and rejects with a TimeoutError. AbortSignal.any([...]) combines signals, so work stops when the user cancels or time runs out.

Try it: Timeouts and cancellation with AbortController

JavaScript

// A cancellable sleep: the same pattern works for any async API
function sleep(ms, { signal } = {}) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    signal?.throwIfAborted();             // already cancelled?
    const id = setTimeout(resolve, ms);
    signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => {
      clearTimeout(id);                   // stop the work
      reject(signal.reason);              // AbortError or TimeoutError
    }, { once: true });
  });
}

// 1. The user presses Cancel after 100 ms
const controller = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 100);
try {
  await sleep(1000, { signal: controller.signal });
  console.log('1: finished');
} catch (err) {
  console.log('1:', err.name);
}

// 2. A signal that aborts itself after 150 ms
try {
  await sleep(1000, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(150) });
} catch (err) {
  console.log('2:', err.name);
}

// 3. A real request with a 3-second limit
try {
  const res = await fetch('https://dummyjson.com/products/1?select=title,price',
    { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);
  const { title, price } = await res.json();
  console.log('3:', title, price);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('3 failed:', err.name === 'TimeoutError' ? 'too slow' : err.message);
}

// 4. Whichever comes first: the user or the clock
const leave = new AbortController();
const signal = AbortSignal.any([leave.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000)]);
leave.abort(new Error('User left the page'));
console.log('4:', signal.aborted, '-', signal.reason.message);

One signal pattern covers a Cancel button, a time limit and fetch. Try changing the 150 ms timeout to 2000.

Two details make cancellation reliable. Check signal.aborted or call signal.throwIfAborted() before starting work, because a listener added after the abort never fires. And tell the difference between a cancel and a real failure: users do not want an error toast for a request they cancelled themselves. AbortSignal.timeout (Chrome 103+, Node 17.3+) and especially AbortSignal.any (Chrome 116+, Node 20.3+) are recent additions. Check the MDN compatibility table if you support older browsers.

Retry with exponential backoff

Networks fail temporarily: a 503 from an overloaded server, a dropped mobile connection. A retry helper runs the operation again, and exponential backoff doubles the wait each time (300, 600, 1200 ms), so a struggling server gets room to recover. Jitter, a small random extra delay, stops thousands of clients from retrying in perfect sync. The checkout below uses the same signal for cancellation, so pressing Cancel also stops the retry loop.

const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
const steps = [...document.querySelectorAll('.step')];

function sleep(ms, signal) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    signal?.throwIfAborted();
    const id = setTimeout(resolve, ms);
    signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => {
      clearTimeout(id);
      reject(signal.reason);
    }, { once: true });
  });
}

// Fake payment gateway: fails the first N calls with a temporary error
let failuresLeft = 0;
async function chargePayment(signal) {
  await sleep(500, signal);
  if (failuresLeft > 0) {
    failuresLeft -= 1;
    throw new Error('Gateway busy (503)');
  }
  return 'PAY-' + (1000 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 9000));
}

async function retry(fn, { retries = 3, base = 300, signal, onRetry } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn(signal);
    } catch (err) {
      if (signal?.aborted || attempt > retries) throw err;
      const delay = base * 2 ** (attempt - 1) + Math.random() * 100;
      onRetry(attempt, delay, err);
      await sleep(delay, signal);         // wait longer each time
    }
  }
}

function mark(i, state, info = '') {
  steps[i].className = 'step ' + state;
  steps[i].querySelector('.info').textContent = info;
}
function setStatus(text, kind = '') {
  $('#status').textContent = text;
  $('#status').className = 'status ' + kind;
}

let controller = null;
async function placeOrder() {
  controller = new AbortController();
  const { signal } = controller;
  failuresLeft = $('#flaky').checked ? 2 : 0;
  steps.forEach((_, i) => mark(i, ''));
  $('#place').disabled = true;
  $('#cancel').disabled = false;
  let i = 0;

    setStatus('Placing your order...');
    mark(i, 'active'); await sleep(400, signal); mark(i++, 'done');
    mark(i, 'active'); await sleep(300, signal); mark(i++, 'done');
    mark(i, 'active');

      signal,
      onRetry(attempt, delay, err) {
        console.warn('Attempt ' + attempt + ' failed: ' + err.message +
          '. Retrying in ' + Math.round(delay) + ' ms');
        mark(2, 'active', 'retry ' + attempt + ' in ' + Math.round(delay) + ' ms');
      },
    });
    mark(i++, 'done', payId);
    mark(i, 'active'); await sleep(300, signal); mark(i, 'done', 'sent');
    setStatus('Order confirmed. Payment ' + payId, 'ok');
    console.log('Order confirmed with', payId);
  } catch (err) {
    mark(i, 'failed');
    const cancelled = err.name === 'AbortError';
    setStatus(cancelled ? 'Order cancelled. You were not charged.' : 'Failed: ' + err.message, 'err');
    console.log(cancelled ? 'Cancelled by the user' : 'Gave up: ' + err.message);
  } finally {
    $('#place').disabled = false;
    $('#cancel').disabled = true;
  }
}

Only retry what is safe to repeat. A GET is safe. A payment POST should only be retried when the API supports an idempotency key (a unique ID per order that makes the server ignore duplicates). Do not retry 4xx client errors such as 400 or 401: sending the same wrong request again will not fix it.

Example: the order dashboard loader

The lab builds the data layer for a Ralfiz Store “My account” page. It talks to a fake API that behaves like real services: the profile, orders and offers each take about 300 ms, recommendations are slow (2 seconds), the exchange-rate service fails twice before working, and the loyalty service is down. The finished loader does this:

  1. Loads profile, orders and offers in parallel with Promise.all and destructuring. The log shows about 300 ms, not 900.
  2. Gives recommendations a 500 ms budget with AbortSignal.timeout. It catches the TimeoutError and logs “skipped” instead of failing the page.
  3. Wraps the exchange rate in retry() with backoff and logs each attempt.
  4. Loads the sidebar widgets with Promise.allSettled, printing a tick or a cross per widget.
  5. Sends invoice reminders one at a time with for...of, because the email API allows one request at a time.
async function loadDashboard() {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const [profile, orders, offers] = await Promise.all([
    api.getProfile(), api.getOrders(), api.getOffers(),
  ]);
  console.log(profile.name + ': ' + orders.length + ' orders, ' +
    offers.length + ' offers in ' + since(t0));
}

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting await. const user = getUser(); console.log(user.name); logs undefined, because user is a promise. Fix: const user = await getUser();. TypeScript and the typescript-eslint rule no-floating-promises both help catch this.
  • Awaiting independent calls one by one. Wrong: const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();. Fix: const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);.
  • Using forEach with an async callback. Wrong: ids.forEach(async (id) => await save(id)); followed by “All saved!”. Fix: for (const id of ids) await save(id); for order, or await Promise.all(ids.map(save)); for speed.
  • Swallowing errors. Wrong: catch (err) { console.log(err); } and then carrying on with undefined data. Fix: show an error state, rethrow, or return a clear fallback value, and keep the original error with new Error('Could not load orders', { cause: err }).
  • Treating a cancel as a failure. Wrong: showing “Something went wrong” after the user pressed Cancel. Fix: if (err.name === 'AbortError') return; before your error UI.
  • Retrying everything. Wrong: retrying a 401 or a non-idempotent POST in a loop. Fix: retry only temporary failures (network errors, 429, 5xx), with a limit and backoff.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What does an async function return?” A promise, always. Explain that await suspends only that function and resumes it as a microtask, so the main thread stays free.
  • “How would you load three endpoints faster?” Start all three and use Promise.all. Mention allSettled when partial data is acceptable, and that Promise.all does not cancel the losers.
  • “What is wrong with await in forEach?” Show the fix both ways and say when order matters.
  • In production, every request that a user waits for should have a timeout, a loading state, an error state and, for searches, cancellation of stale requests. Frameworks and libraries such as TanStack Query add caching and retries on top, but they use these same building blocks.
  • async/await is syntax over promises. Anything you can do with .then() you can do with await, and you can mix them: await fetchData().catch(() => fallback) is a neat one-line fallback.

terms.definition: A function declared with async. It always returns a promise: a returned value fulfils it and a thrown error rejects it.
Pauses the current async function until a promise settles, then gives back its value or throws its rejection reason. Other code keeps running meanwhile.
Awaiting one call before starting the next is sequential (times add up). Starting all calls first and awaiting Promise.all is parallel (you wait for the slowest one).
Using await directly in the body of an ES module, outside any function. It works only in modules, not classic scripts.
A controller creates a signal you pass to fetch or your own functions; calling abort() cancels the work. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) aborts by itself after a delay.
A retry strategy that waits longer after each failure (for example 200, 400, 800 ms), usually plus a little random jitter.

Ralfiz Store

₹4,297
