quiz.question: What does calling async function getTotal() { return 1499; } give you?
options: The number 1499
A promise that fulfils with 1499
undefined until you await it
A generator object
quiz.explanation: An async function always returns a promise. Returning a plain value fulfils that promise; you get the number with await or .then.

quiz.question: You need a profile, orders and offers from three independent endpoints. Which code starts all three at once and waits for every result?
options: for (const load of loaders) await load();
loaders.forEach(async (load) => await load());
const a = await load1(); const b = await load2(); const c = await load3();
const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([load1(), load2(), load3()]);
quiz.explanation: Calling all three functions starts the work; Promise.all waits for the slowest and keeps input order. forEach starts them too, but nothing waits for the results.

quiz.question: What does fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) }) do if the server takes 8 seconds?
options: It rejects after about 5 seconds with a DOMException named TimeoutError
It resolves with a response whose status is 408
It waits the full 8 seconds and then throws
It retries the request automatically
quiz.explanation: The timeout signal aborts the request, so fetch rejects with the signal reason: a TimeoutError DOMException. Nothing is retried for you.

quiz.question: Why do good retry helpers add random jitter to the backoff delay?
options: To make each retry faster than the last
Because setTimeout is not accurate
So thousands of clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant
To stop the browser from caching the response
quiz.explanation: Without jitter, every client that failed during an outage retries on the same schedule and hits the recovering server in synchronised waves.

lessons.title: Fetch and working with APIs
lessons.summaryHtml:
Almost every app talks to a server over HTTP: the browser sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body) and gets back a response (status code, headers, body). fetch() is the built-in way to do this in browsers and in Node 18+.

You will make GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE requests against DummyJSON. You will learn the rule that catches everyone (fetch does not reject on 404 or 500, so you must check response.ok), build query strings safely with URLSearchParams, and send a login token in the Authorization header.

You will also learn what CORS is and why the browser enforces it. Finally, you will wrap all of this in a small reusable API client and use it in a live Ralfiz Store product browser with search, categories, sorting and “Load more”.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An API is a waiter between your page and a kitchen you cannot see. Your page writes an order slip (a request): what you want (GET /products/1), some notes (headers, such as “I want JSON” or “here is my membership card”) and sometimes a filled-in form (the body). The waiter comes back with a response: a status (“here you go”, “we do not have that”, “the kitchen is on fire”), notes of its own and the food itself, usually JSON.

fetch() is how JavaScript hands the slip to the waiter. It returns a promise, so everything from the last two lessons (await, try/catch, timeouts and cancellation) applies directly.

Why it matters

Product lists, logins, carts, dashboards and chat messages all arrive over HTTP. A junior front-end developer spends a large part of the day reading API docs, calling endpoints and handling the unhappy paths: slow networks, expired tokens, 404s and servers that answer with HTML error pages instead of JSON. The code in this lesson becomes the api.js file that sits in almost every front-end project.

How it works

HTTP in five minutes

A request has a method, a URL, headers and an optional body. A response has a status code, headers and a body. In JavaScript these are real objects (Request, Response, Headers), and you can create them yourself, which is handy in tests.

Try it: Requests, responses and headers are objects

JavaScript

// Headers: names are case-insensitive
const headers = new Headers({ 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
headers.set('Authorization', 'Bearer demo-token');
console.log('has content-type?', headers.has('CONTENT-TYPE'));

// A request = method + URL + headers + optional body
const req = new Request('https://dummyjson.com/products/add', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers,
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Ralfiz Steel Bottle', price: 18 }),
});
console.log(req.method, req.url);
console.log('body:', await req.text());

// A response = status + headers + body
const res = new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Product not found' }), {
  status: 404,
  statusText: 'Not Found',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
});
console.log(res.status, res.statusText, '| ok =', res.ok);
console.log('type:', res.headers.get('content-type'));

const data = await res.json();              // read the body once
console.log('message:', data.message, '| bodyUsed =', res.bodyUsed);

No network here: you create a Request, Headers and a 404 Response yourself to see the parts fetch works with.

MethodMeaningBody?Safe to repeat?
GETRead a resource or a listNoYes
POSTCreate something, or run an action (log in)YesNo: may create duplicates
PUTReplace a resource completelyYesYes (same result each time)
PATCHChange some fieldsYesUsually
DELETERemove a resourceRarelyYes
StatusMeaningWhat your UI does
200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No ContentSuccess (204 has no body: do not call json())Show the data
400 Bad Request, 422Your data is invalidShow field errors from the body
401 UnauthorizedNot logged in, or the token expiredRefresh the token or go to login
403 ForbiddenLogged in, but not allowedExplain; do not retry
404 Not FoundNo such resourceShow a “not found” state
429 Too Many RequestsRate limitedBack off, then retry
500, 502, 503The server failedFriendly error, retry with backoff

The body of a response is a stream: res.json(), res.text() and res.blob() each read it once and return a promise. json() is really text() followed by JSON.parse, so it rejects with a SyntaxError if the server sent an HTML error page.

GET and the two kinds of failure

This is the rule that catches everyone. fetch rejects only when no HTTP response arrives: the network is down, the DNS lookup failed, CORS blocked the response, or you aborted it. A 404 or a 500 is still a response, so the promise fulfils, with res.ok === false. Your code must check ok (or status) and turn it into an error itself.

Try it: GET with proper error handling

JavaScript

async function getProduct(id) {
  let res;
  try {
    res = await fetch(`https://dummyjson.com/products/${id}`);
  } catch (err) {
    // Only here when no HTTP response arrived at all
    throw new Error('Network problem, check your connection', { cause: err });
  }
  if (!res.ok) {
    // 4xx and 5xx still resolve: check ok yourself
    const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));
    throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}: ${body.message ?? res.statusText}`);
  }
  return res.json();
}

for (const id of [1, 9999]) {
  try {
    const p = await getProduct(id);
    console.log(`#${id}`, p.title, '-', p.price, 'USD');
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`#${id} failed:`, err.message);
  }
}

// A host that cannot be reached: fetch itself rejects
try {
  await fetch('https://api.ralfiz.invalid/products');
} catch (err) {
  console.log('network error:', err.name, '(a TypeError)');
}

Product 9999 does not exist. Notice that the 404 does not reject: the wrapper turns it into an error on purpose.

Handle the two cases differently. A network error means “check your connection”, and retrying later may help. An HTTP error comes with a status and often a JSON body with details: DummyJSON sends { "message": "Product with id '9999' not found" }. Keep the original error as cause so that debugging tools still show it.

Query strings with URLSearchParams

Filters, search terms and pagination travel in the query string: /products/search?q=mug&limit=10&skip=20. Building it by joining strings breaks as soon as a user types &, =, # or a space. URLSearchParams encodes each value for you. new URL(path, base) joins a path onto a base URL safely, and its searchParams property lets you read and change the query.

Try it: Query strings with URLSearchParams

JavaScript

// Building: special characters are encoded for you
const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'salt & pepper', limit: 5 });
params.set('skip', 10);
params.append('select', 'title,price');
console.log(params.toString());

// Reading a URL someone shared
const shared = new URL('https://shop.ralfiz.dev/search?q=kurta&sort=price&page=2');
const page = Number(shared.searchParams.get('page') ?? 1);
console.log(shared.searchParams.get('q'), page, shared.searchParams.get('size'));
console.log(Object.fromEntries(shared.searchParams));

// A helper that skips empty values
function productsUrl({ q, limit = 10, skip = 0, sortBy, order } = {}) {
  const url = new URL(q ? '/products/search' : '/products', 'https://dummyjson.com');
  const query = { q, limit, skip, sortBy, order, select: 'title,price,rating' };
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(query)) {
    if (value !== undefined && value !== '') url.searchParams.set(key, value);
  }
  return url;
}

const url = productsUrl({ limit: 4, sortBy: 'price', order: 'desc' });
console.log(url.pathname + url.search);
const res = await fetch(url);
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
const { products, total } = await res.json();
console.log(`Top ${products.length} of ${total} by price:`);
console.table(products);

Build, read and send query strings. Look at how the & and the spaces in the search term are encoded.

// Wrong: the & splits the search term into two parameters
fetch('https://dummyjson.com/products/search?q=' + 'salt & pepper');

// Right
const url = new URL('https://dummyjson.com/products/search');
url.searchParams.set('q', 'salt & pepper');
fetch(url);   // ...?q=salt+%26+pepper

DummyJSON uses limit and skip for pagination, select to return fewer fields, and sortBy plus order to sort. List responses have the shape { products, total, skip, limit }, and total tells you whether there is another page.

Sending data: POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE

To send JSON, you do three things: set method, set the Content-Type: application/json header, and pass body: JSON.stringify(data). Forgetting the header is a classic bug. Many servers then ignore the body or answer 400. For file uploads you pass a FormData object instead and let the browser set the header itself.

Try it: POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE

JavaScript

const BASE = 'https://dummyjson.com';

async function send(method, path, body) {
  const res = await fetch(BASE + path, {
    method,
    headers: body ? { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } : {},
    body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
  });
  const data = await res.json();
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${method} ${path}: ${res.status} ${data.message}`);
  console.log(method.padEnd(6), path.padEnd(14), res.status);
  return data;
}

const created = await send('POST', '/products/add', {
  title: 'Ralfiz Steel Bottle', price: 18, category: 'kitchen-accessories',
});
console.log('  created id', created.id, '-', created.title);

const replaced = await send('PUT', '/products/1', { price: 39.99 });
console.log('  new price', replaced.price, 'for', replaced.title);

const patched = await send('PATCH', '/products/1', { stock: 0 });
console.log('  stock is now', patched.stock);

const removed = await send('DELETE', '/products/1');
console.log('  isDeleted:', removed.isDeleted);

try {
  await send('PATCH', '/products/9999', { stock: 1 });
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.message);
}

One small send() helper covers every method. DummyJSON simulates the change and returns the result, but does not store it.

DummyJSON is a practice API: it simulates creates, updates and deletes and returns what the result would be, but nothing is saved. A real API would return the stored record, often with 201 Created for a POST.

Authentication with a Bearer token

Most APIs identify you with a token. You POST your username and password to a login endpoint, the server returns an access token (often a JWT), and you send it with every protected request in the header Authorization: Bearer <token>. Tokens expire. When you get a 401, a real app uses a refresh token to get a new access token, or sends the user back to the login page.

Try it: Log in and send a Bearer token

JavaScript

const BASE = 'https://dummyjson.com';

async function login(username, password) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/auth/login`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ username, password, expiresInMins: 30 }),
  });
  const data = await res.json();
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${data.message}`);
  return data;                               // includes accessToken
}

try {
  await login('emilys', 'wrong-password');
} catch (err) {
  console.log('wrong password:', err.message);
}

const session = await login('emilys', 'emilyspass');
console.log('logged in as', session.firstName);
console.log('token:', session.accessToken.slice(0, 12) + '...');

// Protected endpoint: prove who you are with the token
const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/auth/me`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${session.accessToken}` },
});
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
const me = await res.json();
console.log('GET /auth/me', res.status, '->', me.username, me.email);

Log in with the DummyJSON demo user, then call a protected endpoint with the Authorization header.

Watch out: where you keep the token matters. Anything in localStorage or sessionStorage can be read by any script that runs on your page, so one XSS bug leaks every user’s token. Many production apps let the server set the session in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie that JavaScript cannot read. The DOM track covers these trade-offs in detail. Never put API secrets (keys that must stay private) in front-end code at all: anyone can read them in DevTools.

CORS, explained

An origin is scheme + host + port, for example https://shop.ralfiz.dev. By default, the browser’s same-origin policy lets a page send a request to another origin but not read the response. CORS is how the other server opts in: it answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.ralfiz.dev (or * for public data). DummyJSON and JSONPlaceholder send that header, which is why this lesson works from any page.

A request with a JSON Content-Type, an Authorization header, or a method such as PUT or DELETE is not a “simple” request. The browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request that asks “may I?”, and it sends the real request only if the server agrees. You will see both in the Network panel.

OPTIONS /products/1                     (preflight, sent by the browser)
Origin: https://shop.ralfiz.dev
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization

204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.ralfiz.dev
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, authorization

CORS is enforced by browsers only. The same request works from Node, curl or Postman, which confuses many beginners. The fix for a CORS error is always on the server side: allow your origin, or route the call through your own backend. mode: 'no-cors' does not fix anything. It gives you an “opaque” response whose body you cannot read.

A small API client

Instead of repeating URLs, headers, ok checks and JSON parsing in every component, real projects wrap fetch once. This client also adds a default timeout, a token and a custom error class that carries the status code, so the UI can react to 401 differently from 500.

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(status, message, data) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ApiError';
    this.status = status;
    this.data = data;
  }
}

export function createApi(baseUrl, { getToken } = {}) {
  async function request(path, { method = 'GET', query, body, signal } = {}) {
    const url = new URL(path, baseUrl);
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(query ?? {})) {
      if (v !== undefined && v !== '') url.searchParams.set(k, v);
    }
    const headers = { Accept: 'application/json' };
    if (body !== undefined) headers['Content-Type'] = 'application/json';
    const token = getToken?.();
    if (token) headers.Authorization = 'Bearer ' + token;

    const res = await fetch(url, {
      method, headers, signal: signal ?? AbortSignal.timeout(8000),
      body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
    });
    const isJson = res.headers.get('content-type')?.includes('json');
    const data = res.status === 204 ? null : isJson ? await res.json() : await res.text();
    if (!res.ok) throw new ApiError(res.status, data?.message ?? res.statusText, data);
    return data;
  }
  return {
    get: (path, opts) => request(path, opts),
    post: (path, body, opts) => request(path, { ...opts, method: 'POST', body }),
    patch: (path, body, opts) => request(path, { ...opts, method: 'PATCH', body }),
    del: (path, opts) => request(path, { ...opts, method: 'DELETE' }),
  };
}

Example: Ralfiz Store product browser

The live page below puts it all together: the start-up code loads categories from /products/categories and the first page of products, and every control rebuilds the query with URLSearchParams.

  • Four UI states: a shimmering skeleton while loading, the grid on success, a friendly message with a Try again button on error, and an empty message when a search finds nothing.
  • Search with debounce and abort: the request waits for a 300 ms pause in typing, and each new request aborts the previous one, so a slow old response can never overwrite a newer one.
  • Pagination: Load more increases skip and appends cards until skip reaches total.
  • Safe rendering: product titles go in with textContent, never as HTML. Each card shows a category emoji. Set SHOW_PHOTOS to true to load the real thumbnail images: they get alt, width, height and loading="lazy", and fall back to the emoji if they fail to load.

Try it: Ralfiz Store product browser

HTML

<div class="app">
  <header class="top">
    <div class="brand"><span class="logo">R</span>Ralfiz Store</div>
    <span class="count" id="count"></span>
  </header>
  <div class="controls">
    <input id="q" type="search" placeholder="Search products" aria-label="Search products" autocomplete="off">
    <select id="cat" aria-label="Category"><option value="">All categories</option></select>
    <select id="sort" aria-label="Sort by">
      <option value="">Featured</option>
      <option value="price:asc">Price: low to high</option>
      <option value="price:desc">Price: high to low</option>
      <option value="rating:desc">Top rated</option>
    </select>
  </div>
  <div class="msg" id="msg" role="status"></div>
  <ul class="grid" id="grid"></ul>
  <button class="more" id="more" hidden>Load more</button>
</div>

CSS

:root { --accent: #0f766e; --line: #e5e7eb; --muted: #6b7280; }
body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; background: #f6f7f9; }
.app { max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto; }
.top { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 12px; }
.brand { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; font-weight: 700; font-size: 18px; }
.logo { width: 28px; height: 28px; border-radius: 8px; background: var(--accent); color: #fff;
  display: grid; place-items: center; font-size: 15px; }
.count { font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); }
.controls { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; margin-bottom: 12px; }
input, select { font: inherit; font-size: 14px; padding: 9px 12px; border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 10px; background: #fff; color: inherit; }
input { flex: 1 1 200px; }
select { flex: 0 1 auto; }
input:focus, select:focus, button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 1px; }
.grid { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; display: grid; gap: 12px;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(140px, 1fr)); }
.card { background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 14px; overflow: hidden;
  display: flex; flex-direction: column; box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, .04); }
.thumb { aspect-ratio: 4 / 3; background: #eef2f1; display: grid; place-items: center; font-size: 34px; }
.thumb img { width: 100%; height: 100%; object-fit: cover; grid-area: 1 / 1; }
.thumb span { grid-area: 1 / 1; }
.body { padding: 10px 12px 12px; display: grid; gap: 6px; }
.title { margin: 0; font-size: 14px; font-weight: 600; line-height: 1.3; }
.meta { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; font-size: 12px; color: var(--muted); }
.chip { background: #f0fdfa; color: var(--accent); border-radius: 999px; padding: 2px 8px; }
.price { font-weight: 700; font-size: 15px; }
.skel .thumb, .skel .line { background: linear-gradient(90deg, #eef0f3 25%, #f7f8fa 50%, #eef0f3 75%);
  background-size: 200% 100%; animation: shimmer 1.2s infinite; }
.skel .line { height: 12px; border-radius: 6px; }
@keyframes shimmer { to { background-position: -200% 0; } }
.msg { font-size: 14px; color: var(--muted); }
.msg:not(:empty) { margin: 8px 0 12px; }
.msg.error { color: #b91c1c; }
.msg button, .more { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; border-radius: 10px; cursor: pointer;
  border: 1px solid var(--line); background: #fff; padding: 8px 14px; }
.more { display: block; margin: 16px auto 0; }
.more:disabled { opacity: .5; }

JavaScript

const API = 'https://dummyjson.com';
const PAGE = 8;
const SHOW_PHOTOS = false;   // set to true to load thumbnails from cdn.dummyjson.com
const ICONS = { beauty: '💄', fragrances: '🌸', furniture: '🛋️', groceries: '🥦', laptops: '💻' };
const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
const money = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' });
const state = { q: '', cat: '', sort: '', skip: 0, total: 0 };
let controller;

async function getJSON(url, signal) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

function productsUrl() {
  const path = state.q ? '/products/search'
    : state.cat ? `/products/category/${encodeURIComponent(state.cat)}` : '/products';
  const url = new URL(path, API);
  const [sortBy, order] = state.sort.split(':');
  const query = { q: state.q, limit: PAGE, skip: state.skip, sortBy, order,
    select: 'title,price,rating,category,thumbnail' };
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(query)) if (v) url.searchParams.set(k, v);
  return url;
}

function card(p) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'card';
  li.innerHTML = `<div class="thumb"><span aria-hidden="true"></span></div>
    <div class="body"><h3 class="title"></h3>
    <div class="meta"><span class="chip"></span><span class="rating"></span></div>
    <div class="price"></div></div>`;
  li.querySelector('.thumb span').textContent = ICONS[p.category] ?? '🛍️';
  if (SHOW_PHOTOS) {
    const img = Object.assign(document.createElement('img'),
      { src: p.thumbnail, alt: p.title, width: 160, height: 120, loading: 'lazy' });
    img.addEventListener('error', () => img.remove());  // keep the emoji
    li.querySelector('.thumb').append(img);
  }
  li.querySelector('.title').textContent = p.title;     // text, never HTML
  li.querySelector('.chip').textContent = p.category;
  li.querySelector('.rating').textContent = '★ ' + p.rating.toFixed(1);
  li.querySelector('.price').textContent = money.format(p.price);
  return li;
}

function skeleton() {
  $('#grid').innerHTML = '<li class="card skel"><div class="thumb"></div><div class="body">' +
    '<div class="line"></div><div class="line"></div></div></li>'.repeat(4);
}

function showMessage(text, isError = false) {
  $('#msg').className = 'msg' + (isError ? ' error' : '');
  $('#msg').textContent = text;
  if (isError) {
    const retry = document.createElement('button');
    retry.textContent = 'Try again';
    retry.addEventListener('click', () => load());
    $('#msg').append(' ', retry);
  }
}

async function load({ append = false } = {}) {
  controller?.abort();                       // cancel the previous request
  controller = new AbortController();
  if (!append) { state.skip = 0; skeleton(); }
  showMessage('');
  $('#more').disabled = true;
  try {
    const url = productsUrl();
    console.log('GET', url.pathname + url.search);
    const data = await getJSON(url, controller.signal);
    if (!append) $('#grid').replaceChildren();
    $('#grid').append(...data.products.map(card));
    state.skip += data.products.length;
    state.total = data.total;
    $('#count').textContent = `Showing ${state.skip} of ${state.total}`;
    $('#more').hidden = state.skip >= state.total;
    if (!data.total) showMessage(`No products match "${state.q}".`);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') return;   // a newer request replaced it
    $('#grid').replaceChildren();
    showMessage('Could not load products (' + err.message + ').', true);
  } finally {
    $('#more').disabled = false;
  }
}

let timer;
$('#q').addEventListener('input', (e) => {
  clearTimeout(timer);                       // debounce: wait for a pause
  timer = setTimeout(() => {
    state.q = e.target.value.trim();
    state.cat = '';
    $('#cat').value = '';
    load();
  }, 300);
});
$('#cat').addEventListener('change', (e) => { state.cat = e.target.value; state.q = ''; $('#q').value = ''; load(); });
$('#sort').addEventListener('change', (e) => { state.sort = e.target.value; load(); });
$('#more').addEventListener('click', () => load({ append: true }));

getJSON(`${API}/products/categories`)
  .then((cats) => $('#cat').append(...cats.map((c) => new Option(c.name, c.slug))))
  .catch(() => console.warn('Categories unavailable'));
load();

Type in the search box, pick a category or a sort order, and press Load more. The console lists every request.

Common mistakes

  • Not checking ok. Wrong: const data = await (await fetch(url)).json();. A 404 gives you an error object that you treat as data. Fix: if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status); before parsing.
  • Forgetting to await the body. Wrong: const data = res.json(); data.products is undefined. Fix: const data = await res.json();.
  • Sending an object as the body. Wrong: body: { title: 'Mug' } sends the text [object Object]. Fix: body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Mug' }) plus the JSON Content-Type header.
  • Building URLs by hand. Wrong: '/search?q=' + input.value. Fix: url.searchParams.set('q', input.value).
  • Putting API data into innerHTML. Wrong: card.innerHTML = '<h3>' + product.title + '</h3>'. Any HTML in the data runs on your page. Fix: h3.textContent = product.title.
  • “Fixing” CORS in the browser. Browser extensions and no-cors hide the problem on your machine only. Fix it on the server or with a backend proxy.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the difference between PUT and PATCH, and between 401 and 403. Both come up often.
  • Be ready to explain CORS in two sentences: the browser protects users by not letting one site read another site’s responses, unless the other server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Mention preflight requests.
  • Production clients add a timeout, a single place to attach tokens and handle 401, cancellation of stale searches, and caching. Libraries such as TanStack Query build on these ideas, and axios is a popular alternative to fetch, but fetch is built in everywhere now.
  • The Network panel in DevTools is your best friend: check the method, URL, request headers, payload, status and response for every call before you change your code.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'phone case', limit: 10 });
console.log(params.toString());
  • A q=phone%20case&limit=10
  • B q=phone+case&limit=10
  • C q=phone case&limit=10
  • D ?q=phone+case&limit=10

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const res = new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
console.log(res.ok, res.status);
  • A true 404
  • B undefined 404
  • C false undefined
  • D false 404

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const h = new Headers({ 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
console.log(h.get('content-type'), h.has('CONTENT-TYPE'));
  • A application/json true
  • B null false
  • C application/json false
  • D null true

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const res = new Response('{"id":1,"title":"Mug"}');
res.json()
  .then((data) => {
    console.log(data.title);
    return res.text();
  })
  .catch((err) => console.log(err.name));
  • A 
    Mug
{"id":1,"title":"Mug"}
  • B Mug
  • C 
    Mug
TypeError
  • D TypeError

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const url = new URL('/products/search?q=mug', 'https://dummyjson.com/api/');
url.searchParams.set('limit', 5);
console.log(url.href);
  • A https://dummyjson.com/api/products/search?q=mug&limit=5
  • B https://dummyjson.com/products/search?q=mug&limit=5
  • C https://dummyjson.com/products/search?limit=5
  • D /products/search?q=mug&limit=5

Answers

  1. B. URLSearchParams uses form encoding, where a space becomes +. toString() never adds the leading ?; URL does that when you attach the params to it.
  2. D. ok is true only for statuses 200–299. This is exactly the object fetch would resolve with for a 404, which is why you must check ok.
  3. A. HTTP header names are case-insensitive, and the Headers class follows that rule for get, has and set.
  4. C. A response body is a stream you can read only once. After json() has read it, text() rejects with a TypeError. Use res.clone() if you really need it twice.
  5. B. A path that starts with / replaces the whole path of the base URL, so /api/ is dropped. Write products/search (no leading slash) to keep it.

terms.definition: The verb of a request: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part of a resource and DELETE removes it.
A three-digit result in the response: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client made a mistake, 5xx the server failed.
True when the status is 200–299. fetch resolves even for 404 and 500, so you check ok yourself.
A name-value pair of metadata on a request or response, such as Content-Type: application/json or Authorization: Bearer <token>.
A built-in class that builds and reads query strings and encodes special characters correctly.
A string the server gives you after login. You send it back in the Authorization header to prove who you are.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the browser lets a page read a response from another origin only if the server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-* headers.

lessons.examTip: Interviewers love “does fetch reject on a 404?”. Answer no: it rejects only when no response arrives (network error, CORS block, abort), so every wrapper checks response.ok.

quiz.question: fetch() gets a 500 Internal Server Error response. What happens to the promise it returned?
options: It rejects with an HTTP error
It fulfils with a Response whose ok is false and status is 500
It never settles
It retries three times, then rejects
quiz.explanation: fetch only rejects when no HTTP response arrives. Any response, including 4xx and 5xx, fulfils the promise; you check response.ok or response.status.

quiz.question: Which request best fits “change only the stock of product 7”?
options: GET /products/7?stock=0
POST /products/7
DELETE /products/7
PATCH /products/7 with the body {"stock": 0}
quiz.explanation: PATCH updates part of a resource. PUT replaces the whole resource, POST usually creates one, and GET must never change data.

quiz.question: Your page on shop.ralfiz.dev calls an API on another domain and the console shows a CORS error. Where is the real fix?
options: On the API server: send Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your origin
Add mode: "no-cors" to fetch
Catch the error and parse the body anyway
Switch from fetch to XMLHttpRequest
quiz.explanation: CORS is the server opting in. no-cors only gives you an opaque response you cannot read. The server, or your own backend acting as a proxy, must send the right headers.

quiz.question: Why build query strings with URLSearchParams instead of joining strings?
options: It makes the request faster
It is required by fetch
It encodes characters such as &, = and spaces so user input cannot break the URL
It adds authentication automatically
quiz.explanation: A search for “salt & pepper” joined by hand becomes q=salt & pepper, which the server reads as two parameters. URLSearchParams encodes it correctly.

lessons.title: Modules
lessons.summaryHtml:
A module is a file with its own private scope that shares only what it exports; other files import what they need. ES modules (ESM) are the standard module system, built into every modern browser and into Node.js.

You will learn named, default and namespace imports, renaming and re-exports, and why imports are live bindings to a single shared instance. You will see what changes when code runs as a module: strict mode, top-level await and this being undefined. You will load code on demand with dynamic import() and read import.meta.

Finally, you will learn enough CommonJS (require) to work in older Node code, and how "type": "module" in package.json decides which system Node uses. The lab turns a one-file CommonJS invoice script into clean ES modules.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Imagine a shop where every employee works at one giant shared desk. Anyone can move anyone else’s papers, and two people who both label a folder “total” overwrite each other. That was JavaScript before modules: every <script> shared one global scope. A module gives each file its own office with a door. Nothing inside is visible from outside unless you put it through the hatch with export. Other files ask for exactly what they need with import.

Why it matters

Every real codebase is split into modules: api.js, cart.js, format.js, one component per file. Modules give you encapsulation (private helpers stay private), explicit dependencies (the imports at the top list what a file needs), reuse and tooling. Because imports are static, bundlers can remove unused code (tree-shaking) and editors can rename a function across 50 files safely.

The history explains the odd things you will meet in older code. Developers first used global variables and IIFEs. Node added CommonJS (require) in 2009. ES2015 standardised ES modules, which now run natively in browsers and Node. New code should use ESM, but you will still read CommonJS in older Node projects and packages.

How it works

Module scope and strict mode

A file becomes a module when it is loaded as one: <script type="module"> in a browser, an import from another module, a .mjs file, or a .js file in a package whose package.json says "type": "module". Loading a file as a module changes several rules at once.

Try it: A module has its own rules

JavaScript

// Everything here runs as an ES module (like <script type="module">)
console.log('top-level this:', this);

const cartTotal = 2499;                 // module scope, not a global
var legacyFlag = true;                  // even var stays inside the module
console.log('cartTotal on window?', 'cartTotal' in window);
console.log('legacyFlag on window?', 'legacyFlag' in window);

try {
  discount = 10;                        // undeclared variable
} catch (err) {
  console.log('strict mode:', err.name, '-', err.message);
}

console.log('import.meta.url is a', typeof import.meta.url);

// Top-level await: no async wrapper needed in a module
const res = await fetch('https://dummyjson.com/quotes/1');
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
const { quote, author } = await res.json();
console.log(`"${quote}" (${author})`);

This playground file is an ES module. Check this, the global object, strict mode and top-level await.

BehaviourClassic scriptES module
Top-level var/functionsBecome globals (window.x)Private to the file
Strict modeOnly with 'use strict'Always on
Top-level thiswindowundefined
Top-level awaitSyntax errorAllowed
import/exportSyntax errorAllowed
Loading in the browserBlocks parsing unless defer/asyncDeferred by default, fetched with CORS
Runs how many times?Every <script> tagOnce per URL, however many importers

Exporting and importing

There are two kinds of export. A named export has a fixed name, and a module can have many. A default export is the one main value, and a module can have at most one. On the import side you can rename with as, and collect everything into a namespace object with import * as.

// money.js
export const GST_RATE = 0.18;                  // named
export function addGst(amount) { /* ... */ }   // named
export default function formatINR(amount) {    // default
  /* ... */
}

// main.js
import formatINR, { GST_RATE, addGst as withGst } from './money.js';
import * as money from './money.js';           // money.GST_RATE, money.default

// You can also export at the bottom, which is handy for a quick overview
const round2 = (n) => Math.round(n * 100) / 100;
export { round2, round2 as roundMoney };

In the playground below, a small file() helper turns a string into a module URL, so you can see several “files” in one editor. In your projects each one is a real .js file.

Try it: Named, default and namespace imports

JavaScript

// Playground helper: turns source text into an importable module URL.
// In a real project, each string below would be its own .js file.
const file = (code) =>
  URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([code], { type: 'text/javascript' }));

// ---- money.js ----
const money = file(`
  export const GST_RATE = 0.18;

  export function addGst(amount) {
    return Math.round(amount * (1 + GST_RATE));
  }

  export default function formatINR(amount) {
    return new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {
      style: 'currency', currency: 'INR', maximumFractionDigits: 0,
    }).format(amount);
  }
`);

// ---- main.js ----
const main = file(`
  import formatINR, { GST_RATE, addGst as withGst } from '${money}';
  import * as moneyTools from '${money}';

  const subtotal = 2499;
  console.log('GST rate:', GST_RATE * 100 + '%');
  console.log('Total with GST:', formatINR(withGst(subtotal)));
  console.log('namespace keys:', Object.keys(moneyTools));
  console.log('default is formatINR?', moneyTools.default === formatINR);
`);

await import(main);

money.js has two named exports and a default export. main.js imports them three different ways.

Import specifiers in the browser must be URLs: './money.js', '../lib/cart.js' or a full URL. The .js extension is required, because the browser does not guess. A bare name like 'lodash' only works with a bundler such as Vite, with Node’s package resolution, or with an import map that tells the browser where the name lives.

Live bindings, one instance and evaluation order

Loading a module graph happens in three phases. First the engine parses the entry file, finds its static imports, fetches those files, and repeats until it knows the whole graph. Then it links every import to the matching export. Finally it evaluates each module once, dependencies first. That is why imports are hoisted: the import line can sit anywhere at the top level, and its module has already run before your first statement.

Linking connects names, not values. An import is a live, read-only binding to the exporter’s variable. When cart.js does count += qty, every importer sees the new count. An importer cannot assign to it. And because each module is evaluated only once per URL, all importers share one instance, which makes a module a natural singleton for a store, a cache or a configured API client.

Try it: Live bindings and one shared instance

JavaScript

const file = (code) =>
  URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([code], { type: 'text/javascript' }));

// ---- cart.js ----
const cart = file(`
  console.log('[cart.js] evaluated');
  export let count = 0;
  export function add(qty = 1) {
    count += qty;                        // only the owner may change it
  }
`);

// ---- badge.js: imports count and shows it ----
const badge = file(`
  import { count } from '${cart}';
  export function render() {
    return 'Cart (' + count + ')';
  }
`);

const header = await import(badge);    // loads badge.js AND cart.js
const store = await import(cart);      // already loaded: not run again
console.log(header.render());

store.add(2);                           // change it through cart.js
console.log(header.render());          // badge.js sees the new value

console.log('same instance?', store === await import(cart));
try {
  store.count = 99;                     // importers cannot assign
} catch (err) {
  console.log('assign from outside:', err.name);
}

cart.js runs once, however many files import it. A change made through one importer is visible through the other.

Remember: sharing mutable state through a module is powerful but easy to overuse. Export functions that change the state (add()) rather than the raw object, so there is one place where changes happen.

Circular imports (a.js imports b.js, which imports a.js) are allowed, but one of them will run first and may read a binding that is not initialised yet. The result is a ReferenceError from the temporal dead zone. If you meet one, move the shared piece into a third module.

Re-exports and barrel files

A module can pass on exports from other modules without using them itself. A folder often has an index.js “barrel” that re-exports its public pieces, so the rest of the app imports from one path.

Try it: Re-exports and a barrel file

JavaScript

const file = (code) =>
  URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([code], { type: 'text/javascript' }));

// ---- utils/format.js ----
const format = file(`
  export const formatINR = (n) => '₹' + n.toLocaleString('en-IN');
  export const formatDate = (d) => d.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
`);

// ---- utils/validate.js ----
const validate = file(`
  export const isPincode = (s) => /^[1-9][0-9]{5}$/.test(s);
  export const isMobile = (s) => /^[6-9][0-9]{9}$/.test(s);
  export default function isRequired(value) {
    return String(value ?? '').trim() !== '';
  }
`);

// ---- utils/index.js (the barrel) ----
const utils = file(`
  export * from '${format}';                          // all named exports
  export { default as isRequired } from '${validate}'; // name the default
  export * as validate from '${validate}';            // grouped namespace
`);

// ---- main.js ----
const main = file(`
  import { formatINR, formatDate, isRequired, validate } from '${utils}';

  console.log(formatINR(125000), 'due', formatDate(new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 8, 28))));
  console.log('name filled?', isRequired('   '));
  console.log('PIN 679322 valid?', validate.isPincode('679322'));
  console.log('mobile 98470 valid?', validate.isMobile('98470'));
  console.log('barrel exports:', Object.keys(await import('${utils}')));
`);

await import(main);

utils/index.js gathers several modules behind one import path. Note how the default export is re-exported under a name.

Note that export * from passes on named exports but not the default; re-export it by name with export { default as isRequired } from .... Barrels are convenient, but a huge barrel can slow down dev servers and tests, because importing one helper loads every module behind it. Keep them small and use them for a folder’s public API.

Modules in the browser

<!-- Runs after the HTML is parsed, in order, as a module -->
<script type="module" src="./src/main.js"></script>

<!-- Inline modules work too -->
<script type="module">
  import { formatINR } from './src/money.js';
  document.querySelector('#total').textContent = formatINR(4715.28);
</script>

Module scripts are fetched with CORS, so opening index.html straight from disk (file://) fails with a CORS error. Serve the folder instead, with VS Code Live Server, npx serve or Vite. Without a bundler, each import is a separate request, which is why production sites bundle, as you will see in the next lesson.

Dynamic import()

import(specifier) loads a module at run time and returns a promise for its namespace object. Unlike static import, it can go inside an if, a click handler or a function, and the specifier can be computed. Use it for features most users never touch: a PDF or CSV exporter, a charting library, an admin panel, a language pack. Bundlers turn each import() into a separate file (code splitting), so the first page load stays small.

Try it: Load code on demand with import()

HTML

<main class="invoice">
  <header>
    <div>
      <p class="eyebrow">Ralfiz Billing</p>
      <h1>Invoice INV-2041</h1>
    </div>
    <span class="badge">Paid</span>
  </header>
  <table>
    <thead><tr><th>Item</th><th>Qty</th><th class="num">Amount</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody id="lines"></tbody>
    <tfoot><tr><td colspan="2">Total (incl. 18% GST)</td><td class="num" id="total"></td></tr></tfoot>
  </table>
  <div class="actions">
    <button id="csv">Export CSV</button>
    <button id="chart">Show chart</button>
  </div>
  <div id="chartBox" class="chart" hidden></div>
  <pre id="preview" class="preview" hidden></pre>
  <section class="netlog">
    <h2>Modules</h2>
    <ul id="log"><li>main.js: loaded with the page</li></ul>
  </section>
</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #7c3aed; --line: #e5e7eb; --muted: #6b7280; }
body { margin: 0; padding: 16px; background: #f5f3ff; }
.invoice { max-width: 520px; margin: 0 auto; background: #fff; border: 1px solid var(--line);
  border-radius: 16px; padding: 20px; box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgba(76, 29, 149, .08); }
header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: flex-start; gap: 12px; }
.eyebrow { margin: 0; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; letter-spacing: .06em;
  text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--accent); }
h1 { margin: 2px 0 12px; font-size: 20px; }
.badge { background: #dcfce7; color: #166534; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600;
  padding: 4px 10px; border-radius: 999px; }
table { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 14px; }
th { text-align: left; font-size: 12px; color: var(--muted); font-weight: 600; }
th, td { padding: 8px 4px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); }
.num { text-align: right; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
tfoot td { font-weight: 700; border-bottom: 0; }
.actions { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; margin: 14px 0; }
button { font: inherit; font-weight: 600; font-size: 14px; padding: 9px 14px; border-radius: 10px;
  border: 1px solid var(--accent); background: #fff; color: var(--accent); cursor: pointer; }
button:hover { background: #f5f3ff; }
button:disabled { opacity: .6; cursor: progress; }
.preview { background: #0f172a; color: #e2e8f0; padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px;
  font-size: 12px; overflow-x: auto; margin: 0 0 12px; }
.chart { display: grid; gap: 6px; margin-bottom: 12px; }
.bar { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 130px 1fr; align-items: center; gap: 8px; font-size: 13px; }
.bar i { display: block; height: 14px; border-radius: 7px; background: var(--accent);
  width: var(--w); transition: width .6s ease; }
.netlog h2 { font-size: 13px; margin: 0 0 6px; color: var(--muted); text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: .05em; }

.netlog li::before { content: '● '; color: var(--accent); }

JavaScript

// Playground helper: in a real app these would be files on the server,
// and import('./csv.js') would download them.
const file = (code) =>
  URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([code], { type: 'text/javascript' }));

const MODULES = {
  'csv.js': file(`
    function cell(value) {                 // quote cells that need it
      const s = String(value);
      return /[",]/.test(s) ? '"' + s.replaceAll('"', '""') + '"' : s;
    }
    export function toCsvLines(rows) {
      return rows.map((row) => row.map(cell).join(','));
    }
  `),
  'chart.js': file(`
    export default function barChart(el, items) {
      const max = Math.max(...items.map((i) => i.value));
      el.replaceChildren(...items.map((i) => {
        const row = document.createElement('div');
        row.className = 'bar';
        const label = document.createElement('span');
        label.textContent = i.label;
        const bar = document.createElement('i');
        requestAnimationFrame(() => bar.style.setProperty('--w', (i.value / max) * 100 + '%'));
        row.append(label, bar);
        return row;
      }));
    }
  `),
};

const items = [
  { name: 'Cotton Kurta, size M', qty: 2, price: 1299 },
  { name: 'Steel Bottle 1L', qty: 1, price: 499 },
  { name: 'Laptop Sleeve 14"', qty: 1, price: 899 },
];
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);

for (const it of items) {
  const tr = $('#lines').insertRow();
  tr.insertCell().textContent = it.name;
  tr.insertCell().textContent = it.qty;
  const amount = tr.insertCell();
  amount.className = 'num';
  amount.textContent = inr.format(it.qty * it.price);
}
const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, it) => sum + it.qty * it.price, 0);
$('#total').textContent = inr.format(subtotal * 1.18);

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const downloaded = new Set();

async function load(name) {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const first = !downloaded.has(name);
  if (first) await sleep(350);             // pretend download time
  const mod = await import(MODULES[name]); // the browser caches modules
  downloaded.add(name);
  const ms = Math.round(performance.now() - t0);
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = name + ': ' + (first ? 'downloaded in ' + ms + ' ms' : 'from cache, ' + ms + ' ms');
  $('#log').append(li);
  console.log(li.textContent);
  return mod;
}

async function withButton(btn, task) {
  btn.disabled = true;
  try {
    await task();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Could not load the feature:', err.message);
  } finally {
    btn.disabled = false;
  }
}

$('#csv').addEventListener('click', (e) => withButton(e.currentTarget, async () => {
  const { toCsvLines } = await load('csv.js');
  const rows = [['Item', 'Qty', 'Price'], ...items.map((i) => [i.name, i.qty, i.price])];
  $('#preview').textContent = toCsvLines(rows).join('\n');
  $('#preview').hidden = false;
}));

$('#chart').addEventListener('click', (e) => withButton(e.currentTarget, async () => {
  const { default: barChart } = await load('chart.js');
  $('#chartBox').hidden = false;
  barChart($('#chartBox'), items.map((i) => ({ label: i.name.split(',')[0], value: i.qty * i.price })));
}));

console.log('main.js ready: csv.js and chart.js are not loaded yet');

The CSV exporter and the chart are separate modules that load only when you click. Click each button twice and compare the timings.

The first click on each button “downloads” its module. The second click is instant, because the browser keeps evaluated modules in its module map. Always handle failure (the network can drop between page load and click) and show a loading state on the button.

import.meta

import.meta is an object that describes the current module. import.meta.url is the module’s full URL, so new URL('./data.json', import.meta.url) finds a file next to the module, wherever the page lives. In Node 20.11+ you also get import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename, the ESM replacements for __dirname and __filename. Vite adds import.meta.env for environment variables, covered in the next lesson.

CommonJS in older Node code

// cart.cjs (CommonJS)
const { writeFile } = require('node:fs/promises');
function formatINR(n) { /* ... */ }
module.exports = { formatINR };        // or exports.formatINR = formatINR

// main.cjs
const { formatINR } = require('./cart.cjs');
console.log(__dirname);                // exists in CommonJS only
CommonJSES modules
Syntaxrequire(), module.exportsimport, export
LoadingSynchronous, at the line where require runsStatic graph first; async-capable
What you getA copy of the exported value (an object)Live bindings
Top-level awaitNoYes
Runs in browsersOnly after bundlingNatively

Node decides per file. .mjs is always ESM and .cjs is always CommonJS. For .js, the nearest package.json decides: "type": "module" means ESM, and a missing field means CommonJS. (Node 22 can also detect import syntax in a typeless file, but it prints a warning, so set the field.) An ES module can import a CommonJS package, and module.exports becomes the default import. Node 22.12+ can also require() an ES module that has no top-level await.

Example: from one CommonJS file to ES modules

The lab starts with start/index.js, a one-file CommonJS invoice script with money helpers, a Cart class and the main program all in one file. You split it like this:

  1. Create package.json with "type": "module" so .js files are ES modules.
  2. Move GST_RATE and formatINR into cart.js as named exports, and Cart as the default export.
  3. In index.js, write import Cart, { formatINR, GST_RATE } from './cart.js'; and delete the module.exports line.
  4. Replace the require('node:fs/promises') at the top with const { writeFile } = await import('node:fs/promises'); inside the --save branch, so the file system module loads only when needed.
  5. Remove the main().catch() wrapper and use top-level await. Build the output path with new URL('./invoice.txt', import.meta.url).
// solution/index.js
import Cart, { formatINR, GST_RATE } from './cart.js';

const cart = new Cart()
  .add('Cotton Kurta', 1299, 2)
  .add('Steel Bottle', 499)
  .add('Laptop Sleeve', 899);

console.log(cart.lines().join('\n'));
console.log('GST ' + GST_RATE * 100 + '%: ' + formatINR(cart.gst));

if (process.argv.includes('--save')) {
  const { writeFile } = await import('node:fs/promises');
  await writeFile(new URL('./invoice.txt', import.meta.url), cart.lines().join('\n'));
}

Common mistakes

  • Leaving out the file extension. Wrong: import { formatINR } from './cart'; fails in the browser and in Node ESM. Fix: './cart.js'. Bundlers are more forgiving, which hides the problem until you run without one.
  • Mixing up default and named imports. Wrong: import formatINR from './money.js' when money.js only has export function formatINR. You get “does not provide an export named default”. Fix: import { formatINR } from './money.js'.
  • Using require in an ES module. Wrong: const fs = require('fs'); in a "type": "module" project throws “require is not defined in ES module scope”. Fix: import fs from 'node:fs'; or import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';.
  • Opening module pages from file://. The browser blocks the imports with a CORS error. Fix: run a local server.
  • Assigning to an import. Wrong: import { count } from './cart.js'; count++; throws a TypeError. Fix: export a function such as add() from the owning module.
  • Expecting export * to include the default. Fix: add export { default } from './x.js' or re-export it under a name.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “ESM vs CommonJS?” Static vs dynamic loading, live bindings vs copied values, top-level await, browser support, and why static imports enable tree-shaking.
  • “What is a live binding?” Show the counter example and say that importers cannot assign to it.
  • “How would you reduce bundle size?” Dynamic import() for rarely used features, import only what you use, and check the bundle with a visualiser.
  • Team conventions vary. Many teams ban default exports in app code so that names stay consistent. Frameworks sometimes require them (for example, a Next.js page file exports its component as default).
  • Know how to read an error like “Cannot use import statement outside a module”. It means the file is being run as CommonJS or a classic script: add "type": "module", rename it .mjs, or use <script type="module">.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. In what order are the lines logged? (This runs as a module.)

console.log('main body');
import 'data:text/javascript,console.log("dependency")';
  • A 
    main body
dependency
  • B 
    dependency
main body
  • C main body
  • D SyntaxError

Snippet 2. What is logged? (This runs as a module.)

console.log(typeof this);
try {
  total = 5;
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name);
}
  • A 
    object
ReferenceError
  • B undefined
  • C object
  • D 
    undefined
ReferenceError

Snippet 3. What is logged? (This runs as a module.)

const m = await import('data:text/javascript,export let n = 0; export function inc() { n++; }');
m.inc();
m.inc();
console.log(m.n);
  • A 0
  • B 1
  • C 2
  • D undefined

Snippet 4. What is logged? (This runs as a module.)

const url = 'data:text/javascript,console.log("init")';
await import(url);
await import(url);
console.log('done');
  • A 
    init
init
done
  • B 
    init
done
  • C done
  • D 
    done
init

Snippet 5. What is logged? (This runs as a module.)

const m = await import('data:text/javascript,export default 7; export const a = 1;');
console.log(m.default + m.a, 'default' in m);
  • A 8 true
  • B 1 false
  • C NaN true
  • D 8 false

Answers

  1. B. Static imports are hoisted: the whole dependency graph is loaded and evaluated before the importing module’s body runs, wherever the import line appears.
  2. D. At the top of a module this is undefined, and modules are always in strict mode, so assigning to an undeclared variable throws a ReferenceError instead of creating a global.
  3. C. The namespace object exposes live bindings. inc() changes n inside the module, and reading m.n always gives the current value.
  4. B. A module is evaluated once per URL. The second import() finds it in the module map and returns the same namespace without running the code again.
  5. A. A default export is simply an export named default. Dynamic import() gives you the namespace object, so you read it as m.default.

terms.definition: The standard JavaScript module system: files that use import and export, run in strict mode and have their own top-level scope.
An export with a fixed name (export const GST_RATE = 0.18). Import it with braces: import { GST_RATE } from './money.js'.
The single main value of a module (export default function formatINR…). The importer chooses its name: import formatINR from './money.js'.
An import is a read-only view of the exporter’s variable, not a copy. If the module changes the variable, every importer sees the new value.
A function-like expression that loads a module at run time and returns a promise for its namespace object. Used for code splitting and optional features.
An object with information about the current module, such as import.meta.url (and import.meta.dirname in Node, import.meta.env in Vite).
Node’s original module system: require() to import and module.exports to export. It loads synchronously and is still common in older packages.

lessons.examTip: Prefer named exports in app code: editors auto-import them, renames stay consistent across files, and typos fail loudly at load time instead of at run time.

quiz.question: cart.js has export let count = 0 and a function that increments it. main.js does import { count } from './cart.js'. What does main.js see after the function runs?
options: Always 0: an import is a copy
The updated value: imports are live bindings
undefined, because let cannot be exported
A TypeError on every read
quiz.explanation: An import is a live, read-only binding to the exporter’s variable. The exporting module can change it and every importer sees the change; importers cannot assign to it.

quiz.question: Which statement about <script type="module"> in a browser is true?
options: It runs before the HTML below it is parsed, like a classic script
It can use require() to load files
It works from file:// URLs without a server
It is deferred by default and runs in strict mode with its own top-level scope
quiz.explanation: Module scripts behave like defer: they run after parsing, in order. They are always strict, their top-level variables are not globals, and they are fetched with CORS, so you need a local server.

quiz.question: When is dynamic import() the right tool?
options: To load a heavy feature (a chart library, a PDF exporter) only when the user asks for it
To make every import faster
To import CommonJS modules only
To avoid using a bundler
quiz.explanation: import() loads a module on demand and returns a promise. Bundlers such as Vite split it into a separate file, so the first page load stays small.

quiz.question: A Node project has no "type" field in package.json and index.js uses require(). What happens if you add "type": "module"?
options: Nothing changes
require keeps working because Node supports both
.js files become ES modules, so require is not defined there and the file must use import (or be renamed .cjs)
Node converts require calls to imports automatically
quiz.explanation: "type": "module" makes Node treat .js files as ES modules. Inside them require, module.exports and __dirname do not exist; use import/export and import.meta, or rename the file to .cjs.

lessons.title: npm, Vite and the tooling stack
lessons.summaryHtml:
Professional JavaScript projects are built with a small set of tools. npm installs packages and runs project commands. package.json describes the project, and a lockfile pins the exact versions. Vite serves your code during development and bundles it for production. ESLint finds bugs, and Prettier formats the code.

You will learn the difference between dependencies and devDependencies, how semantic versioning ranges such as ^8.3.0 work, why you commit package-lock.json and use npm ci, and how npm scripts and npx find tools.

You will also see how Vite handles environment variables (import.meta.env, and why secrets never belong in front-end code), why built files have hashed names, and a clean folder structure. In the lab you set up the Ralfiz Store project with Vite, ESLint and Prettier from scratch.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Think of a restaurant kitchen. package.json is the recipe card: which ingredients (packages) the dish needs, and which kitchen tools (build tools) the cooks use. npm is the supplier that delivers them. The lockfile is the exact delivery receipt, down to the batch number, so every branch cooks with identical ingredients. Vite is the kitchen itself: fast while you are experimenting, and able to pack a tidy takeaway box (the dist folder) for customers. ESLint is the head chef who spots mistakes, and Prettier plates everything the same way.

Why it matters

On your first day at a job you will clone a repository and type npm ci and npm run dev. The same week you will add a package, fix a lint error in a pull request, and ask why the staging site shows the wrong API URL. Understanding the tooling turns these from mysteries into routine. It also protects you from real risks: a “harmless” update that breaks the build, a secret key shipped to every visitor, or a huge bundle that makes the site slow on mobile.

How it works

package.json: the project’s ID card

npm init -y creates a package.json, and Vite’s starter creates one for you. The fields you will touch most are shown below. JSON allows no comments, so the notes are listed after the file.

{
  "name": "ralfiz-store",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "format": "prettier --write ."
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "dompurify": "^3.2.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "eslint": "^10.11.0",
    "prettier": "^3.9.9",
    "vite": "^8.3.0"
  }
}
  • "private": true stops you from publishing the app to the npm registry by accident.
  • "type": "module" makes .js files ES modules in Node, as you saw in the last lesson. That applies to config files such as eslint.config.js.
  • npm install dompurify adds a dependency. npm install -D vite (or --save-dev) adds a devDependency.
FieldPut hereExamples
dependenciesCode your app runs in productiondompurify, a date library, a chart library
devDependenciesTools for building, testing and checkingvite, eslint, prettier, vitest, typescript
peerDependencies(Libraries only) something the host app must provideA React component library lists react

For a Vite front-end, both kinds end up in the same bundle only if you import them, so the split mainly documents intent. It matters for Node servers and published packages, where npm ci --omit=dev skips devDependencies to keep production images small.

Semantic versioning and ranges

Versions follow semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change bumps MAJOR (7.4.2 to 8.0.0), a backwards-compatible feature bumps MINOR, and a bug fix bumps PATCH. In package.json you write a range. The caret ^ (npm’s default) allows minor and patch updates. The tilde ~ allows only patches. A bare version pins it exactly. Versions below 1.0.0 are special: ^0.3.2 allows only 0.3.x, because any 0.x minor release may break things.

Try it: Semver ranges: what ^ and ~ allow

JavaScript

// A tiny semver checker (npm uses the full "semver" package)
const parse = (v) => v.split('.').map(Number);   // '4.2.1' -> [4, 2, 1]

function compare(a, b) {
  const [x, y] = [parse(a), parse(b)];
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    if (x[i] !== y[i]) return x[i] - y[i];       // compare as numbers
  }
  return 0;
}

// A range becomes [lowest allowed, first NOT allowed]
function bounds(range) {
  const op = range[0];
  const base = '^~'.includes(op) ? range.slice(1) : range;
  const [major, minor, patch] = parse(base);
  if (op === '~') return [base, `${major}.${minor + 1}.0`];
  if (op === '^') {
    if (major > 0) return [base, `${major + 1}.0.0`];
    if (minor > 0) return [base, `0.${minor + 1}.0`];
    return [base, `0.0.${patch + 1}`];
  }
  return [base, `${major}.${minor}.${patch + 1}`]; // exact version
}

function satisfies(version, range) {
  const [min, max] = bounds(range);
  return compare(version, min) >= 0 && compare(version, max) < 0;
}

const published = ['4.2.0', '4.2.1', '4.2.9', '4.3.0', '4.10.2', '5.0.0'];
const ranges = ['4.2.1', '~4.2.1', '^4.2.1'];
console.table(published.map((v) => ({
  version: v,
  ...Object.fromEntries(ranges.map((r) => [r, satisfies(v, r) ? 'yes' : '-'])),
})));

for (const r of ['^4.2.1', '~4.2.1', '^0.3.2', '^0.0.3']) {
  const [min, max] = bounds(r);
  console.log(r.padEnd(7), 'means', `>=${min} <${max}`);
}

A tiny version of the rules npm uses. Add a version to the published list or try a range such as ^0.0.3.

Semver is a promise made by humans, so it is sometimes broken. That is exactly why lockfiles exist.

Lockfiles, npm install and npm ci

A range such as ^2.3.0 can mean a different version next week. package-lock.json records the exact version, download URL and integrity hash of every package in the tree, including the dependencies of your dependencies. Commit it. Never commit node_modules, which the lockfile can recreate.

Try it: Lockfiles: same package.json, different installs

JavaScript

// Versions on the registry (it only ever grows)
const registry = {
  'date-kit': ['2.3.0', '2.4.0', '2.5.1'],
  vite: ['8.3.0', '8.3.1'],
};

const pkg = {
  dependencies: { 'date-kit': '^2.3.0' },
  devDependencies: { vite: '^8.3.0' },
};

// Highest published version with the same major (a caret range)
function resolve(range, versions) {
  const major = range.slice(1).split('.')[0];
  return versions.filter((v) => v.split('.')[0] === major).at(-1);
}

function install(pkg, { lock, omitDev = false } = {}) {
  const wanted = { ...pkg.dependencies, ...(omitDev ? {} : pkg.devDependencies) };
  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(wanted).map(([name, range]) =>
    [name, lock?.[name] ?? resolve(range, registry[name])]));
}

// Monday: Asha runs npm install and commits package-lock.json
const lock = install(pkg);
console.log('Monday, npm install :', lock);

// Tuesday: date-kit 2.6.0 is published (with a bug)
registry['date-kit'].push('2.6.0');
console.log('Tuesday, no lockfile:', install(pkg));
console.log('Tuesday, npm ci     :', install(pkg, { lock }));

// On a server that only runs the built app
console.log('npm ci --omit=dev   :', install(pkg, { lock, omitDev: true }));

A new, buggy date-kit is published on Tuesday. Compare a fresh install with one that follows the lockfile.

CommandWhat it doesUse it
npm installInstalls, and may update the lockfile within your rangesOn your machine, when adding or changing packages
npm install pkg@latestUpgrades one package and updates both filesDeliberate upgrades, in their own commit
npm ciDeletes node_modules and installs exactly the lockfile; fails if it does not match package.jsonCI pipelines, fresh clones, deploys
npm outdated / npm auditLists newer versions / known vulnerabilitiesRegular maintenance

npm scripts and npx

The scripts field gives your team shared, named commands. When a script runs, npm adds node_modules/.bin to the PATH. That is why "lint": "eslint ." works without a global ESLint install, and why every developer uses the project’s exact version. npm start and npm test have shortcuts; every other script needs npm run. If a prebuild or postbuild script exists, npm runs it before or after build.

npm run dev                  # start the Vite dev server
npm run build                # production build into dist/
npm run lint -- --fix        # everything after -- goes to eslint
npx eslint src/main.js       # run a local binary directly
npx serve dist               # run a package without installing it
npm create vite@latest shop  # runs the create-vite package (npm init works too)

npx runs a binary from node_modules/.bin, or downloads the package temporarily if it is not installed. Be careful with typos in npx package names: you are running code from the internet.

Vite: dev server and production build

In development, Vite does not bundle your code. It starts a server (by default at http://localhost:5173) that serves your source files as native ES modules, transforming them on request. It pre-bundles your npm dependencies once, so a package made of hundreds of files becomes one request. When you save a file, hot module replacement (HMR) swaps just that module in the running page. That is why the dev server starts in well under a second, even on big projects.

For production, vite build bundles the module graph starting from index.html. It removes unused exports (tree-shaking), splits dynamic import()s into separate chunks, minifies the output and writes it to dist/ with content-hashed file names. Vite 8 does this with Rolldown, a bundler written in Rust. Earlier versions used esbuild and Rollup, and the idea is the same. vite preview serves dist/ locally so you can test the real build before deploying it to any static host.

Try it: Why built files have hashed names

JavaScript

// FNV-1a: a small, fast hash. Vite uses a stronger one; the idea is the same.
function hash(text) {
  let h = 0x811c9dc5;
  for (const ch of text) {
    h ^= ch.codePointAt(0);
    h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193) >>> 0;
  }
  return h.toString(36).padStart(7, '0');
}

function build(files) {
  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(files).map(([name, code]) => {
    const [base, ext] = name.split('.');
    return [name, `assets/${base}-${hash(code)}.${ext}`];
  }));
}

const release1 = {
  'index.js': 'renderShop(); console.log("v1");',
  'vendor.js': 'export function purify(html) { /* big library */ }',
  'style.css': 'body { font-family: system-ui; }',
};
const release2 = { ...release1, 'index.js': 'renderShop(); console.log("v2");' };

const a = build(release1);
const b = build(release2);
console.table(Object.keys(a).map((name) => ({
  file: name,
  release1: a[name],
  release2: b[name],
  download: a[name] === b[name] ? 'cached' : 'new',
})));
console.log('index.html always points at the current names, and is never cached for long.');

Change one file and only its hash changes, so browsers re-download just that file.

Environment variables

Settings that differ between your laptop, staging and production, such as the API base URL, go in .env files. Vite loads .env, then .env.local, then .env.[mode], then .env.[mode].local, and later files win. Mode is development for vite and production for vite build. Only variables that start with VITE_ are exposed to your code, as import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE, next to built-ins such as MODE, DEV and PROD.

Try it: How Vite builds import.meta.env

JavaScript

// Files in the project root (a real project would not commit secrets)
const files = {
  '.env': 'VITE_API_BASE=https://dummyjson.com\nVITE_STORE_NAME=Ralfiz Store\nDB_PASSWORD=s3cret',
  '.env.development': 'VITE_STORE_NAME=Ralfiz Store (dev)',
  '.env.production': 'VITE_API_BASE=https://api.ralfiz.dev',
  '.env.local': '# personal, git-ignored\nVITE_SHOW_DEBUG=true',
};

function parseEnv(text = '') {
  const vars = {};
  for (const line of text.split('\n')) {
    if (!line.trim() || line.startsWith('#')) continue;
    const i = line.indexOf('=');
    vars[line.slice(0, i).trim()] = line.slice(i + 1).trim(); // always strings
  }
  return vars;
}

function loadEnv(mode) {
  // Later files win: mode-specific beats generic, .local beats shared
  const order = ['.env', '.env.local', `.env.${mode}`, `.env.${mode}.local`];
  const merged = Object.assign({}, ...order.map((name) => parseEnv(files[name])));
  const exposed = Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(merged).filter(([key]) => key.startsWith('VITE_')));
  return { ...exposed, MODE: mode, DEV: mode !== 'production', PROD: mode === 'production' };
}

console.log('npm run dev   ->', loadEnv('development'));
console.log('npm run build ->', loadEnv('production'));
console.log('DB_PASSWORD reaches the browser?', 'DB_PASSWORD' in loadEnv('production'));
console.log('typeof VITE_SHOW_DEBUG:', typeof loadEnv('development').VITE_SHOW_DEBUG);

A simplified model of Vite’s env loading. Change the mode or add a variable without the VITE_ prefix.

Watch out: Vite replaces import.meta.env.VITE_* with the literal values at build time, so they are plain text in the JavaScript every visitor downloads. The VITE_ prefix means “this is public”. Payment keys, database passwords and private API tokens must stay on a server. The browser calls your backend, and the backend uses the secret. Also remember that values are strings: 'false' is truthy.

The Vite starter’s .gitignore ignores *.local files, so keep personal values in .env.local and commit a .env.example that lists the variable names with safe defaults.

ESLint and Prettier

ESLint (linter)Prettier (formatter)
JobFinds likely bugs and bad patternsRewrites layout: quotes, commas, line breaks
ExamplesUnused variables, ==, undeclared globals, unreachable codeSingle vs double quotes, 2-space indent, wrapping at 80 or 100 columns
Configeslint.config.js (flat config).prettierrc

Modern ESLint (version 9 and newer) uses a “flat config”: one eslint.config.js that exports an array of config objects. ESLint’s recommended set contains no formatting rules (ESLint has deprecated them), so the two tools do not fight. Install the VS Code extensions for both and turn on “format on save”, and the editor fixes most issues as you type. Newer, faster tools such as Oxlint and Biome follow the same ideas.

// eslint.config.js
import js from '@eslint/js';
import globals from 'globals';
import { defineConfig } from 'eslint/config';

export default defineConfig([
  { ignores: ['dist/'] },
  {
    files: ['**/*.js'],
    extends: [js.configs.recommended],
    languageOptions: { sourceType: 'module', globals: { ...globals.browser } },
    rules: { eqeqeq: 'error', 'prefer-const': 'error' },
  },
]);

A project structure for a vanilla app

ralfiz-store/
  index.html            entry point Vite starts from
  public/               copied to dist as-is (favicon.svg, robots.txt)
  src/
    main.js             starts the app: wires modules to the page
    api.js              the API client from lesson 5.4
    state.js            app state and functions that change it
    components/         productCard.js, cartDrawer.js ...
    utils/format.js     formatINR, formatDate
    styles/main.css
  .env                  shared, non-secret defaults (committed)
  .env.local            personal overrides (git-ignored)
  eslint.config.js
  .prettierrc
  package.json
  package-lock.json     committed

Keep main.js thin: it imports modules and connects them to the page. Group files by feature once the app grows, and keep pure logic (formatting, calculations) separate from DOM code, so it is easy to test in lesson 7.2.

Example: setting up the Ralfiz Store project

The lab builds the project in about fifteen minutes:

  1. npm create vite@latest ralfiz-store -- --template vanilla, then cd ralfiz-store, npm install and npm run dev.
  2. npm install -D eslint @eslint/js globals prettier, then add eslint.config.js, .prettierrc and the lint, format and check scripts.
  3. Replace the demo code with a main.js that reads import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE and VITE_STORE_NAME and renders six products with textContent.
  4. Create .env and .env.development, then compare the dev server with npm run build and npm run preview.
  5. Open dist/assets: find the hashed file name, check that DB_PASSWORD is nowhere in it, and check that the store name is.
