JavaScript

const sample = {
  name: 'ralfiz-store',
  version: '0.1.0',
  private: true,
  type: 'module',
  scripts: {
    dev: 'vite',
    build: 'vite build',
    preview: 'vite preview',
    lint: 'eslint .',
    format: 'prettier --write .',
    prebuild: 'npm run lint',
  },
  dependencies: { dompurify: '^3.2.0' },
  devDependencies: {
    '@eslint/js': '^10.0.1',
    eslint: '^10.11.0',
    globals: '^17.12.0',
    prettier: '~3.9.9',
    vite: '^8.3.0',
  },
};

const $ = (sel) => document.querySelector(sel);
$('#src').value = JSON.stringify(sample, null, 2);

function explainRange(range) {
  const m = /^([\^~]?)(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)$/.exec(range.trim());
  if (!m) return range === '*' || range === 'latest' ? 'any version (risky)' : 'custom range';
  const [, op, major, minor, patch] = m;
  const [x, y, z] = [major, minor, patch].map(Number);
  if (op === '~') return `>=${x}.${y}.${z} <${x}.${y + 1}.0 (patches)`;
  if (op === '^') {
    const max = x > 0 ? `${x + 1}.0.0` : y > 0 ? `0.${y + 1}.0` : `0.0.${z + 1}`;
    return `>=${x}.${y}.${z} <${max} (${x > 0 ? 'minor + patches' : 'careful: 0.x'})`;
  }
  return 'exactly this version';
}

function row(left, right, hint = '') {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  const name = Object.assign(document.createElement('code'), { className: 'cmd', textContent: left });
  const value = Object.assign(document.createElement('code'), { textContent: right });
  li.append(name, value);
  if (hint) li.append(Object.assign(document.createElement('span'), { className: 'hint', textContent: hint }));
  return li;
}

function fill(list, items) {
  list.replaceChildren(...items);
  if (!items.length) {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.className = 'empty';
    li.textContent = 'none';
    list.append(li);
  }
}

function render() {
  let pkg;
  try {
    pkg = JSON.parse($('#src').value);
  } catch (err) {
    $('#error').textContent = 'Invalid JSON: ' + err.message;
    $('#error').hidden = false;
    return;
  }
  $('#error').hidden = true;
  $('#name').textContent = pkg.name ?? '(no name)';
  $('#version').textContent = 'v' + (pkg.version ?? '0.0.0');
  $('#type').textContent = pkg.type === 'module' ? 'ES modules' : 'CommonJS';

  const scripts = Object.entries(pkg.scripts ?? {});
  fill($('#scripts'), scripts.map(([name, cmd]) => {
    const hook = /^(pre|post)(.+)$/.exec(name);
    const run = ['start', 'test'].includes(name) ? `npm ${name}` : `npm run ${name}`;
    const hint = hook && pkg.scripts[hook[2]] ? `runs ${hook[1] === 'pre' ? 'before' : 'after'} ${hook[2]}` : '';
    return row(run, cmd, hint);
  }));
  const deps = (obj) => Object.entries(obj ?? {}).map(([n, r]) => row(n, r, explainRange(r)));
  fill($('#deps'), deps(pkg.dependencies));
  fill($('#dev'), deps(pkg.devDependencies));
  console.log(`${pkg.name}: ${scripts.length} scripts, ` +
    `${Object.keys(pkg.dependencies ?? {}).length} deps, ` +
    `${Object.keys(pkg.devDependencies ?? {}).length} devDeps`);
}

let timer;
$('#src').addEventListener('input', () => {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  timer = setTimeout(render, 250);
});
render();

Common mistakes

  • Committing node_modules, or ignoring the lockfile. Fix: node_modules in .gitignore, package-lock.json committed, npm ci in CI.
  • Installing tools globally. Wrong: npm install -g eslint, so every developer has a different version. Fix: npm install -D eslint and run it through a script or npx.
  • Secrets in VITE_ variables. Wrong: VITE_PAYMENT_SECRET=sk_live_.... Fix: keep secrets on the server and call your own backend.
  • Treating env values as booleans or numbers. Wrong: if (import.meta.env.VITE_BETA) is true for 'false'. Fix: import.meta.env.VITE_BETA === 'true' and Number(import.meta.env.VITE_PAGE_SIZE).
  • Opening dist/index.html by double-clicking. Module scripts need a server. Fix: npm run preview.
  • Upgrading everything at once. Wrong: a pull request that bumps 20 packages across major versions. Fix: upgrade one major version at a time, read the changelog, and run the tests.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be able to explain ^ vs ~, why lockfiles exist, and the difference between npm install and npm ci.
  • “Why is Vite’s dev server fast?” It serves native ES modules on demand instead of bundling first, pre-bundles dependencies once and uses HMR. The production build is still bundled.
  • “How do you handle config per environment in a front-end app?” .env files with VITE_ variables for public values, and a backend for secrets. Mention that front-end env values are public by design.
  • pnpm and Yarn are alternative package managers with the same concepts (pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock). Use whichever lockfile the repository already has.
  • Supply-chain safety: install well-known packages, check weekly downloads and maintenance, review what npm audit reports, and do not add a dependency for a five-line function.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const versions = ['1.10.0', '1.9.0', '1.2.0'];
console.log(versions.sort());
  • A [ '1.2.0', '1.9.0', '1.10.0' ]
  • B [ '1.10.0', '1.2.0', '1.9.0' ]
  • C [ '1.9.0', '1.2.0', '1.10.0' ]
  • D [ '1.10.0', '1.9.0', '1.2.0' ]

Snippet 2. What is logged?

function caretMax(v) {
  const [major, minor] = v.split('.').map(Number);
  return major > 0 ? `<${major + 1}.0.0` : `<0.${minor + 1}.0`;
}
console.log(caretMax('2.3.1'), caretMax('0.3.1'));
  • A <3.0.0 <1.0.0
  • B <3.0.0 <0.4.0
  • C <2.4.0 <0.4.0
  • D <3.0.0 <0.3.2

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const env = { VITE_PAGE_SIZE: '12', VITE_BETA: 'false', DB_PASSWORD: 'x' };
const exposed = Object.keys(env).filter((k) => k.startsWith('VITE_'));
console.log(exposed.length, env.VITE_PAGE_SIZE + 1, Boolean(env.VITE_BETA));
  • A 3 13 false
  • B 2 13 false
  • C 2 121 true
  • D 2 121 false

Snippet 4. npm runs pre and post hooks around a script. What does this model log?

const scripts = { prebuild: 'eslint .', build: 'vite build', postbuild: 'node report.js' };
function runOrder(name) {
  if (!(name in scripts)) return 'Missing script: ' + name;
  return ['pre' + name, name, 'post' + name].filter((s) => s in scripts).join(' > ');
}
console.log(runOrder('build'));
console.log(runOrder('dev'));
  • A 
    build
Missing script: dev
  • B 
    prebuild > build > postbuild
prebuild > build > postbuild
  • C 
    build > prebuild > postbuild
Missing script: dev
  • D 
    prebuild > build > postbuild
Missing script: dev

Answers

  1. B. sort() compares strings character by character, and "1" comes before "2" and "9", so 1.10.0 sorts first. That is why semver tools compare each number separately.
  2. B. A caret allows changes that do not touch the left-most non-zero number. For 2.x that is the major; for 0.3.x it is the minor, because 0.x versions may break things in any minor release.
  3. C. Only the two VITE_ keys pass the filter. Environment values are always strings, so + 1 concatenates, and the non-empty string "false" is truthy. Convert with Number() and === "true".
  4. D. npm run build runs prebuild, then build, then postbuild if they exist. A script that is not defined fails with a Missing script error.

terms.definition: The project’s manifest: name, version, "type", npm scripts and the packages it depends on, with version ranges.
Packages needed only to develop, test or build (Vite, ESLint, Prettier). Runtime code that ships to users goes in dependencies.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking changes bump MAJOR, new features bump MINOR, fixes bump PATCH. ^1.4.2 allows <2.0.0 and ~1.4.2 allows <1.5.0.
package-lock.json records the exact version of every installed package, so every machine and CI run installs the same tree.
Named commands in package.json ("dev": "vite") run with npm run dev; node_modules/.bin is on the PATH while they run.
A build tool with a fast dev server that serves native ES modules with hot module replacement, and a production build that bundles, minifies and hashes files.
Vite’s object of environment values (MODE, DEV, PROD and any VITE_* variables) that are inlined into the bundle at build time.

quiz.question: Your app imports DOMPurify in the browser code, and you use Vite and ESLint to build it. Where should each go?
options: All three in devDependencies
DOMPurify in dependencies; Vite and ESLint in devDependencies
All three in dependencies
DOMPurify in devDependencies; Vite and ESLint in dependencies
quiz.explanation: Code that runs in the product is a dependency. Tools used only to develop and build are devDependencies. For a front-end app, Vite bundles whatever your code imports (tools such as ESLint never reach dist), so the split mainly documents intent and keeps npm install --omit=dev lean on servers.

quiz.question: package.json says "eslint": "^10.2.0". Which version can npm install?
options: Only 10.2.0
quiz.explanation: The caret allows any version at least 10.2.0 and below 11.0.0. Versions compare number by number, so 10.11.0 is newer than 10.2.0.

quiz.question: In a Vite project, what happens to DB_PASSWORD=abc in the .env file?
options: It is not exposed to your code, because only VITE_ variables are
It is available as import.meta.env.DB_PASSWORD
Vite encrypts it in the bundle
It is sent to the server with each request
quiz.explanation: Vite exposes only VITE_-prefixed variables to client code. Those are inlined into the public bundle as plain text, so nothing secret should ever be given that prefix.

quiz.question: Why does vite build name a file assets/index-CrVNE-W7.js instead of index.js?
options: To hide the source code
Because Vite minifies file names
The hash changes when the content changes, so browsers can cache files forever and still get updates
To prevent other sites from linking to it
quiz.explanation: Content-hashed names allow long-lived caching. When you deploy a change, only the files whose content changed get new names, and index.html points to them.

lessons.title: Modern JavaScript roundup (ES2020–ES2025)
lessons.summaryHtml:
JavaScript gets a new edition every year. Since 2020 the yearly editions have added small features that remove whole categories of bugs: ?. and ?? for missing data, logical assignment, at(), Object.hasOwn, array copy methods such as toSorted, Object.groupBy, Promise.withResolvers, top-level await, error cause, Set methods, iterator helpers and the RegExp v flag.

In this lesson you learn what each feature replaces, how new features move through the TC39 stages, and how to check whether your users’ browsers and your Node version support them. The lab turns a legacy order report into modern JavaScript and fixes two real bugs along the way.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

JavaScript is not a finished language. Every June, Ecma International approves a new edition of the ECMAScript standard, named after its year: ES2020, ES2021 and so on up to ES2025. Each edition is small. It adds a few operators, methods or functions that people kept writing by hand, usually with bugs.

A developer who still writes a && a.b && a.b.c, JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) and a ten-line reduce to group an array looks out of date in a code review, and those old patterns hide real bugs.

This lesson is a roundup. You met some of these features earlier in the course; here you see them side by side, learn what each one replaces, and learn how to decide whether you can use a feature today.

Why it matters

Imagine the Ralfiz Store order report. A coupon with percent: 0 is treated as “missing”, so the customer gets a 5% default discount they were never promised. A snapshot of the orders turns every Date into a string, so the “orders this week” filter silently returns nothing. Sorting orders for a “top 3” widget reorders the main list on the page. None of these throw an error. They just produce wrong numbers.

Each of those bugs has a modern fix in one line: ??, structuredClone and toSorted. Knowing the modern toolbox makes your code shorter, and more importantly it makes the intent visible: toSorted tells the reader “I am not changing the original”.

How it works

How a feature gets into JavaScript

The language is designed by TC39, a committee of browser makers, companies and invited experts. Anyone can suggest an idea, and a proposal moves through stages:

StageMeaningShould you use it?
0An idea, not yet taken up by the committeeNo
1The committee agrees the problem is worth solvingNo
2A draft design and specification text existNo, it may still change a lot
2.7Design approved in principle; tests and prototypes are being writtenExperiments only
3Ready for engines to implement; only small changes expectedOnly where it has shipped, after checking support
4Finished: tests exist and at least two engines ship itYes, once your target browsers and Node have it

Stage 4 features are included in the next June edition. Notice the order: engines often ship a feature before the edition that names it is published, and some ship it later. The edition year tells you when the feature was standardised, not when your users’ browsers got it.

So how do you check? Three habits:

  • MDN compatibility tables: every MDN page ends with a table showing the first browser and Node versions that support the feature. Check caniuse.com for the same information with usage percentages.
  • Know your targets: a Node 22 server is one fixed engine you control. A public website must support whatever your users run, which usually means “the last two versions of evergreen browsers” plus Safari on older iPhones.
  • Feature detection at run time for APIs: if ('groupBy' in Object) { … }. This works for functions and methods. It does not work for new syntax such as ?.: an old engine fails to parse the whole file before any of your checks run. Build tools such as Vite handle syntax by compiling down to an older target.
Remember: structuredClone, fetch and AbortController are not ECMAScript features at all. They are web platform APIs, defined by browser standards and also provided by Node. MDN marks which is which.

Safe access and defaults: ?. ?? and logical assignment

Optional chaining (?., ES2020) checks the value on its left. If it is null or undefined, the whole chain stops and returns undefined instead of throwing “Cannot read properties of null”. It works for properties (a?.b), computed keys (a?.[key]) and calls (fn?.()).

Nullish coalescing (??, ES2020) picks the right side only when the left is null or undefined. The older || picks the right side for every falsy value: 0, '', false and NaN too. For quantities, prices, discounts and flags, that difference is a bug waiting to happen.

Logical assignment (ES2021) combines the two ideas with =: a ||= b, a &&= b and a ??= b. They are short-circuiting: a ??= b only evaluates b and only writes to a when a is nullish. Small additions from the same years are numeric separators (1_00_000, ignored by the engine and allowed between any digits, so Indian lakh grouping works), Array.prototype.at (negative indexes count from the end) and Object.hasOwn, a safe replacement for obj.hasOwnProperty(key).

Try it: Safe defaults: ?. ?? and logical assignment

JavaScript

const order = {
  id: 'ORD-1001',
  customer: { name: 'Anu', address: null },
  discount: 0,
  items: [
    { sku: 'PEN', price: 20, qty: 3 },
    { sku: 'BAG', price: 1_250, qty: 1 },
  ],
};

// ?. returns undefined instead of throwing on null/undefined
console.log('city:', order.customer.address?.city);
console.log('phone:', order.customer.phone?.trim() ?? 'not given');

// || replaces every falsy value; ?? only null and undefined
console.log('|| gives', order.discount || 10);
console.log('?? gives', order.discount ?? 10);

// logical assignment: assign only when needed
const settings = { currency: '', pageSize: 0 };
settings.currency ||= 'INR';   // '' is falsy, so it is replaced
settings.pageSize ??= 20;      // 0 is kept
settings.theme ??= 'light';    // missing, so it is added
console.log(settings);

console.log('last item:', order.items.at(-1).sku);
console.log('own id?', Object.hasOwn(order, 'id'));
console.log('budget:', 1_00_000 + 50_000); // separators are ignored

Change discount to null and see which line changes. Then try settings.pageSize ||= 20 and compare.

Copy instead of mutate

Spread ({ ...cart }) makes a shallow copy: the top-level object is new, but nested arrays and objects are shared. The old trick JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) makes a deep copy but loses anything JSON cannot represent: a Date becomes a string, undefined properties vanish, and a Map becomes {}.

structuredClone(value) uses the same algorithm the browser uses to pass data to a Web Worker. It deep-copies plain objects, arrays, Date, Map, Set, typed arrays and even circular references. It throws a DataCloneError for functions and DOM nodes, and class instances come back as plain objects without their methods.

For arrays, ES2023 added the “change array by copy” methods. Each has an old, mutating twin:

Mutates the originalReturns a new array
arr.sort(fn)arr.toSorted(fn)
arr.reverse()arr.toReversed()
arr.splice(start, count, ...items)arr.toSpliced(start, count, ...items)
arr[i] = valuearr.with(i, value)

They matter most in state-driven UIs (the DOM track and React), where changing the array that the current screen was drawn from causes stale or missing updates. ES2023 also added findLast and findLastIndex, which search from the end.

Try it: Copy, don’t mutate

JavaScript

const cart = {
  items: [{ sku: 'PEN', qty: 1 }, { sku: 'INK', qty: 2 }],
  updatedAt: new Date('2026-09-28T10:00:00Z'),
};

const shallow = { ...cart };
shallow.items[0].qty = 99;             // items array is shared!
console.log('after shallow edit:', cart.items[0].qty);

const deep = structuredClone(cart);
deep.items[1].qty = 5;
console.log('after deep edit:', cart.items[1].qty);
console.log('Date kept:', deep.updatedAt instanceof Date);

const json = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(cart));
console.log('JSON copy date type:', typeof json.updatedAt);

const prices = [499, 99, 1299, 249];
const sorted = prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);
console.log('original:', prices, 'sorted:', sorted);
console.log('reversed:', prices.toReversed());
console.log('replace index 1:', prices.with(1, 149));
console.log('remove 2 from index 1:', prices.toSpliced(1, 2));
console.log('last under 500:', prices.findLast(p => p < 500));

Spread copies only the top level, so the shallow edit leaks into cart. structuredClone copies nested objects and keeps the Date.

Grouping and Set methods

Object.groupBy(items, keyFn) (ES2024) replaces the classic reduce that builds { key: [...] }. The result is an object with a null prototype, so it has no toString or hasOwnProperty; read it with Object.entries or Object.hasOwn. Map.groupBy does the same but returns a Map, which is better when keys are not strings (objects, numbers you want to keep as numbers) or when order and size matter.

ES2025 finally gave Set the operations from school maths: union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf and isDisjointFrom. They return new sets and never mutate. Before, you wrote new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x))). They are supported in current Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Node 22; check the MDN table if you support older Safari.

Try it: Grouping and Set methods

JavaScript

const orders = [
  { id: 1, city: 'Kochi', total: 1200, customer: 'anu' },
  { id: 2, city: 'Chennai', total: 450, customer: 'ravi' },
  { id: 3, city: 'Kochi', total: 300, customer: 'sara' },
  { id: 4, city: 'Pune', total: 2499, customer: 'anu' },
  { id: 5, city: 'Chennai', total: 1250, customer: 'tom' },
];

const byCity = Object.groupBy(orders, o => o.city);
for (const [city, list] of Object.entries(byCity)) {
  console.log(city.padEnd(8), list.map(o => o.id));
}

const bySize = Map.groupBy(orders, o => (o.total >= 1000 ? 'large' : 'small'));
console.log('large orders:', bySize.get('large').length);

const monday = new Set(['anu', 'ravi', 'sara']);
const tuesday = new Set(['ravi', 'sara', 'tom']);
console.log('both days:', monday.intersection(tuesday));
console.log('any day:', monday.union(tuesday));
console.log('only Monday:', monday.difference(tuesday));
console.log('exactly one day:', monday.symmetricDifference(tuesday));
console.log('ravi ⊆ Monday?', new Set(['ravi']).isSubsetOf(monday));
console.log('no overlap?', monday.isDisjointFrom(new Set(['zoe'])));

Object.groupBy gives a plain lookup object; Map.groupBy lets you use any key. The Set methods are ES2025.

Async improvements: top-level await, withResolvers and error cause

Top-level await (ES2022) lets a module use await outside any function. The module pauses while it waits, and anything that imports it waits too. It does not work in classic scripts, so in the browser you need <script type="module"> and in Node a .mjs file or "type": "module".

Promise.withResolvers() (ES2024) returns { promise, resolve, reject }. It replaces the awkward pattern of declaring let resolve outside new Promise(r => { resolve = r; }), which you need when the code that settles the promise lives somewhere else, such as a timer, an event listener or a queue.

Error cause (ES2022) lets you wrap a low-level error in a clearer one without losing the original: new Error('Could not load product 7', { cause: err }). Logging tools and DevTools show the chain. Related older additions: Promise.allSettled (ES2020) waits for every promise and reports each outcome, and Promise.any (ES2021) resolves with the first success.

Try it: Top-level await, withResolvers and error cause

JavaScript

function loadConfig() {
  const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers();
  setTimeout(() => resolve({ currency: 'INR', taxRate: 0.18 }), 300);
  return promise;
}

const config = await loadConfig();   // top-level await: modules only
console.log('config ready:', config);

async function fetchProduct(id) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`https://dummyjson.com/products/${id}`);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    return await res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    // keep the low-level reason, add a message for humans
    throw new Error(`Could not load product ${id}`, { cause: err });
  }
}

try {
  await fetchProduct(99999);
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.message);
  console.log('cause:', err.cause.message);
}

const results = await Promise.allSettled([fetchProduct(1), fetchProduct(99999)]);
console.log(results.map(r => r.status));

This runs as a module, so await works at the top level. Try product 3 instead of 99999 to see the success path.

Iterator helpers and modern regular expressions

Iterator helpers (ES2025) add map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, reduce, some, every, find, forEach and toArray to iterators such as generators and map.values(). Unlike array methods they are lazy: nothing runs until a value is pulled, and take(3) stops pulling after three values. That is why they work even on infinite generators, and why map.values().map(...) does not build a temporary array. Iterator.from(obj) wraps any iterable.

For regular expressions, ES2024 added the v flag (“unicodeSets”), an upgraded u flag. It supports set operations inside character classes ([\p{L}--[aeiou]] means “letters except these vowels”) and properties of strings such as \p{RGI_Emoji}, which matches a whole emoji even when it is built from several code points. ES2025 standardised RegExp.escape(text), which makes user input safe to put inside new RegExp(); it shipped in engines later than the other ES2025 features, so feature-detect it. Promise.try is in the same position. You will use both flags in the next lesson on regular expressions.

What about dates? Temporal is the new date and time API, designed to fix the problems of Date (zero-based months, mutable objects, weak time zone support). It is rolling out across engines, so check MDN before relying on it; this course keeps using Date with Intl.DateTimeFormat.

Try it: Iterator helpers, the v flag and RegExp.escape

JavaScript

function* orderIds() {
  let n = 1001;
  while (true) yield n++;          // infinite, but lazy
}

const firstEven = orderIds()
  .filter(id => id % 2 === 0)
  .map(id => `ORD-${id}`)
  .take(3)
  .toArray();
console.log(firstEven);

const stock = new Map([['pen', 20], ['bag', 1250], ['lamp', 2499]]);
console.log(stock.values().map(p => Math.round(p * 1.18)).toArray());

// v flag: set subtraction inside a character class
const noVowels = /^[\p{L}--[aeiouAEIOU]]+$/v;
console.log('rhythm', noVowels.test('rhythm'), 'ralfiz', noVowels.test('ralfiz'));
// v flag: match a whole emoji, even when it is several code points
console.log('one emoji?', /^\p{RGI_Emoji}$/v.test('👩🏽‍💻'));

const search = 'C++ (2025)';
if (typeof RegExp.escape === 'function') {
  const re = new RegExp(RegExp.escape(search), 'i');
  console.log('escaped:', re.source, re.test('Learn c++ (2025) now'));
} else {
  console.log('RegExp.escape is not supported here yet');
}

The generator is infinite, but the helpers are lazy: take(3) stops it. RegExp.escape is feature-detected because it is new in runtimes.

Example: a feature radar for your team

Before adopting new APIs, a team lead at Ralfiz wants a page that shows which ones the current browser supports. The live page below does exactly that, and it is built with the features it tests.

  1. Each feature is a row [name, edition, test]. The test is a tiny function such as () => 'groupBy' in Object. Each test runs inside try/catch, so a broken check cannot crash the page.
  2. The edition chips come from Object.keys(Object.groupBy(features, f => f.year)). Keys keep insertion order, so the chips appear from ES2020 upwards.
  3. Cards are built with createElement and textContent, never innerHTML, and the grid is swapped in one step with replaceChildren.
  4. A single delegated click listener on the chip row uses closest('button') and updates aria-pressed for screen readers.

Open it at phone width with the toggle, then look at the console: it lists anything this browser is missing.

Try it: Feature radar

HTML

<main class="radar">
  <header class="top">
    <div>
      <p class="eyebrow">Ralfiz Dev Tools</p>
      <h1>Feature radar</h1>

    </div>

    </div>

</main>

CSS

:root { --accent: #b45309; --bg: #f7f7f8; --card: #fff; --line: #e6e6ea;
  --text: #17171c; --muted: #6b6b76; --ok: #15803d; --no: #b91c1c; }
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin: 0; background: var(--bg); color: var(--text);
  font: 14px/1.45 system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif; }
.radar { max-width: 880px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 20px 16px 28px; }
.top { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between; margin-bottom: 16px; }
.eyebrow { margin: 0; color: var(--accent); font-weight: 600; font-size: 12px;
  letter-spacing: .06em; text-transform: uppercase; }
h1 { margin: 2px 0 4px; font-size: 24px; }
.sub { margin: 0; color: var(--muted); }

.score span { color: var(--muted); font-size: 12px; }
.chips { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px; margin-bottom: 16px; }

  border-radius: 999px; padding: 6px 12px; font: inherit; cursor: pointer; }
.chips button[aria-pressed="true"] { background: var(--accent); border-color: var(--accent);
  color: #fff; }
.chips button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 2px; }

JavaScript

const features = [
  ['globalThis', 'ES2020', () => typeof globalThis === 'object'],
  ['Promise.allSettled', 'ES2020', () => 'allSettled' in Promise],
  ['String#matchAll', 'ES2020', () => 'matchAll' in String.prototype],
  ['BigInt', 'ES2020', () => typeof BigInt === 'function'],
  ['String#replaceAll', 'ES2021', () => 'replaceAll' in String.prototype],
  ['Promise.any', 'ES2021', () => 'any' in Promise],
  ['WeakRef', 'ES2021', () => typeof WeakRef === 'function'],
  ['Array#at', 'ES2022', () => 'at' in Array.prototype],
  ['Object.hasOwn', 'ES2022', () => 'hasOwn' in Object],
  ['Error cause', 'ES2022', () => new Error('x', { cause: 1 }).cause === 1],
  ['Array#toSorted', 'ES2023', () => 'toSorted' in Array.prototype],
  ['Array#findLast', 'ES2023', () => 'findLast' in Array.prototype],
  ['Object.groupBy', 'ES2024', () => 'groupBy' in Object],
  ['Promise.withResolvers', 'ES2024', () => 'withResolvers' in Promise],
  ['RegExp v flag', 'ES2024', () => 'unicodeSets' in RegExp.prototype],
  ['Set#union', 'ES2025', () => 'union' in Set.prototype],
  ['Iterator helpers', 'ES2025',
    () => typeof Iterator === 'function' && 'map' in Iterator.prototype],
  ['Promise.try', 'ES2025', () => 'try' in Promise],
  ['RegExp.escape', 'ES2025', () => 'escape' in RegExp],
  ['Temporal', 'Rolling out', () => typeof Temporal === 'object'],
].map(([name, year, test]) => {
  let ok = false;
  try { ok = Boolean(test()); } catch { ok = false; }
  return { name, year, ok };
});

const grid = document.querySelector('#grid');
const chips = document.querySelector('#chips');
const years = ['All', ...Object.keys(Object.groupBy(features, f => f.year))];
let active = 'All';

function card(f) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.className = 'card';
  const name = document.createElement('code');
  name.textContent = f.name;
  const meta = document.createElement('div');
  meta.className = 'meta';
  const year = document.createElement('span');
  year.className = 'year';
  year.textContent = f.year;
  const pill = document.createElement('span');
  pill.className = `pill ${f.ok ? 'ok' : 'no'}`;
  pill.textContent = f.ok ? '✓ Supported' : '✕ Missing';
  meta.append(year, pill);
  li.append(name, meta);
  return li;
}

function render() {
  const shown = features.filter(f => active === 'All' || f.year === active);
  grid.replaceChildren(...shown.map(card));
  const ok = shown.filter(f => f.ok).length;
  document.querySelector('#score').textContent = `${ok}/${shown.length}`;
  for (const b of chips.children) {
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b.dataset.year === active));
  }
}

for (const y of years) {
  const b = document.createElement('button');
  b.type = 'button';
  b.dataset.year = y;
  b.textContent = y;
  chips.append(b);
}
chips.addEventListener('click', e => {
  const b = e.target.closest('button');
  if (!b) return;
  active = b.dataset.year;
  render();
});

render();
const missing = features.filter(f => !f.ok).map(f => f.name);
console.log(`${features.length - missing.length} of ${features.length} detected`);
console.log('missing:', missing.length ? missing : 'none');

Every card runs a small feature test in this browser. Syntax such as ?. cannot be tested this way: an old engine fails to parse the whole script.

// The same idea in a real app: load a fallback only when needed
if (!('groupBy' in Object)) {
  const { groupBy } = await import('./polyfills/group-by.js');
  Object.groupBy = groupBy;
}

Common mistakes

1. Using || for values where 0 or '' is valid.

// Wrong: a coupon with percent 0 gets the 5% default
const percent = coupon.percent || 5;
// Right: only a missing value gets the default
const percent = coupon.percent ?? 5;

2. Assigning through optional chaining. ?. is for reading. user?.profile.name = 'Anu' is a syntax error.

// Right: make sure the object exists, then assign
user.profile ??= {};
user.profile.name = 'Anu';

3. Expecting structuredClone to copy class instances or functions.

const copy = structuredClone(account); // BankAccount instance
copy.deposit(100); // TypeError: copy.deposit is not a function
// Right: give the class its own copy method
clone() { return new BankAccount(this.owner, this.balance); }

4. Sorting state in place.

// Wrong: reorders state.products for everyone
const cheapest = state.products.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)[0];
// Right
const cheapest = state.products.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price)[0];

5. Top-level await in a classic script. await outside an async function is a syntax error in a normal <script> or a CommonJS file. Use type="module" or "type": "module".

6. Calling methods on an Object.groupBy result. groups.hasOwnProperty('Kochi') throws because the object has no prototype. Use Object.hasOwn(groups, 'Kochi') or 'Kochi' in groups.

Interview and real-world notes

  • “What is the difference between || and ???” Answer with a price or quantity example: 0 || 10 is 10, 0 ?? 10 is 0.
  • “How do you deep clone?” structuredClone for data; mention what it cannot copy (functions, DOM nodes, class methods) and why JSON round-tripping loses dates.
  • “How does a feature get into JavaScript?” TC39 stages 0 to 4, two shipping implementations, then the yearly June edition.
  • On a real project, write down your targets (for example “Node 22, last two versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari”), configure the build tool to match, and check MDN before using anything from the last two editions.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const qty = 0;
const note = '';
console.log(qty || 10, qty ?? 10, JSON.stringify(note ?? 'none'));
  • A 10 10 "none"
  • B 0 0 "none"
  • C 10 0 ""
  • D 10 0 "none"

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const a = [3, 1, 2];
const b = a.toSorted();
const c = a.sort().reverse();
console.log(a.join(''), b.join(''), c === a);
  • A 312 123 false
  • B 321 123 true
  • C 123 123 true
  • D 321 321 false

Snippet 3. What is logged?

const s = { theme: '', lang: undefined, size: 0 };
s.theme ||= 'dark';
s.lang ??= 'en';
s.size &&= 16;
console.log(s.theme, s.lang, s.size);
  • A dark en 16
  • B dark undefined 0
  • C en 0
  • D dark en 0

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
const b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);
console.log(a.difference(b).size, a.intersection(b).size, a.union(b).size);
  • A 1 2 4
  • B 2 1 4
  • C 1 2 7
  • D 3 2 4

Answers

  1. C. || replaces any falsy value, so 0 becomes 10. ?? only replaces null and undefined, so 0 and the empty string are both kept.
  2. B. toSorted returns a new array and leaves a alone. sort and reverse mutate a in place and return the same array, so a ends as 321 and c === a is true.
  3. D. ||= assigns because the empty string is falsy; ??= assigns because lang is undefined; &&= assigns only when the value is truthy, and 0 is falsy, so size stays 0.
  4. A. difference keeps what is only in a ({1}), intersection keeps what is in both ({2, 3}) and union keeps each value once ({1, 2, 3, 4}).

terms.definition: The Ecma committee that designs JavaScript. Proposals move through stages 0 to 4; stage 4 features join the next yearly edition.
The yearly language standard (ES2020, ES2021 … ES2025), approved each June.
Stops a property access or call and returns undefined when the value on the left is null or undefined.
Returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined, so 0, false and empty strings are kept.
ES2023 methods toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with that return a new array instead of mutating the original.
ES2024 function that groups items into a null-prototype object using a key function (Map.groupBy returns a Map).
Checking at run time that an API exists before using it, instead of guessing from the browser name.

lessons.examTip: In code reviews, a || default on a number or string field is a classic bug: ask whether 0 or an empty string is a valid value, and use ?? if it is.

quiz.question: A settings object has pageSize: 0, which is a valid value. Which line keeps 0 and only fills in a default when the value is missing?
options: settings.pageSize ||= 20
settings.pageSize ??= 20
settings.pageSize &&= 20
settings.pageSize = settings.pageSize || 20
quiz.explanation: ??= assigns only when the current value is null or undefined. ||= and || also replace 0, false and the empty string, because they test for any falsy value.

quiz.question: Your team wants to show a product list sorted by price without changing the array held in state. What is the best choice?
options: products.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)
products.reverse().sort()
products.toSorted((a, b) => a.price - b.price)
Object.groupBy(products, p => p.price)
quiz.explanation: toSorted (ES2023) returns a new sorted array and leaves the original untouched. sort and reverse mutate in place, which breaks state that other code relies on.

quiz.question: Which statement about a proposal at TC39 stage 3 is correct?
options: It is part of the published standard and safe everywhere
It is an idea with no specification text yet
It was rejected and will be removed
The design is complete and engines are implementing it, but you must still check support before relying on it
quiz.explanation: Stage 3 means the specification is ready and implementations are under way. It reaches stage 4 after tests and two shipping implementations, then joins the next yearly edition.

quiz.question: Why does code sometimes need Object.groupBy results to be read with Object.entries rather than result.hasOwnProperty?
options: The result is a null-prototype object, so it has no inherited methods such as hasOwnProperty
Object.groupBy returns an array of arrays
The result is frozen
Object.groupBy only works with Map keys
quiz.explanation: Object.groupBy creates an object with a null prototype so a group called "toString" cannot clash with inherited properties. Use Object.hasOwn, Object.keys or Object.entries with it.

lessons.title: Regular expressions in practice
lessons.summaryHtml:
A regular expression (regex) is a small pattern language for finding, checking and rewriting text: “six digits that do not start with 0”, “every amount after a ₹ sign”, “a date written as dd/mm/yyyy”. In JavaScript a regex is a RegExp object, written as a literal such as /^[1-9]\d{5}$/ or built with new RegExp().

You learn the building blocks (character classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups and lookarounds), the flags g i m s u y d v, and the string methods that use them: test, match, matchAll, replace with a function, and split. You also learn to validate email, mobile numbers and PIN codes sensibly, and when a parser or a built-in API beats a regex.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A regular expression is a pattern for text. Instead of writing a loop that checks “is this character a digit? and the next one? and are there exactly six?”, you write /^\d{6}$/ and let the regex engine do the checking. Think of it as a very precise “find” box: the same pattern can test a value (is it valid?), find parts of a text (every order id in a log), extract pieces (the day, month and year of a date) and replace them (reformat or redact).

Regex has a reputation for being unreadable. That comes from long patterns written in one line with no explanation. Small, anchored, well-named patterns are easy to read, and they are one of the most practical skills you can have: form validation, log analysis, data cleaning, search and replace in VS Code, and many interview questions all use them.

Why it matters

Ralfiz receives lead lists from partners as pasted text: names, emails, phone numbers in five different formats (+91 98470 12345, 098470-12345, 9847012345) and PIN codes with random spaces. Before the leads go into the CRM, someone has to clean, validate and normalise every row. With regex, that is a few lines per field. Without it, it is hundreds of lines of character-by-character checks.

The flip side: regex is also a common source of bugs and even outages. A pattern without anchors accepts garbage. A g flag on a shared regex makes every second check fail. A badly nested pattern can freeze a server when someone sends a crafted string. This lesson covers both sides.

How it works

Anatomy of a pattern

You create a regex with a literal, /pattern/flags, when you know the pattern while writing the code. Use the constructor, new RegExp(string, flags), when the pattern comes from data, such as a search box. In a string, backslashes must be doubled: new RegExp('\\d+') equals /\d+/.

PieceMeaningExample
abcLiteral characters/ORD-/ finds “ORD-”
.Any character except a line break/a.c/ matches abc, a-c
\d \w \sDigit, word character (letter, digit, _), whitespace/\d\d/ two digits
\D \W \SThe opposite of each/\S+/ a run of non-spaces
[abc] [a-z] [^0-9]One character from a set, a range, or not in a set/[6-9]/ one of 6, 7, 8, 9
* + ? {n} {n,m}0 or more, 1 or more, optional, exactly n, n to m/\d{2,3}/
^ $ \bStart, end, word boundary (positions, not characters)/^\d+$/ only digits
a|bEither side/paid|refunded/

Special characters (. * + ? ^ $ { } ( ) | [ ] \ /) must be escaped with a backslash to match literally: /\$\d+/ matches “$20”. When a pattern is built from user input, escape the input first, or a user who searches for “C++” gets a syntax error. ES2025 added RegExp.escape() for this; it reached browsers and Node later than other ES2025 features, so check MDN before relying on it and keep a small escape function as a fallback.

Quantifiers are greedy: they take as much as they can, then give back characters until the rest of the pattern matches. Adding ? makes them lazy: they take as little as possible. That is the difference between matching one bold tag and everything from the first tag to the last one.

Try it: Anchors, classes and quantifiers

JavaScript

// Indian PIN code: 6 digits, first digit 1-9
const pin = /^[1-9]\d{5}$/;
for (const s of ['673001', '073001', '67300', '6730011', 'PIN 673001']) {
  console.log(s.padEnd(11), pin.test(s));
}

// Greedy .* grabs as much as possible; .*? as little as possible
const html = '<b>Sale</b> ends <b>today</b>';
console.log('greedy:', html.match(/<b>.*<\/b>/)[0]);
console.log('lazy:  ', html.match(/<b>.*?<\/b>/)[0]);

// \b is a word boundary: "cat" as a whole word only
console.log('cat catalog concat cat.'.match(/\bcat\b/g));

// Character classes and ranges
console.log('SKU: PEN-01, bag-2, LAMP-003'.match(/[A-Z]+-\d{2,3}/g));
console.log('Hex colour?', /^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i.test('#B45309'));

// Building a regex from user input: escape special characters first
const word = 'price (INR)';
const escaped = word.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
const re = new RegExp(escaped, 'i');
console.log(re.source, re.test('Total PRICE (inr): 450'));

Remove the ^ or $ from the PIN pattern and run again: some bad values start passing.

Flags

Flags go after the closing slash (or as the second constructor argument) and change how the whole pattern behaves:

FlagNameEffect
gglobalFind all matches; makes test/exec stateful through lastIndex
iignoreCaseCase-insensitive
mmultiline^ and $ match at the start and end of every line
sdotAll. also matches line breaks
uunicodeWorks with code points, enables \p{…}, stricter syntax
vunicodeSets (ES2024)Everything u does, plus set operations in classes and emoji properties; cannot be combined with u
ystickyMatch only exactly at lastIndex (useful for tokenisers)
dhasIndicesAdds indices with start and end positions of each group

The flag that causes the most bugs is g. A global regex remembers where the last match ended in re.lastIndex, and test() and exec() continue from there. If you keep one global regex in a constant and call test() on each form field, results alternate between true and false. For yes/no checks, do not use g. Use u or v whenever your text may contain emoji or other characters outside the basic range, so that . matches a whole code point rather than half of a surrogate pair. (An emoji built from several code points still needs \p{RGI_Emoji} with v.)

Try it: Flags and the lastIndex trap

JavaScript

const log = 'Order ORD-1001 paid\norder ord-1002 pending\nORDER ORD-1003 paid';

console.log('g+i:', log.match(/ord-\d+/gi));
console.log('no m:', log.match(/^order/gi)?.length ?? 0);
console.log('m:   ', log.match(/^order/gim).length);    // ^ at every line
console.log('no s:', /paid.order/i.test(log));
console.log('s:   ', /paid.order/is.test(log));           // . matches \n

// g makes a regex stateful: test() continues from lastIndex
const paid = /paid/g;
console.log(paid.test(log), paid.lastIndex);
console.log(paid.test(log), paid.lastIndex);
console.log(paid.test(log), paid.lastIndex);   // false, resets to 0

// y (sticky) must match exactly at lastIndex
const digits = /\d+/y;
digits.lastIndex = 4;
console.log('sticky at 4:', digits.exec('ORD-1001')?.[0]);
digits.lastIndex = 2;
console.log('sticky at 2:', digits.exec('ORD-1001')?.[0]);

// d gives start/end indices for each group
const m = /ORD-(?<num>\d+)/d.exec('Paid: ORD-1001');
console.log('num at', m.indices.groups.num);

// u / v: count by code points, not UTF-16 units
console.log('😀'.length, '😀'.match(/./gu).length);

Each flag changes how the same pattern behaves. Look at how lastIndex moves after each test() on a g regex.

Groups and the string methods

Parentheses create a capturing group. Groups are numbered from 1 by their opening parenthesis. Give them names with (?<name>…) and you read them from match.groups.name, which survives later edits to the pattern much better than match[3]. Use (?:…) when you need grouping for | or a quantifier but do not need to capture. Inside the pattern, \1 or \k<name> refers back to what a group already matched.

MethodReturnsUse it for
re.test(str)true / falseValidation
str.match(re)First match with groups, or all matched strings with g, or nullExtracting one thing, or a quick list
str.matchAll(re)An iterator of full match objects (needs g)Every match with its groups and index
str.replace(re, x)A new stringReformatting, redacting; x can be a function
str.replaceAll(re, x)A new string (needs g)Makes “replace every match” explicit
str.split(re)An arraySplitting on several separators
str.search(re)Index or -1Where the first match starts

In a replacement string, $1, $<name> and $& (the whole match) insert captured text. When the new text needs logic, pass a function: it receives the match, then each group, then the index, and whatever it returns is inserted. Note that match with g returns only strings; if you need groups for every match, use matchAll.

Try it: Groups, named groups and replace with a function

JavaScript

const line = 'INV-2026-0042 | 28/09/2026 | ₹12,450.00 | Kochi';
const invoice =
  /^INV-(?<year>\d{4})-(?<seq>\d{4}) \| (?<date>[\d/]+) \| ₹(?<amount>[\d,.]+)/;

const { year, seq, date, amount } = line.match(invoice).groups;
console.log({ year, seq, date, amount: Number(amount.replaceAll(',', '')) });

// Named references in the replacement string
const iso = '28/09/2026'.replace(
  /(?<d>\d{2})\/(?<m>\d{2})\/(?<y>\d{4})/,
  '$<y>-$<m>-$<d>',
);
console.log('ISO date:', iso);

// A replacer function runs once per match
const note = 'Pen x2 @20, Bag x1 @1250';
const pretty = note.replace(/@(\d+)/g, (match, n) =>
  `@ ₹${Number(n).toLocaleString('en-IN')}`);
console.log(pretty);

// matchAll: every match with its groups and index
const item = /(?<name>\w+) x(?<qty>\d+) @(?<price>\d+)/g;
for (const m of note.matchAll(item)) {
  const { name, qty, price } = m.groups;
  console.log(name.padEnd(4), qty * price, 'at index', m.index);
}

// Backreference \1: remove doubled words
console.log('the the price is is final'.replace(/\b(\w+) \1\b/g, '$1'));

// (?:…) groups without capturing; split with a regex
console.log('red, green;blue |  pink'.split(/\s*(?:,|;|\|)\s*/));

Named groups make the code read like the data. The replacer function receives the match and each group.

Lookarounds

A lookaround checks the text next to the current position without consuming it, so it is not part of the match. There are four:

  • (?=…) lookahead: followed by …
  • (?!…) negative lookahead: not followed by …
  • (?<=…) lookbehind: preceded by …
  • (?<!…) negative lookbehind: not preceded by …

Lookbehind is how you extract “the digits after ₹” without the symbol. Several lookaheads at the start of a pattern act like a list of independent rules, all checked from the same position; that is the classic “at least one lowercase, one uppercase, one digit” password pattern. It works, but for passwords, length matters more than character mix, and a readable check with a clear message for each rule is kinder to users than one clever regex.

Try it: Lookarounds

JavaScript

// Lookbehind: amounts that follow a ₹ sign (the ₹ is not in the match)
console.log('Pen ₹20, 3 pcs, Bag ₹1250'.match(/(?<=₹)\d+/g));

// Negative lookbehind: numbers NOT after a ₹ sign
console.log('Pen ₹20, 3 pcs, Bag ₹1250'.match(/(?<![₹\d])\d+/g));

// Lookahead: several independent rules at the same start position
const rules = /^(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d).{8,}$/;
for (const p of ['ralfiz2026', 'Ralfiz2026', 'Rz1', 'RALFIZacademy']) {
  console.log(p.padEnd(14), rules.test(p));
}

// Negative lookahead: SKUs not followed by -OLD
console.log('PEN-01 BAG-02-OLD LAMP-03'.match(/\b[A-Z]+-\d+\b(?!-OLD)/g));

// Western thousands separators with a lookahead ...
console.log('1234567'.replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, ','));
// ... but Intl knows Indian grouping and currency
console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN').format(1234567));

Lookarounds check what is next to the match without including it. The last line shows why Intl beats a regex for number formatting.

Validating email, mobile numbers and PIN codes sensibly

Good validation is a two-step process: normalise, then check a simple anchored pattern. Trim spaces, lowercase emails, and strip spaces and dashes from phone numbers and PIN codes. Then store the normalised value, so the database never holds five formats of the same number.

  • Email: the full standard allows forms that no simple regex handles, and the only real proof is a confirmation email. Check the basic shape, /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/, use <input type="email"> in forms, and send a verification link.
  • Indian mobile: ten digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9, with an optional +91 or 0: /^(?:\+91|0)?[6-9]\d{9}$/ after removing spaces and dashes. For international numbers, use a phone library rather than your own regex.
  • PIN code: six digits, first digit 1 to 9: /^[1-9]\d{5}$/. This checks the format only; whether the PIN exists needs a lookup.

Also limit the input length before running any pattern. That protects you from catastrophic backtracking: a pattern with nested quantifiers, such as /^(a+)+$/, can take exponential time on input like “aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!” because the engine tries every way of splitting the a’s between the inner and outer loop. On a server that means one request can block the event loop. Avoid nested or overlapping quantifiers, keep patterns anchored, and cap input length.

Try it: Validating sensibly

JavaScript

const patterns = {
  email: /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/,     // loose on purpose
  mobile: /^(?:\+91|0)?[6-9]\d{9}$/,       // Indian mobile
  pin: /^[1-9]\d{5}$/,                     // Indian PIN code
};

const normalise = (field, raw) =>
  field === 'email' ? raw.trim().toLowerCase() : raw.replace(/[\s-]/g, '');

function validate(field, raw) {
  const value = normalise(field, raw);
  return { field, raw, value, valid: patterns[field].test(value) };
}

console.table([
  validate('email', ' Anu@Ralfiz.dev '),
  validate('email', 'anu@ralfiz'),
  validate('mobile', '+91 98470 12345'),
  validate('mobile', '098470-12345'),
  validate('mobile', '58470 12345'),
  validate('pin', '673 001'),
  validate('pin', '073001'),
]);

// Reject absurd input before any regex runs
const MAX = 254;
const tooLong = 'a'.repeat(300) + '@ralfiz.dev';
console.log('long email:', tooLong.length <= MAX && patterns.email.test(tooLong));

Normalise first (trim, remove spaces and dashes), then validate a simple, anchored pattern.

When not to use regex

TaskUse instead
Parse HTML or XMLDOMParser or the DOM, then textContent
Read parts of a URL or query stringnew URL() and URLSearchParams
Parse JSONJSON.parse
Parse or compare datesDate with Intl (Temporal as it rolls out)
CSV with quoted fieldsA CSV parser library
Format numbers and currencyIntl.NumberFormat
Simple contains / starts withincludes, startsWith, endsWith

The rule of thumb: regex is great for flat patterns. Anything nested (HTML, JSON, arithmetic with brackets) needs a real parser.

Example: a regex tester for Ralfiz Academy

Students keep asking “why doesn’t my pattern match?”. This tool answers that visually.

  1. The pattern and flags come from the page, so the regex is built with new RegExp(input.value, flags) inside try/catch. An invalid pattern shows the engine’s message in a role="alert" paragraph and marks the input aria-invalid.
  2. With g on, matchAll returns every match with index and groups. Empty matches (for example from \b alone) are skipped and the list is capped at 200, so a pattern like .* cannot flood the page.
  3. The highlight is built from plain text slices and <mark> elements whose textContent is set. The test text is never passed to innerHTML, so typing <img onerror=…> just shows the characters.
  4. Presets are stored as regex literals; clicking one copies re.source and re.flags into the form.

Try the presets, toggle g off to see only the first match, and type an unclosed ( to see the error state.

JavaScript

const presets = [
  { name: 'Amounts', re: /₹(?<amount>\d+(?:,\d+)*(?:\.\d{2})?)/g },
  { name: 'Email', re: /[^\s@,]+@[^\s@,]+\.[a-z]{2,}/gi },
  { name: 'PIN code', re: /\b[1-9]\d{5}\b/g },
  { name: 'Mobile', re: /(?:\+91[\s-]?)?[6-9]\d{4}[\s-]?\d{5}/g },
  { name: 'Order id', re: /ORD-(?<num>\d+)/g },
];
const FLAGS = ['g', 'i', 'm', 's', 'u'];
const $ = sel => document.querySelector(sel);
const input = $('#pattern');
const text = $('#text');
let flags = new Set(['g']);

for (const p of presets) {
  const b = document.createElement('button');
  b.type = 'button';
  b.textContent = p.name;
  b.addEventListener('click', () => {
    input.value = p.re.source;
    flags = new Set(p.re.flags);
    render();
  });
  $('#presets').append(b);
}
for (const f of FLAGS) {
  const b = document.createElement('button');
  b.type = 'button';
  b.textContent = f;
  b.dataset.flag = f;
  b.addEventListener('click', () => {
    flags.has(f) ? flags.delete(f) : flags.add(f);
    render();
  });
  $('#flags').append(b);
}

function findMatches(re) {
  if (!re.global) {
    const m = re.exec(text.value);
    return m ? [m] : [];
  }
  return [...text.value.matchAll(re)].filter(m => m[0] !== '').slice(0, 200);
}

function render() {
  for (const b of $('#flags').children) {
    b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(flags.has(b.dataset.flag)));
  }
  let re;
  try {
    re = new RegExp(input.value, [...flags].join(''));
    $('#error').textContent = '';
    input.removeAttribute('aria-invalid');
  } catch (err) {
    $('#error').textContent = err.message;
    input.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    return;
  }
  const matches = input.value ? findMatches(re) : [];
  const parts = [];
  let pos = 0;
  for (const m of matches) {
    parts.push(text.value.slice(pos, m.index));
    const mark = document.createElement('mark');
    mark.textContent = m[0];
    parts.push(mark);
    pos = m.index + m[0].length;
  }
  parts.push(text.value.slice(pos));
  $('#preview').replaceChildren(...parts);
  $('#count').textContent = `${matches.length} match${matches.length === 1 ? '' : 'es'}`;

  $('#list').replaceChildren(...matches.map(m => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    const code = document.createElement('code');
    code.textContent = m[0];
    const groups = m.groups
      ? Object.entries(m.groups).map(([k, v]) => `${k} = ${v}`).join(', ')
      : '';
    li.append(code, ` at ${m.index}${groups ? ' · ' + groups : ''}`);
    return li;
  }));
  return matches.length;
}

input.addEventListener('input', render);
text.addEventListener('input', render);
input.value = presets[0].re.source;
flags = new Set(presets[0].re.flags);
console.log(`/${input.value}/${[...flags].join('')} →`, render(), 'matches');

Common mistakes

1. Forgetting anchors in validation.

/\d{6}/.test('PIN: 6730019');    // true: six digits found somewhere
/^[1-9]\d{5}$/.test('6730019');  // false: the whole value must match

2. Sharing a global regex for test().

const DIGITS = /^\d+$/g;              // wrong: g makes it stateful
fields.every(f => DIGITS.test(f));     // alternates true/false
const DIGITS_OK = /^\d+$/;            // right: no g for yes/no checks

3. Building a regex from raw user input.

new RegExp(search);                    // 'C++' throws a SyntaxError
const escape = s => s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
new RegExp(escape(search), 'i');       // or RegExp.escape where supported

4. Using match with g when you need groups.

text.match(/ORD-(\d+)/g);   // ['ORD-1001', 'ORD-1002']: groups are lost
[...text.matchAll(/ORD-(?<num>\d+)/g)].map(m => m.groups.num);

5. Forgetting that replace with a string pattern replaces once.

'a-b-c'.replace('-', ' ');     // 'a b-c'
'a-b-c'.replaceAll('-', ' ');  // 'a b c'
'a-b-c'.replace(/-/g, ' ');    // 'a b c'

6. Regex for dates, HTML or money formatting. Use Date/Intl, DOMParser and Intl.NumberFormat; they handle the edge cases you would miss.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Be ready to explain greedy vs lazy with the bold-tag example, and why a g regex changes lastIndex.
  • A common task: “extract all hashtags” (/#(\w+)/g with matchAll) or “convert camelCase to kebab-case” (str.replace(/[A-Z]/g, c => '-' + c.toLowerCase())).
  • Mention ReDoS when you talk about validating input on a server. It shows you think about security and performance.
  • In VS Code, the search box has a regex toggle (Alt+R on Windows/Linux) and replacement supports $1. Renaming across a project with a capture group is a real daily skill.
  • Name your patterns: const INDIAN_PIN = /^[1-9]\d{5}$/; is self-documenting. For long patterns, build them from smaller named pieces or add a comment for each part.

  • B 531
  • C 450+81
  • D 450+81+2

Answers

  1. B. $1, $2 and $3 refer to the three capturing groups (year, month, day), so the replacement rebuilds the string as day/month/year.
  2. D. The g flag makes test() start at lastIndex. The first call matches and sets lastIndex to 1; the second finds nothing after index 1, returns false and resets lastIndex to 0; the third matches again.
  3. A. .+ is greedy: it runs to the end and backs off only to the last >, so it matches the whole 9-character string. .+? is lazy and stops at the first >, matching <b>.
  4. C. The lookbehind (?<=₹) requires a ₹ before the digits but does not include it in the match. The 2 has no ₹ before it, so it is skipped. join builds a string; nothing adds the numbers.

terms.definition: A pattern that describes a set of strings, used to test, find, extract or replace text.
A set of allowed characters in square brackets, such as [0-9] or [^@\s], or a shorthand such as \d, \w or \s.
How many times the previous item may repeat: *, +, ?, {n} or {n,m}. Greedy by default; add ? to make it lazy.
A position rather than a character: ^ (start), $ (end) and \b (word boundary).
Parentheses that remember what they matched, by number ($1) or by name with (?<name>…).
A zero-width check for what comes after (?=…) or before (?<=…) the current position, without consuming it.
Exponential slow-down caused by nested or overlapping quantifiers such as (a+)+ on input that almost matches (ReDoS).

lessons.examTip: Anchor validation patterns with ^ and $. Without anchors, /\d{6}/ happily “validates” abc1234567xyz because it only needs to find six digits somewhere.

quiz.question: A form checks a PIN code with /\d{6}/.test(value). Which input is wrongly accepted?
options: abc
quiz.explanation: Without ^ and $ the pattern only has to find six digits somewhere in the string, so any text containing six digits in a row passes. Use /^[1-9]\d{5}$/.

quiz.question: You call re.test() in a loop with the same /…/g regex and every second call returns false. Why?
options: The g flag makes the regex case-sensitive
A regex with g or y stores lastIndex and the next search starts from there
test() only works once per regex
The loop runs too fast for the regex engine
quiz.explanation: Global and sticky regexes are stateful: after a match, lastIndex points past it. Remove g for a yes/no check, or reset lastIndex to 0.

quiz.question: Which task should NOT be solved with a regular expression?
options: Extracting every ORD-1234 order id from a log line
Checking that a PIN code has six digits
Swapping dd/mm/yyyy to yyyy-mm-dd
Reading the text of every link in an HTML page
quiz.explanation: HTML is nested and irregular; parse it with DOMParser (or the DOM itself) and read textContent. The other three are flat patterns that suit regex well.

quiz.question: What does "a1b22".replace(/\d+/g, n => n * 2) return?
options: "aNaNbNaN"
quiz.explanation: With g, the replacer function runs for every match. Each match arrives as a string ("1", "22"), and * converts it to a number, so the results are 2 and 44.

lessons.title: Clean code and design patterns
lessons.summaryHtml:
Clean code is code the next person (often you, six months later) can read, change and test without fear. It comes from a few habits: names that explain intent, small functions that do one thing, a pure core of business logic with the messy input and output pushed to an outer shell, and a clear strategy for errors.

Design patterns are named solutions to problems that keep coming back. In JavaScript the most useful ones are small: the module and factory patterns for private state, observer (pub/sub, an event emitter) for “tell everyone who cares”, strategy for swappable rules, and dependency injection by passing collaborators in as parameters. The lab refactors a real messy checkout script without changing what it prints.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Code is read far more often than it is written. Clean code is not about clever tricks or following rules for their own sake; it is about making the next change cheap and safe. When a shop owner asks “can we add a festive discount?”, clean code lets you answer “yes, one new function, tested, live today” instead of “let me see what breaks”.

Design patterns are the vocabulary of that work. When a colleague says “make shipping a strategy” or “the cart should emit an event and the badge subscribes”, everyone knows the shape of the solution without drawing it. You do not need the full catalogue of patterns from 1990s object-oriented books. JavaScript has functions as values, closures and modules, so the useful patterns are small, and many are just a function that takes or returns another function.

Why it matters

Every agency has the script that “works, but nobody wants to touch it”: a 200-line go() function with variables called t, d and tmp2, where pricing, shipping, email and logging are tangled together. A new requirement arrives, someone adds another if, and a bug appears in a part they did not touch. Without tests, nobody notices until a customer does.

Clean structure fixes three business problems at once: speed of change (new rules are one entry in a map), confidence (a pure core can be unit-tested, which is the next lesson) and onboarding (a new developer can read priceOrder and understand the rules). Interviewers test this directly with “refactor this function” and “how would you structure this feature?” questions.

How it works

Names, small functions and single responsibility

A good name removes the need for a comment. Some rules that work:

Instead ofWriteWhy
d, data, tmporders, unpaidInvoicesSay what it holds
flag, checkisPaid, hasStock, canCheckoutBooleans read as questions
calc(), process()priceOrder(), sendReceipt()Functions are verbs with an object
0.18, 999GST_RATE, FREE_SHIPPING_FROMNo magic numbers
price (in paise?)priceInPaise, timeoutMsUnits in the name
save(order, true)save(order, { notify: true }) or saveAndNotify(order)A bare boolean argument says nothing at the call site

Single responsibility means a function or module has one reason to change. In a checkout, the pricing rules change when the business changes prices; the receipt format changes when design changes; the email changes when marketing changes. If one function does all three, every change risks the other two. Small functions also compose: orderTotal becomes a readable pipeline of subtotal, a discount and addGst. When you refactor, change structure but not behaviour, and prove it: here a console.assert compares old and new; in real projects, tests do this.

Try it: Naming and small functions: before and after

JavaScript

// BEFORE: short names, magic numbers, one function does everything
function calc(d, m) {
  let t = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < d.length; i++) {
    if (d[i].st != 'cancelled') t += d[i].p * d[i].q;
  }
  if (m == 1) t = t * 0.9;
  if (m == 2) t = t - 100;
  return Math.round(t * 1.18 * 100) / 100;
}

// AFTER: each function does one thing and its name says what
const GST_RATE = 0.18;
const isActive = line => line.status !== 'cancelled';
const lineTotal = line => line.price * line.qty;
const subtotal = lines => lines.filter(isActive).reduce((sum, l) => sum + lineTotal(l), 0);
const discounts = {
  none: amount => amount,
  tenPercent: amount => amount * 0.9,
  flat100: amount => amount - 100,
};
const addGst = amount => Math.round(amount * (1 + GST_RATE) * 100) / 100;

function orderTotal(lines, discount = 'none') {
  return addGst(discounts[discount](subtotal(lines)));
}

const lines = [
  { name: 'Pen', price: 20, qty: 5, status: 'ok' },
  { name: 'Bag', price: 1250, qty: 1, status: 'ok' },
  { name: 'Lamp', price: 2499, qty: 1, status: 'cancelled' },
];
const old = lines.map(l => ({ p: l.price, q: l.qty, st: l.status }));

console.log('before:', calc(old, 0), calc(old, 1), calc(old, 2));
console.log('after: ', orderTotal(lines), orderTotal(lines, 'tenPercent'),
  orderTotal(lines, 'flat100'));
console.assert(calc(old, 1) === orderTotal(lines, 'tenPercent'), 'totals differ');

Both versions give the same totals. Which one could you change safely on a Friday evening? Try adding a “flat50” discount to each.

Pure core, impure shell, and an error strategy

A pure function depends only on its arguments and only returns a value: no DOM, no network, no console, no Date.now(), no Math.random(), no mutation of its inputs. Pure functions are easy to test (call them, compare the result), easy to reuse (the same pricing code on the server and in the browser) and easy to reason about.

Of course a program must do I/O at some point. The trick, often called functional core, imperative shell, is to push all side effects to a thin outer layer. The shell reads input (form fields, a request, a file), calls the pure core, and performs output (renders, saves, sends). Most of your logic, and most of your bugs, then live in code you can test without a browser.

Errors need a strategy too, decided once for the project:

  • Validate at the boundaries: data coming from users, APIs and storage is checked in the shell before it reaches the core.
  • Expected failures return a result: an invalid coupon is not exceptional; { ok: false, error } forces the caller to handle it.
  • Bugs and impossible states throw: a TypeError when items is not an array. Add context with { cause } as you rethrow.
  • Catch once, at the top: a single handler per request, per event handler or per job logs the error and shows a friendly message. Never write an empty catch {}.

Try it: Pure core, impure shell and an error strategy

JavaScript

// ---- pure core: data in, data out ----
function priceCart(items, { taxRate, coupon = null }) {
  if (!Array.isArray(items)) throw new TypeError('items must be an array');
  const subtotal = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  const discount = coupon
    ? Math.min((subtotal * coupon.percent) / 100, coupon.max)
    : 0;
  const tax = Math.round((subtotal - discount) * taxRate * 100) / 100;
  return { subtotal, discount, tax, total: subtotal - discount + tax };
}

// Expected failure: return a result object instead of throwing
function parseCoupon(code) {
  const match = /^SAVE(\d{1,2})$/.exec(code.trim().toUpperCase());
  if (!match) return { ok: false, error: `Unknown coupon "${code}"` };
  return { ok: true, value: { percent: Number(match[1]), max: 500 } };
}

// ---- impure shell: input, output, logging ----
function checkout(items, code) {
  const coupon = parseCoupon(code);
  if (!coupon.ok) console.warn(coupon.error, '- continuing without it');
  const bill = priceCart(items, {
    taxRate: 0.18,
    coupon: coupon.ok ? coupon.value : null,
  });
  console.log(bill);
}

const items = [{ price: 1250, qty: 2 }, { price: 20, qty: 5 }];
checkout(items, 'save10');
checkout(items, 'HALFPRICE');

// One top-level handler for real bugs, with context in cause
try {
  checkout({ price: 10 }, 'SAVE5');
} catch (err) {
  const wrapped = new Error('Checkout failed', { cause: err });
  console.error(wrapped.message, '←', wrapped.cause.message);
}

priceCart never logs or reads the clock, so it is trivial to test. Expected problems (a bad coupon) return a result; bugs (bad input) throw and are caught once, at the top.

The module pattern and factory functions

Before ES modules, JavaScript had no private scope for a file, so developers used an IIFE (immediately invoked function expression) that returned only the public parts. Variables inside the function stayed private thanks to closures. ES modules replaced this: anything you do not export is private to the file.

// Old module pattern (you will meet it in legacy code)
const CartModule = (function () {
  const items = [];                      // private
  return {
    add: item => items.push(item),
    count: () => items.length,
  };
})();

// Today: an ES module file, cart.js
const items = [];                        // private to the module
export const add = item => items.push(item);
export const count = () => items.length;

A module holds one instance. When you need many (one cart per user, one store per widget), use a factory function: createCart() returns a new object each time, with private state in its closure. Factories are a lightweight alternative to classes; use a class when you want instanceof, inheritance or many methods shared on a prototype, and a factory when you want simple private state and no this problems.

Observer: pub/sub and event emitters

The observer pattern decouples “something happened” from “what should react”. The cart emits cart:changed; the badge, the analytics tracker and the “free delivery” tip each subscribe. The cart does not import any of them, so you can add or remove reactions without touching it. You already use this pattern: addEventListener is the DOM’s version, and Node’s EventEmitter is the server’s.

A good emitter has three details right: on returns an unsubscribe function (so components can clean up and avoid memory leaks), emit loops over a copy of the handlers (so a handler can unsubscribe during the loop), and once removes itself. In the browser and in Node, EventTarget with CustomEvent gives you a standard emitter for free.

Try it: Observer: a tiny event emitter

JavaScript

class Emitter {
  #handlers = new Map();

  on(event, fn) {
    if (!this.#handlers.has(event)) this.#handlers.set(event, new Set());
    this.#handlers.get(event).add(fn);
    return () => this.off(event, fn);           // unsubscribe function
  }
  off(event, fn) {
    this.#handlers.get(event)?.delete(fn);
  }
  once(event, fn) {
    const off = this.on(event, payload => { off(); fn(payload); });
    return off;
  }
  emit(event, payload) {
    // copy first, so handlers can unsubscribe while we loop
    for (const fn of [...(this.#handlers.get(event) ?? [])]) fn(payload);
  }
}

function createCart(events) {
  const items = [];
  return {
    add(item) {
      items.push(item);
      events.emit('cart:changed', { count: items.length, item });
    },
  };
}

const events = new Emitter();
const cart = createCart(events);

const stopBadge = events.on('cart:changed', ({ count }) =>
  console.log(`badge shows ${count}`));
events.on('cart:changed', ({ item }) =>
  console.log(`analytics: add_to_cart ${item.sku}`));
events.once('cart:changed', () => console.log('first item: show free-delivery tip'));

cart.add({ sku: 'PEN' });
cart.add({ sku: 'BAG' });
stopBadge();                     // the badge component was removed
cart.add({ sku: 'LAMP' });

// The platform has one built in: EventTarget + CustomEvent
const bus = new EventTarget();
bus.addEventListener('order:placed', e => console.log('EventTarget got', e.detail.id));
bus.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('order:placed', { detail: { id: 'ORD-1001' } }));

The cart does not know who listens. Subscribers can be added and removed freely; once() removes itself after one call.

Strategy, factory and dependency injection

The strategy pattern replaces a growing if/else or switch with a map of interchangeable functions that share one signature. Shipping rules, tax rules per product type, sort orders in a table and payment providers are all strategies. Adding a rule means adding an entry; the code that calls strategies[name](input) never changes. Always handle an unknown name explicitly.

Dependency injection sounds like a framework feature, but in JavaScript it is simply this: do not reach out for collaborators, receive them as parameters. A service that calls new Date(), fetch and localStorage directly can only be tested in a real environment at a real time. A service created with createOrderService({ clock, nextId, http }) can be given a fixed clock and a fake HTTP client in tests, a real one in production and a logging one while debugging. Combine it with a factory and you have most of what large “DI containers” do, with no library.

Try it: Strategy, factory and dependency injection

JavaScript

// Strategy: interchangeable rules, chosen by name at run time
const shippingStrategies = {
  standard: ({ subtotal }) => (subtotal >= 999 ? 0 : 49),
  express: ({ weightKg }) => 99 + Math.ceil(weightKg) * 20,
  pickup: () => 0,
};

// Factory + dependency injection by parameters
function createOrderService({ clock, nextId, shipping = shippingStrategies }) {
  return {
    place(cart, method) {
      const cost = shipping[method];
      if (!cost) throw new Error(`Unknown shipping method: ${method}`);
      return {
        id: nextId(),
        placedAt: clock().toISOString(),
        shipping: cost(cart),
      };
    },
  };
}

const cart = { subtotal: 1250, weightKg: 1.4 };

// Test setup: fixed clock and predictable ids, so output never changes
let n = 0;
const testService = createOrderService({
  clock: () => new Date('2026-09-28T10:00:00Z'),
  nextId: () => `TEST-${++n}`,
});
console.log(testService.place(cart, 'standard'));
console.log(testService.place(cart, 'express'));

// Production setup: the real clock and random ids
const liveService = createOrderService({
  clock: () => new Date(),
  nextId: () => crypto.randomUUID(),
});
const live = liveService.place(cart, 'pickup');
console.log('live id looks like a UUID:', /^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/.test(live.id));

// Adding a rule = adding an entry, nothing else changes
const festive = createOrderService({
  clock: () => new Date(),
  nextId: () => 'F-1',
  shipping: { ...shippingStrategies, festive: () => 0 },
});
console.log('festive shipping:', festive.place(cart, 'festive').shipping);

The service gets its clock, id generator and shipping rules as parameters. Production and test use the same code with different collaborators.

Example: refactoring a messy checkout script

The lab starts from a checkout script written in a hurry before a sale. It works, but pricing, shipping, coupons, stock warnings, email and logging all live in one go(d) function with var, magic numbers and string comparisons. The goal is to change its structure without changing a single character of its output.

  1. Pin the behaviour: run the old script and save its output. That is your safety net (the next lesson replaces it with real tests).
  2. Rename: t becomes subtotal, w becomes weightKg, 0.18 becomes GST_RATE. Run again and compare.
  3. Extract pure functions: subtotal(items), parseCoupon(code) returning a result object, priceOrder(order) returning all the numbers, and formatReceipt(order, pricing) returning lines of text.
  4. Replace the shipping if/else with a strategy map, and make an unknown method a thrown error instead of silently free delivery.
  5. Replace direct side effects with events: the core emits stock:low and order:placed; the shell subscribes the console warning, the fake email sender and the analytics log.
  6. Move the core to its own module (checkout.js) and keep index.js as the shell.

The live page shows the same architecture in a UI: price(state) is pure, delivery options are strategies, and four independent subscribers render the lines, the delivery buttons, the totals and the event log from one store.

Try it: Ralfiz Store checkout

HTML

<main class="shop">
  <section class="panel">
    <h1>Your cart</h1>
    <ul id="lines" class="lines"></ul>
    <div class="ship" role="group" aria-label="Delivery">
      <span class="label">Delivery</span>
      <div id="ship" class="seg"></div>
    </div>
    <form id="coupon" class="coupon">
      <input id="code" value="SAVE10" aria-label="Coupon code" autocomplete="off"
        placeholder="Coupon, e.g. SAVE10">
      <button>Apply</button>

</main>

CSS
