JavaScript

// ---------- pure core ----------
const TAX_RATE = 0.18;
const shipping = {
  standard: { label: 'Standard', cost: ({ subtotal }) => (subtotal >= 999 ? 0 : 49) },
  express: { label: 'Express', cost: ({ weightKg }) => 99 + Math.ceil(weightKg) * 20 },
  pickup: { label: 'Pickup', cost: () => 0 },
};

function parseCoupon(code) {
  const match = /^SAVE(\d{1,2})$/.exec(code.trim().toUpperCase());
  if (!match) return { ok: false, error: `“${code.trim()}” is not a valid coupon` };
  return { ok: true, value: { code: match[0], percent: Number(match[1]), max: 500 } };
}

function price({ lines, ship, coupon }) {
  const subtotal = lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.price * l.qty, 0);
  const weightKg = lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.kg * l.qty, 0);
  const discount = coupon ? Math.min((subtotal * coupon.percent) / 100, coupon.max) : 0;
  const delivery = shipping[ship].cost({ subtotal, weightKg });
  const tax = Math.round((subtotal - discount) * TAX_RATE * 100) / 100;
  return { subtotal, discount, delivery, tax, total: subtotal - discount + delivery + tax };
}

// ---------- observer: a tiny store ----------
function createStore(initial) {
  let state = initial;
  const subscribers = new Set();
  return {
    get: () => state,
    update(event, change) {
      state = { ...state, ...change(state) };
      for (const fn of subscribers) fn(state, event);
    },
    subscribe(fn) {
      subscribers.add(fn);
      return () => subscribers.delete(fn);
    },
  };
}

// ---------- impure shell: DOM ----------
const store = createStore({
  lines: [
    { sku: 'PEN', name: 'Gel pen set', icon: '🖊️', price: 180, kg: 0.2, qty: 2 },
    { sku: 'BAG', name: 'Laptop bag', icon: '💼', price: 1250, kg: 0.9, qty: 1 },
    { sku: 'LAMP', name: 'Desk lamp', icon: '💡', price: 2499, kg: 1.3, qty: 0 },
  ],
  ship: 'standard',
  coupon: null,
});
const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
const $ = sel => document.querySelector(sel);

function el(tag, props = {}, ...children) {
  const node = Object.assign(document.createElement(tag), props);
  node.append(...children);
  return node;
}

function renderLines({ lines }) {
  $('#lines').replaceChildren(...lines.map(l => el('li', { className: 'line' },
    el('span', { className: 'icon', ariaHidden: 'true' }, l.icon),
    el('div', { className: 'info' }, el('strong', {}, l.name), el('span', {}, inr.format(l.price))),
    el('div', { className: 'stepper' },
      el('button', { type: 'button', ariaLabel: `Remove one ${l.name}` }, '−'),
      el('span', {}, String(l.qty)),
      el('button', { type: 'button', ariaLabel: `Add one ${l.name}` }, '+')),
  )));
  $('#lines').querySelectorAll('.stepper').forEach((box, i) => {
    const [minus, , plus] = box.children;
    minus.dataset.sku = plus.dataset.sku = lines[i].sku;
    minus.dataset.step = '-1';
    plus.dataset.step = '1';
  });
}

function renderShip({ ship }) {
  $('#ship').replaceChildren(...Object.entries(shipping).map(([key, s]) =>
    el('button', { type: 'button', ariaPressed: String(key === ship), value: key }, s.label)));
}

function renderTotals(state) {
  const p = price(state);
  const rows = [
    ['Subtotal', inr.format(p.subtotal)],
    [`Discount${state.coupon ? ' (' + state.coupon.code + ')' : ''}`, '−' + inr.format(p.discount)],
    ['Delivery', p.delivery ? inr.format(p.delivery) : 'Free'],
    ['GST 18%', inr.format(p.tax)],
  ];
  const nodes = rows.flatMap(([k, v]) => [el('dt', {}, k), el('dd', {}, v)]);
  nodes.push(el('dt', { className: 'grand' }, 'Total'),
    el('dd', { className: 'grand' }, inr.format(p.total)));
  $('#totals').replaceChildren(...nodes);
}

const log = [];
function renderLog(state, event) {
  log.unshift(`${event} → ${inr.format(price(state).total)}`);
  $('#log').replaceChildren(...log.slice(0, 6).map(t => el('li', {}, t)));
}

// Each part of the UI is an independent subscriber
store.subscribe(renderLines);
store.subscribe(renderShip);
store.subscribe(renderTotals);
store.subscribe(renderLog);
store.subscribe((state, event) => console.log('[analytics]', event));

$('#lines').addEventListener('click', e => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('button[data-sku]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const step = Number(btn.dataset.step);
  store.update(`qty ${btn.dataset.sku} ${step > 0 ? '+1' : '−1'}`, s => ({
    lines: s.lines.map(l => (l.sku === btn.dataset.sku
      ? { ...l, qty: Math.max(0, l.qty + step) } : l)),
  }));
});
$('#ship').addEventListener('click', e => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('button');
  if (btn) store.update(`ship ${btn.value}`, () => ({ ship: btn.value }));
});
$('#coupon').addEventListener('submit', e => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const result = parseCoupon($('#code').value);
  const msg = $('#couponMsg');
  msg.className = `msg ${result.ok ? 'ok' : 'bad'}`;
  msg.textContent = result.ok ? `${result.value.percent}% off applied (max ₹500)` : result.error;
  store.update(result.ok ? `coupon ${result.value.code}` : 'coupon rejected',
    () => ({ coupon: result.ok ? result.value : null }));
});

store.update('cart loaded', () => ({}));
$('#coupon').requestSubmit();

The pricing is a pure function, the shipping options are strategies and the UI parts are observers of one store. Change quantities, delivery and coupons, and watch the event log.

Common mistakes

1. Swallowing errors.

try { saveOrder(order); } catch {}          // wrong: the failure disappears
try { saveOrder(order); } catch (err) {
  throw new Error(`Could not save ${order.id}`, { cause: err });
}

2. Boolean flag arguments.

render(list, true, false);                          // what do these mean?
render(list, { compact: true, showPrices: false }); // readable at the call site

3. Subscribing without unsubscribing.

store.subscribe(updateBadge);                  // leaks after the widget is gone
const unsubscribe = store.subscribe(updateBadge);
// on teardown:
unsubscribe();

4. Hidden side effects in a “get” function.

function getTotal(cart) {
  cart.items.sort(byPrice);   // surprise: reorders the caller’s cart
  return sum(cart.items);
}
// Right: read-only helpers never mutate their input
const getTotal = cart => sum(cart.items);

5. Patterns for their own sake. A strategy map with one entry, an event bus for two functions that always run together, or a factory that wraps a single constant makes code harder to follow. Introduce a pattern when the second or third variation appears, not before.

6. The utils.js dumping ground. A 900-line helpers file has no single responsibility. Group helpers by domain: money.js, dates.js, validation.js.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the SOLID ideas at a sentence level: single responsibility, open for extension and closed for modification (the strategy map), substitutable implementations, small interfaces, and depending on abstractions (dependency injection).
  • DRY (don’t repeat yourself) is good, but premature abstraction is worse than a little duplication. Many teams follow “AHA”: avoid hasty abstractions; wait until you see the real pattern.
  • In a “refactor this” exercise, talk through the smells, protect behaviour first (a test or a saved output), and make small steps that each keep the program working.
  • Frameworks use these patterns everywhere: React state libraries are observers, Express middleware and Vite plugins are strategies in a list, and testing libraries depend on dependency injection or module mocking. Recognising them makes new tools faster to learn.
  • Formatting and small style issues belong to tools (Prettier, ESLint), not to code review. Save review time for naming, structure and behaviour.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const handlers = [];
const on = fn => {
  handlers.push(fn);
  return () => handlers.splice(handlers.indexOf(fn), 1);
};
const emit = x => handlers.forEach(fn => fn(x));

const off = on(x => console.log('A' + x));
on(x => console.log('B' + x));
emit(1);
off();
emit(2);
  • A 
    A1
B1
A2
B2
  • B 
    A1
B1
B2
  • C 
    A1
B1
  • D 
    B1
A1
B2

Snippet 2. What is logged?

const rates = { standard: 0.18, food: 0.05 };
const tax = (amount, type) => amount * (rates[type] ?? 0);
console.log(tax(100, 'food'), tax(100, 'books'));
  • A 5 0
  • B 5 NaN
  • C 5 undefined
  • D 0.05 0

Snippet 3. What is logged?

function createCounter() {
  let n = 0;
  return { inc: () => ++n, get value() { return n; } };
}
const c = createCounter();
c.inc();
c.inc();
c.n = 10;
console.log(c.value, c.n);
  • A 10 10
  • B 2 undefined
  • C 2 10
  • D NaN 10

Snippet 4. What is logged?

function addItem(cart, item) {
  cart.push(item);
  return cart;
}
const a = [];
const b = addItem(a, 'pen');
console.log(a === b, a.length);
  • A false 0
  • B false 1
  • C true 0
  • D true 1

Answers

  1. B. Handlers run in the order they subscribed. off() removes handler A, so the second emit only reaches B. This is the unsubscribe function pattern.
  2. A. The strategy map gives 0.05 for food. books is not in the map, so rates[type] is undefined and ?? falls back to 0, giving 0 instead of NaN.
  3. C. n lives in the closure, not on the object. c.n = 10 just adds an unrelated property, so value still reads the private n, which is 2. This is the factory / module pattern for private state.
  4. D. addItem is impure: it mutates the array it receives and returns the same reference. A pure version would return [...cart, item] and leave a empty.

terms.definition: A function or module should have one reason to change: pricing rules, formatting and sending email are three separate jobs.
Returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects (no I/O, no mutation of its arguments, no clock or random).
Keep decisions in pure functions and push I/O (DOM, network, console, storage) to a thin outer layer that calls them.
Subscribers register with a subject or event bus and are notified when something happens, without the publisher knowing who they are.
A family of interchangeable functions (for example shipping rules) selected at run time instead of a growing if/else chain.
A function that builds and returns an object, often keeping private state in a closure (createCart, createStore).
Passing collaborators such as a clock, fetch or storage in as parameters so code is testable and easy to reconfigure.

lessons.examTip: When asked “how would you improve this code?” in an interview, name the smell first (long function, magic numbers, boolean flag argument, hidden side effect), then show one small refactor and how you would keep behaviour the same.

quiz.question: A function calculates the order total, writes it to the DOM and sends an analytics event. What is the main problem?
options: It should use a class
It mixes pure calculation with side effects, so the pricing rules cannot be tested or reused without a page
It is too short
It should use var for speed
quiz.explanation: The calculation is business logic; the DOM write and analytics call are I/O. Split them: a pure priceOrder function that returns numbers, and a shell that renders and reports.

quiz.question: Shipping cost depends on the method chosen (standard, express, pickup), and marketing adds new methods every quarter. Which pattern fits best?
options: Singleton
A deeper if/else chain
Strategy: an object that maps each method to its own cost function
Global variables for each rate
quiz.explanation: With a strategy map, adding a method means adding one entry. The code that uses it (strategies[method](cart)) never changes.

quiz.question: Why pass a clock function into createOrderService instead of calling new Date() inside it?
options: new Date() is deprecated
It makes the code run faster
It is required by ES modules
Tests can pass a fixed clock and get the same output every time
quiz.explanation: That is dependency injection by parameter. Production passes () => new Date(); a test passes a fixed date and can assert exact results.

quiz.question: A component subscribes to a store in its setup code but never unsubscribes. What happens after it is removed from the page?
options: The store keeps a reference to the handler, so the handler keeps running and its memory is never freed
Nothing: JavaScript removes handlers automatically
The browser throws an error
The store is garbage-collected
quiz.explanation: The subscriber set still references the function and everything its closure holds. Return an unsubscribe function from subscribe and call it on teardown.

lessons.title: Testing JavaScript with Vitest
lessons.summaryHtml:
An automated test is a small program that calls your code with known input and checks the result. Vitest is a fast, modern test runner built on Vite: you write describe blocks and it (or test) cases, and check results with expect(value) and a matcher such as toBe, toEqual or toThrow.

You learn to test synchronous and async code, to replace collaborators with mocks (vi.fn, vi.spyOn), to control time with fake timers, to work test-first with the red–green–refactor cycle, and to read coverage reports sensibly. The playground runs a tiny hand-written test helper with the same shape as Vitest, and the lab tests a real cart module with Vitest itself.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A test is a tiny program that uses your code the way the rest of the app would, and checks that the answer is what you expect. “Add two pens at ₹20 and a bag at ₹1,250: the subtotal should be ₹1,290.” You write that once, and a test runner such as Vitest checks it for you every time you save a file, in milliseconds.

Think of tests as a safety net under a trapeze. The net does not make you a better acrobat, but it lets you try the bold move, such as refactoring a checkout, upgrading a library or fixing a bug on a Friday, because a mistake is caught immediately instead of by a customer.

Why it matters

In the last lesson you refactored a messy checkout and compared text output by hand. That works once. Tests make it automatic and precise: each rule of the business (“coupons are capped at ₹500”, “expired coupons are rejected”, “a declined card keeps the cart”) becomes a named check that runs in the terminal, in the editor and in CI (continuous integration, the server that runs your tests on every push).

Employers care because tests are how teams move fast without breaking things. Most job descriptions for front-end developers mention unit tests, and a take-home project with a small, clear test suite stands out immediately. Tests are also the best documentation: a test called 'caps a percentage coupon at its max' says exactly what the code promises.

How it works

Setting up Vitest

Vitest is a test runner built on Vite. It understands ES modules, TypeScript and JSX out of the box, has a fast watch mode, and uses an API compatible with Jest, the older popular runner, so most examples online work in both.

npm install -D vitest
npx vitest          # watch mode: reruns affected tests on every save
npx vitest run      # run once and exit (use this in CI)
{
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest",
    "test:run": "vitest run",
    "coverage": "vitest run --coverage"
  },
  "devDependencies": { "vitest": "^5.0.0" }
}

Vitest finds files named *.test.js or *.spec.js. Put cart.test.js next to cart.js. By default you import the helpers explicitly, which keeps editors and linters happy:

import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { createCart } from './cart.js';

describe, it and expect

describe(name, fn) groups related tests. it(name, fn) (or its alias test) is one test case. Inside, expect(actual) returns an object of matchers; when a matcher fails it throws, the runner catches the error, marks the test as failed and shows expected versus received values. A good test follows Arrange, Act, Assert: set up the data, call the code once, check the result.

Name tests as sentences about behaviour ('rejects an expired coupon'), not about implementation ('test applyCoupon 2'). When a test fails in CI six months from now, its name is the first thing someone reads. Use beforeEach to create fresh data for every test, so tests never depend on each other or on the order they run in.

The playground cannot run Vitest itself, so the examples below use a tiny hand-written helper with the same shape. Once you have seen how expect works inside (a function that returns an object of checks that throw), Vitest has no magic left.

Try it: Your first tests: describe, it and expect

JavaScript

// ---- a tiny stand-in for Vitest ----
const fmt = v => JSON.stringify(v);
function describe(name, fn) { console.log(name); fn(); }
function it(name, fn) {
  try {
    fn();
    console.log(`  ✓ ${name}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`  ✗ ${name}\n      ${err.message}`);
  }
}
function expect(actual) {
  return {
    toBe(expected) {
      if (!Object.is(actual, expected)) {
        throw new Error(`expected ${fmt(expected)}, received ${fmt(actual)}`);
      }
    },
  };
}

// ---- code under test ----
const lineTotal = (price, qty) => price * qty;
function applyDiscount(amount, percent) {
  return amount - percent;            // bug: should be a percentage
}

// ---- tests: Arrange, Act, Assert ----
describe('lineTotal', () => {
  it('multiplies price by quantity', () => {
    expect(lineTotal(20, 5)).toBe(100);
  });
  it('is 0 for quantity 0', () => {
    expect(lineTotal(1250, 0)).toBe(0);
  });
});

describe('applyDiscount', () => {
  it('takes 10% off 1000', () => {
    const amount = 1000;                        // arrange
    const result = applyDiscount(amount, 10);   // act
    expect(result).toBe(900);                   // assert
  });
  it('leaves the amount alone for 0%', () => {
    expect(applyDiscount(450, 0)).toBe(450);
  });
});

This 20-line helper has the same shape as Vitest. One test fails because of a real bug: read the message, fix applyDiscount and run again.

Choosing the right matcher

MatcherChecksExample
toBe(x)Same value or same reference (Object.is)Numbers, strings, booleans
toEqual(x)Same structure, recursivelyObjects and arrays
toStrictEqual(x)Like toEqual, but also checks undefined keys and classesAPI response shapes
toMatchObject(x)Contains at least these propertiesBig objects where only some fields matter
toBeCloseTo(n, digits)Equal within rounding (default 2 digits)Money, percentages
toContain(x), toHaveLength(n)Array or string contents and sizeLists
toThrow(msg or class)The function throwsexpect(() => add(0)).toThrow()
toBeTruthy(), toBeNull(), toBeUndefined()Special valuesOptional results
.notNegates any matcherexpect(list).not.toContain('LAMP')

Two traps catch everyone. First, toBe on objects compares references, so two identical objects fail; use toEqual. Second, toThrow needs a function to call: expect(add(0)).toThrow() runs add(0) before expect even starts, so the error escapes the matcher.

Try it: Matchers: toBe, toEqual, toThrow, toBeCloseTo, not

JavaScript

function expect(actual) {
  const check = (pass, msg) => { if (!pass) throw new Error(msg); };
  const m = {
    toBe: e => check(Object.is(actual, e),
      `expected ${JSON.stringify(e)}, got ${JSON.stringify(actual)}`),
    toEqual: e => check(JSON.stringify(actual) === JSON.stringify(e),
      `expected ${JSON.stringify(e)}, got ${JSON.stringify(actual)}`),
    toBeCloseTo: (e, digits = 2) =>
      check(Math.abs(actual - e) < 10 ** -digits / 2, `${actual} is not close to ${e}`),
    toContain: item => check(actual.includes(item), `missing ${item}`),
    toThrow: text => {
      try { actual(); } catch (err) {
        return check(!text || err.message.includes(text),
          `threw "${err.message}", expected "${text}"`);
      }
      check(false, 'expected the function to throw');
    },
  };
  m.not = { toBe: e => check(!Object.is(actual, e), `expected not ${e}`) };
  return m;
}
function it(name, fn) {
  try { fn(); console.log('✓', name); }
  catch (err) { console.log('✗', name, '→', err.message); }
}

const cart = { items: ['PEN', 'BAG'], total: 0.1 + 0.2 };
const addQty = qty => {
  if (qty <= 0) throw new RangeError('Quantity must be positive');
};

it('toBe on objects compares references', () => expect({ qty: 1 }).toBe({ qty: 1 }));
it('toEqual compares structure', () => expect({ qty: 1 }).toEqual({ qty: 1 }));
it('toBe on money fails: 0.1 + 0.2', () => expect(cart.total).toBe(0.3));
it('toBeCloseTo handles floating point', () => expect(cart.total).toBeCloseTo(0.3));
it('toContain checks arrays and strings', () => expect(cart.items).toContain('BAG'));
it('toThrow wraps the call in a function', () =>
  expect(() => addQty(0)).toThrow('must be positive'));
it('not flips any matcher', () => expect(cart.items.length).not.toBe(0));

The failing lines are on purpose: they show why objects need toEqual and money needs toBeCloseTo.

Testing async code

Give the test an async function and await inside it. Vitest waits for the returned promise and fails the test if it rejects. For promises you expect to succeed or fail, use resolves and rejects, and always await them:

it('loads a product', async () => {
  const product = await getProduct(1, fakeFetch);
  expect(product.title).toBe('Gel pen');
});

it('rejects a missing product', async () => {
  await expect(getProduct(999, fakeFetch)).rejects.toThrow('not found');
});

Without await, the test function returns before the assertion has finished. Older runners (and Jest) could report such a test as passing, with the failure surfacing later as an unhandled rejection or not at all. Current Vitest detects an unawaited resolves/rejects assertion and fails the test with a clear message, but write the await yourself. Unit tests should not call real APIs: they become slow, flaky and dependent on someone else’s server. Inject a fake fetch, as here, or mock it.

Try it: Testing async code

JavaScript

const tests = [];
const it = (name, fn) => tests.push({ name, fn });
function expect(actual) {
  const fail = msg => { throw new Error(msg); };
  return {
    toBe: e => Object.is(actual, e) || fail(`expected ${e}, got ${actual}`),
    rejects: {
      async toThrow(text) {
        try { await actual; } catch (err) {
          if (err.message.includes(text)) return;
          fail(`rejected with "${err.message}"`);
        }
        fail('expected the promise to reject');
      },
    },
  };
}

// ---- code under test: the fetch function is injected ----
async function getPrice(id, fetchFn) {
  const res = await fetchFn(`https://dummyjson.com/products/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Product ${id} not found`);
  const product = await res.json();
  return Math.round(product.price * 83);      // USD to INR, demo rate
}

// A fake fetch: instant, offline and deterministic
const fakeFetch = async url => {
  const id = Number(url.split('/').pop());
  return id === 1
    ? { ok: true, json: async () => ({ id: 1, price: 9.99 }) }
    : { ok: false, status: 404, json: async () => ({}) };
};

it('converts the price to rupees', async () => {
  const price = await getPrice(1, fakeFetch);
  expect(price).toBe(829);
});
it('rejects for a missing product', async () => {
  await expect(getPrice(999, fakeFetch)).rejects.toThrow('not found');
});
it('works against the real API shape too', async () => {
  const price = await getPrice(1, fetch);     // real fetch (online)
  expect(typeof price).toBe('number');
});

for (const t of tests) {
  try { await t.fn(); console.log('✓', t.name); }
  catch (err) { console.log('✗', t.name, '→', err.message); }
}

Each test is awaited before the next starts. Remove await from the rejects test and watch it pass for the wrong reason.

Mocks and spies

A mock function, created with vi.fn(), is a fake that records every call. You can give it behaviour with mockReturnValue, mockResolvedValue, mockRejectedValue or mockImplementation, and then assert how it was used with toHaveBeenCalled, toHaveBeenCalledTimes(n) and toHaveBeenCalledWith(...args). A spy, created with vi.spyOn(object, 'method'), wraps an existing method: it records calls, keeps the original behaviour unless you override it, and mockRestore() (or vi.restoreAllMocks() in afterEach) puts the original back.

it('charges the total in INR', async () => {
  const payments = { charge: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'PAY-1' }) };
  const cart = createCart();
  cart.add(pen, 5);
  await cart.checkout(payments);
  expect(payments.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith(118, 'INR');
});

it('warns on low stock', () => {
  const warn = vi.spyOn(console, 'warn').mockImplementation(() => {});
  checkStock([{ sku: 'BAG', stock: 1 }]);
  expect(warn).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  warn.mockRestore();
});

Mock at the boundaries: payments, network, time, randomness, storage, email. Do not mock your own small functions, or your tests end up checking that the code calls itself the way it currently does, and they break on every refactor. This is where the dependency injection from the last lesson pays off: a service that receives payments as a parameter needs no special mocking tools at all. For modules you cannot inject, Vitest has vi.mock('./payments.js'), which replaces a whole import.

Try it: Mocks and spies

JavaScript

// ---- mini versions of vi.fn() and vi.spyOn() ----
function fn(impl = () => undefined) {
  const mock = (...args) => {
    mock.calls.push(args);
    return mock.impl(...args);
  };
  mock.calls = [];
  mock.impl = impl;
  mock.mockResolvedValue = value => { mock.impl = async () => value; return mock; };
  mock.mockRejectedValue = err => { mock.impl = async () => { throw err; }; return mock; };
  return mock;
}
function spyOn(obj, method) {
  const original = obj[method];
  const spy = fn((...args) => original.apply(obj, args));
  spy.restore = () => { obj[method] = original; };
  obj[method] = spy;
  return spy;
}

// ---- code under test ----
async function checkout(cart, { payments, logger }) {
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  try {
    const receipt = await payments.charge(total, 'INR');
    logger.info(`paid ${receipt.id}`);
    return { ok: true, total };
  } catch (err) {
    logger.warn(`payment failed: ${err.message}`);
    return { ok: false, total };
  }
}

const cart = [{ price: 1250, qty: 1 }, { price: 20, qty: 5 }];
const logger = { info: msg => msg, warn: msg => msg };

// Test 1: success path
const payments = { charge: fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'PAY-7' }) };
const info = spyOn(logger, 'info');
const ok = await checkout(cart, { payments, logger });
console.log('result:', ok);
console.log('charge calls:', payments.charge.calls);   // [[1350, 'INR']]
console.log('info called with:', info.calls[0][0]);
info.restore();

// Test 2: failure path
const declined = { charge: fn().mockRejectedValue(new Error('card declined')) };
const warn = spyOn(logger, 'warn');
const bad = await checkout(cart, { payments: declined, logger });
console.log('result:', bad, '| warn:', warn.calls.length === 1 ? warn.calls[0][0] : 'none');
warn.restore();

fn() records every call, like vi.fn(). spyOn wraps a real method, like vi.spyOn(), and restore() puts it back.

Fake timers and dates

Debounced search, autosave, toast timeouts and coupon expiry all depend on time. Real waiting makes tests slow and flaky. vi.useFakeTimers() replaces setTimeout, setInterval and Date with fakes you control:

beforeEach(() => vi.useFakeTimers());
afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

it('autosaves once after 300 ms of quiet', () => {
  const save = vi.fn();
  const autosave = debounce(save, 300);
  autosave('R'); autosave('Ra'); autosave('Ralfiz');
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(299);
  expect(save).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(1);
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Ralfiz');
});

it('treats Diwali coupons as expired after the sale', () => {
  vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2026-11-15T00:00:00Z'));
  expect(() => cart.applyCoupon(diwali)).toThrow('expired');
});

Always switch back to real timers in afterEach, or a later test that relies on real time will hang or behave strangely.

Try it: Fake timers

JavaScript

// ---- a mini fake clock (Vitest: vi.useFakeTimers) ----
function createFakeTimers() {
  let now = 0;
  let nextId = 1;
  const timers = new Map();
  return {
    setTimeout(fn, ms) {
      const id = nextId++;
      timers.set(id, { fn, at: now + ms });
      return id;
    },
    clearTimeout(id) { timers.delete(id); },
    advance(ms) {                               // vi.advanceTimersByTime
      const end = now + ms;
      for (;;) {
        const due = [...timers].filter(([, t]) => t.at <= end)
          .sort((a, b) => a[1].at - b[1].at)[0];
        if (!due) break;
        timers.delete(due[0]);
        now = due[1].at;
        due[1].fn();
      }
      now = end;
    },
    pending: () => timers.size,
  };
}

// ---- code under test: timers are injected ----
function debounce(fn, ms, timers = globalThis) {
  let id;
  return (...args) => {
    timers.clearTimeout(id);
    id = timers.setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}

const clock = createFakeTimers();
const saved = [];
const autosave = debounce(text => saved.push(text), 300, clock);

autosave('R');
autosave('Ra');
autosave('Ralfiz');                // typing quickly
clock.advance(299);
console.log('after 299 ms:', saved, 'pending:', clock.pending());
clock.advance(1);
console.log('after 300 ms:', saved);

autosave('Ralfiz Store');
clock.advance(1000);
console.log('after another second:', saved);
console.assert(saved.length === 2, 'autosave should run twice');

The fake clock runs callbacks when you advance it, so a 300 ms debounce is tested instantly. Vitest does the same with vi.useFakeTimers().

The TDD cycle and coverage

Test-driven development turns the order around: write the test first, then the code.

  1. Red: write one small failing test for the next behaviour, for example “a 50% coupon on ₹2,500 is capped at ₹500”. Run it and see it fail for the right reason.
  2. Green: write the simplest code that makes it pass: Math.min(subtotal * percent / 100, max).
  3. Refactor: tidy names and structure while all tests stay green. Then pick the next behaviour.

TDD is especially good for bug fixes: first write a test that reproduces the bug (red), then fix it (green). The bug can never silently return. You do not have to use TDD for everything, but try it in the lab.

Coverage measures which lines and branches ran during the tests. Run npx vitest run --coverage; Vitest uses the V8 engine’s built-in coverage through the @vitest/coverage-v8 package and offers to install it the first time. Read the report to find untested areas, such as an else branch nobody tried. Do not chase 100%: coverage shows that code ran, not that the assertions were meaningful.

Example: testing the Ralfiz cart module

The lab gives you cart.js, a real ES module with createCart, applyCoupon, an async checkout(payments) and a debounce helper, plus a starter cart.test.js with three passing tests and several it.todo entries.

  1. Write a test that adds the same product twice and expects the quantities to add up. It fails: add overwrites the quantity. Fix the bug; the test turns green.
  2. Test the error paths with toThrow: zero, negative and fractional quantities, and more than the stock.
  3. Test totals with toEqual for the whole object and toBeCloseTo for money that needs rounding.
  4. Use TDD for the new coupon cap: red, green, refactor.
  5. Test coupon expiry twice: once with an injected now function, once with vi.setSystemTime.
  6. Test checkout with vi.fn().mockResolvedValue and mockRejectedValue, including err.cause.
  7. Test debounce with fake timers.

The live page shows the same idea as a report: the tests run against a cart in the page. Toggle “Introduce a bug” to reintroduce the overwrite bug and read how the failing tests describe it.

JavaScript

// ---- the module under test (with an optional bug) ----
function createCart({ buggy = false } = {}) {
  const lines = new Map();
  return {
    add(product, qty = 1) {
      if (!Number.isInteger(qty) || qty <= 0) throw new RangeError(`Invalid quantity: ${qty}`);
      const current = lines.get(product.sku)?.qty ?? 0;
      lines.set(product.sku, { ...product, qty: buggy ? qty : current + qty });
    },
    get count() { return [...lines.values()].reduce((n, l) => n + l.qty, 0); },
    totals() {
      const subtotal = [...lines.values()].reduce((s, l) => s + l.price * l.qty, 0);
      const tax = Math.round(subtotal * 0.18 * 100) / 100;
      return { subtotal, tax, total: subtotal + tax };
    },
  };
}

// ---- a tiny runner with Vitest-like output ----
const suites = [];
let current;
const describe = (name, fn) => { current = { name, tests: [] }; suites.push(current); fn(); };
const it = (name, fn) => current.tests.push({ name, fn });
const show = v => JSON.stringify(v);
function expect(actual) {
  const fail = (exp) => {
    throw Object.assign(new Error('mismatch'), { expected: show(exp), received: show(actual) });
  };
  return {
    toBe: e => Object.is(actual, e) || fail(e),
    toEqual: e => show(actual) === show(e) || fail(e),
    toThrow: text => {
      try { actual(); } catch (err) { if (err.message.includes(text)) return; }
      fail(`throws "${text}"`);
    },
  };
}

function defineTests(buggy) {
  suites.length = 0;
  const pen = { sku: 'PEN', price: 20 };
  const bag = { sku: 'BAG', price: 1250 };
  describe('adding items', () => {
    it('starts empty', () => expect(createCart({ buggy }).count).toBe(0));
    it('adds a product with a quantity', () => {
      const cart = createCart({ buggy });
      cart.add(pen, 3);
      expect(cart.count).toBe(3);
    });
    it('adding the same product twice adds the quantities', () => {
      const cart = createCart({ buggy });
      cart.add(pen, 2);
      cart.add(pen, 3);
      expect(cart.count).toBe(5);
    });
    it('rejects a quantity of 0', () =>
      expect(() => createCart({ buggy }).add(pen, 0)).toThrow('Invalid quantity'));
  });
  describe('totals', () => {
    it('adds 18% GST', () => {
      const cart = createCart({ buggy });
      cart.add(pen, 5);
      cart.add(bag);
      expect(cart.totals()).toEqual({ subtotal: 1350, tax: 243, total: 1593 });
    });
    it('counts repeat adds in the subtotal', () => {
      const cart = createCart({ buggy });
      cart.add(bag);
      cart.add(bag);
      expect(cart.totals().subtotal).toBe(2500);
    });
  });
}

const $ = sel => document.querySelector(sel);
function el(tag, className, text) {
  const node = document.createElement(tag);
  if (className) node.className = className;
  if (text !== undefined) node.textContent = text;
  return node;
}

function run() {
  defineTests($('#bug').checked);
  const start = performance.now();
  let passed = 0;
  let failed = 0;
  const blocks = suites.map(suite => {
    const box = el('article', 'suite');
    const list = el('ul');
    for (const t of suite.tests) {
      const t0 = performance.now();
      let error = null;
      try { t.fn(); passed++; } catch (err) { error = err; failed++; }
      const row = el('li', `test ${error ? 'fail' : 'pass'}`);
      row.append(el('span', 'icon', error ? '✗' : '✓'), el('span', '', t.name),
        el('span', 'ms', `${(performance.now() - t0).toFixed(2)} ms`));
      if (error) {
        row.append(el('pre', 'diff', error.expected
          ? `Expected: ${error.expected}\nReceived: ${error.received}`
          : `${error.name}: ${error.message}`));
      }
      list.append(row);
    }
    box.append(el('h2', '', suite.name), list);
    return box;
  });
  $('#suites').replaceChildren(...blocks);
  $('#summary').replaceChildren(
    el('span', 'chip pass', `${passed} passed`),
    ...(failed ? [el('span', 'chip fail', `${failed} failed`)] : []),
    el('span', 'time', `${passed + failed} tests · ${(performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)} ms`),
  );
  console.log(`Tests: ${failed ? failed + ' failed, ' : ''}${passed} passed`);
}

$('#bug').addEventListener('change', run);

Common mistakes

1. Calling the function inside expect when testing throws.

expect(cart.add(pen, 0)).toThrow();        // wrong: throws before expect runs
expect(() => cart.add(pen, 0)).toThrow();  // right

2. Forgetting await on async assertions.

expect(cart.checkout(payments)).rejects.toThrow();        // not awaited: unreliable
await expect(cart.checkout(payments)).rejects.toThrow();  // really checks

3. Sharing state between tests.

const cart = createCart();              // one cart for every test: order matters
let cart;
beforeEach(() => { cart = createCart(); });  // fresh cart for each test

4. Leaving fakes installed. Pair vi.useFakeTimers() with vi.useRealTimers() and spies with mockRestore() or vi.restoreAllMocks() in afterEach.

5. Testing implementation details. Asserting that a private helper was called, or on the exact internal structure of a Map, breaks on every refactor. Test what users of the module can observe: return values, thrown errors and calls to external boundaries.

6. Exact equality for money. expect(total).toBe(8849.96) may fail by a tiny floating-point amount. Use toBeCloseTo, or keep money in paise as integers.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Know the testing pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests (modules working together, for example with a fake server), and a handful of end-to-end tests in a real browser with a tool such as Playwright.
  • For DOM code, Vitest can run tests in a simulated browser environment (environment: 'jsdom' or 'happy-dom' in the config), or in a real browser with its browser mode.
  • “What makes a good test?” Fast, isolated, deterministic (same result every run), readable, and failing for exactly one reason.
  • Run vitest run in CI on every pull request and block merging when it fails. That single habit prevents most regressions.
  • In a take-home project, even eight well-named tests for the core logic (pricing, validation, reducers) make a strong impression. Mention what you chose not to test and why.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 0.005);
  • A true true
  • B false false
  • C false true
  • D true false

Snippet 2. What is logged? (toBe uses Object.is; toEqual compares structure.)

const a = { qty: 1 };
const b = { qty: 1 };
console.log(Object.is(a, b), JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b),
  Object.is(NaN, NaN), NaN === NaN);
  • A false true true false
  • B true true true true
  • C false true false false
  • D false false true false

Snippet 3. What is logged?

function fn() {
  const f = (...args) => { f.calls.push(args); return 42; };
  f.calls = [];
  return f;
}
const charge = fn();
[100, 250].forEach(amount => charge(amount, 'INR'));
console.log(charge.calls.length, charge.calls[1][0], charge(1));
  • A 2 250 undefined
  • B 3 250 42
  • C 2 100 42
  • D 2 250 42

Snippet 4. This runner does not await tests. What is logged?

const results = [];
function test(name, fn) {
  try {
    const r = fn();
    results.push(`${name}:pass`);
    return r;
  } catch {
    results.push(`${name}:fail`);
  }
}
test('sync', () => { throw new Error('boom'); });
test('async', async () => { throw new Error('boom'); })
  ?.catch(() => results.push('async:late-fail'));
console.log(results.join(' '));
setTimeout(() => console.log(results.join(' ')), 0);
  • A 
    sync:fail async:fail
sync:fail async:fail
  • B 
    sync:fail async:pass
sync:fail async:pass async:late-fail
  • C 
    sync:fail
sync:fail async:late-fail
  • D 
    sync:fail async:pass
sync:fail async:pass

Answers

  1. C. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in floating point, so === fails. toBeCloseTo works like the second check: with the default 2 digits it passes when the difference is under 0.005.
  2. A. Two object literals are different references, so Object.is (and toBe) says false while a structural comparison (toEqual) says true. Object.is also treats NaN as equal to itself, unlike ===.
  3. D. The arguments to console.log are evaluated left to right. At that moment the mock has recorded two calls and the second one’s first argument is 250; then charge(1) returns 42 (and records a third call afterwards).
  4. B. An async function never throws synchronously: it returns a rejected promise, so the try block records a pass. The rejection is only seen later, in a microtask. That is why Vitest awaits async tests, and why you must await expect(...).rejects.

terms.definition: A test of one small piece (a function or module) in isolation, fast enough to run on every save.
A method on expect() that performs a check, such as toBe (same value, Object.is), toEqual (same structure) or toThrow.
A fake function (vi.fn) that records its calls and can return canned values, so you can check how your code used it.
A wrapper (vi.spyOn) around an existing method that records calls, optionally replaces the implementation, and can be restored.
Replacements for setTimeout, setInterval and Date that let a test move time forward instantly (vi.useFakeTimers, vi.advanceTimersByTime).
Test-driven development: write a failing test (red), make it pass with the simplest code (green), then clean up (refactor).
A report of which lines and branches ran during the tests. It shows what is untested, not whether tests are good.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say what you test (behaviour through the public API, edge cases, errors) and what you mock (only slow or external boundaries such as network, time and payments), not just which library you use.

quiz.question: A test does expect({ qty: 2 }).toBe({ qty: 2 }) and fails. Why?
options: toBe compares with Object.is, and two separate objects are never the same reference; use toEqual
qty must be a string
toBe only works with arrays
The test needs to be async
quiz.explanation: toBe checks identity, like ===. For objects and arrays with the same contents, use toEqual (or toStrictEqual to also compare undefined properties and classes).

quiz.question: An async test calls expect(loadCart()).rejects.toThrow() without await. What is wrong?
options: rejects only works with fake timers
The assertion is a promise; without await (or return) the test can finish before it runs
toThrow cannot be used with promises
Async tests must use done callbacks
quiz.explanation: Assertions on promises are asynchronous. Write await expect(promise).rejects.toThrow(...) so the test waits for, and fails on, the result. Current Vitest versions detect the missing await and fail the test with a clear message; older runners (and Jest) could let such a test pass silently.

quiz.question: You test a debounced autosave that waits 500 ms. What is the best approach in Vitest?
options: await a real 500 ms sleep in every test
Remove the debounce in the test build
Call vi.useFakeTimers(), trigger the save, then vi.advanceTimersByTime(500) and assert
Mock setTimeout with a function that never runs
quiz.explanation: Fake timers make time-based code fast and deterministic. Remember vi.useRealTimers() in afterEach so other tests are not affected.

quiz.question: Your checkout calls payments.charge(). Which test design is best?
options: Charge a real card in every test run
Do not test checkout at all
Copy the checkout code into the test file
Pass in a payments object whose charge is vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(...), then assert it was called with the right amount
quiz.explanation: Mock the external boundary, not your own logic. Injecting a fake payments object keeps the test fast, free and deterministic, and toHaveBeenCalledWith proves the contract.

lessons.title: TypeScript essentials
lessons.summaryHtml:
TypeScript is JavaScript with a type system on top. You describe the shape of your data (a Product has a numeric price, an order status is one of four words) and the compiler checks every use of it before the code ever runs. Then the types are erased and plain JavaScript is left.

In this lesson you learn annotations and inference, union and literal types, interfaces and type aliases, generics, narrowing, strict mode and tsconfig.json, how TypeScript fits into a Vite project and how to type data that comes from fetch safely. The live examples run the plain JavaScript that TypeScript would produce; the lab builds a typed Ralfiz Store order module and compiles it with tsc.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

JavaScript lets any variable hold anything. That freedom is pleasant for ten lines and painful for ten thousand. TypeScript adds a layer where you write down what your data looks like: a price is a number, a status is one of 'pending', 'paid' or 'shipped', a function takes a Product and returns a number. A compiler called tsc reads your code and tells you, before anything runs, where you broke those promises.

Think of it as a spell checker for the shape of your data. It underlines mistakes while you type. When you build, the types are erased and ordinary JavaScript is left, which is what browsers and Node actually run.

TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript: every JavaScript file is almost valid TypeScript already. You add types gradually, where they help most.

Why it matters

Most job adverts for front-end and Node roles list TypeScript, and frameworks such as React, Angular, Vue and Next.js all have first-class support for it. The reason is practical. In a real codebase, a renamed field or a function that now returns null can break forty files. With TypeScript, the editor shows all forty errors at once and F2 renames safely across the project.

Types also document your code. A new developer reading function refund(order: Order, reason: RefundReason): Result<Refund> learns more than from a paragraph of comments, and autocomplete shows every property of Order as they type.

The first example shows three bugs that plain JavaScript happily runs: a misspelt property, a number that is really a string, and a misspelt method. TypeScript reports each of them in the editor.

Try it: Bugs TypeScript would catch

JavaScript

// Plain JavaScript: nothing stops these mistakes until you look closely.
const product = { title: 'Ralfiz Notebook', price: 250, stock: 12 };

// 1. A typo in a property name gives undefined, not an error.
console.log('Price with GST:', product.prise * 1.18);

// 2. A number arrives as a string (from an input or a query string).
const qty = '3';
console.log('Line total:', product.price * qty);
console.log('Stock after sale:', product.stock - qty);
console.log('Items in cart:', 2 + qty);

// 3. A misspelt method only fails when this line runs.
try {
  product.title.toUpperCas();
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name + ':', err.message);
}

// TypeScript errors you would see instead (shortened):
// Property 'prise' does not exist on type '{ ... }'. Did you mean 'price'?
// The right-hand side of an arithmetic operation must be of type
//   'any', 'number', 'bigint' or an enum type.
// Property 'toUpperCas' does not exist on type 'string'.
//   Did you mean 'toUpperCase'?
// Note: 2 + qty is allowed, because + also joins strings. Convert input
// with Number() at the boundary and type qty as number.

Every line runs and every result is wrong. In a .ts file the editor underlines all three before you press Run.

How it works

Annotations and inference

You add a type after a colon. For most local variables you do not need to, because TypeScript infers the type from the value. Annotate the edges instead: function parameters, return types of exported functions, and data from outside.

const shopName = 'Ralfiz Store'; // inferred: the literal type 'Ralfiz Store'
let itemsInCart = 0;                  // inferred: number

function lineTotal(price: number, qty: number): number {
  return price * qty;
}

lineTotal(250, '3');
// Error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable
// to parameter of type 'number'.

const tags: string[] = ['new', 'sale'];
const point: [number, number] = [11.07, 76.07]; // a tuple: fixed length and types

The basic types match JavaScript’s values: string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, null, undefined, arrays and objects. Three special types matter in interviews: any turns checking off, unknown means “anything, but prove it before you use it”, and never means “this cannot happen”, such as the return type of a function that always throws.

Union and literal types, and narrowing

A union says a value is one of several types: string | number. A literal type is an exact value used as a type. Together they model real business rules far better than a bare string:

type OrderStatus = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped' | 'cancelled';

type Payment =
  | { kind: 'upi'; vpa: string }
  | { kind: 'card'; last4: string; network: 'visa' | 'rupay' }
  | { kind: 'cod' };

function paymentFee(p: Payment, amount: number): number {
  switch (p.kind) {
    case 'upi':  return 0;
    case 'card': return Math.round(amount * 0.018); // p.last4 is available here
    case 'cod':  return 40;
    default:     return assertNever(p); // p is never here
  }
}

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error('Unhandled case: ' + JSON.stringify(x));
}

The shared kind field makes this a discriminated union. Inside each case, TypeScript narrows p to that one variant, so p.last4 is allowed only in the card branch. If a colleague later adds { kind: 'wallet' }, the call to assertNever fails to compile until the new case is handled. That is how large teams keep every switch up to date.

Narrowing works with the checks you already know: typeof, instanceof, Array.isArray, the in operator, equality checks and truthiness. The example runs the JavaScript that this TypeScript compiles to.

Try it: Discriminated unions and narrowing

JavaScript

// TypeScript version:
// type Payment =
//   | { kind: 'upi'; vpa: string }
//   | { kind: 'card'; last4: string }
//   | { kind: 'cod' };
function describe(payment) {
  switch (payment.kind) {
    case 'upi':
      return `UPI to ${payment.vpa}`;
    case 'card':
      return `Card ending ${payment.last4}`;
    case 'cod':
      return 'Cash on delivery';
    default:
      // In TypeScript: return assertNever(payment);
      throw new Error(`Unknown payment kind: ${payment.kind}`);
  }
}

const payments = [
  { kind: 'upi', vpa: 'asha@okbank' },
  { kind: 'card', last4: '4242' },
  { kind: 'cod' },
];
payments.forEach((p) => console.log(describe(p)));

// typeof and instanceof narrow too: value is string | number | Date
function toRupees(value) {
  if (typeof value === 'string') return Number(value.replace(/[₹,]/g, ''));
  if (value instanceof Date) return NaN;
  return value; // only number is left here
}
console.log(toRupees('₹1,250'), toRupees(99));

try {
  describe({ kind: 'crypto' });
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.message);
}

The switch on payment.kind is exactly how TypeScript narrows a union. Try adding a { kind: 'wallet' } payment.

Interfaces and type aliases

Both describe the shape of an object. An interface can only describe objects (and classes can implements it). A type alias can name anything: unions, tuples, functions and computed types.

interface Product {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  price: number;
  discountPercentage?: number;   // optional: number | undefined
  readonly sku: string;          // cannot be reassigned
}

interface DigitalProduct extends Product {
  downloadUrl: string;
}

type CartLine = { product: Product; qty: number };
type Money = number;
type Handler = (event: Event) => void;
Featureinterfacetype alias
Object shapesYesYes
Unions, tuples, primitives, functionsNoYes
ExtendingextendsIntersection A & B
Declaration merging (same name twice)MergesError
Typical usePublic object and class contractsUnions, helpers, everything else

Either is fine for plain objects; pick one convention per project. TypeScript is structural: any object with the right properties matches Product, whether or not it was created from a class or declared with that name.

Generics

A generic is a type parameter. It lets one function work for many types while keeping the input and output connected. Without generics, first(items: any[]): any loses all information; with them, first of a Product[] returns a Product | undefined.

function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return items[0];
}

function groupBy<T, K extends string>(
  items: readonly T[],
  keyOf: (item: T) => K,
): Partial<Record<K, T[]>> {
  const groups: Partial<Record<K, T[]>> = {};
  for (const item of items) (groups[keyOf(item)] ??= []).push(item);
  return groups;
}

type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string };

K extends string is a constraint: whatever K is, it must be a string type, so it can be an object key. Built-in utility types are generics too: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, Record<K, V> and ReturnType<F>. You can also get TypeScript checking in plain .js files with JSDoc comments and // @ts-check, which is a gentle way to start in an existing codebase.

Try it: Generics with JSDoc in a .js file

JavaScript

// @ts-check

/**
 * Return the first item, or undefined for an empty array.
 * @template T
 * @param {T[]} items
 * @returns {T | undefined}
 */
function first(items) {
  return items[0];
}

/**
 * Group items by a string key.
 * @template T
 * @template {string} K
 * @param {T[]} items
 * @param {(item: T) => K} keyOf
 * @returns {Partial<Record<K, T[]>>}
 */
function groupBy(items, keyOf) {
  /** @type {Partial<Record<K, T[]>>} */
  const groups = {};
  for (const item of items) {
    const key = keyOf(item);
    (groups[key] ??= []).push(item);
  }
  return groups;
}

const orders = [
  { id: 'A1', status: 'paid', total: 1200 },
  { id: 'A2', status: 'pending', total: 450 },
  { id: 'A3', status: 'paid', total: 800 },
];
console.log(first(orders));      // T is the order type
console.log(first([]));          // T is never, result undefined
const byStatus = groupBy(orders, (o) => o.status);
console.log(Object.keys(byStatus));
console.log('Paid orders:', byStatus.paid?.length ?? 0);

The // @ts-check comment and JSDoc tags give you TypeScript checking in plain .js files. Hover the functions in VS Code to see the inferred types.

The utility types describe operations you already do by hand. The next example runs their JavaScript equivalents, plus as const, which turns an array of strings into a union of literal types.

Try it: Utility types, as runtime code

JavaScript

const product = { id: 7, title: 'Ralfiz Pen', price: 40, stock: 90, cost: 18 };

// type ProductPatch = Partial<Product>   (any subset of fields)
const applyPatch = (p, patch) => ({ ...p, ...patch });
console.log(applyPatch(product, { price: 35 }));

// type ProductCard = Pick<Product, 'id' | 'title' | 'price'>
const pick = (obj, keys) => Object.fromEntries(keys.map((k) => [k, obj[k]]));
console.log(pick(product, ['id', 'title', 'price']));

// type PublicProduct = Omit<Product, 'cost'>
const omit = (obj, keys) =>
  Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).filter(([k]) => !keys.includes(k)));
console.log(omit(product, ['cost']));

// const STATUSES = ['pending', 'paid', 'shipped'] as const;
// type Status = (typeof STATUSES)[number];  -> 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped'
const STATUSES = ['pending', 'paid', 'shipped'];
const isStatus = (s) => STATUSES.includes(s);
console.log(isStatus('paid'), isStatus('lost'));

Partial, Pick, Omit and as const describe these everyday operations. The comments show the types; the code shows what they model.

Strict mode and tsconfig.json

tsconfig.json tells the compiler which files to check and how. The most important switch is strict. It turns on a family of checks, including strictNullChecks (a string can no longer be null by accident) and noImplicitAny (an untyped parameter is an error). Recent TypeScript versions switch strict on by default, but write it explicitly so every tool and version agrees.

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "skipLibCheck": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
OptionWhat it does
strictEnables the full set of safety checks. Always on for new code.
targetWhich JavaScript version to emit, e.g. ES2022 keeps modern syntax.
moduleModule system: NodeNext for Node, ESNext with a bundler.
noUncheckedIndexedAccessarr[i] becomes T | undefined, catching out-of-range reads.
outDir / noEmitWhere compiled files go, or only type-check without writing files.
erasableSyntaxOnlyForbids enums and other syntax that needs code generation, so type stripping works.

Using TypeScript with Vite and Node

Vite has TypeScript templates. Vite itself only strips types, which is why it is so fast; the template’s build script runs tsc first to do the actual checking.

npm create vite@latest ralfiz-store -- --template vanilla-ts
cd ralfiz-store
npm install
npm run dev        # fast dev server, no type checking
npm run build      # runs tsc (type check) and then vite build
npx tsc --noEmit   # check types on demand, e.g. in CI

Node 22.18 and later can run a .ts file directly with node index.ts. It also only strips types and does not check them, and it rejects syntax such as enum. For that reason many teams prefer union types over enums. Always install TypeScript locally (npm install -D typescript) or use npx -p typescript tsc: a bare npx tsc without TypeScript installed downloads an unrelated package called tsc.

Typing fetch responses

This is where beginners get burned. response.json() returns data the compiler has never seen. Writing const data = await res.json() as Product does not check anything; it is a promise you make to the compiler. If the API changes, your code crashes somewhere far away. Treat outside data as unknown and prove its shape once, at the boundary, with a type guard (a function whose return type is x is Product).

function isProduct(x: unknown): x is Product {
  return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null
    && 'id' in x && typeof x.id === 'number'
    && 'title' in x && typeof x.title === 'string'
    && 'price' in x && typeof x.price === 'number';
}

async function getProduct(id: number): Promise<Product> {
  const res = await fetch('https://dummyjson.com/products/' + id);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);
  const data: unknown = await res.json();
  if (!isProduct(data)) throw new Error('Unexpected product shape');
  return data; // narrowed to Product
}

For bigger APIs, teams use a schema library such as Zod or Valibot, which writes the guard and the type from one definition.

Try it: Types vanish: validate API data

JavaScript

// TypeScript: function isProduct(x: unknown): x is Product
function isProduct(x) {
  return (
    typeof x === 'object' && x !== null &&
    typeof x.id === 'number' &&
    typeof x.title === 'string' &&
    typeof x.price === 'number'
  );
}

// TypeScript: async function getProduct(id: number): Promise<Product>
async function getProduct(id) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://dummyjson.com/products/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status} for product ${id}`);
  const data = await res.json(); // treat as unknown, not any
  if (!isProduct(data)) throw new Error('Unexpected product shape');
  return data; // from here on it is a Product
}

try {
  const p = await getProduct(1);
  console.log(p.id, p.title, p.price);
  console.log('Fake passes?', isProduct({ id: '1', title: 'Fake', price: 10 }));
  await getProduct(9999);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('Handled:', err.message);
}

response.json() gives you unknown data. One type guard at the edge turns it into a trusted Product. Try changing the id to 9999.

Example: a typed Ralfiz Store order module

The lab turns an untyped order script into TypeScript. The key moves are:

  1. Model the domain first: Category and OrderStatus as literal unions, Product and CartLine as interfaces, Payment as a discriminated union.
  2. Type the functions at their edges: lineTotal(line: CartLine): number. Let inference handle the locals.
  3. Replace throw in expected failures with Result<T>, so the caller is forced by the compiler to handle the error branch.
  4. Validate the incoming JSON with isProduct before trusting it.
  5. Compile with tsc, run the output with Node, then add a new payment kind and watch the compiler point at every place to update.
function addToCart(
  lines: CartLine[],
  id: number,
  qty: number,
): Result<CartLine[]> {
  const product = catalogue.find((p) => p.id === id);
  if (!product) return { ok: false, error: 'No product ' + id };
  if (qty > product.stock) {
    return { ok: false, error: 'Only ' + product.stock + ' left' };
  }
  return { ok: true, value: [...lines, { product, qty }] };
}

const added = addToCart([], 3, 2);
// value exists only when ok is true, error only when it is false
if (added.ok) console.log(added.value.length);
else console.log(added.error);

Common mistakes

  • Using any to silence errors. function total(items: any) spreads unchecked data everywhere. Fix: write the type, or use unknown and narrow.
  • Casting instead of checking. const p = data as Product; lies to the compiler. Fix: if (isProduct(data)) { … }.
  • The non-null assertion everywhere. document.querySelector('#q')!.value crashes when the element is missing. Fix: const q = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('#q'); if (!q) return;
  • Forgetting typeof null === 'object'. Wrong: if (typeof x === 'object') x.id. Fix: if (typeof x === 'object' && x !== null).
  • Thinking types exist at runtime. You cannot write if (x instanceof Product) for an interface. Fix: check a discriminant field or use a type guard.
  • Over-typing locals. const count: number = 0 adds noise. Fix: let inference work and annotate parameters and exports.

Interview and real-world notes

  • type vs interface: both describe objects; interfaces can be extended and merged, type aliases can express unions and computed types. Say which convention your team uses and why.
  • any vs unknown vs never: any disables checks, unknown requires narrowing, never is the empty type used for impossible states and exhaustive checks.
  • satisfies: const config = { theme: 'dark' } satisfies Config; checks a value against a type but keeps its precise inferred type.
  • Structural typing: compatibility is decided by shape, not by name.
  • Migration story: start with // @ts-check and JSDoc, rename files to .ts one by one, turn on strict, then remove any. Interviewers like hearing a gradual, low-risk plan.
  • TypeScript 7 moved the compiler to native code, which makes type checking much faster. The language you learn here stays the same.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. In TypeScript this was written as const qty = input as unknown as number. What does the compiled JavaScript log?

const input = '5';
const qty = input; // the cast disappears when compiled
console.log(qty + 1);
  • A 6
  • B 51
  • C NaN
  • D TypeError

Snippet 2. What is logged?

function kind(v) {
  if (typeof v === 'object') return 'object';
  if (typeof v === 'string') return 'string';
  return 'other';
}
console.log(kind(null), kind([]), kind('x'));
  • A other object string
  • B other other string
  • C object other string
  • D object object string

Snippet 3. What is logged?

function fee(p) {
  switch (p.kind) {
    case 'upi': return 0;
    case 'card': return p.amount * 0.02;
    default: return 'unhandled ' + p.kind;
  }
}
console.log(fee({ kind: 'card', amount: 500 }), fee({ kind: 'cod', amount: 500 }));
  • A 10 unhandled cod
  • B 10 0
  • C 0 unhandled cod
  • D 10 undefined

Snippet 4. The type says pageSize?: number and theme?: { name: string }. What is logged?

const settings = { pageSize: 0 };
const a = settings.pageSize || 20;
const b = settings.pageSize ?? 20;
const c = settings.theme?.name ?? 'light';
console.log(a, b, c);
  • A 0 0 light
  • B 20 20 light
  • C 20 0 light
  • D 20 0 undefined

Answers

  1. B. A cast (as) only silences the compiler. It does not convert anything, so qty is still the string '5' and + concatenates to '51'. Convert with Number(input) instead.
  2. D. typeof null is 'object' and so is typeof of an array. That is why TypeScript does not narrow away null after typeof v === 'object': you must also check v !== null.
  3. A. card pays 2% of 500, which is 10. cod has no case, so the default runs. In TypeScript, assertNever in the default would turn this forgotten case into a compile error.
  4. C. || replaces every falsy value, including a valid 0. ?? replaces only null and undefined, so b keeps 0. Optional chaining returns undefined for the missing theme and ?? supplies 'light'.

terms.definition: A label such as : number or : Product that tells TypeScript what a variable, parameter or return value must hold.
TypeScript works out a type from the value, so const total = 0 is a number without an annotation.
A type that is one of several options, such as 'upi' | 'card' | 'cod'. Literal types are exact values used as types.
Checks such as typeof, in, instanceof or a switch on a kind field that let TypeScript know the more specific type inside a branch.
A type parameter (like T) that lets one function or type work with many types while keeping them connected, e.g. first of an array of T returns a T.
any switches checking off; unknown means “could be anything, prove it before use”. Use unknown for data from outside.
The project file that tells the compiler which files to check and how strict to be.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, say “TypeScript checks at compile time and is erased at runtime, so I still validate data that crosses a boundary such as an API response or a form.” It shows you understand where types stop.

quiz.question: A teammate says “TypeScript will stop bad data from the API reaching our code.” What is the accurate reply?
options: Right: tsc inserts runtime checks for every interface
Types are erased when compiled, so API data must still be validated at runtime
Only if strict mode is on
Only when the response is typed as any
quiz.explanation: TypeScript checks your source code. The emitted JavaScript contains no types, so a response typed as Product can hold anything. Treat it as unknown and validate it with a type guard or a schema library.

quiz.question: What does a discriminated union give you?
options: Faster code at runtime
Automatic JSON validation
A shared literal field (such as kind) that TypeScript uses to narrow to the exact variant in each branch
A way to merge two interfaces
quiz.explanation: Each variant has a common field with a different literal value. When you switch on that field, TypeScript knows which properties exist in each case, and assertNever can prove every case is handled.

quiz.question: Which is the best type for a value you just parsed from JSON.parse or response.json()?
options: unknown, then narrow it with checks
any, because it is flexible
never
object, because JSON is always an object
quiz.explanation: unknown forces you to check the shape before using it. any silently turns off checking for everything it touches. JSON can also be a number, string, array, boolean or null, so object is wrong.

quiz.question: In a Vite project, what checks your types during npm run build?
options: Vite itself, always
The browser
Nothing can check types in Vite
The tsc step in the build script (for example tsc && vite build); Vite only strips types
quiz.explanation: Vite transpiles TypeScript very fast by removing types without checking them. The template runs tsc before vite build, and your editor shows errors while you type.

lessons.title: Performance and memory
lessons.summaryHtml:
Fast JavaScript is mostly about doing less work and not holding the main thread. You pick data structures with the right lookup cost (a Set or Map instead of searching an array in a loop), you measure before and after with performance.now() and the DevTools Performance panel, and you avoid repeating work with memoization.

For user input you use debounce (wait until the user stops) and throttle (at most once per interval). You split long jobs into chunks so the page stays responsive, and move heavy computation to a Web Worker. Finally you learn how garbage collection decides what to free, and the four classic leaks: forgotten listeners, running timers, closures holding big data and detached DOM nodes.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A fast page is not one with clever tricks. It is one that does less work, does it at the right time, and lets go of memory it no longer needs. JavaScript in the browser runs on a single main thread that also handles clicks, typing and painting. Every millisecond your code holds that thread is a millisecond the user cannot interact.

Think of a billing counter with one cashier. Looking up each customer by walking through a paper register is slow (use an index card box instead). Recalculating the same tax rate for every item is wasteful (write it down once). Processing a 500-item bulk order while a queue forms is rude (serve others between batches). And never throwing away old receipts eventually fills the room. Those four ideas are this lesson: data structures, memoization, scheduling and memory.

Why it matters

Many of your users are on mid-range phones where JavaScript runs several times slower than on your laptop. Google’s Core Web Vitals include INP (Interaction to Next Paint), which measures how quickly the page responds to input; a good INP is 200 ms or less. Long JavaScript tasks are the main cause of poor INP.

Memory matters for apps that stay open all day: an admin dashboard, a POS screen, a chat window. A small leak per screen change becomes hundreds of megabytes by evening, and the tab slows down or crashes. Interviewers love this topic because it separates people who can write code from people who can keep it running.

How it works

Big-O intuition: pick the right data structure

Big-O describes how work grows as data grows. You rarely need the maths; you need the instinct.

CostNameExample10,000 items
O(1)Constantmap.get(id), set.has(x), arr[i]About 1 step
O(log n)LogarithmicBinary search in a sorted arrayAbout 14 steps
O(n)Lineararr.includes(x), find, one loop10,000 steps
O(n log n)Linearithmicarr.toSorted()About 140,000 steps
O(n²)Quadraticfind or includes inside a loop100,000,000 steps

The most common real-world slowdown is the hidden O(n²): a find, filter or includes inside a map or for loop. The fix is almost always to build a Map or Set once (O(n)) and then look up in O(1).

// O(orders × customers): find scans the whole array for every order
const slowRows = orders.map((o) => ({
  ...o,
  customer: customers.find((c) => c.id === o.customerId),
}));

// O(orders + customers): index once, then constant-time lookups
const byId = new Map(customers.map((c) => [c.id, c]));
const fastRows = orders.map((o) => ({ ...o, customer: byId.get(o.customerId) }));

Measure instead of guessing. performance.now() gives a high-resolution timestamp in milliseconds, and console.time(label) with console.timeEnd(label) wraps the same idea. Run a measurement several times: the first run is often slower while the engine’s JIT compiler warms up, and browsers deliberately reduce timer precision for security. For real pages, record a trace in the DevTools Performance panel, which shows long tasks as red-flagged blocks and the functions inside them.

const arrayMs = performance.now() - t;

t = performance.now();
const vipSet = new Set(vipIds);                                  // O(m), once
const fast = orders.filter((o) => vipSet.has(o.customer));       // O(n)

console.log(`Array.includes: ${arrayMs.toFixed(1)} ms`);

console.timeEnd('Build a Map index by id');

Same answer, very different cost. Change the sizes and watch how the array version grows much faster than the Set version.

Memoization

Memoization caches the result of a pure function (same input, same output, no side effects) by its input. The second call with the same argument returns instantly. It is perfect for expensive calculations that repeat: shipping quotes by PIN code, formatted prices, parsed templates, filtered lists for the same query.

Two rules keep it safe. First, only memoize pure functions: caching a function that reads the clock or the network returns stale answers. Second, bound the cache. An unlimited cache is a memory leak with good intentions. The example uses a Map, which remembers insertion order, to evict the least recently used entry.

Try it: Memoize with a size limit

JavaScript

function memoize(fn, { max = 100 } = {}) {
  const cache = new Map(); // a Map remembers insertion order
  return (arg) => {
    if (cache.has(arg)) {
      const value = cache.get(arg);
      cache.delete(arg);       // move to the end: most recently used
      cache.set(arg, value);
      return value;
    }
    const value = fn(arg);
    cache.set(arg, value);
    if (cache.size > max) cache.delete(cache.keys().next().value); // oldest
    return value;
  };
}

let calls = 0;
function shippingQuote(pincode) {
  calls++;
  let h = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 3e6; i++) h = (h + pincode * i) % 97; // slow on purpose
  return 40 + h;
}

const quote = memoize(shippingQuote, { max: 2 });
console.time('first call');
quote(679322);
console.timeEnd('first call');
console.time('cached call');
quote(679322);
console.timeEnd('cached call');

quote(682001);
quote(560001); // cache is over its limit: 679322 is evicted
quote(679322); // computed again
console.log('Real computations:', calls);

The cache keeps at most two entries and evicts the least recently used one. Count the real computations.

Debounce and throttle

Some events fire far more often than you need: input on every keystroke, scroll and pointermove dozens of times per second, resize while dragging a window edge.

DebounceThrottle
RunsOnce, after calls stop for wait msAt most once per interval while calls continue
Good forSearch boxes, autosave, validation after typingScroll progress, infinite scroll checks, drag, analytics
RiskNever runs if calls never pauseCan miss the final value without a trailing call
function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);                       // cancel the previous plan
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait); // plan a new one
  };
}

Debounce is a closure over one timer variable: each call cancels the previous timer and starts a new one. Throttle remembers when it last ran and schedules one trailing call so the last value is never lost.

Try it: Debounce and throttle on a timeline

JavaScript

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), wait);
  };
}

function throttle(fn, interval) {
  let last = -Infinity;
  let timer = null;
  let pending;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = performance.now();
    if (now - last >= interval) {
      clearTimeout(timer); // a late trailing call is now redundant
      timer = null;
      last = now;
      fn(...args);
    } else {
      pending = args; // remember the latest call for the trailing run
      timer ??= setTimeout(() => {
        last = performance.now();
        timer = null;
        fn(...pending);
      }, interval - (now - last));
    }
  };
}

const start = performance.now();
const at = () => `${Math.round((performance.now() - start) / 10) * 10} ms`;
const report = (kind) => (n) => console.log(`${kind} -> event ${n} at ${at()}`);
const onDebounced = debounce(report('debounced'), 150);
const onThrottled = throttle(report('throttled'), 200);

let n = 0;
const id = setInterval(() => {
  n++;
  onDebounced(n);
  onThrottled(n);
  if (n === 30) {
    clearInterval(id);
    console.log(`raw events: ${n}`);
  }
}, 20);

A fake input fires every 20 ms for 600 ms. Debounce waits for silence; throttle lets one call through per 200 ms.

const $ = (s) => document.querySelector(s);
const input = $('#q');
const list = $('#results');
const status = $('#status');
const count = { keys: 0, reqs: 0, aborts: 0 };
const show = () => {
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(count)) $('#' + k).textContent = v;

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });

let controller;
async function search(q) {
  controller?.abort();             // cancel the previous request if still running
  if (!q) {
    list.replaceChildren();
    status.textContent = 'Start typing to search.';
    return;
  }
  controller = new AbortController();
  count.reqs++; show();
  status.textContent = `Searching for “${q}”…`;
  try {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({ q, limit: 5, select: 'title,price,category' });
    const url = `https://dummyjson.com/products/search?${params}`;
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const { products, total } = await res.json();
    render(products);
    status.textContent = `${total} result(s) for “${q}”`;
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') { count.aborts++; show(); return; }
    status.textContent = 'Could not load results. Check your connection.';
    console.error(err.message);
  }
}

}

    const li = el('li', 'item', '');
    const name = el('span', 'name', p.title);
    name.append(el('small', 'cat', p.category));
    li.append(el('span', 'badge', p.title[0]), name, el('span', 'price', inr.format(p.price)));
    return li;
