Avoiding long tasks

A long task is any main-thread task over 50 ms. During it, clicks queue up and nothing repaints. Making a function async does not help: the synchronous part still runs in one go. You have three tools:

  1. Do less. Better data structures, fewer DOM updates, pagination and virtualised lists.
  2. Split the work into chunks and yield to the main thread between them. await scheduler.yield() is designed for this and resumes your work ahead of other queued tasks; it is available in Chromium-based browsers and Firefox but not yet in Safari, so check the MDN compatibility table and fall back to setTimeout(resolve, 0).
  3. Move it off the main thread with a Web Worker, which runs a separate script on its own thread and talks through messages.

Try it: Chunk a long task

JavaScript

// One million invoice rows: sum the GST.
const rows = Array.from({ length: 1_000_000 }, (_, i) => ({
  amount: (i % 500) + 1,
  rate: i % 3 ? 0.18 : 0.05,
}));

function yieldToMain() {
  // scheduler.yield() keeps your place in line; fall back to a new task.
  if (globalThis.scheduler?.yield) return scheduler.yield();
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

async function sumGstInChunks(items, budgetMs = 4) {
  let total = 0;
  let tasks = 1;
  let deadline = performance.now() + budgetMs;
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    total += items[i].amount * items[i].rate;
    if (i % 5000 === 0 && performance.now() > deadline) {
      await yieldToMain();
      tasks++;
      deadline = performance.now() + budgetMs;
    }
  }
  return { total: Math.round(total), tasks };
}

let t = performance.now();
let blocking = 0;
for (const r of rows) blocking += r.amount * r.rate;
console.log(`Blocking loop: ${(performance.now() - t).toFixed(1)} ms in ONE task`);

t = performance.now();
const { total, tasks } = await sumGstInChunks(rows);
console.log(`Chunked: ${tasks} tasks, ${(performance.now() - t).toFixed(1)} ms in total`);
console.log('Same result:', total === Math.round(blocking));
console.log('GST total: ₹' + total.toLocaleString('en-IN'));
const hasYield = typeof globalThis.scheduler?.yield === 'function';
console.log('scheduler.yield available:', hasYield);

The blocking loop runs as one task. The chunked version yields every few milliseconds so clicks and paints can happen in between.

// main.js
const url = new URL('./report-worker.js', import.meta.url);
const worker = new Worker(url, { type: 'module' });
worker.postMessage({ orders });                 // data is copied (structured clone)
worker.onmessage = (e) => renderReport(e.data); // the UI stays responsive

// report-worker.js
self.onmessage = (e) => {
  const report = buildReport(e.data.orders); // heavy work, no DOM here
  self.postMessage(report);
};

Workers cannot touch the DOM, and copying large data has a cost, so use them for genuinely heavy jobs: parsing big CSV files, image processing, search indexes, report crunching.

Garbage collection and memory leaks

You never free memory by hand in JavaScript. The engine’s garbage collector starts from roots (global variables, the current call stack, the live DOM, active timers and listeners) and marks everything it can reach. Anything unreachable is freed. Modern engines do this in generations: short-lived objects are collected often and cheaply, long-lived ones less often.

So a leak is never “memory JavaScript forgot to free”. It is memory you are still pointing at without meaning to. The four classics:

LeakWhy it stays reachableFix
Forgotten listenerswindow holds the listener, the listener’s closure holds your dataremoveEventListener, or pass { signal } and abort on unmount
Running timersAn active setInterval is a rootclearInterval on unmount
Closures holding big dataA small callback captures a huge arrayCapture only what you need; set big references to null
Detached DOMA removed element is still stored in a variable or arrayDrop the reference, or key metadata with a WeakMap

Unbounded caches and ever-growing arrays (logs, histories) belong on that list too. A WeakMap helps when you attach data to objects you do not own: the entry disappears when the key object is collected. To find leaks, take two heap snapshots in the DevTools Memory panel, one before and one after repeating an action several times, and compare; type “Detached” in the class filter to find removed DOM nodes still held in memory.

Try it: Find and fix a listener leak

JavaScript

// A tiny event bus, like the ones dashboards use for live prices.
class Bus {
  #listeners = new Set();
  on(fn, { signal } = {}) {
    this.#listeners.add(fn);
    signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => this.#listeners.delete(fn), { once: true });
    return () => this.#listeners.delete(fn);
  }
  emit(data) {
    this.#listeners.forEach((fn) => fn(data));
  }
  get size() {
    return this.#listeners.size;
  }
}

// LEAK: the widget subscribes on mount and never unsubscribes.
const leaky = new Bus();
function mountLeakyWidget() {
  const history = new Array(100_000).fill(0); // kept alive by the closure
  leaky.on((price) => history.push(price));
}
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) mountLeakyWidget();
console.log('Listeners after 5 leaky mounts:', leaky.size);

// FIX: one AbortController per mount; unmount aborts it and clears timers.
const clean = new Bus();
function mountWidget() {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  clean.on((price) => console.log('price', price), { signal: controller.signal });
  const timer = setInterval(() => clean.emit(Date.now()), 1000);
  return function unmount() {
    controller.abort();
    clearInterval(timer);
  };
}
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) mountWidget()();
console.log('Listeners after 5 clean mount/unmount cycles:', clean.size);

// WeakMap: data that is freed together with its key object.
const meta = new WeakMap();
let row = { id: 1 };
meta.set(row, { renderedAt: Date.now() });
console.log('Row has metadata:', meta.has(row));
row = null; // nothing else points at the object, so the entry can be collected

Five leaky mounts leave five listeners (and five big arrays) alive. Tying each subscription to an AbortController cleans up in one line.

Example: speeding up the nightly order report

The lab starts with a Ralfiz Store report that takes 30,000 orders and 3,000 customers and produces revenue by city plus VIP revenue. The original is correct but slow. The steps:

  1. Measure the slow version with performance.now() and write the number down.
  2. Index customers in a Map by id: the O(n) find per order becomes an O(1) get.
  3. Convert the VIP list to a Set: includes becomes has.
  4. Memoize gstRate(category): there are 4 categories but 30,000 calls.
  5. Bound the memo cache with LRU eviction so it cannot grow without limit.
  6. Verify the fast report equals the slow one, then measure again.
function reportFast({ customers, vip, orders }) {
  const byId = new Map(customers.map((c) => [c.id, c]));
  const vipSet = new Set(vip);
  const rate = memoize(gstRate, { max: 16 });
  const byCity = {};
  let vipRevenue = 0;
  for (const o of orders) {
    const c = byId.get(o.customerId);
    const gross = o.amount * (1 + rate(o.category));
    byCity[c.city] = (byCity[c.city] ?? 0) + gross;
    if (vipSet.has(c.id)) vipRevenue += gross;
  }
  return summarise(byCity, vipRevenue);
}

Note what did not change: the loop, the maths and the output. Most real speed-ups are this undramatic.

Common mistakes

  • Optimising without measuring. Rewriting a map as a for loop rarely matters. Measure, then fix the algorithm.
  • Lookup in a loop. Wrong: orders.filter((o) => vipIds.includes(o.customer)). Fix: const vip = new Set(vipIds); orders.filter((o) => vip.has(o.customer)).
  • Debouncing inside the handler. Wrong: input.oninput = () => debounce(search, 300)() creates a new timer each time, so nothing is debounced. Fix: create it once, const onInput = debounce(search, 300), and reuse it.
  • Believing async means non-blocking. Wrong: async function build() { heavyLoop(); }. Fix: chunk with await scheduler.yield() (or a setTimeout fallback), or use a Worker.
  • Listeners without cleanup. Wrong: window.addEventListener('resize', onResize) in every mount. Fix: window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal }) and controller.abort() on unmount.
  • Unbounded memo caches. Fix: set a maximum size, or use a WeakMap when keys are objects.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Expect “implement debounce” and “what is the difference between debounce and throttle?”. Write debounce from memory in under two minutes, and mention preserving this and the arguments.
  • For “this page is slow”, describe a process: reproduce, record a Performance trace, find the long task, check the algorithm and DOM work, fix, measure again.
  • Know that Map and Set give roughly constant-time lookups, and that includes, indexOf and find are linear.
  • Explain garbage collection as reachability from roots, and name the four classic leaks with their fixes.
  • Mention Web Workers for CPU-heavy work and why they cannot touch the DOM.

Snippet 5. What is logged?

const cache = new Map();

Answers

  1. C. The three quick calls reset the timer, so only 'lap' fires at 50 ms. The call at 100 ms comes after that pause, so it starts a new timer and 'laptop' fires at 150 ms.
  2. D. Only the first call for each of the ids 1, 2 and 3 does the work. The other three calls are cache hits, so calls is 3 and the Map holds 3 entries.
  3. A. Sets compare primitives by value, so the duplicate 'A1' collapses. Objects are compared by reference: two separate { id: 1 } literals are two different objects, so b keeps both.
  4. B. indexOf uses strict equality, and NaN === NaN is false, so it returns -1. includes and Set use SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to NaN.
  5. D. Map keys are compared by reference, so a new { id: 1 } is a different key and get returns undefined. The first entry can never be read again, yet the Map still holds it: a small memory leak.

terms.definition: A way to describe how work grows with input size: O(1) constant, O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic.
Caching a pure function’s result by its input so repeated calls return instantly.
Run a function only after calls have stopped for a set time, e.g. search 300 ms after the last keystroke.
Run a function at most once per interval while calls keep coming, e.g. update a scroll indicator every 100 ms.
A piece of main-thread work that takes more than 50 ms. While it runs, the page cannot respond to clicks or typing.
The engine frees memory that can no longer be reached from roots such as globals, the stack and live DOM.
Memory that stays reachable by mistake (a listener, timer, cache or closure you forgot) so it can never be freed.

quiz.question: You check 10,000 orders against a list of 5,000 VIP ids with vipIds.includes(id) inside a loop. What is the best fix?
options: Sort the orders first
Build a Set of VIP ids once and use set.has(id)
Use a for loop instead of filter
Use indexOf instead of includes
quiz.explanation: includes scans the array, so the loop is O(n × m). A Set lookup is close to O(1), which makes the whole check O(n + m). Changing the loop style does not change the algorithm.

quiz.question: A search box calls an API on every keystroke. Which technique fits best?
options: Throttle to once per second
Memoize the input element
Debounce, and abort the previous request with AbortController
Move the fetch into a Web Worker
quiz.explanation: Debounce waits until typing pauses, so “laptop” triggers one request instead of six. Aborting the previous request stops a slow old response from overwriting newer results.

quiz.question: Which of these is a memory leak in a single-page app?
options: A component adds a window resize listener on mount and never removes it
A local array inside a function that returns
A WeakMap entry whose key object is no longer referenced
A const string at the top of a module
quiz.explanation: The window keeps the listener alive, and the listener keeps its closure (and often DOM nodes) alive, even after the component is gone. Remove it on unmount, for example with an AbortController signal.

quiz.question: A report function blocks the page for 800 ms. What keeps the page responsive without changing the result?
options: Wrap it in a Promise
Mark the function async
Call it inside setTimeout(fn, 0)
Process the data in chunks and yield to the main thread between chunks (or run it in a Web Worker)
quiz.explanation: Promise, async and a single setTimeout still run the whole job in one task. Chunking with yields lets the browser handle input and paint between pieces; a Worker moves the job off the main thread entirely.

lessons.title: Interview preparation
lessons.summaryHtml:
Junior front-end interviews usually test three things: whether you understand the language (closures, this, the event loop, copying objects), whether you can solve a small problem out loud, and whether you can ship a clean small project.

This lesson gives you the 25 concepts that come up most, each with a crisp answer and a tiny example, then solves 8 classic coding challenges step by step: reverse words, anagram check, FizzBuzz variants, flatten, deep clone, debounce, curry, and sleep with retry. You also practise a way to explain your thinking and get tips for take-home projects. The lab is a kata pack with its own tiny test runner.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A junior JavaScript interview is not a trivia contest. The interviewer wants to know three things: do you understand how the language behaves, can you turn a small problem into working code while explaining yourself, and would your code be pleasant to maintain? This lesson prepares you for all three.

A typical process has a short screening call, a concepts round (“what is a closure?”), a live-coding round of 30 to 60 minutes, sometimes a take-home project, and a final conversation about your projects. You will not know every answer. What you can control is having crisp answers for the common concepts, a repeatable way to attack coding problems, and a calm habit of thinking out loud.

Why it matters

Many candidates know the material but lose the interview in the delivery. They give a two-minute ramble instead of a two-sentence answer, jump into code without checking what the input looks like, or go silent for five minutes. Interviewers can only score what they can see and hear.

The fix is practice with a structure. For every concept below, learn the one-line definition, a tiny example you can type from memory, and one real-world use. For every challenge, practise the same six steps until they are automatic. The quick demo below proves six of the most-asked answers with real output.

Try it: Six concepts in one run

JavaScript

// 1. Closure: count lives on after makeCounter returns.
function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return () => ++count;
}
const next = makeCounter();
next();
console.log('closure:', next());

// 2. this depends on how a function is called (modules are strict).
const shop = { name: 'Ralfiz Store', hi() { return this?.name; } };
const hi = shop.hi;
console.log('method:', shop.hi(), '| extracted:', hi(), '| bound:', hi.bind(shop)());

// 3. Spread is shallow; structuredClone is deep.
const order = { id: 1, items: ['pen'] };
const shallow = { ...order };
const deep = structuredClone(order);
shallow.items.push('ink');
console.log('original:', order.items, '| deep copy:', deep.items);

// 4. == converts types first; === does not.
console.log("0 == '':", 0 == '', "| 0 === '':", 0 === '');

// 5. || replaces any falsy value; ?? only null and undefined.
const discount = 0;
console.log('||', discount || 10, '| ??', discount ?? 10);

// 6. Sync code, then microtasks, then tasks.
setTimeout(() => console.log('task: setTimeout'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask: then'));
console.log('sync: done');

Closures, this, copying, equality, ?? and the event loop: the answers interviewers expect, proved by output. Read the last three lines carefully.

How it works

The 25 most-asked concepts: language core

ConceptCrisp answerTiny example
1. let, const, varlet and const are block-scoped and sit in the temporal dead zone until declared; var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined. const stops reassignment, not mutation.const a = []; a.push(1); // fine
2. HoistingDeclarations are registered before code runs. Function declarations are usable early; var reads undefined; let/const throw before their line.f(); function f() {}
3. Primitives vs referencesPrimitives are copied by value. Objects are shared by reference, so two variables can point at one object.const b = a; b.x = 1; // a.x is 1
4. == vs ====== compares without converting types. == converts first and has surprising rules. Use ===; x == null is the one common exception.0 == '' // true
5. Truthy, falsy, ?? and ?.Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. ?? falls back only on null or undefined; ?. stops at null or undefined.user?.address?.city ?? 'N/A'
6. Types and typeofSeven primitive types plus objects. typeof null is 'object' (a historical bug) and arrays are objects, so use Array.isArray.typeof null // 'object'
7. Shallow vs deep copySpread and Object.assign copy one level. structuredClone copies deeply, including Date, Map, Set and cycles.structuredClone(order)
8. map, filter, reduceReturn a new array of transformed items, a subset, or a single accumulated value. They do not mutate the original.cart.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0)

The 25 most-asked concepts: functions and objects

ConceptCrisp answerTiny example
9. ScopeWhere a name is visible: global, module, function or block. Inner scopes see outer ones, not the reverse.{ let x = 1; } // x not visible here
10. ClosuresA function remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has returned. Used for private state, factories and callbacks.const inc = (() => { let n = 0; return () => ++n; })();
11. thisSet by the call: obj.m() gives obj, a plain call gives undefined in strict mode, new gives the new object, call/apply/bind set it explicitly.const f = obj.m; f(); // lost this
12. Arrow functionsShorter syntax, no own this or arguments (they use the outer ones), cannot be used with new.setTimeout(() => this.save(), 0)
13. call, apply, bindcall and apply invoke now with a chosen this (arguments listed or as an array); bind returns a new function with this fixed.const save = form.save.bind(form)
14. PrototypesObjects link to a prototype; a missing property is looked up along that chain. Methods live once on the prototype and are shared.Object.getPrototypeOf([]) === Array.prototype
15. ClassesSyntax over prototypes with constructor, extends, super, static members and truly private #fields.class Account { #balance = 0; }
16. Higher-order functions and curryingFunctions that take or return functions. Currying turns f(a, b) into f(a)(b) so you can pre-fill arguments.const addGst = (r) => (p) => p * (1 + r)
17. Pure functions and immutabilitySame input, same output, no side effects. Easier to test, cache and reason about. Prefer toSorted and spread over mutation.const sorted = list.toSorted(byPrice)

The 25 most-asked concepts: async, browser and tooling

ConceptCrisp answerTiny example
18. Event loopRun the call stack to empty, then all microtasks (promise callbacks), then render if needed, then the next task (timer, event).then logs before setTimeout(…, 0)
19. PromisesAn object for a future value: pending, then fulfilled or rejected, once. then returns a new promise, which enables chaining.fetch(url).then((r) => r.json())
20. async and awaitSyntax over promises: an async function always returns a promise; await pauses that function only, not the page. Handle errors with try/catch.const data = await res.json();
21. Promise combinatorsall fails fast, allSettled waits for every result, race takes the first to settle, any takes the first success.await Promise.all([getUser(), getCart()])
22. Debounce vs throttleDebounce runs after calls stop; throttle runs at most once per interval.Search box vs scroll handler
23. Event delegationEvents bubble, so one listener on a parent can handle clicks for many children using event.target.closest().list.addEventListener('click', onItem)
24. ModulesES modules use import/export, are strict and scoped per file, and load asynchronously; CommonJS uses require in older Node code.export const tax = 0.18;
25. Security and storageNever put untrusted data in innerHTML (XSS); use textContent or sanitise. Tokens in localStorage can be read by any XSS script. CORS is enforced by the browser, not a server firewall.el.textContent = comment

Memory leaks and garbage collection (lesson 7.4) and TypeScript basics (lesson 7.3) are common follow-up questions, so review those two lessons as well.

How to explain your thinking

Use the same six steps for every coding question. Say each step out loud.

  1. Restate and clarify. “So I get a string and return the words in reverse order. Can there be extra spaces? Should I keep punctuation?”
  2. Write two or three examples, including an edge case: empty input, one item, duplicates.
  3. Say the brute-force idea and its cost. “I could compare every pair, which is O(n²).”
  4. Improve it. “If I count letters in a Map, one pass is enough: O(n).”
  5. Code it cleanly, with clear names, narrating the tricky lines.
  6. Test it by hand with your examples, then state time and space complexity.

If you get stuck, say what you are trying: “I am not sure how to handle nested arrays, so let me solve one level first.” Silence is the one thing an interviewer cannot help with.

Challenges 1–3: strings

1. Reverse words. Clarify spaces first. Trim, split on one or more whitespace characters with a regular expression, reverse the array and join with single spaces. O(n) time and space.

const reverseWords = (s) => s.trim().split(/\s+/).reverse().join(' ');
reverseWords('  learn   JavaScript  '); // 'JavaScript learn'

2. Anagram check. Brute force: sort both strings and compare, O(n log n). Better: normalise case, strip spaces and punctuation, compare lengths, count letters of the first string in a Map, then decrement with the second. Any missing or negative count means false. O(n).

3. FizzBuzz variants. The interviewer usually follows up with “now add 7 for Bazz”. If your rules live in a table, the variant is one more array entry instead of another if branch. Mention that the order of the rules decides the order of the words.

Try it: Strings: reverse words, anagrams, FizzBuzz

JavaScript

// 1. Reverse the order of words, ignoring extra spaces.
const reverseWords = (s) => s.trim().split(/\s+/).reverse().join(' ');
console.log(reverseWords('  learn   JavaScript at Ralfiz  '));

// 2. Anagram check with a letter count: O(n) time.
function isAnagram(a, b) {
  const clean = (s) => s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '');
  const x = clean(a);
  const y = clean(b);
  if (x.length !== y.length) return false;
  const counts = new Map();
  for (const ch of x) counts.set(ch, (counts.get(ch) ?? 0) + 1);
  for (const ch of y) {
    const n = counts.get(ch);
    if (!n) return false; // missing letter or used too often
    counts.set(ch, n - 1);
  }
  return true;
}
console.log(isAnagram('Listen', 'Silent'), isAnagram('Dormitory', 'dirty room'));
console.log(isAnagram('rat', 'car'), isAnagram('aab', 'abb'));

// 3. FizzBuzz driven by a rules table, so variants need no new if/else.
function fizzBuzz(n, rules = [[3, 'Fizz'], [5, 'Buzz']]) {
  return Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => {
    const k = i + 1;
    const word = rules
      .filter(([d]) => k % d === 0)
      .map(([, w]) => w)
      .join('');
    return word || String(k);
  });
}
console.log(fizzBuzz(15).join(' '));
console.log(fizzBuzz(7, [[2, 'Even'], [7, 'Lucky']]).join(' '));

Three classic warm-ups. Try isAnagram with accents or emoji, and add a [7, 'Bazz'] rule to FizzBuzz.

Challenges 4–5: arrays and objects

4. Flatten an array. Clarify the depth. The recursive idea: for each item, if it is an array and depth remains, flatten it one level deeper and push its items; otherwise push the item. Mention the built-in arr.flat(Infinity), then show you can write it.

function flatten(arr, depth = Infinity) {
  const out = [];
  for (const item of arr) {
    if (Array.isArray(item) && depth > 0) out.push(...flatten(item, depth - 1));
    else out.push(item);
  }
  return out;
}

A good follow-up answer: for extremely deep nesting, use an explicit stack instead of recursion to avoid a stack overflow.

5. Deep clone. Start by saying “in production I would use structuredClone”. Then write it: return primitives as they are, copy Date specially, create an empty array or object, and recurse over the entries. The step many candidates miss is circular references: keep a WeakMap from original to copy, and return the existing copy when you meet an object again. Also mention why JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is weak: it turns Dates into strings, drops undefined and functions, and throws on cycles.

Try it: Flatten and deep clone

JavaScript

// 1. Flatten to a given depth (like Array.prototype.flat).
function flatten(arr, depth = Infinity) {
  const out = [];
  for (const item of arr) {
    if (Array.isArray(item) && depth > 0) out.push(...flatten(item, depth - 1));
    else out.push(item);
  }
  return out;
}
const nested = [1, [2, [3, [4]]], 5];
console.log(flatten(nested));
console.log(flatten(nested, 1));
console.log(nested.flat(Infinity)); // the built-in answer

// 2. Deep clone: primitives, arrays, plain objects, Date, cycles.
function deepClone(value, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (value === null || typeof value !== 'object') return value;
  if (value instanceof Date) return new Date(value);
  if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value); // circular reference
  const copy = Array.isArray(value) ? [] : {};
  seen.set(value, copy);
  for (const [key, v] of Object.entries(value)) copy[key] = deepClone(v, seen);
  return copy;
}

const invoice = {
  no: 'INV-7',
  due: new Date(2026, 9, 1),
  lines: [{ sku: 'PEN', qty: 2 }],
};
invoice.self = invoice; // circular
const copy = deepClone(invoice);
copy.lines[0].qty = 99;
console.log('original qty:', invoice.lines[0].qty, '| copy qty:', copy.lines[0].qty);
console.log('Date kept:', copy.due instanceof Date, '| cycle kept:', copy.self === copy);
console.log('structuredClone agrees:', structuredClone(invoice).self.lines[0].qty);
try {
  JSON.stringify(invoice);
} catch (err) {
  console.log('JSON fails:', err.name);
}

Recursion with a depth counter, and a clone that survives Dates and circular references. Compare with structuredClone at the end.

Challenges 6–7: functions

6. Debounce. Explain the closure: one timer variable shared by every call. Each call clears the old timer and sets a new one. Use a regular function for the returned wrapper and fn.apply(this, args) so methods keep their this. Follow-ups: add a cancel() method, or a leading-edge option.

7. Curry. fn.length tells you how many parameters the function declares. Collect arguments until you have that many, then call the original; otherwise return a function that collects more. Note the limitation: fn.length ignores rest parameters and parameters with defaults.

function curry(fn) {
  return function curried(...args) {
    if (args.length >= fn.length) return fn.apply(this, args);
    return (...more) => curried.apply(this, [...args, ...more]);
  };
}

Try it: Debounce and curry

JavaScript

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer;
  return function (...args) {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait);
  };
}

const box = {
  label: 'search',
  log: debounce(function (q) {
    console.log(`${this.label}: ${q}`);
  }, 100),
};
box.log('p');
box.log('ph');
box.log('phone'); // only this one runs, 100 ms later

function curry(fn) {
  return function curried(...args) {
    if (args.length >= fn.length) return fn.apply(this, args);
    return (...more) => curried.apply(this, [...args, ...more]);
  };
}

const price = (base, gst, qty) => Math.round(base * (1 + gst) * qty);
const cPrice = curry(price);
console.log(cPrice(100)(0.18)(3), cPrice(100, 0.18)(3), cPrice(100)(0.18, 3));

const withGst = cPrice(250, 0.05); // partial application
console.log([1, 2, 4].map((q) => withGst(q)));

debounce keeps this and the latest arguments; curry keeps collecting arguments until it has as many as the function expects.

Challenge 8: sleep and retry

sleep wraps setTimeout in a promise: const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));. retry calls an async task, and on failure waits and tries again, doubling the wait each time (exponential backoff) so a struggling server is not flooded. After the last attempt it throws, keeping the original error as cause. Good follow-ups: add random jitter to the delay, only retry errors that make sense (a 503 yes, a 400 no), and accept an AbortSignal so the caller can cancel.

Try it: sleep and retry with backoff

JavaScript

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function retry(task, { retries = 3, delay = 50, factor = 2 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await task(attempt);
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt >= retries) {
        throw new Error(`Failed after ${attempt + 1} attempts`, { cause: err });
      }
      const wait = delay * factor ** attempt;
      console.log(`attempt ${attempt + 1} failed (${err.message}), waiting ${wait} ms`);
      await sleep(wait);
    }
  }
}

function flakyPayment(failures) {
  let calls = 0;
  return async () => {
    calls++;
    await sleep(10);
    if (calls <= failures) throw new Error('503 Service Unavailable');
    return { status: 'paid', calls };
  };
}

const started = performance.now();
const result = await retry(flakyPayment(2));
console.log(result, `in about ${Math.round((performance.now() - started) / 10) * 10} ms`);

try {
  await retry(flakyPayment(5), { retries: 2, delay: 20 });
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.message, '| last cause:', err.cause.message);
}

A flaky task fails twice and then succeeds. retry waits 50, then 100 ms between attempts. Set failures to 5 to see it give up.

Example: a mock live-coding round

Interviewer: “Write a function that returns the first non-repeating character in a string.”

  1. Clarify: “Is it case-sensitive? What should I return if every character repeats?” The interviewer says case-sensitive, return null.
  2. Examples: 'ralfiz' gives 'r', 'aabbc' gives 'c', 'aabb' gives null, '' gives null.
  3. Brute force: “For each character, count it with a second loop. That is O(n²).”
  4. Improve: “Count every character in a Map in one pass, then walk the string again and return the first with count 1. Two passes, O(n) time, and the Map holds at most one entry per distinct character.”
  5. Code and test: walk through 'aabbc' by hand, then the empty string.
function firstUnique(s) {
  const counts = new Map();
  for (const ch of s) counts.set(ch, (counts.get(ch) ?? 0) + 1);
  for (const ch of s) if (counts.get(ch) === 1) return ch;
  return null;
}

Notice that the finished code is short. The narration around it is what earned the score. The lab gives you all eight challenges with a test runner, so you can practise against the clock.

Take-home project tips

  • Meet the brief first. Build exactly what was asked, then polish. Extra features never make up for a missing requirement.
  • Handle the states: loading, error, empty and success for every fetch, and validation messages for every form.
  • Structure the code: small modules (api.js, state.js, render.js), clear names, no dead code or leftover console.log.
  • Add a few meaningful tests for the core logic, such as the cart total or the filter function.
  • Write a README with how to run it, the decisions you made, the trade-offs, and what you would do with more time.
  • Commit in logical steps with clear messages, and deploy it if you can so reviewers can click a link.
  • Stay safe: no API keys in the code, textContent for user data, accessible labels on inputs.

Common mistakes

  • Coding before clarifying. You solve the wrong problem. Fix: ask about input shape and edge cases first.
  • Losing this in debounce. Wrong: return (...args) => { … fn(...args) } when fn is a method. Fix: return function (...args) { … fn.apply(this, args) }.
  • Using var in loop closures. Wrong: for (var i = 0; …) btns[i].addEventListener('click', () => show(i)); shows the last index. Fix: for (let i = 0; …).
  • Forgetting await inside try. Wrong: try { return task(); } catch … in an async function lets rejections escape. Fix: return await task();.
  • Mutating inputs. Wrong: arr.sort() inside a helper changes the caller’s array. Fix: arr.toSorted() or copy first.
  • Claiming instead of testing. Saying “this works” without running an example. Fix: trace one normal and one edge case aloud.

Interview and real-world notes

  • Prepare a two-minute story for each portfolio project: the problem, your role, one hard bug and how you found it, and what you would change.
  • When you do not know something, say so and reason from what you do know. “I have not used WeakRef, but I know WeakMap holds keys weakly, so I expect…” scores better than guessing confidently.
  • Ask questions at the end: how code review works, how they test, what a new developer ships in the first month.
  • Practise on paper or a plain editor too: some interviews turn off autocomplete.
  • Repeat the eight challenges until each takes under ten minutes, then vary them: reverse each word’s letters, group anagrams, throttle instead of debounce, retry with a timeout.

Predict the output

Read each snippet and decide what it prints before you run it. The answers are at the end of this section.

Snippet 1. What is logged?

const fns = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
const first = fns.map((f) => f()).join(',');
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) fns[j] = () => j;
console.log(first, fns.map((f) => f()).join(','));
  • A 0,1,2 0,1,2
  • B 3,3,3 3,3,3
  • C 3,3,3 0,1,2
  • D 0,1,2 3,3,3

Snippet 2. What is logged?

'use strict';
const cart = {
  items: 3,
  count() { return this?.items ?? 'no this'; },
};
const count = cart.count;
console.log(cart.count(), count());
  • A 3 no this
  • B 3 3
  • C 3 undefined
  • D TypeError

Snippet 3. What order are the numbers logged in?

console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);
(async () => {
  console.log(3);
  await null;
  console.log(4);
})();
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(5));
console.log(6);
  • A 
    1
2
3
4
5
6
  • B 
    1
3
6
5
4

  • C 
    1
3

Snippet 4. What is logged?

const a = { user: { name: 'Asha' }, tags: ['new'] };
const b = { ...a };
const c = structuredClone(a);
b.user.name = 'Ravi';
c.tags.push('vip');
console.log(a.user.name, a.tags.length);
  • A Asha 1
  • B Ravi 1
  • C Asha 2
  • D Ravi 2

Snippet 5. What is logged?

console.log([] == false, [0] == false, null == 0, null >= 0);
  • A false false false false
  • B true false false true
  • C true true true true
  • D true true false true

Answers

  1. C. var creates one i shared by all three closures, and it is 3 when they run. let creates a fresh j for every iteration, so each closure keeps its own value.
  2. A. Called as cart.count(), this is cart. The extracted function is called plainly, so in strict mode this is undefined; optional chaining avoids the TypeError and ?? supplies the fallback.
  3. D. An async function runs synchronously until its first await, so 3 comes right after 1. The code after await is queued as a microtask before the then callback, so 4 comes before 5. The timer is a task and runs last.
  4. B. Spread copies only the top level, so b.user is the same object as a.user and the rename shows in a. structuredClone copies deeply, so pushing into c.tags does not touch a.tags.
  5. D. Arrays convert to strings, then numbers: [] becomes '' then 0 and [0] becomes '0' then 0, both equal to false (0). null == 0 is false because null is only loosely equal to undefined, but >= converts null to 0, so null >= 0 is true.

terms.definition: A function together with the variables it captured from the scope where it was created.
The mechanism that runs the call stack, then all microtasks (promise callbacks), then one task (timer, event) at a time.
How the number of steps grows with input size, written in Big-O, e.g. O(n) for one pass.
An unusual input that often breaks code: empty arrays, empty strings, zero, null, very large values, duplicates.
The simplest correct solution, even if slow. State it first, then improve it.
A small app you build in a few days; judged on correctness, code quality, tests and the README.

lessons.examTip: Talk while you code: restate the problem, give an example, say the brute-force idea and its cost, then improve. Interviewers score your reasoning, not only the final answer.

plays.title: Six concepts in one run
plays.caption: Closures, this, copying, equality, ?? and the event loop: the answers interviewers expect, proved by output. Read the last three lines carefully.

plays.title: Strings: reverse words, anagrams, FizzBuzz
plays.caption: Three classic warm-ups. Try isAnagram with accents or emoji, and add a [7, 'Bazz'] rule to FizzBuzz.

plays.title: Flatten and deep clone
plays.caption: Recursion with a depth counter, and a clone that survives Dates and circular references. Compare with structuredClone at the end.

plays.title: Debounce and curry
plays.caption: debounce keeps this and the latest arguments; curry keeps collecting arguments until it has as many as the function expects.

plays.title: sleep and retry with backoff
plays.caption: A flaky task fails twice and then succeeds. retry waits 50, then 100 ms between attempts. Set failures to 5 to see it give up.

quiz.question: An interviewer asks you to find duplicates in a large array. What should you say first?
options: The final optimised code, without comments
Clarifying questions and a brute-force idea with its cost, then an improvement using a Set
That you would search online for the answer
Nothing: start typing immediately
quiz.explanation: Clarify the input and expected output, give the simple O(n²) idea, then improve it to O(n) with a Set. This shows structured thinking even before the code works.

quiz.question: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
options: They are the same
Throttle waits until calls stop; debounce runs at a fixed rate
Debounce runs after calls stop for a set time; throttle runs at most once per interval while calls continue
Debounce only works with promises
quiz.explanation: Debounce suits search boxes (run once typing pauses). Throttle suits scroll and resize handlers (run regularly, but not on every event).

quiz.question: Why is JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) a weak deep clone?
options: It loses Dates (they become strings), undefined, functions, Map and Set, and throws on circular references
It is too fast
It copies prototypes and methods
It only works in Node
quiz.explanation: JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. Use structuredClone, which handles Date, Map, Set and cycles, or write a clone that tracks visited objects.

quiz.question: In a take-home project, what usually matters most to reviewers?
options: Using as many libraries as possible
Adding features that were not asked for
A long commit history with one commit per line
Meeting the brief, clean structure, handled edge cases, a few tests and a clear README
quiz.explanation: Reviewers check that it works, that the code is easy to read, that loading, error and empty states are handled, and that the README explains how to run it and what you would do next.
